Compile, Schedule, Serve
Go · runtime · backend
A language you can hold in your head, running systems you cannot

Go, from the syntax to the scheduler to production

Four books in one. The language, learned properly rather than by analogy to the last one you used. The runtime — what the compiler emits, where memory goes, how goroutines are scheduled onto threads, how the collector runs beside your code. The backend engineering that Go is overwhelmingly used for: HTTP services, databases, queues, gRPC, observability, and the operational decisions that keep them up. And then a complete build: Quill, a collaborative notebook, from an empty directory to a running six-service system with offline-first sync, sharing by email and link, and the deployment around it — followed by its account-security surface in full: devices and sessions, passkeys, two-factor and step-up, Google, GitHub and Apple sign-in, email codes, and the linking rules that stop all of it becoming an account-takeover vector. Every file, nothing elided.

00

What Go optimises for

Every language is a set of trades. Go's are unusually explicit, unusually opinionated, and unusually stable — and most of what confuses newcomers is a trade they have not been told about yet.

01 · Write
Small spec25 keywords, one formatter
02 · Compile
Secondsone static binary
03 · Schedule
GoroutinesM:N onto OS threads
04 · Collect
Concurrent GCsub-millisecond pauses
05 · Observe
pprof built inCPU, heap, block, trace
06 · Ship
Scratch imageno runtime to install

The trades, stated plainly

Go gives upTo get
Inheritance, class hierarchiesComposition and small interfaces you can actually reason about
ExceptionsErrors as ordinary values — every failure path is visible in the code
Expressive type-level abstractionA language a new hire is productive in within a week
Manual memory controlA garbage collector tuned for latency, not throughput
Formatting debates, unused-import tolerancegofmt, and a compiler that refuses to build sloppiness
Dynamic linking, a runtime to installOne binary you copy onto a machine and run
The sentence that explains the whole design

Go was built at Google to be maintained by large teams, over long periods, across enormous codebases, by engineers who rotate. That is why it is boring on purpose: readability by a stranger beats expressiveness for the author, and the language will consistently choose the first. Once you accept that, the things that feel like limitations start reading as decisions.

The three questions this book answers

  1. What does this code mean? — Part I, the language: types, interfaces, slices, errors, generics, goroutines and channels, with the semantics that bite rather than the tour.
  2. What does it actually do? — Part II, the runtime: compilation, escape analysis, the GMP scheduler, the garbage collector, what a channel and an interface are in memory, and how to profile all of it.
  3. How do I build a real service with it? — Parts III and IV: HTTP, databases, caching, auth, gRPC, jobs, testing and observability, then the production concerns — containers, GOMAXPROCS, graceful shutdown, resilience, security and cost.
  4. Can I see all of it at once? — Part V builds Quill end to end across sixteen chapters: six services, a shared platform module, Postgres with row-level security, an offline-first sync protocol with a local SQLite replica, invitations by email and by link, and the Kubernetes manifests to run it. Part VI then takes the identity service apart and rebuilds it as a real one — every authenticator, every device, every linking rule.
Interview follow-up

“Why would you pick Go for this service?” The good answer is specific and unromantic: predictable latency from a low-pause collector, cheap concurrency so a request-per-goroutine model is viable at high connection counts, a single static binary that makes deployment trivial, fast compilation that keeps CI short, and a standard library that covers HTTP, TLS, JSON and testing without dependencies. The weak answer is “it's fast” — so is everything it competes with.

L01

The toolchain and your first program

Go's tooling is part of the language design, not an ecosystem that grew around it. One binary formats, builds, tests, benchmarks, profiles, vets, and manages dependencies. Learn it first — it removes most of the decisions other languages ask you to make.

A module, from nothing

shell
$ mkdir hello && cd hello
$ go mod init github.com/acme/hello
go: creating new go.mod: module github.com/acme/hello

$ cat go.mod
module github.com/acme/hello

go 1.24

$ go run .
hello, 世界

$ go build -o bin/hello .
$ file bin/hello
bin/hello: Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64      # one file, no runtime to install
go · main.go
// Package main is special: it is the entry point, and it must contain func main.
package main

import (
	"fmt"
	"os"
)

func main() {
	// fmt.Println writes to stdout. There is no implicit `console`,
	// no global print in production code — everything comes from a package.
	fmt.Println("hello, 世界")

	// Exit codes matter for CLIs and containers. os.Exit skips deferred
	// functions, so it belongs at the very top of main and nowhere else.
	if len(os.Args) > 1 && os.Args[1] == "--fail" {
		fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, "asked to fail")
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}
The module path is an identity, not a location

github.com/acme/hello names the module and prefixes every import path inside it. It does not have to be fetchable for a private service, but if it ever is published, the path is how the world imports it — so use the real repository URL from the start. Renaming later means touching every importer.

The commands you will actually run

CommandWhat it does
go mod init pathCreate go.mod and name the module
go mod tidyAdd what is imported, remove what is not, update go.sum. Run it before every commit
go get pkg@verAdd or change a dependency version (@latest, @v1.2.3, @none to drop)
go build ./...Compile everything; writes a binary only for main packages
go run .Build to a temp dir and run — for development, never for production
go test ./...Run every test in the module
go test -race ./...The same, with the race detector. Run this in CI, always
go vet ./...Catch suspicious-but-legal code: bad Printf verbs, lost cancels, copied locks
gofmt -l .List files that are not formatted. In CI, a non-empty output fails the build
go doc pkg.SymRead documentation offline, including for your own code
go env GOPATH GOMODCACHEWhere the toolchain keeps things
go tool pprofThe profiler (Part II)
go work init ./a ./bWorkspace mode: develop several modules together without replace

Files, packages and directories

service/ ├── go.mod module github.com/acme/service ├── go.sum cryptographic checksums — commit this ├── main.go package main ├── cmd/ │ └── worker/main.go package main → a second binary └── internal/ ├── orders/ │ ├── order.go package orders │ ├── store.go package orders same dir = same package │ └── order_test.go package orders (or orders_test) └── http/ └── server.go package http shadows stdlib name — legal, but import it aliased Three rules that are not obvious: 1 One directory is exactly one package. You cannot have two packages in a directory, and you cannot split a package across directories. 2 internal/ is enforced by the compiler: only code rooted at the parent of internal/ may import it. It is real encapsulation. 3 The directory name and the package name are conventionally the same but need not be. The package clause is what importers get.

Exported means capitalised

go · visibility is a property of the identifier, not a keyword
package orders

type Order struct {   // exported: visible to importers
	ID     string     // exported field
	Total  int64
	secret string     // unexported: invisible outside package orders
}

func New(id string) *Order { return &Order{ID: id} }  // exported constructor
func validate(o *Order) error { return nil }          // package-private helper

// Consequence people miss: encoding/json can only see EXPORTED fields.
// `secret` will never be marshalled, unmarshalled, or reflected over.
// That is a feature — but it surprises everyone once.
The compiler refuses things other languages tolerate

An unused import is a compile error. An unused local variable is a compile error (unused package-level variables and struct fields are fine). A missing return is a compile error. This is deliberate: dead code is the beginning of rot, and catching it at build time rather than in review scales to a very large codebase. Use _ = x or _ "package" deliberately when you genuinely want the side effect, and let the error catch the rest.

Formatting is not a preference

shell
$ gofmt -l .                 # files needing formatting
internal/orders/store.go

$ gofmt -w .                 # rewrite them in place
$ gofmt -d internal/orders/store.go   # or see the diff first

$ go vet ./...
internal/orders/store.go:41: Printf format %d has arg name of wrong type string

$ golangci-lint run          # the community meta-linter, in most CI setups
Tabs, and no debate about it

gofmt indents with tabs and aligns with spaces, brace placement is fixed, and there is no configuration. The entire category of formatting argument is gone from Go code review, which is worth more than any individual formatting preference. Wire it into your editor's save hook on day one and never think about it again.

Interview follow-up

“What is in go.sum, and should it be committed?” Yes, commit it. go.mod records the module versions you depend on; go.sum records cryptographic hashes of those exact module contents. On every build the toolchain verifies the downloaded module against the recorded hash, so a dependency that is re-tagged or tampered with upstream fails the build loudly instead of silently changing your binary. It is the supply-chain check, and deleting it to “fix” a build is a mistake — the correct fix is go mod tidy.

L02

Types, zero values and constants

Go has no null, no implicit conversion, and no uninitialised memory. Those three facts together remove an entire class of bug, and explain several things that look verbose until you see why.

Every type has a zero value, and it is always usable

TypeZero valueUsable as-is?
numeric (int, float64, …)0yes
boolfalseyes
string"" (not nil)yes
pointer, func, chan, interfacenilno — dereference panics
slicenilyes — len, cap, range, append all work
mapnilread yes, write panics
structevery field zeroed, recursivelyyes
arrayevery element zeroedyes
go · design for the zero value and constructors mostly disappear
type Counter struct {
	mu sync.Mutex     // zero value is an unlocked mutex — ready to use
	n  map[string]int // zero value is nil — NOT ready to write
}

var c Counter
c.mu.Lock()          // fine: zero Mutex works
c.n["a"]++           // PANIC: assignment to entry in nil map

// Two fixes. Prefer the first when the type is meant to be used as `var x T`.
type Counter2 struct {
	mu sync.Mutex
	n  map[string]int
}

func (c *Counter2) Inc(k string) {
	c.mu.Lock()
	defer c.mu.Unlock()
	if c.n == nil {          // lazily make the map: zero value now works
		c.n = make(map[string]int)
	}
	c.n[k]++
}

// Or require a constructor, and say so by unexporting the struct fields.
func NewCounter() *Counter2 { return &Counter2{n: make(map[string]int)} }
“Make the zero value useful”

This is one of the strongest idioms in the standard library. var buf bytes.Buffer, var mu sync.Mutex, var wg sync.WaitGroup, var once sync.Once, http.Client{} — all work immediately with no constructor. When you design a type, ask whether its zero value can be the sensible default. When it can, callers get simpler code and you get fewer initialisation bugs.

Declarations

go · four forms, and when each is right
var a int              // explicit type, zero value — use when zero is meaningful
var b = 42             // type inferred from the value (int)
var c int = 42         // both — redundant; gofmt won't remove it but reviewers will
d := 42                // short form: only inside a function

// := requires at least one NEW variable on the left, and that trips people:
x, err := f()          // both new
y, err := g()          // y is new, err is REASSIGNED — legal and idiomatic
// err := h()          // illegal if err already exists and nothing else is new

// Grouped declarations read better for related values:
var (
	ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")
	ErrConflict = errors.New("conflict")
	timeout     = 5 * time.Second
)
Shadowing is the bug := causes

Inside an if or for body, err := … creates a new err that shadows the outer one. The inner assignment is then thrown away at the end of the block, and the outer err stays nil — so the failure is silently swallowed. go vet -vettool=shadow and every serious linter check for this; turn it on. When you mean to assign to an existing variable, use =, not :=.

Numeric types are explicit, and conversions are never implicit

TypeUse for
int / uintDefault for counts, indices, lengths. 64-bit on modern platforms, but not guaranteed
int64Money in minor units, IDs, timestamps, anything crossing a wire or a database
int32, uint8…Binary formats, protocol fields, memory-sensitive arrays
float64Default float. Never for money
byteAlias for uint8 — raw data
runeAlias for int32 — one Unicode code point
Integer division truncates and overflow wraps silently

7 / 2 is 3, not 3.5 — integer division truncates toward zero. And signed overflow is defined to wrap, with no panic: math.MaxInt64 + 1 is math.MinInt64. Go chose defined wrapping over undefined behaviour, which is safer, but it means bounds checks on arithmetic are yours to write. For money, use int64 minor units (cents) or a decimal package — never float64, where 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3.

Constants are arbitrary-precision until they are used

go · untyped constants, and iota
const big = 1 << 62          // fine: untyped constants are arbitrary precision
const pi = 3.14159265358979323846264338327950288  // more precision than float64 holds

var f float64 = pi           // rounded to float64 only at the point of use
// var i int = pi            // error: constant truncated — the compiler catches it

// Untyped constants adapt to context, which is why this works:
var d time.Duration = 5 * time.Second   // 5 is untyped, becomes Duration

// iota: an auto-incrementing counter, reset to 0 in each const block.
type Status int

const (
	StatusPending Status = iota   // 0
	StatusActive                  // 1  — expression repeats implicitly
	StatusClosed                  // 2
)

// The classic byte-size idiom:
const (
	_  = iota             // discard 0
	KB = 1 << (10 * iota) // 1 << 10
	MB                    // 1 << 20
	GB                    // 1 << 30
)

// Always give enum types a String method — otherwise logs show "2".
func (s Status) String() string {
	switch s {
	case StatusPending: return "pending"
	case StatusActive:  return "active"
	case StatusClosed:  return "closed"
	}
	return fmt.Sprintf("Status(%d)", int(s))
}
stringer generates that method for you

//go:generate stringer -type=Status at the top of the file, then go generate ./.... It writes the String() method into status_string.go and keeps it in sync as you add values — including a compile-time check that catches a renamed constant. Committing generated code is normal in Go.

Defined types versus aliases

go · one keeps you safe, the other is a rename
type UserID string      // DEFINED type: new type, distinct from string
type Email = string      // ALIAS: literally the same type, interchangeable

func send(to Email) {}
func lookup(id UserID) {}

var s string = "x"
send(s)            // fine — Email IS string
// lookup(s)       // error — cannot use string as UserID
lookup(UserID(s))  // explicit conversion required

// Defined types are how you stop passing a customer ID where an order ID
// goes. They cost one conversion at the boundary and catch a real class of
// bug forever. Aliases exist mainly for gradual refactors across packages.
Interview follow-up

“What is the difference between a nil slice and an empty slice?” A nil slice (var s []int) has no backing array, len and cap of 0, and s == nil is true. An empty slice (s := []int{}) has a non-nil pointer to a zero-length array. Behaviourally they are identical for len, cap, range and append — which is why the idiom is to declare var s []T and just append. The one place it matters is encoding/json: a nil slice marshals to null, an empty slice to []. If an API contract promises an array, initialise it explicitly.

L03

Control flow

Go has one loop keyword, a switch that does not fall through, and no ternary. The surface is small enough to learn in ten minutes — so this chapter spends most of its time on the two places it still surprises people.

for is the only loop

go · five shapes, one keyword
for i := 0; i < n; i++ { }        // C-style
for i < n { }                     // while
for { break }                     // infinite
for i, v := range xs { }          // range
for range 10 { }                  // Go 1.22+: range over an int, no variable needed

// range gives different pairs per type — this is worth memorising:
for i, v := range slice   { }   // index, copy of element
for k, v := range m       { }   // key, value  — ORDER IS RANDOMISED
for i, r := range str     { }   // byte offset, rune (decoded UTF-8)
for v := range ch         { }   // received value, until the channel is closed
for i := range array      { }   // index only
for range ticker.C        { }   // value discarded

// Go 1.23+: range over a function — iterators
for k, v := range maps.All(m) { }
Map iteration order is deliberately randomised

Not "unspecified but stable" — actively randomised on every run, with a random start offset. This is intentional: it stops anyone depending on an order that the implementation never promised. If you need deterministic output, collect the keys, sort them, then range over the sorted slice. Tests that pass locally and fail in CI one time in twenty are almost always this.

The loop variable, before and after Go 1.22

This is governed by the go line in go.mod, not your toolchain

A module declaring go 1.21 keeps the old per-loop semantics even when compiled by Go 1.24 — the language version is per-module so that upgrading the toolchain cannot silently change behaviour. So when you read unfamiliar code, check go.mod before reasoning about a closure in a loop. And when you bump that line, re-read every goroutine-in-a-loop in the module: the change usually fixes bugs, but it can also change timing.

if with a statement

go · scope the variable to the branch that needs it
if v, ok := m[key]; ok {
	use(v)                    // v and ok exist only inside this if/else
}

if err := do(); err != nil {
	return fmt.Errorf("do: %w", err)
}

// The dominant shape in Go: handle the error, return early, and keep the
// happy path at the leftmost indentation. Code reads top-to-bottom with no
// nesting, which is why Go code looks the way it does.
func process(id string) (*Order, error) {
	o, err := load(id)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("load %s: %w", id, err)
	}
	if err := validate(o); err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("validate %s: %w", id, err)
	}
	if err := save(o); err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("save %s: %w", id, err)
	}
	return o, nil
}

switch does more than you expect

go · four kinds of switch
// 1. Ordinary — no break needed, cases do NOT fall through.
switch status {
case "active", "trial":       // comma = OR
	allow()
case "suspended":
	deny()
default:
	unknown()
}

// 2. Expressionless — replaces an if/else-if chain, and reads far better.
switch {
case n < 0:
	return ErrNegative
case n == 0:
	return nil
case n > 1_000_000:
	return ErrTooLarge
}

// 3. With an initialiser.
switch v := compute(); {
case v > threshold:
	escalate(v)
}

// 4. Type switch — see L06.
switch x := any.(type) {
case string:
	fmt.Println(len(x))
case int, int64:              // NOTE: with several types, x keeps the
	fmt.Println(x)            //       interface type, not the concrete one
case nil:
	fmt.Println("nil interface")
default:
	fmt.Printf("%T\n", x)
}

// fallthrough exists, is rare, and transfers unconditionally to the NEXT
// case body without evaluating its condition.
switch n {
case 1:
	fmt.Println("one")
	fallthrough
case 2:
	fmt.Println("two")   // printed for n == 1 as well
}

Labels, goto, and breaking the right thing

go · break inside a select or switch does not break the loop
// This is the classic bug: `break` binds to the SWITCH, so the loop spins.
for {
	select {
	case msg := <-ch:
		if msg == "stop" {
			break        // breaks the select. The for loop continues.
		}
	}
}

// Label the loop and break the label.
loop:
	for {
		select {
		case msg := <-ch:
			if msg == "stop" {
				break loop
			}
		case <-ctx.Done():
			break loop
		}
	}

// continue also takes a label — useful in nested loops.
outer:
	for _, a := range as {
		for _, b := range bs {
			if conflicts(a, b) {
				continue outer
			}
		}
		keep(a)
	}
Prefer a named loop condition to a label when you can

Labels work, but a boolean for running { } or a small function with an early return is usually clearer. goto exists and is legal — it cannot jump into a block or over a variable declaration — but in modern Go it appears almost exclusively in generated code and in a handful of hot standard-library loops. If you reach for it, look for the missing function first.

Interview follow-up

“Why does Go not have a ternary operator?” The official answer is readability: a ? b : c invites nesting, and nested ternaries are where expressions become unreadable. The practical answer is that a three-line if assigning to a pre-declared variable is nearly as short and always legible, and that Go consistently trades author convenience for reader convenience. The same reasoning explains no while, no do..while, and no implicit fall-through in switch — each removes a way to write something that reads ambiguously.

L04

Functions, closures and defer

Functions are values, multiple returns are the reason Go has no exceptions, and defer has three rules that, once known, explain every surprise it produces.

Signatures

func Divide(a, b float64) (result float64, err error)
go · returns, variadics, and function types
// Multiple returns. The (value, error) pair is the single most common shape
// in the language — it is why Go does not need exceptions.
func Divide(a, b float64) (float64, error) {
	if b == 0 {
		return 0, errors.New("divide by zero")
	}
	return a / b, nil
}

// Named results document intent and enable bare returns — but bare returns
// in a long function hide what is being returned. Name them for the
// documentation, then still return explicitly.
func split(sum int) (x, y int) {
	x = sum * 4 / 9
	y = sum - x
	return          // legal; in anything over ~10 lines, write `return x, y`
}

// Variadic: xs is a []int inside the function.
func Sum(xs ...int) int {
	total := 0
	for _, x := range xs { total += x }
	return total
}
Sum(1, 2, 3)
Sum(nums...)            // spread an existing slice — note: NOT copied

// Functions are first-class values with types.
type Middleware func(http.Handler) http.Handler
var ops = map[string]func(int, int) int{
	"add": func(a, b int) int { return a + b },
	"mul": func(a, b int) int { return a * b },
}
f(xs...) passes the slice itself

The variadic parameter is not a copy of the backing array — it is your slice. A function that sorts or appends in place will mutate the caller's data. The standard library is careful about this; your code should be too. If the callee may retain or modify the argument, copy it with slices.Clone first.

Closures capture variables, not values

go · a closure holds a reference to the variable itself
func counter() func() int {
	n := 0                  // escapes to the heap: the closure outlives the call
	return func() int {
		n++                 // same n every call
		return n
	}
}

c := counter()
c() // 1
c() // 2

next := counter()           // a separate n
next() // 1

// Closures are how you build middleware, options, and callbacks:
func WithTimeout(d time.Duration) Option {
	return func(s *Server) { s.timeout = d }   // captures d
}
srv := New(WithTimeout(5*time.Second), WithLogger(log))

defer: three rules explain everything

1 Arguments are evaluated NOW; the call happens LATER. i := 0 defer fmt.Println(i) // prints 0 — i was copied at defer time i = 42 To capture the later value, defer a closure instead: defer func() { fmt.Println(i) }() // prints 42 2 Deferred calls run LIFO, when the function returns — by any path: normal return, an early return, or a panic unwinding the stack. They do not run on os.Exit, and they are not scoped to a block. 3 A deferred closure can read and MODIFY named return values, because it runs after the return values are assigned but before the caller sees them. This is how recover-and-convert-to-error works.
go · the three rules in practice
// Rule 3 — the only correct way to turn a panic into an error.
func safe() (err error) {
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			err = fmt.Errorf("recovered: %v", r)   // assigns the NAMED result
		}
	}()
	mightPanic()
	return nil
}

// Rule 3 again — never silently discard a Close error on a writer.
func writeFile(name string, data []byte) (err error) {
	f, err := os.Create(name)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer func() {
		if cerr := f.Close(); cerr != nil && err == nil {
			err = cerr        // a failed Close can mean unflushed data lost
		}
	}()
	_, err = f.Write(data)
	return err
}

// Rule 2 — LIFO order, and the classic lock idiom.
func (s *Store) Get(k string) (string, error) {
	s.mu.RLock()
	defer s.mu.RUnlock()      // unlocks on EVERY return path, including panics
	v, ok := s.data[k]
	if !ok {
		return "", ErrNotFound
	}
	return v, nil
}
defer in a loop is a resource leak

Deferred calls run when the function returns, not when the loop iteration ends. A loop over ten thousand files that defers f.Close() holds ten thousand descriptors open until the function exits, and will hit the process limit. Two fixes: move the body into its own function (so each call's defer fires), or call Close explicitly at the end of the iteration and on each error path.

panic and recover

Use
Return an errorAnything a caller could plausibly handle: bad input, a failed request, a missing file. This is 99% of failures.
panicA bug that makes continuing meaningless: an impossible switch branch, a broken invariant, a failed MustCompile at init
recoverAt a process boundary you must not let die — an HTTP handler, a worker loop — and only to log, convert, and return a 500
go · recovery middleware, the one legitimate broad recover
func Recoverer(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		defer func() {
			rec := recover()
			if rec == nil {
				return
			}
			// ErrAbortHandler is the stdlib's signal that the connection
			// was already torn down. Re-panic so net/http handles it.
			if rec == http.ErrAbortHandler {
				panic(rec)
			}
			slog.Error("panic in handler",
				"err", rec,
				"path", r.URL.Path,
				"stack", string(debug.Stack()))   // ALWAYS log the stack
			w.WriteHeader(http.StatusInternalServerError)
		}()
		next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
	})
}
recover only works directly inside a deferred function

Calling recover() anywhere else — including from a helper the deferred function calls — returns nil and the panic keeps unwinding. And it cannot catch a panic in a different goroutine: an unrecovered panic in any goroutine crashes the entire process. That is why every long-lived goroutine you spawn needs its own recover at the top, or a helper that wraps it.

Interview follow-up

“What does defer cost?” Almost nothing now. Go 1.13 added open-coded defers, where the compiler inlines the deferred call directly into the function's exit paths when the set of defers is statically known — roughly the cost of a normal call. The heap-allocated path remains only for defers inside a loop or under a condition the compiler cannot resolve. The old advice to avoid defer in hot functions is obsolete; write the correct code, then profile if it matters.

L05

Structs, methods and embedding

Go has no classes. It has structs that hold data, methods that can be attached to any named type, and embedding — which looks like inheritance, behaves like composition, and is the single most misread feature in the language.

Structs are values

go · declaration, literals, tags, comparability
type Order struct {
	ID        string    `json:"id"         db:"id"`
	Total     int64     `json:"total_cents" db:"total_cents"`
	Currency  string    `json:"currency"   db:"currency"`
	CreatedAt time.Time `json:"created_at" db:"created_at"`
	notes     string    // unexported: invisible to json, db drivers, reflection
}

o := Order{ID: "o_1", Total: 4999, Currency: "EUR"}   // field names: always use them
p := &Order{ID: "o_2"}                                 // pointer to a new value
var z Order                                            // every field zeroed

// Assignment COPIES the whole struct. There are no references by default.
a := o
a.ID = "changed"
// o.ID is still "o_1"

// Structs are comparable with == if every field is comparable.
// Slices, maps and functions are NOT comparable, so a struct containing one
// cannot be compared, used as a map key, or put in a set.
type Point struct{ X, Y int }
m := map[Point]string{{1, 2}: "origin-ish"}   // legal: Point is comparable
Struct tags are just strings the compiler ignores

They are metadata read at runtime by reflection — encoding/json, sqlx, validators, protobuf. A typo in a tag is not a compile error; it silently changes behaviour, which is why go vet has a structtag check and why you should let it run. The common tags: json:"-" excludes a field, json:"x,omitempty" drops zero values, and json:",string" encodes a number as a JSON string (useful for int64 IDs that JavaScript would round).

Methods can be attached to any named type in your package

go · not just structs
type Celsius float64

func (c Celsius) Fahrenheit() Celsius { return c*9/5 + 32 }
func (c Celsius) String() string      { return fmt.Sprintf("%.1f°C", float64(c)) }

type IDs []string

func (ids IDs) Contains(x string) bool { return slices.Contains(ids, x) }

// You cannot define a method on a type from another package — including
// builtin types. That restriction is what makes `go build` able to know
// every method of a type by looking at one package.
// func (s string) Reverse() string   // illegal

Value receiver or pointer receiver

Value receiver func (t T)Pointer receiver func (t *T)
Getsa copythe original
Can mutateno (mutations are lost)yes
Costcopies the struct on every callone word
Nil receiverimpossiblepossible — and legal to handle
Use whensmall, immutable, value-like (time.Time, Point)mutating, large, or the type contains a lock
Pick one and use it for every method on the type

Mixing receivers on one type is the mistake that produces the hardest bugs in this area. A type with any pointer-receiver method should use pointer receivers everywhere — because only *T then satisfies an interface containing those methods, and a T value silently will not. The second reason: a value receiver on a type containing a sync.Mutex copies the mutex, so each call locks a different lock and the protection quietly does nothing. go vet catches that one as copylocks.

go · the method set rule, which is where interfaces trip people
type Counter struct{ n int }

func (c *Counter) Inc()     { c.n++ }
func (c Counter) Value() int { return c.n }

// Method sets:
//   Counter  has:  Value
//   *Counter has:  Value AND Inc
//
// Calling is forgiving — Go auto-takes the address of an ADDRESSABLE value:
var c Counter
c.Inc()              // compiles: shorthand for (&c).Inc()

// Interface satisfaction is NOT forgiving:
type Incrementer interface{ Inc() }
var _ Incrementer = &Counter{}   // ok
// var _ Incrementer = Counter{} // COMPILE ERROR: Inc has pointer receiver

// And map elements are not addressable, so this fails too:
m := map[string]Counter{"a": {}}
// m["a"].Inc()      // cannot take the address of m["a"]
// Use map[string]*Counter instead.
A nil pointer receiver is legal and sometimes useful

func (l *Logger) Print(s string) { if l == nil { return }; … } compiles and runs — a method call on a nil pointer only panics if the body dereferences it. This lets a nil *Logger act as a working no-op, which the standard library uses in places. Use it sparingly: most readers assume nil means broken.

Embedding

go · a field with no name, whose methods get promoted
type Base struct {
	ID        string
	CreatedAt time.Time
}

func (b *Base) Age() time.Duration { return time.Since(b.CreatedAt) }

type User struct {
	Base                 // embedded: no field name
	Email string
}

u := User{Base: Base{ID: "u_1", CreatedAt: time.Now()}, Email: "a@b.c"}
u.ID        // promoted field  — shorthand for u.Base.ID
u.Age()     // promoted method — shorthand for u.Base.Age()
u.Base.ID   // the long form always works

// Embedding an INTERFACE is the more powerful move: you satisfy the whole
// interface while implementing only what you need.
type LoggingStore struct {
	Store               // interface — inherits every method
	log *slog.Logger
}

func (s LoggingStore) Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (*Order, error) {
	s.log.Info("get", "id", id)
	return s.Store.Get(ctx, id)     // the rest of Store passes straight through
}
Embedding is NOT inheritance. The difference that matters: ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Inheritance │ Embedding │ ├───────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────┤ │ Base method calls │ Base method calls the BASE's own │ │ the OVERRIDE │ method — it has no idea an outer │ │ (dynamic dispatch │ type exists │ │ to the subclass) │ │ └───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────┘ type Base struct{} func (b Base) Name() string { return "base" } func (b Base) Greet() string { return "hi, " + b.Name() } type Child struct{ Base } func (c Child) Name() string { return "child" } Child{}.Name() → "child" (promotion is shadowed as expected) Child{}.Greet() → "hi, base" NOT "hi, child" There is no virtual dispatch. Base.Greet was compiled against Base. If you want the outer behaviour, pass an interface in — do not embed and hope.
Ambiguous promotion is a compile error only at the point of use

Embed two types that both have a Close() method and the struct compiles fine. The error appears the moment someone writes x.Close() — "ambiguous selector". Depth wins over breadth: a method at depth 1 shadows one at depth 2, and only equal-depth collisions are ambiguous. Resolve it by writing the explicit path, or by naming one of the fields so its methods stop being promoted.

Struct layout costs real memory

Fields are laid out in declaration order with alignment padding. type Bad struct { type Good struct { a bool 1 byte x int64 8 _ [7]byte padding y int64 8 x int64 8 a bool 1 b bool 1 b bool 1 _ [7]byte padding _ [6]byte padding y int64 8 } } 24 bytes 32 bytes Order fields widest-to-narrowest. At a million rows that is 8 MB, and it also changes how many structs fit in a cache line. fieldalignment in go vet (or golangci-lint) finds these automatically — but only reorder in hot, high-count types. Readable grouping beats byte-shaving everywhere else.
Interview follow-up

“When would you use embedding over a plain field?” When you genuinely want the outer type to be usable as the inner one — decorating an interface implementation, or adding methods to a value while keeping its whole API. For plain code reuse a named field is clearer, because u.base.ID tells the reader where the data lives while u.ID hides it. The strongest argument against reflexive embedding is that promoted methods become part of your public API by accident: embed a sync.Mutex and you have exported Lock and Unlock to every caller.

L06

Interfaces

Interfaces in Go are structural, not nominal — a type satisfies one by having the right methods, never by declaring that it does. That single decision changes how you design packages, and produces the one Go gotcha that catches everybody.

Implicit satisfaction, and what it buys

go · nobody declares anything
type Stringer interface {
	String() string
}

type Temp float64
func (t Temp) String() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%.1f°", float64(t)) }
// Temp now satisfies fmt.Stringer. It did not import fmt to do so, and
// fmt does not know Temp exists.

// The consequence: the CONSUMER declares the interface, not the producer.
// Your package says what it needs; any type that happens to fit works.
package report

type Store interface {                  // defined HERE, next to the user
	Orders(ctx context.Context, since time.Time) ([]Order, error)
}

func Monthly(ctx context.Context, s Store) (*Report, error) { … }
// postgres.Store fits. memory.Store fits. A test fake fits. None of them
// import `report`, and `report` imports none of them.
“Accept interfaces, return structs”

Take the narrowest interface you need as a parameter, and return a concrete type. Returning an interface hides the concrete type's other methods from callers and forces everyone downstream through your abstraction. Taking one keeps your package testable and decoupled. The corollary, which matters more: define the interface where it is used, not where it is implemented — a storage package that exports type Store interface with fifteen methods has usually got this backwards.

Small interfaces compose; large ones do not

go · the standard library's most-copied design
type Reader interface { Read(p []byte) (n int, err error) }
type Writer interface { Write(p []byte) (n int, err error) }
type Closer interface { Close() error }

type ReadWriter interface { Reader; Writer }           // embedding interfaces
type ReadWriteCloser interface { Reader; Writer; Closer }

// One method each — and therefore *os.File, *bytes.Buffer, net.Conn,
// *strings.Reader, gzip writers, HTTP bodies and a hundred third-party
// types all interoperate without any of them coordinating.

func Copy(dst Writer, src Reader) (int64, error)   // works on all of them
The interface-per-struct anti-pattern

A UserService struct with a UserServiceInterface containing exactly its methods, written only so a mock can be generated, adds an indirection layer with no design content. If the interface has one implementation and one fake, and its method set is identical to the struct's, it is ceremony. Write the interface when a second real implementation appears, or when the consumer genuinely needs less than the whole type — and then make it as small as that consumer's actual use.

What an interface value actually is

An interface value is two words: a type descriptor and a data pointer. var s Shape = Circle{R: 2} ┌──────────────┬──────────────┐ │ itab │ data │ │ ↓ │ ↓ │ │ type Circle │ *Circle{R:2}│ │ method tbl: │ │ │ Area →fn │ │ │ Perim →fn │ │ └──────────────┴──────────────┘ nil interface both words nil → s == nil is TRUE non-nil interface type set, data nil → s == nil is FALSE holding a nil pointer That second row is the entire gotcha below.

The typed-nil trap

go · the most common Go bug in production code
type MyErr struct{ Code int }
func (e *MyErr) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("code %d", e.Code) }

func doWork(ok bool) error {
	var e *MyErr          // nil *MyErr
	if !ok {
		e = &MyErr{Code: 500}
	}
	return e              // BUG: returns a non-nil error interface
}                         //      holding a nil *MyErr

err := doWork(true)
fmt.Println(err == nil)   // false  — and the caller now handles a "failure"
fmt.Println(err)          // panics if Error() dereferences e

// The fix is to never put a typed nil into an interface. Return a
// literal nil on the success path:
func doWork2(ok bool) error {
	if !ok {
		return &MyErr{Code: 500}
	}
	return nil            // an untyped nil — both words are nil
}
Where this bites in real services

Any function whose signature returns a concrete error type — func f() *MyErr — and is then assigned to an error variable. Also: a struct field declared as error assigned a nil *MyErr, and a channel of a concrete pointer type read into an error. The rule: declare error-returning functions as returning error, never a concrete error type. That one habit eliminates the whole class.

Type assertions and type switches

go · getting back to the concrete type
var v any = "hello"

s := v.(string)        // panics if v is not a string
s, ok := v.(string)    // comma-ok: never panics; s is "" and ok is false

// Asserting to an INTERFACE asks "does the dynamic type implement this?"
// This is how optional capabilities work throughout the stdlib:
if f, ok := w.(http.Flusher); ok {
	f.Flush()                       // stream if the writer supports it
}
if rs, ok := body.(io.ReadSeeker); ok {
	http.ServeContent(w, r, name, modTime, rs)   // range requests possible
}

// Type switch — the multi-way form.
func describe(v any) string {
	switch x := v.(type) {
	case nil:
		return "nil"
	case error:                       // interface cases work, and are checked
		return "error: " + x.Error()  //   in source order — put them last
	case string:
		return "string of " + strconv.Itoa(len(x))
	case []byte:
		return "bytes of " + strconv.Itoa(len(x))
	case fmt.Stringer:
		return "stringer: " + x.String()
	default:
		return fmt.Sprintf("%T", x)
	}
}

Compile-time assertions

go · fail at build time, not at wiring time
// Put this next to the type. It costs nothing at runtime and turns
// "forgot to update the implementation" into a compile error with a
// precise message about which method is missing.
var _ Store = (*PostgresStore)(nil)
var _ http.Handler = (*Server)(nil)
var _ json.Marshaler = Money{}      // value receiver → assert with a value

any, and when to resist it

SituationReach for
A container that works for all typesgenerics (L11) — type-safe, no boxing
A set of known, closed alternativesan interface with a marker method, or a type switch
Genuinely dynamic data: JSON, config, loggingany is correct — this is what it is for
“I could not decide on a type”decide on a type
any is an alias for interface{}

Added in Go 1.18, identical in every way — gofmt -r 'interface{} -> any' rewrites the old spelling mechanically. Note that the empty interface has no methods, so every type satisfies it; putting a value in one boxes it, which means an allocation for anything that is not already pointer-shaped, and an interface call cannot be inlined. That cost is invisible until it shows up in a profile.

Interview follow-up

“How do you test code that talks to a database?” The Go answer is to define a narrow interface in the package that consumes the store — two or three methods, exactly what that package calls — and implement it twice: with the real database, and with an in-memory fake in the test package. No mocking framework, no generated code, and the fake is real Go you can put assertions in. For anything where SQL correctness is the thing under test, run the real database in a container (testcontainers) rather than faking it, because a fake that accepts your broken query proves nothing.

L07

Arrays and slices

A slice is three words pointing at an array you cannot see. Almost every slice bug in Go comes from forgetting the array is shared — so this chapter draws it, then shows the four ways it bites.

Arrays are values; slices are views

go · the length is part of an array's type
var a [3]int          // [3]int and [4]int are DIFFERENT types
b := a                // copies all 3 elements
b[0] = 99             // a[0] is still 0

func f(arr [3]int)    // copies on every call — arrays are rare in Go APIs
func g(s []int)       // slices: three words, the data is shared

// Arrays earn their place in three situations:
//   fixed-size protocol fields   var hdr [16]byte
//   map keys                     map[[32]byte]bool   (a sha256 digest)
//   avoiding an allocation       buf := [64]byte{}; use(buf[:])
A slice header is exactly three words: s := make([]int, 3, 8) ┌─────────┬─────┬─────┐ │ ptr │ len │ cap │ len = elements you may index │ ────────┼── 3 ┼── 8 │ cap = elements from ptr to the end └────┬────┴─────┴─────┘ of the backing array │ ▼ backing array (8 slots) ┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐ │ 0 │ 0 │ 0 │ · │ · │ · │ · │ · │ └───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘ └─── len ───┘└──── spare cap ────┘ Passing a slice to a function copies the HEADER, not the data. So the callee can change your elements (same backing array) but cannot change your length (its own copy of the header). That asymmetry is the source of the "why didn't my append show up" question.

Slicing, and the capacity that comes with it

go · s[low:high:max]
s := []int{0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7}   // len 8, cap 8

a := s[2:5]       // len 3, cap 6   — cap runs from index 2 to the END
b := s[2:5:5]     // len 3, cap 3   — three-index form CAPS it

a[0] = 99         // s[2] is now 99 — same backing array
_ = b

// Why the three-index form matters: it makes a later append on the
// sub-slice allocate a new array instead of overwriting the parent's data.
func (b *Buffer) Bytes() []byte {
	return b.buf[:b.n:b.n]    // callers can append without corrupting b
}

append: the four ways it surprises people

go · 1 — append may or may not allocate
s := make([]int, 0, 4)
t := append(s, 1)     // cap was spare → SAME array, t and s share it
u := append(s, 2)     // also writes index 0 → t[0] is now 2, not 1!

// Once cap is exceeded, append allocates a NEW array and copies:
v := make([]int, 4, 4)
w := append(v, 5)     // new array; v and w are now independent

// So: `append` returns a slice that MAY OR MAY NOT alias the input.
// Never rely on either. Always use the returned value:
//   s = append(s, x)       correct
//   append(s, x)           compile error (result unused) — the language helps
go · 3 — the filter-in-place idiom, and its hidden leak
// Reuse the backing array instead of allocating a second slice:
keep := xs[:0]
for _, x := range xs {
	if x.Valid {
		keep = append(keep, x)
	}
}
xs = keep

// Correct — but if x is a pointer or contains one, the tail of the backing
// array still holds references to the dropped elements, so the GC cannot
// free them. Zero the tail when elements are pointer-shaped:
clear(xs[len(keep):])          // Go 1.21+ builtin
xs = keep

// Or just use the stdlib, which does this for you:
xs = slices.DeleteFunc(xs, func(x Item) bool { return !x.Valid })
4 — a small slice can pin a huge array

head := body[:100] on a 10 MB response keeps the entire 10 MB alive for as long as head is reachable, because the slice header points into that array and the GC frees whole objects. This is a classic "memory grows and never falls" cause in services that keep a prefix of a large buffer in a cache. The fix is one line: head := slices.Clone(body[:100]), or bytes.Clone for a []byte.

Growth, and why preallocating is free performance

append grows capacity when it runs out. Since Go 1.18 the factor slides from ~2× for small slices toward ~1.25× for large ones, then the result is rounded up to a size class — so never assume an exact number. Appending 1,000,000 ints with no preallocation: ~20 reallocations, and every one copies everything so far total copied ≈ 2× the final size If you know the length, say so: out := make([]Result, 0, len(in)) len 0, cap len(in) for _, x := range in { out = append(out, f(x)) } One allocation, zero copies. This is the single most common easy win in a Go CPU profile, and it shows up as runtime.growslice. Watch the classic typo: make([]T, len(in)) gives you len(in) ZERO VALUES and then appends after them — a slice of double length whose first half is empty.

Copy, compare, and the modern stdlib

go · slices, and what replaced the hand-rolled helpers
n := copy(dst, src)        // copies min(len(dst), len(src)); handles overlap
b := []byte("hi")
copy(b, "ok")              // string → []byte is a special case

// Slices are NOT comparable with ==. Only against nil.
// if a == b            // compile error
slices.Equal(a, b)         // element-wise
slices.EqualFunc(a, b, eq) // with your own comparison

// Go 1.21+ standard library — prefer these to hand-written loops:
slices.Contains(s, v)
slices.Index(s, v)                       // -1 if absent
slices.Sort(s)                           // ordered types
slices.SortFunc(s, func(a, b T) int { return cmp.Compare(a.N, b.N) })
slices.SortStableFunc(s, cmpFn)
slices.BinarySearch(s, v)                // on a sorted slice
slices.Reverse(s)
slices.Clone(s)                          // shallow copy — one level only
slices.Max(s); slices.Min(s)
slices.Compact(s)                        // dedupe ADJACENT equal elements
slices.Insert(s, i, vs...)
slices.Delete(s, i, j)
slices.Concat(a, b, c)                   // Go 1.22+
slices.Chunk(s, n)                       // Go 1.23+, an iterator
slices.Clone is shallow

It copies the header and the backing array, so the elements themselves are copied — but if the element type contains a pointer, a slice, or a map, both copies point at the same underlying data. Cloning []*User gives you a new slice of the same *User values. For a genuine deep copy you write it yourself; Go has no generic deep-copy, deliberately.

Interview follow-up

“What happens when you append to a slice inside a function?” The function receives a copy of the three-word header. If append fits within the existing capacity it writes into the shared backing array — so the caller sees the new element only if it happens to reslice, and it sees element mutations either way. If capacity is exceeded, append allocates a new array and the callee's slice now points somewhere else entirely, leaving the caller completely unaffected. Because the behaviour differs based on capacity, the rule is absolute: a function that grows a slice must return it, or take a *[]T.

L08

Maps, strings and runes

Maps are the workhorse container and have three rules worth memorising. Strings are immutable byte slices that happen to usually hold UTF-8 — and that "usually" is where the bugs live.

Maps

go · create, read, write, delete
m := make(map[string]int)          // ready to write
m := map[string]int{"a": 1}        // literal
m := make(map[string]int, 1000)    // preallocate buckets — real speedup
var m map[string]int               // NIL: reads OK, writes PANIC

v := m["missing"]                  // 0 — reading an absent key never errors
v, ok := m["missing"]              // v=0, ok=false — the comma-ok form
delete(m, "a")                     // no-op if absent, never panics
n := len(m)
clear(m)                           // Go 1.21+: empty it, keep the buckets

// Counting and grouping — the two idioms you will write constantly.
counts := map[string]int{}
for _, w := range words { counts[w]++ }         // zero value makes this work

byUser := map[string][]Order{}
for _, o := range orders {
	byUser[o.UserID] = append(byUser[o.UserID], o)   // append to a nil slice
}
RuleConsequence
Iteration order is randomisedSort keys for deterministic output; never rely on insertion order
Not safe for concurrent useConcurrent read+write is detected by the runtime and crashes the process — not a data race you can ignore
Elements are not addressable&m[k] and m[k].Field = v are compile errors. Use map[K]*V, or read-modify-write the whole value
Keys must be comparableNo slice, map, or func keys. Structs and arrays are fine if their fields are
Maps never shrinkA map that held 10M entries keeps its buckets after delete. Reassign a fresh map to release memory
go · the addressability rule in practice
type Stat struct{ N int }

m := map[string]Stat{"a": {}}
// m["a"].N++                       // compile error: not addressable

s := m["a"]; s.N++; m["a"] = s      // read, modify, write back
// or store pointers:
p := map[string]*Stat{"a": {}}
p["a"].N++                          // fine

// Concurrency: a plain map guarded by a RWMutex beats sync.Map for almost
// every workload. sync.Map is optimised for exactly two cases — keys
// written once and read many times, or disjoint key sets per goroutine.
type Cache struct {
	mu sync.RWMutex
	m  map[string]string
}

func (c *Cache) Get(k string) (string, bool) {
	c.mu.RLock()
	defer c.mu.RUnlock()
	v, ok := c.m[k]
	return v, ok
}
Deterministic map output in three lines

keys := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m)) (Go 1.23+) then range over keys. Before 1.23, keys := make([]string, 0, len(m)); for k := range m { keys = append(keys, k) }; slices.Sort(keys). Use it in every place output is compared: golden-file tests, generated code, config dumps, and anything hashed.

Sets, since Go has none

go · map[T]struct{} costs zero bytes per value
seen := map[string]struct{}{}
seen["a"] = struct{}{}
if _, ok := seen["a"]; ok { … }

// map[string]bool is more readable and costs one byte per entry. Use it
// unless the set is large enough for that byte to matter — then the
// struct{} form is genuinely zero-width.

Strings are immutable bytes

A string header is two words: a pointer and a length. No capacity, because it cannot grow — strings are immutable. s := "héllo" ┌─────────┬─────┐ │ ptr │ len │ len is in BYTES, not characters │ ────────┼── 6 │ └────┬────┴─────┘ ▼ ┌────┬────┬────┬────┬────┬────┐ │ 68 │ c3 │ a9 │ 6c │ 6c │ 6f │ │ h │ ←── é ──→│ l │ l │ o │ └────┴────┴────┴────┴────┴────┘ len(s) → 6 bytes s[1] → 0xc3 a byte, NOT 'é' utf8.RuneCountInString(s) → 5 code points []rune(s) → 5 runes, and this allocates Indexing a string gives you a byte. Ranging gives you runes. That single asymmetry causes most string bugs involving non-ASCII input.
go · bytes, runes and the conversions between them
s := "héllo"

for i := 0; i < len(s); i++ { _ = s[i] }   // 6 iterations, raw bytes
for i, r := range s {                       // 5 iterations
	fmt.Printf("%d: %c\n", i, r)            // i jumps 0,1,3,4,5 — BYTE offsets
}

b := []byte(s)      // copies (string is immutable, []byte is not)
r := []rune(s)      // decodes UTF-8 → []int32; allocates
s2 := string(b)     // copies back
s3 := string(r)     // encodes back to UTF-8

// string(65) is "A" — an int is treated as a rune. To render a number:
strconv.Itoa(65)                  // "65"
strconv.FormatInt(x, 10)
strconv.Quote(s)                  // adds quotes and escapes
n, err := strconv.Atoi("65")      // parse; ALWAYS check the error
Reversing a string by bytes corrupts it

for i := len(s)-1; i >= 0; i-- over bytes produces invalid UTF-8 for anything non-ASCII. Reverse over []rune instead — and even that is wrong for grapheme clusters: an emoji with a skin-tone modifier, or "é" written as e plus a combining accent, is several runes that render as one character. Correct grapheme handling needs golang.org/x/text. This is a favourite interview question precisely because the naive answer looks right.

Building strings

NeedUse
join a slicestrings.Join(xs, ", ") — one allocation, sized exactly
build in a loopstrings.Builder (or bytes.Buffer if you need []byte)
format oncefmt.Sprintf — convenient, reflection-based, the slowest option
concatenate twoa + b is fine and the compiler optimises it
search / splitstrings.Contains, HasPrefix, Cut, SplitN, Fields, TrimSpace
replacestrings.ReplaceAll, or strings.NewReplacer for many pairs (reusable, faster)
case-insensitive comparestrings.EqualFold — not ToLower(a) == ToLower(b)
strings.Cut is the one to learn

before, after, found := strings.Cut(s, "=") replaces the SplitN(s, "=", 2) plus length-check dance that used to be everywhere, allocates nothing, and reads exactly like what it does. Added in Go 1.18; strings.CutPrefix and CutSuffix followed in 1.20.

Interview follow-up

“Why is len("héllo") 5 in Python and 6 in Go?” Because Go's string is a read-only byte slice with no character semantics attached, and len reports bytes. Go made strings byte-oriented because that is what I/O, networking and files actually produce, and it puts the decoding cost exactly where you ask for it — range, []rune, or the utf8 package. A string in Go is not even required to hold valid UTF-8; it can carry arbitrary bytes, which is why reading a file into a string is safe and why utf8.ValidString exists.

L09

Errors

Errors are ordinary values implementing a one-method interface. That is the whole mechanism — no stack unwinding, no catch, no hidden control flow. What takes practice is not the mechanism but the discipline: what to wrap, what to add, and what a caller is meant to do with it.

The interface

type error interface { Error() string }
go · three ways to make one
errors.New("connection refused")                 // static
fmt.Errorf("read %s: %w", name, err)             // wrapped, with context
type ValidationError struct{ Field, Reason string }   // typed, carries data
func (e *ValidationError) Error() string {
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s: %s", e.Field, e.Reason)
}

Wrapping builds a chain

Each layer adds what it knows and keeps the layer below intact. handler "create order: " └── service "charge card: " └── client "POST /v1/charges: " └── net "dial tcp 10.0.3.4:443: i/o timeout" Printed: create order: charge card: POST /v1/charges: dial tcp 10.0.3.4:443: i/o timeout And still inspectable at every level: errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) → true errors.As(err, &netErr) → true, and netErr.Timeout() %w wraps (keeps the chain) · %v formats (flattens to text, chain lost) Use %w when a caller might want to inspect the cause. Use %v when the cause is an implementation detail you do not want to make part of your package's contract.
go · wrap with context that the caller does not already have
func (s *Service) PlaceOrder(ctx context.Context, userID string, items []Item) (*Order, error) {
	u, err := s.users.Get(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		// Add the ID: the caller passed it, but the log line three layers
		// up did not. Do NOT repeat "users.Get" — that is in the inner error.
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("load user %s: %w", userID, err)
	}

	total, err := price(items)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("price %d items: %w", len(items), err)
	}

	o := &Order{UserID: u.ID, Total: total}
	if err := s.orders.Insert(ctx, o); err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("insert order: %w", err)
	}
	return o, nil
}

// Go 1.20+ can wrap several errors at once:
err := errors.Join(errValidateName, errValidateEmail)
// errors.Is finds either one; Error() prints them newline-separated.
Do not start an error string with a capital or end it with punctuation

Error strings get concatenated: "create order: Charge failed." reads badly in the middle of a chain. The convention is lowercase, no trailing period, no "failed to" prefix — the fact that it is an error already says it failed. go vet's ST1005 (via staticcheck) enforces this.

Inspecting: Is for identity, As for data

go · never compare with == across a wrap
var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found")     // sentinel: exported, comparable

// WRONG once anything wraps it:
if err == ErrNotFound { … }

// RIGHT — unwraps the whole chain:
if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) {
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNotFound)
	return
}

// errors.As finds the first error in the chain assignable to the target
// and assigns it — so you can read its fields.
var ve *ValidationError
if errors.As(err, &ve) {
	http.Error(w, "bad "+ve.Field, http.StatusBadRequest)
	return
}

// Real example: distinguishing a Postgres unique-violation from any other
// database failure.
var pgErr *pgconn.PgError
if errors.As(err, &pgErr) && pgErr.Code == "23505" {
	return ErrConflict
}

// A type can define its own Is to match a family of errors:
func (e *HTTPError) Is(target error) bool {
	t, ok := target.(*HTTPError)
	return ok && t.Status == e.Status
}
errors.As takes a pointer to the target, and will panic if you forget

The argument must be a non-nil pointer to a type implementing error, or to an interface. For an error type with a pointer receiver — the usual case — that means declaring var ve *ValidationError and passing &ve: a pointer to a pointer. Passing ve directly compiles (the parameter is any) and panics at runtime. This is the single most common errors mistake.

Sentinel or typed?

Sentinel var ErrX = errors.New(…)Typed type XError struct{…}
Carries datanoyes — field, code, retry-after
Checked witherrors.Iserrors.As
API costa package-level variable callers depend on forevera type callers depend on forever
Use whenthe caller only needs to know which failurethe caller needs details to act
Export an error only when a caller must branch on it

Every exported sentinel and error type is a public API commitment — once someone writes errors.Is(err, pkg.ErrBusy), you can never remove it. Most errors are not branched on; they are logged and returned. Keep those unexported and wrapped. A package with three exported errors that all mean something is better designed than one with twenty.

Where to handle, where to return

The rule: either handle it or return it — never both

Logging and returning is double reporting, and it produces incident timelines where one failure appears six times at six different layers with six different wordings. Decide at each layer: can I do something about this (retry, fall back, default)? Then handle it and do not return it. Otherwise wrap it with context and return. Log at the boundary where the error stops travelling — the HTTP handler, the worker loop, main.

Errors that tell the caller what to do

go · behaviour beats identity for cross-package contracts
// Instead of exporting a list of errors callers must know about, expose a
// behaviour they can test for. net.Error does exactly this.
type temporary interface{ Temporary() bool }

func isRetryable(err error) bool {
	var t temporary
	if errors.As(err, &t) {
		return t.Temporary()
	}
	// Context errors are never worth retrying with the same context.
	if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) || errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) {
		return false
	}
	return errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNRESET) || errors.Is(err, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF)
}

// An HTTP-shaped error type that the top layer can turn into a response
// without knowing anything about the packages below it.
type APIError struct {
	Status  int
	Code    string          // stable, machine-readable: "order_not_found"
	Message string          // safe to show a user
	err     error           // the internal cause — never sent to the client
}

func (e *APIError) Error() string { return e.Code + ": " + e.Message }
func (e *APIError) Unwrap() error { return e.err }   // keeps the chain alive
Stack traces are not built in, and often you do not need them

A well-wrapped error chain names every layer it passed through, which is usually more useful than a stack trace and far cheaper. When you do want frames — a library where the call path is genuinely ambiguous — github.com/pkg/errors is the historical answer and log/slog plus a wrapper that captures runtime.Callers is the modern one. Capturing a stack on every error in a hot path is a measurable cost; do it at the boundary, not everywhere.

Interview follow-up

“Isn't if err != nil everywhere just noise?” It is verbose, and that is the trade Go made deliberately: every failure path is visible in the source, so reading a function tells you exactly what can go wrong and where. Exceptions make the happy path shorter and the failure paths invisible — and in a service, the failure paths are the ones that wake you at night. The honest criticism is not the check itself but the wrapping boilerplate, which is why proposals keep appearing; none has been accepted because none preserved that visibility.

L10

Packages, modules and initialisation

Go's dependency story is unusual: versions are resolved by picking the minimum that satisfies everyone, the import graph must be acyclic, and the order in which your program's variables come to life is fully specified. All three affect how you lay out a real codebase.

Modules and versions

ini · go.mod, annotated
module github.com/acme/service      // import path prefix for everything here

go 1.24                             // LANGUAGE version: gates semantics
                                    // (e.g. per-iteration loop variables)
toolchain go1.24.2                  // minimum toolchain; go will fetch it

require (
    github.com/jackc/pgx/v5 v5.6.0          // direct
    golang.org/x/sync       v0.8.0
)

require (
    github.com/rogpeppe/go-internal v1.12.0 // indirect
)

replace github.com/acme/shared => ../shared  // local dev only — never commit
exclude github.com/bad/pkg v1.4.0            // skip a known-broken version
Minimal version selection — Go's answer to dependency hell your module requires A v1.2.0 A requires C v1.1.0 B requires C v1.4.0 ──────────── selected: C v1.4.0 ← the MAXIMUM of the MINIMUMS Not "the newest that satisfies the range" — there are no ranges. Every requirement is an exact minimum, and the build picks the highest one anyone asked for. Consequences: · builds are reproducible without a lock file (go.sum is integrity, not resolution) · adding a dependency cannot silently upgrade an unrelated one · upgrades are explicit: go get -u or go get pkg@v1.5.0 · v2 and above live at a different import path: github.com/x/y/v2 — so v1 and v2 can coexist in one build
CommandEffect
go mod tidyReconcile go.mod/go.sum with actual imports. Run before every commit
go mod why pkgExplain why a module is in the graph — the answer to "who pulled this in"
go mod graphThe full requirement graph, one edge per line
go list -m allEvery module in the build, at its selected version
go list -m -u allThe same, annotated with available upgrades
go mod vendorCopy dependencies into vendor/; builds then use it automatically
go mod verifyCheck the module cache against go.sum
go get -u ./...Upgrade direct and indirect deps to latest minor/patch
GOFLAGS=-mod=readonlyFail instead of editing go.mod — the right CI setting
The proxy and the checksum database

By default GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct means modules come from an immutable cache rather than straight from GitHub, so a deleted or force-pushed tag cannot break your build. GOSUMDB=sum.golang.org independently attests to each module's hash. In a corporate environment you point GOPROXY at an internal mirror (Athens, Artifactory) and set GOPRIVATE=github.com/acme/* so private modules bypass both the proxy and the sum database.

Import cycles are a hard error

package a imports b, package b imports a → compile error There is no flag to allow it. The three fixes, in order of preference: 1 Move the shared thing down. Extract the types both need into a third package that neither imports the other for. a ──┐ a ──┐ ├── cycle ⇒ ├──▶ model ◀──┐ b ──┘ b ────────┘ 2 Invert with an interface. If a needs to call into b, define the interface in a and have b's type satisfy it. b imports a; a imports nothing. 3 Merge them. Two packages that genuinely need each other are usually one package that was split too early. This restriction is why Go codebases tend toward a shallow dependency tree with leaf packages holding types — and why internal/ subtrees work so well.

Initialisation order is fully specified

go · what runs before main
package main

var a = b + 1     // 3 — Go resolves DEPENDENCY order, not source order
var b = c * 2     // 2
var c = 1

func init() { fmt.Println("init 1") }   // several init funcs per file are legal
func init() { fmt.Println("init 2") }   // they run in source order

func main() { fmt.Println(a, b, c) }    // 3 2 1
The full order, for the whole program: 1 Every imported package is initialised first, depth-first, each exactly once — so a dependency is always ready before its importer. 2 Within a package, package-level variables initialise in dependency order (unreferenced ones in file-name order). 3 Then every init() in that package, file by file in the order the compiler is given them (alphabetical, in practice). 4 Finally, main.main. All of this happens on a single goroutine, so no locking is needed — but a goroutine you start in init escapes that guarantee.
init is mostly a smell

It runs before main can parse a flag, read config, or set up a logger; it cannot return an error, so failure means panic or a silently broken program; and it makes tests depend on import side effects. Legitimate uses are narrow: registering a database driver or image format with a registry, and compiling a package-level regexp.MustCompile. Everything else — connections, config, clients — belongs in an explicit constructor called from main, where errors are values and the order is visible.

go · the blank import, which exists for exactly this
import (
	"database/sql"
	_ "github.com/lib/pq"        // imported ONLY for its init(), which calls
)                                // sql.Register("postgres", &Driver{})

db, err := sql.Open("postgres", dsn)   // the name only resolves because of it

Laying out a service

service/ ├── cmd/ │ ├── api/main.go wiring only: flags, config, deps, serve │ └── worker/main.go ├── internal/ compiler-enforced private │ ├── order/ domain: types + business rules, no I/O │ │ ├── order.go │ │ └── service.go │ ├── postgres/ one adapter per external system │ ├── http/ transport: handlers, routing, middleware │ └── config/ ├── pkg/ only if you truly publish it — most don't ├── migrations/ └── api/openapi.yaml Name packages for what they provide, not what they contain. util, common, helpers, models, base — these are buckets that grow forever and import everything. order, billing, postgres, ratelimit tell a reader what is inside. And avoid stuttering. The package name is part of every call: order.OrderService → order.Service http.HTTPServer → http.Server
Workspaces beat replace for multi-module development

go work init ./service ./shared writes a go.work file that makes the toolchain resolve those modules locally, across every go command, without touching any go.mod. Add go.work and go.work.sum to .gitignore — it is a developer-machine artefact. The old replace directive did the same job but lived in a committed file, and shipping one to production is a classic mistake.

Interview follow-up

“What goes in internal/ versus pkg/?” internal/ is a language feature: the compiler refuses imports from outside the subtree rooted at its parent, so everything that is not a deliberate public API belongs there — which, for a service, is essentially all of it. pkg/ is only a convention with no enforcement, and it is worth having exactly when you intend other repositories to import that code. For an application, the honest layout is cmd/ plus internal/ and no pkg/ at all; adding one because a template had it is how packages end up public by accident.

L11

Generics

Added in Go 1.18 after a decade of deliberation, and deliberately limited. Generics let you write one implementation for many types without any and without reflection — and the community norm, which the standard library follows, is to use them sparingly.

Type parameters

func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U
go · the shape, and inference
func Map[T, U any](s []T, f func(T) U) []U {
	out := make([]U, 0, len(s))
	for _, v := range s {
		out = append(out, f(v))
	}
	return out
}

names := Map(users, func(u User) string { return u.Name })   // T, U inferred
ids   := Map[User, int64](users, func(u User) int64 { return u.ID })  // explicit

// Generic types, not just functions:
type Stack[T any] struct{ items []T }

func (s *Stack[T]) Push(v T) { s.items = append(s.items, v) }
func (s *Stack[T]) Pop() (T, bool) {
	if len(s.items) == 0 {
		var zero T          // the idiom for "zero value of an unknown type"
		return zero, false
	}
	v := s.items[len(s.items)-1]
	s.items = s.items[:len(s.items)-1]
	return v, true
}

s := &Stack[string]{}      // instantiate with a concrete type
Methods cannot have their own type parameters

func (s *Stack[T]) MapTo[U any](f func(T) U) []U does not compile. A method may only use the type parameters of its receiver — adding new ones would require constructing method sets at runtime, which breaks how interfaces are implemented. The workaround is always the same: make it a free function taking the receiver as the first argument, which is why the standard library's generic helpers are package-level functions rather than methods.

Constraints are interfaces with type sets

go · what a constraint can say
// 1. Method-based — an ordinary interface used as a constraint.
type Stringer interface{ String() string }
func Join[T Stringer](xs []T) string { … }

// 2. Type-set based — the new part. A union of permitted types.
type Number interface {
	~int | ~int8 | ~int16 | ~int32 | ~int64 |
		~uint | ~uint8 | ~uint16 | ~uint32 | ~uint64 |
		~float32 | ~float64
}

func Sum[T Number](xs []T) T {
	var total T
	for _, x := range xs { total += x }   // + is legal: every type in the set has it
	return total
}

// The ~ means "any type whose UNDERLYING type is this". Without it,
// `type Celsius float64` would not satisfy Number. Almost always use ~.

// 3. Both at once:
type Keyed interface {
	~string | ~int
	Key() string
}

// 4. From the standard library — use these before inventing your own:
//    any               anything
//    comparable        supports == and != (map keys, slices.Contains)
//    cmp.Ordered       supports < <= > >=  (all numerics and string)
import "cmp"
func Max[T cmp.Ordered](a, b T) T { if a > b { return a }; return b }
comparable is about compile-time comparability, not runtime

It accepts types where == is guaranteed to work — numerics, strings, pointers, channels, and structs or arrays of those. It excludes slices, maps and funcs. Since Go 1.20 an ordinary interface type also satisfies comparable, even though comparing two interfaces holding slices panics at runtime. So a generic map keyed on a comparable type parameter instantiated with any compiles and can still panic. Constrain more tightly than comparable when you can.

Real uses, from the standard library

go · slices, maps and cmp — the generic packages that shipped
import ("slices"; "maps"; "cmp")

slices.Sort(xs)                                    // xs is []E, E cmp.Ordered
slices.SortFunc(users, func(a, b User) int {
	return cmp.Compare(a.Name, b.Name)             // -1, 0, +1
})
slices.SortStableFunc(rows, func(a, b Row) int {
	return cmp.Or(                                 // Go 1.22: first non-zero
		cmp.Compare(a.Group, b.Group),
		cmp.Compare(b.Score, a.Score),             // descending: args swapped
	)
})
i, found := slices.BinarySearch(sorted, target)
xs = slices.DeleteFunc(xs, func(x T) bool { return x.Expired })

keys := slices.Sorted(maps.Keys(m))                // Go 1.23: iterator → slice
vals := slices.Collect(maps.Values(m))
maps.Copy(dst, src)
maps.DeleteFunc(m, func(k string, v int) bool { return v == 0 })

// cmp.Or is also the clean way to express fallback defaults:
host := cmp.Or(os.Getenv("HOST"), cfg.Host, "localhost")

When generics are the right answer — and when they are not

Use genericsDo not
Containers: stack, set, queue, LRU, ring bufferWhen one interface with one method would do
Algorithms over any element type: sort, map, filter, dedupeTo avoid writing two short concrete functions
Removing any plus a type assertion from a hot pathWhen the behaviour differs per type — that is an interface
A result/option wrapper used across many types“It might be reusable later”
A typed sync.Pool, cache, or channel helperIn a public API where it complicates every call site
The community rule of thumb

Write the concrete version first. When you have written it a third time for a third type, and the bodies are genuinely identical, make it generic. Rob Pike's older advice — "a little copying is better than a little dependency" — survives generics intact: two twenty-line functions are often better than one generic function with a constraint nobody can read.

How the compiler implements them

Go uses GC shape stenciling — a middle path between C++ templates (one copy per type, huge binaries, fast) and Java erasure (one copy for all, boxing everywhere, slower). Instantiations are grouped by GC shape: types with the same size and pointer layout share one compiled body. Sum[int] ┐ Sum[int64] ├─▶ one copy (all 8-byte, no pointers) Sum[float64] ┘ Sum[string] ──▶ another (16 bytes, contains a pointer) Sum[*T] ──▶ shared pointer shape, plus a hidden dictionary argument carrying per-type info at runtime Practical consequences: · binaries grow less than C++ templates, more than pre-1.18 Go · a generic call through the shared pointer shape has a small indirection cost and is harder for the compiler to inline · so generics are not automatically faster than any — they are type-safe, which is the actual reason to use them. Benchmark before claiming a generic rewrite made anything quicker.
Interview follow-up

“Why did Go wait so long for generics, and what did it give up?” The team's stated concern was that generics complicate the language for everyone to benefit a minority of code, so nothing shipped until a design existed that kept the type system simple and compilation fast — type sets, and no specialisation the programmer has to reason about. What was left out is deliberate: no generic methods, no type-parameterised type aliases until very recently, no specialisation, no operator overloading, and no higher-kinded types. If you find yourself fighting those limits, the answer in Go is almost always a plain interface.

L12

Goroutines and channels

A goroutine costs about two kilobytes and starts in microseconds, so Go programs create them freely. Channels are the typed pipes between them. The hard part is not starting concurrent work — it is knowing when it stops.

Goroutines

go · starting one is trivial; stopping one is the design work
go doWork()                          // fire and forget
go func() { doWork(ctx) }()          // closure — captures ctx

// Three things that are true and often forgotten:
//
// 1. main returning kills every goroutine immediately, mid-statement.
// 2. An unrecovered panic in ANY goroutine crashes the whole process.
// 3. There is no goroutine ID, no join handle, no Thread object. If you
//    want to wait, you build the waiting yourself.

var wg sync.WaitGroup
for _, url := range urls {
	wg.Add(1)                        // BEFORE `go` — never inside the goroutine
	go func() {
		defer wg.Done()              // defer, so a panic still decrements
		fetch(url)                   // Go 1.22+: url is per-iteration
	}()
}
wg.Wait()
Every goroutine needs an owner who knows how it ends

Before writing go, answer three questions: when does it exit, who waits for it, and where does its error go? A goroutine blocked forever on a channel nobody will write to is a leak — it holds its stack, its captured variables, and everything they reference, and it never appears in a CPU profile because it uses none. Leaks accumulate silently until the process is killed for memory. go.uber.org/goleak in your tests catches most of them at build time.

Channels

Unbuffered make(chan T) cap 0 A send blocks until a receiver is ready, and vice versa. The two goroutines rendezvous — the handoff itself is the synchronisation. Use when you want a guarantee that the other side took the value. Buffered make(chan T, n) cap n A send blocks only when the buffer is full; a receive blocks only when it is empty. The buffer decouples the two sides — which also means a send succeeding no longer proves anyone received it.
