Directions in a signature document intent and are compiler-checked: func produce(out chan<- T) send-only func consume(in <-chan T) receive-only The state table — memorise this: ┌────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┐ │ │ nil chan │ open │ closed │ ├────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┼──────────────┤ │ send │ blocks forever│ ok or blocks │ PANIC │ │ receive │ blocks forever│ ok or blocks │ zero, ok=false│ │ close │ PANIC │ ok │ PANIC │ └────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┘ Only the sender closes a channel, and only when no further sends will happen. Closing is a broadcast that there is no more data — it is not a way to cancel, and it is not reference counting.
go · sending, receiving, closing, ranging
ch := make(chan int, 3)
ch <- 1                     // send
v := <-ch                   // receive
v, ok := <-ch               // ok is false once the channel is closed AND drained
close(ch)

// range receives until the channel is closed. Without a close, it blocks
// forever — this is the most common deadlock in beginner Go.
for v := range ch { use(v) }

// The producer owns the close:
func produce(n int) <-chan int {
	out := make(chan int)
	go func() {
		defer close(out)            // guarantees the range in the consumer ends
		for i := 0; i < n; i++ {
			out <- i
		}
	}()
	return out                      // returning a receive-only channel is the
}                                   // idiom: callers cannot send or close

select

go · wait on several channels; the workhorse of Go concurrency
select {
case v := <-a:
	use(v)
case b <- x:
	sent()
case <-time.After(time.Second):     // timeout — allocates a timer each call
	timedOut()
case <-ctx.Done():                  // cancellation — put this in EVERY select
	return ctx.Err()
}

// Ready cases are chosen UNIFORMLY AT RANDOM, not in order. That is
// deliberate: it prevents a busy channel from starving a quiet one.

// A default clause makes the select non-blocking:
select {
case ch <- v:
	// sent
default:
	dropped.Inc()      // channel full — shed rather than block. This is how
}                      // metrics and log pipelines avoid stalling a request.

// An empty select blocks forever — occasionally useful in main.
// select {}
time.After in a loop leaks until it fires

Each call allocates a timer that stays in the runtime's heap until its duration elapses — in a tight loop with a one-minute timeout, that is a minute of accumulating timers. In a hot loop use a time.Timer and Reset it, or in Go 1.23+ rely on the new behaviour where unreferenced timers become collectable immediately. For anything with a deadline, prefer context.WithTimeout: it is composable and it cancels the work as well as the wait.

The nil-channel trick

go · disabling a select case by nilling its channel
// A receive on a CLOSED channel succeeds instantly and forever, so a
// closed channel in a select spins the loop at 100% CPU. Setting the
// variable to nil removes that case from consideration.
func merge(a, b <-chan int) <-chan int {
	out := make(chan int)
	go func() {
		defer close(out)
		for a != nil || b != nil {
			select {
			case v, ok := <-a:
				if !ok { a = nil; continue }   // disable this case
				out <- v
			case v, ok := <-b:
				if !ok { b = nil; continue }
				out <- v
			}
		}
	}()
	return out
}

Signalling without data

go · chan struct{} — zero bytes per element
done := make(chan struct{})
go func() {
	defer close(done)       // close broadcasts to EVERY waiter at once
	work()
}()
<-done                      // wait

// A semaphore limiting concurrency to N:
sem := make(chan struct{}, 10)
for _, job := range jobs {
	sem <- struct{}{}                    // acquire (blocks at 10 in flight)
	go func() {
		defer func() { <-sem }()         // release
		process(job)
	}()
}
“Do not communicate by sharing memory; share memory by communicating”

The slogan is often read as "always use channels". The author of the memory model has since been blunter: use whichever is clearer. Channels are for passing ownership of data and for orchestration — pipelines, fan-out, cancellation. A mutex is for protecting a piece of shared state, and for that job it is simpler, faster, and easier to reason about. A counter behind a channel is worse code than a counter behind a sync.Mutex.

Interview follow-up

“How do you stop a goroutine?” You do not — you ask it to stop and it returns. Go has no kill or interrupt, because unwinding another goroutine's stack safely is impossible in general. The mechanism is cooperative: pass a context.Context, and have the goroutine select on ctx.Done() in its loop or pass the context down to whatever call blocks. Any goroutine doing long work without a context and without a done channel cannot be shut down, which is why "does it take a context?" is the first thing to check when reviewing concurrent code.

L13

sync, the memory model and context

Channels are for orchestration. For protecting shared state, the sync package is simpler and faster — and behind both sits the memory model, which defines the only guarantees you are allowed to rely on.

The sync toolkit

TypeUseNote
sync.MutexExclusive access to shared stateZero value ready. Not reentrant — locking twice deadlocks
sync.RWMutexMany readers, occasional writerOnly wins when reads dominate and are slow; otherwise Mutex is faster
sync.WaitGroupWait for N goroutinesAdd before go, Done in a defer
sync.OnceExactly-once initialisationOnceValue/OnceFunc (1.21+) are usually nicer
sync.PoolReuse short-lived allocationsCleared at every GC. Only for profiler-proven allocation pressure
sync.MapTwo narrow cases onlyWrite-once-read-many, or disjoint keys per goroutine. Otherwise use a map + RWMutex
sync/atomicLock-free counters and flagsPrefer the typed atomic.Int64, atomic.Bool, atomic.Pointer[T]
errgroup.GroupWaitGroup + first error + cancellationgolang.org/x/sync. Use this, not a bare WaitGroup
go · the patterns you will write most
type Registry struct {
	mu sync.RWMutex                 // guards everything below it — say so
	m  map[string]*Service
}

func (r *Registry) Get(name string) (*Service, bool) {
	r.mu.RLock()
	defer r.mu.RUnlock()
	s, ok := r.m[name]
	return s, ok
}

func (r *Registry) Put(name string, s *Service) {
	r.mu.Lock()
	defer r.mu.Unlock()
	if r.m == nil { r.m = make(map[string]*Service) }
	r.m[name] = s
}

// Lazy init, done right — and OnceValue removes even the boilerplate:
var loadConfig = sync.OnceValue(func() *Config {
	return mustParse(os.Getenv("CONFIG"))
})

// Typed atomics: no CPU-word juggling, no alignment footguns.
type Stats struct {
	requests atomic.Int64
	healthy  atomic.Bool
	current  atomic.Pointer[Snapshot]     // lock-free config swap
}
s.requests.Add(1)
s.current.Store(newSnapshot)             // readers never block
Copying a struct that contains a lock breaks it silently

A sync.Mutex is a plain struct; copying it copies its state, so the copy is a different lock and the protection evaporates. This happens through value receivers, passing a struct by value, appending it to a slice, or storing it in a map. Always use pointer receivers on lock-holding types and pass them as pointers. go vet's copylocks check catches it — make sure go vet ./... runs in CI.

The memory model, in one page

A data race is two goroutines accessing the same memory, at least one writing, with no synchronisation between them. A racy Go program has no defined behaviour for the racing values — the compiler and CPU may reorder, cache, or tear them. What establishes happens-before — the only orderings you may rely on: 1 Within a single goroutine, program order. 2 go f() happens after everything before the go statement. 3 A send on a channel happens before the corresponding receive completes. 4 A receive from an unbuffered channel happens before the corresponding send completes. (the rendezvous, both ways) 5 close(ch) happens before a receive that returns zero because the channel is closed. 6 The nth Unlock happens before the (n+1)th Lock returns. 7 once.Do(f): f completes before any Do returns. 8 wg.Done() calls happen before wg.Wait() returns. 9 Atomic operations are sequentially consistent with each other. What does NOT synchronise: time.Sleep, a "long enough" delay, printing, a plain bool flag, or the fact that it worked on your laptop. If two goroutines touch a variable and none of rules 3-9 sits between them, it is a race even if you never observe it.
The race detector finds races that happened, not races that exist

go test -race and go build -race instrument memory access and report a race only when two conflicting accesses actually occur during the run — so coverage matters more than cleverness. Run your full test suite, your integration tests, and ideally a staging canary with -race. It costs roughly 2–10× CPU and 5–10× memory, which is why it is a CI and staging tool rather than a production one. A clean -race run is evidence, not proof; a reported race is always real.

context

A Context carries three things across an API boundary: cancellation a Done() channel closed when the work should stop a deadline so every layer below inherits the remaining time request values request ID, trace span, authenticated user Contexts form a tree. Cancelling a parent cancels every descendant, which is how one client disconnect unwinds a whole call graph: context.Background() └── WithTimeout(30s) ← HTTP server, per request ├── WithTimeout(5s) ← database query └── WithTimeout(3s) ← payment API call └── WithCancel() ← retry attempt Cancel the 30s node and all four stop. A child can only ever be shorter-lived than its parent, never longer.
go · the rules, and the code they produce
// 1. First parameter, always named ctx. Never stored in a struct field.
func (s *Service) Charge(ctx context.Context, id string) error {

	// 2. ALWAYS call cancel, even on the success path — defer it
	//    immediately. Not doing so leaks the timer and the child context,
	//    and `go vet` has a check (lostcancel) for exactly this.
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 3*time.Second)
	defer cancel()

	// 3. Pass it down to everything that blocks.
	req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, url, body)
	if err != nil { return err }
	resp, err := s.client.Do(req)
	if err != nil {
		// 4. Distinguish the two causes — they mean different things.
		if errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) { return ErrTimeout }
		if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled)         { return ErrAborted }
		return fmt.Errorf("charge %s: %w", id, err)
	}
	defer resp.Body.Close()
	return nil
}

// 5. In your own loops, check it.
func (w *Worker) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return ctx.Err()
		case job := <-w.jobs:
			w.handle(ctx, job)
		}
	}
}

// 6. Values: use an unexported key type so nobody can collide with you.
type ctxKey struct{}
func WithRequestID(ctx context.Context, id string) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, ctxKey{}, id)
}
func RequestID(ctx context.Context) string {
	id, _ := ctx.Value(ctxKey{}).(string)
	return id
}
context.Value is not a parameter-passing mechanism

It is untyped, invisible in signatures, and unverifiable at compile time — a function's real dependencies become impossible to read. Restrict it to values that are genuinely request-scoped and cross-cutting: request ID, trace span, auth principal, locale. Anything the function needs in order to do its job is a parameter or a struct field. A handler that pulls a database handle out of a context is the canonical abuse.

Cancellation without losing the values

Go 1.21 added context.WithoutCancel(ctx) — it keeps the values and drops the cancellation, which is exactly what you want when a background cleanup, audit write, or metric flush must finish after the request is gone. Before that, people copied values into a fresh Background() by hand and lost the trace. Also useful: context.AfterFunc (1.21) to run a callback on cancellation, and WithDeadlineCause/WithTimeoutCause (1.21) so context.Cause(ctx) tells you why something was cancelled rather than just that it was.

Interview follow-up

“Mutex or channel?” Ask what you are protecting. If the answer is a piece of state — a map, a counter, a cache — use a mutex: it is one lock, one critical section, and trivially reviewable. If the answer is a flow of work between stages, or ownership of a value moving from one goroutine to another, use a channel. The failure mode of picking wrong is recognisable: a channel wrapping a single variable turns a two-line critical section into a goroutine, a request type and a reply channel, and a mutex used for coordination turns into condition variables and polling.

L14

Concurrency patterns

Six shapes cover almost all concurrent Go in production. Each one is a small amount of code — what matters is the failure handling and the exit path, which is where hand-rolled versions go wrong.

1 · Bounded parallelism with errgroup

go · the single most useful concurrency type in Go
import "golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"

func FetchAll(ctx context.Context, urls []string) ([]Result, error) {
	g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)   // ctx is cancelled on the first error
	g.SetLimit(10)                        // at most 10 in flight — ALWAYS set this

	results := make([]Result, len(urls))  // index per goroutine: no lock needed
	for i, u := range urls {
		g.Go(func() error {
			r, err := fetch(ctx, u)
			if err != nil {
				return fmt.Errorf("fetch %s: %w", u, err)
			}
			results[i] = r
			return nil
		})
	}
	if err := g.Wait(); err != nil {      // waits for all, returns the FIRST error
		return nil, err
	}
	return results, nil
}
Why writing to results[i] needs no mutex

Each goroutine writes to a distinct element of a pre-sized slice, so no two ever touch the same memory, and g.Wait() establishes happens-before for every read afterwards. This is the cleanest way to collect parallel results — no channel, no lock, order preserved. It is only safe because the slice is allocated up front and never grown; append from multiple goroutines is a race.

Unbounded fan-out is a self-inflicted outage

for _, x := range items { go work(x) } over a 100,000-row result set starts 100,000 goroutines, opens 100,000 connections, and takes down the dependency you are calling rather than your own process. Always bound it — g.SetLimit(n), a buffered-channel semaphore, or a worker pool — and pick n from the downstream system's capacity, not your CPU count.

2 · Worker pool

go · fixed workers, a job channel, a result channel
func Pool(ctx context.Context, jobs <-chan Job, workers int) <-chan Result {
	out := make(chan Result)

	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	for i := 0; i < workers; i++ {
		wg.Add(1)
		go func() {
			defer wg.Done()
			for job := range jobs {              // ends when jobs is closed
				select {
				case out <- process(ctx, job):
				case <-ctx.Done():               // do not block forever on a
					return                       // consumer that went away
				}
			}
		}()
	}

	go func() { wg.Wait(); close(out) }()        // close ONCE, after all workers
	return out
}
Pool vs errgroup — pick by lifetime, not by taste errgroup a finite batch, known now, all results needed together. Goroutine per item, capped. Exits when the batch is done. → fan out 200 API calls for one request worker pool an open-ended stream, running for the life of the process. Fixed goroutines, work arrives forever. → a queue consumer, an ingestion pipeline Using errgroup for a stream means unbounded goroutine churn. Using a pool for a batch means writing the wait and the error plumbing yourself.

3 · Pipeline

go · stages connected by channels, each closing its own output
func gen(ctx context.Context, ids []string) <-chan string {
	out := make(chan string)
	go func() {
		defer close(out)
		for _, id := range ids {
			select {
			case out <- id:
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return              // downstream gave up — stop producing
			}
		}
	}()
	return out
}

func enrich(ctx context.Context, in <-chan string) <-chan Record {
	out := make(chan Record)
	go func() {
		defer close(out)
		for id := range in {
			r, err := load(ctx, id)
			if err != nil { continue }
			select {
			case out <- r:
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return
			}
		}
	}()
	return out
}

// Composition reads like the data flow:
for rec := range enrich(ctx, gen(ctx, ids)) { save(rec) }
Every stage must be cancellable or the pipeline leaks

If a downstream stage stops reading — an error, a caller timeout, a break out of the range loop — every upstream goroutine blocks forever on its send and is never collected. The select with ctx.Done() on every send is not optional decoration; it is the only thing that lets the pipeline unwind. Test this deliberately: cancel the context halfway and assert with goleak that no goroutines remain.

4 · Fan-out, fan-in

go · N consumers of one channel, merged back into one
func merge[T any](cs ...<-chan T) <-chan T {
	out := make(chan T)
	var wg sync.WaitGroup
	wg.Add(len(cs))
	for _, c := range cs {
		go func() {
			defer wg.Done()
			for v := range c { out <- v }
		}()
	}
	go func() { wg.Wait(); close(out) }()
	return out
}

// Fan-out is just several goroutines ranging over the SAME channel —
// Go distributes values among them automatically, one value to one
// receiver. No round-robin logic needed.
work := gen(ctx, ids)
merged := merge(stage(ctx, work), stage(ctx, work), stage(ctx, work))

5 · singleflight — collapse duplicate work

go · the cache-stampede fix, in six lines
import "golang.org/x/sync/singleflight"

type Loader struct {
	g     singleflight.Group
	cache *Cache
	db    *DB
}

func (l *Loader) Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (*User, error) {
	if u, ok := l.cache.Get(id); ok { return u, nil }

	// 500 concurrent misses for the same key issue ONE database query.
	// The other 499 block and receive that same result.
	v, err, _ := l.g.Do(id, func() (any, error) {
		u, err := l.db.LoadUser(ctx, id)
		if err != nil { return nil, err }
		l.cache.Set(id, u)
		return u, nil
	})
	if err != nil { return nil, err }
	return v.(*User), nil
}
Two sharp edges in singleflight

First, the shared context: the goroutine that actually runs the function uses its context, so if that caller cancels, every waiter fails too — use a context detached from any single request, or DoChan with your own select. Second, a failure is shared: one error is returned to all 500 waiters, so a transient blip fails every one of them rather than 1-in-500. Both are usually acceptable, but decide rather than discover.

6 · Graceful shutdown

go · the shape every Go service should have in main
func run() error {
	// NotifyContext cancels ctx when SIGINT/SIGTERM arrives.
	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(),
		os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	srv := &http.Server{Addr: ":8080", Handler: mux}

	g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)

	g.Go(func() error {
		if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})

	g.Go(func() error { return worker.Run(gctx) })   // background consumers

	g.Go(func() error {
		<-gctx.Done()                                // signal, or any error
		// Fresh context: gctx is already cancelled, and Shutdown needs
		// time to drain. Keep this shorter than the platform's grace period.
		shutCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
		defer cancel()
		return srv.Shutdown(shutCtx)                 // stop accepting, drain in-flight
	})

	return g.Wait()
}

Finding leaks

goroutine leak, diagnosed
$ curl -s localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1 | head -20
goroutine profile: total 48213          # 48k — something is not exiting

47980 @ 0x43e2f6 0x40d8dc 0x40d4bb 0x7f2a11
#	0x7f2a10	main.(*Fetcher).worker+0x90	/app/fetch.go:112
#	                                            chan send, nobody receiving

   233 @ 0x43e2f6 0x46d1a5 0x7c4b22
#	0x7c4b21	net/http.(*conn).serve+0x361

$ # In tests, catch it before it ships:
$ go test -run TestPipeline ./...
    leaks_test.go:14: found unexpected goroutines:
    [Goroutine 47 in state chan send, with main.gen.func1 on top of the stack]
go · goleak in TestMain covers the whole package
import "go.uber.org/goleak"

func TestMain(m *testing.M) {
	goleak.VerifyTestMain(m,
		// Known long-lived goroutines you do not control:
		goleak.IgnoreTopFunction("go.opencensus.io/stats/view.(*worker).start"),
	)
}
Interview follow-up

“How would you limit concurrency when calling a slow downstream service?” Name the constraint first: the limit belongs to the dependency, not to your machine, so it comes from its documented rate limit or connection pool, not from runtime.NumCPU(). Then errgroup with SetLimit for a request-scoped batch, or a worker pool with a fixed size for a stream. Add a per-call timeout via context so one hung request cannot occupy a slot forever, and a circuit breaker so you stop sending when it is already failing. The answer that stands out mentions what happens to the work you cannot start — queued, shed, or backpressured — because that is the decision the code is really making.

R01

From source to binary

Go compiles fast because the design says it must. Understanding the pipeline explains why builds are quick, why the binary is large, why there is no dynamic linking by default, and what the compiler is actually deciding on your behalf.

01
Parsesource → AST
02
Type checktypes, constants, generics
03
IR & inlineescape analysis here
04
SSA~40 optimisation passes
05
Codegenmachine instructions
06
Linkone static binary

Why it is fast

1 No header files, no preprocessor. A package's export data is compiled once and read as a compact binary blob, not re-parsed from source for every importer as C++ headers are. 2 The import graph is a DAG, so packages compile in parallel and each exactly once. Cycles are illegal, which is partly why. 3 Export data is transitively closed. Compiling package A needs only B's export data — not C's, even though B imports C. The compiler never walks the whole tree. 4 The build cache keys every action on the hash of its inputs (source, flags, toolchain version, dependencies' export data). An unchanged package is never recompiled. 5 The language avoids expensive analysis — no templates needing instantiation-time type checking, no whole-program type inference. The trade: optimisation is deliberately less aggressive than LLVM's. Go picks a 10-second build over a 3% faster binary, on the theory that developer iteration speed compounds and 3% rarely does.
the cache is why the second build is instant
$ go build ./...          # cold
12.4s

$ go build ./...          # nothing changed
0.2s

$ go build -x ./... 2>&1 | head -3    # what it actually runs
mkdir -p $WORK/b001/
cat >/tmp/go-build/b001/importcfg << 'EOF'
packagefile fmt=/Users/x/Library/Caches/go-build/4c/4c9f...-d

$ go clean -cache          # nuke it (rarely the right fix)
$ go build -a ./...        # force rebuild of everything
$ go env GOCACHE GOMODCACHE
/Users/x/Library/Caches/go-build
/Users/x/go/pkg/mod

Seeing what the compiler decided

FlagShows
-gcflags='-m'Escape analysis and inlining decisions. -m -m for the reasoning
-gcflags='-S'The generated assembly
-gcflags='-l'Disable inlining (to read a profile honestly)
-gcflags='-N -l'No optimisation, no inlining — required for a usable debugger
-gcflags='-d=ssa/check_bce/debug=1'Which bounds checks were not eliminated
-ldflags='-s -w'Strip the symbol table and DWARF — smaller binary, no stack symbols
-ldflags='-X main.version=1.2.3'Inject a string variable at link time
-trimpathRemove local filesystem paths — needed for reproducible builds
-race / -msan / -asanInstrumented builds
-coverCoverage instrumentation, now available for whole binaries
reading -m output
$ go build -gcflags='-m' ./internal/order 2>&1 | head
./order.go:22:6: can inline (*Order).Total          # inlined: cheap, no call
./order.go:31:6: cannot inline process: function too complex: cost 213
./order.go:14:13: &Order{...} escapes to heap         # heap allocation
./order.go:19:17: buf does not escape                 # stack — free
./order.go:44:21: leaking param: o to result ~r0 level=0

# the inline budget is 80 nodes. "too complex" means the function body
# exceeded it — split it and the hot path can be inlined.

The linker, and why the binary is big

A "hello world" binary is around 1.5-2 MB. It contains: your code ~a few KB the standard library you used ~hundreds of KB the runtime scheduler, GC, allocator, channel and map implementations type metadata needed by reflect, interfaces, and the GC's pointer maps DWARF debug info ~25% of the file the symbol table, pclntab for stack traces and panics Making it smaller, in order of value: -ldflags="-s -w" −25-30% but you lose readable panics -trimpath tiny, and gains reproducibility avoid reflect-heavy deps the linker's dead-code elimination gives up when reflection may reach anything UPX compression −60%, but slower start and AV false positives Usually the right answer is: do not. A 12 MB binary in a scratch container is a 12 MB image. That is already smaller than almost any alternative runtime.

Cross-compilation is a two-variable problem

no toolchain to install
$ GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 go build -o bin/app-linux-amd64 .
$ GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 go build -o bin/app-linux-arm64 .
$ GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64 go build -o bin/app-darwin-arm64 .
$ GOOS=windows GOARCH=amd64 go build -o bin/app.exe .

$ go tool dist list | head -5          # ~45 supported pairs
aix/ppc64
android/386
darwin/amd64
darwin/arm64
linux/amd64

$ GOAMD64=v3 go build .   # assume AVX2 etc. — faster, needs newer CPUs
CGO is what breaks cross-compilation

With CGO_ENABLED=1 (the default when a C toolchain is present) the build needs a C cross-compiler for the target, and the result links against the host's libc — so a binary built on a glibc machine will not run on Alpine, which uses musl. Setting CGO_ENABLED=0 gives a fully static binary that runs anywhere, at the cost of losing cgo-dependent packages. The two that bite in practice are os/user and DNS resolution: pure-Go Go resolves DNS itself, which behaves subtly differently from the system resolver for /etc/nsswitch.conf setups. For a container image, CGO_ENABLED=0 is nearly always right.

Build tags

go · conditional compilation, by filename and by directive
//go:build linux && amd64 && !race

package sys

// The modern //go:build form (Go 1.17+) replaced // +build. gofmt keeps
// the old line in sync if both are present; new files need only the new one.

// Filename suffixes are implicit tags — no directive needed:
//   sys_linux.go        GOOS=linux
//   sys_darwin_arm64.go GOOS=darwin GOARCH=arm64
//   sys_test.go         test files only

// Custom tags gate optional features:
//go:build integration
// → go test -tags=integration ./...

// Other directives worth knowing:
//go:generate mockgen -source=store.go -destination=mock_store.go
//go:embed templates/*.html          // compile files INTO the binary
//go:noinline                        // benchmarking aid
//go:linkname                        // unsafe access to runtime internals
go · embed puts assets in the binary — no files to ship
import "embed"

//go:embed templates/*.html
var templateFS embed.FS

//go:embed migrations
var migrationsFS embed.FS

//go:embed VERSION
var version string          // a single file can embed straight into a string

var tmpl = template.Must(template.ParseFS(templateFS, "templates/*.html"))
Interview follow-up

“Why does a Go binary not need a runtime installed?” Because the runtime is in the binary. The scheduler, garbage collector, allocator and all the type metadata are linked statically alongside your code, so there is no JVM, no interpreter, and with CGO_ENABLED=0 not even a libc dependency. That is why the canonical Go container image is FROM scratch with one file copied in, and why deployment is scp plus ./app. The cost is a multi-megabyte binary and no way to patch the runtime without rebuilding — a trade that strongly favours operations.

R02

Memory, the stack, and escape analysis

Go has pointers but no malloc and no free. The compiler decides, per allocation, whether a value lives on the stack (free) or the heap (collected later). Reading that decision is the highest-leverage optimisation skill in the language.

Stack or heap — the compiler chooses

Stack Heap ───────────────────────── ────────────────────────── per goroutine shared by the process allocation = bump a pointer allocation = size class lookup, free = pop the frame possibly a new span from the OS zero GC cost the GC must trace and free it starts at 2 KB, grows grows to whatever you allocate by copying fragmentation is possible The rule: a value goes on the heap if the compiler cannot prove its lifetime ends when the function returns. That proof failing is called escaping, and it is a static, conservative analysis — when in doubt, it heaps.
go build -gcflags='-m'
$ go build -gcflags='-m' ./...
./main.go:12:13: &User{...} escapes to heap
./main.go:12:13:   ... from ~r0 (return) at ./main.go:12:2
./main.go:19:17: buf does not escape
./main.go:24:21: leaking param: s
./main.go:31:9:  make([]byte, n) escapes to heap    # n is not constant
./main.go:33:9:  make([]byte, 64) does not escape   # constant, small → stack
./main.go:41:26: ... argument does not escape
./main.go:41:27: id escapes to heap                  # passed to an interface

The six things that make a value escape

go · each of these is a heap allocation you can often avoid
// 1. Returning a pointer to a local.
func New() *User { return &User{} }              // escapes — and that's fine

// 2. Storing a pointer somewhere that outlives the call.
func (c *Cache) Put(u *User) { c.m[u.ID] = u }   // u escapes through c

// 3. Passing to an interface whose method set is not statically known.
fmt.Println(x)        // x escapes: Println takes ...any, and the compiler
                      // cannot see what the implementation does with it
// This is why fmt.Sprintf in a hot loop allocates even for an int.

// 4. Capturing by a closure that outlives the frame.
func handler() func() { n := 0; return func() { n++ } }   // n escapes

// 5. A size the compiler cannot bound at compile time.
buf := make([]byte, n)        // escapes: n is a variable
buf := make([]byte, 4096)     // stack, if it fits the frame budget

// 6. Slices/maps that grow beyond what the frame can hold, or anything
//    over ~64 KB (the implicit maximum for a stack-allocated object).
var big [100000]int           // too large for a stack frame → heap
“Avoid pointers to avoid allocations” is backwards

A pointer does not cause a heap allocation; escaping does. p := &User{}; use(p) where use is inlined and does not retain p stays entirely on the stack. Conversely, a large struct passed by value into an interface is copied to the heap. Do not guess from the syntax — read -gcflags='-m', which tells you exactly what the compiler concluded and why.

Reducing allocations, in order of payoff

ChangeTypical effect
Preallocate with a known capacityRemoves every growslice; usually the largest single win
strconv instead of fmt.SprintfRemoves boxing and reflection — often 5-10× on that line
strings.Builder instead of +=O(n) instead of O(n²)
Return a struct, not *struct, for small valuesKeeps it on the stack when the caller does not retain it
Reuse buffers via sync.PoolBig for large, short-lived buffers; noise for small ones
Pass []byte instead of converting to stringEach conversion copies
Avoid interface boxing in hot loopsEvery non-pointer value stored in an any allocates
The compiler optimises two specific string/byte conversions

m[string(byteSlice)] as a map lookup does not allocate — the compiler recognises the pattern and hashes the bytes directly. So does for i, r := range string(byteSlice). Comparisons like string(b) == "x" are also allocation-free. Outside those recognised forms, every string(b) and []byte(s) copies, which is why high-throughput parsers stay in []byte end to end.

sync.Pool, and when it earns its complexity

go · reuse large buffers across requests
var bufPool = sync.Pool{
	New: func() any { return new(bytes.Buffer) },
}

func render(w io.Writer, data any) error {
	buf := bufPool.Get().(*bytes.Buffer)
	defer func() {
		// Do NOT pool a buffer that grew enormous — you would cache the
		// peak forever. Drop oversized ones on the floor.
		if buf.Cap() < 64<<10 {
			buf.Reset()               // reset BEFORE putting it back
			bufPool.Put(buf)
		}
	}()

	if err := tmpl.Execute(buf, data); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	_, err := w.Write(buf.Bytes())
	return err
}
A pool is a cache, not an allocator — and it is emptied by the GC

Objects in a sync.Pool are dropped at every garbage collection, so a pool does not guarantee reuse and is useless for a low-traffic path. It also has real failure modes: forgetting to Reset leaks the previous request's data into the next one (a genuine security bug when the buffer held another user's response), and pooling variable-size buffers pins the largest one ever needed. Use it only when a heap profile shows a specific large, frequent, short-lived allocation — and measure afterwards.

Reading a heap profile

go tool pprof
$ go tool pprof -alloc_space http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap
(pprof) top10
Showing nodes accounting for 41.2GB, 88.3% of 46.6GB total
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
   18.1GB 38.8% 38.8%     18.1GB 38.8%  runtime.growslice
                                            ↑ missing preallocation
    9.4GB 20.2% 59.0%     11.8GB 25.3%  encoding/json.Marshal
    6.2GB 13.3% 72.3%      6.2GB 13.3%  fmt.Sprintf
    4.1GB  8.8% 81.1%      4.1GB  8.8%  runtime.makemap_small

(pprof) list growslice        # source view, line by line
(pprof) web                   # the call graph in a browser

# FOUR different heap views — know which question you are asking:
#   -inuse_space  bytes live NOW          → find a leak
#   -inuse_objects objects live NOW       → find pointer-heavy structures
#   -alloc_space  bytes ever allocated    → find GC pressure   ← usually this
#   -alloc_objects allocations ever made  → find allocation COUNT hotspots

unsafe, briefly

go · what it is for, and the rule that governs it
import "unsafe"

unsafe.Sizeof(x)      // compile-time size in bytes — useful and harmless
unsafe.Alignof(x)
unsafe.Offsetof(s.F)

// Go 1.20+ gave the zero-copy conversions a supported spelling:
func b2s(b []byte) string { return unsafe.String(&b[0], len(b)) }
func s2b(s string) []byte { return unsafe.Slice(unsafe.StringData(s), len(s)) }

// The rule: the resulting string MUST be treated as immutable. Mutating
// the []byte afterwards mutates a "string", which the runtime, the map
// implementation and the compiler all assume cannot happen. The result
// is memory corruption, not a panic.
The unsafe.Pointer rules are not guidelines

The unsafe package documents six legal conversion patterns; anything outside them is undefined, and "it worked" is not evidence, because the garbage collector is precise and moves goroutine stacks. The most common real bug is holding a uintptr across a statement — it is an integer, so the GC does not see it as a reference and may free or relocate what it pointed to. Run go vet (which has an unsafeptr check) and GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 on anything that uses it.

Interview follow-up

“How do you know whether something is allocated on the stack or the heap?” You ask the compiler: go build -gcflags='-m', and -m -m for the chain of reasoning. Add that it is decided statically and conservatively, that it has nothing to do with new versus a literal — Go has no such distinction — and that the practical workflow is to find allocation hotspots with -alloc_space in pprof or -benchmem in a benchmark first, then read -m for those specific lines. Guessing from syntax is how people spend a day removing pointers and make the program slower.

R03

The scheduler

Go multiplexes many goroutines onto few OS threads. The machinery has three letters — G, M and P — and once you can name them, every scheduler question, GOMAXPROCS decision and stuck-goroutine stack trace becomes readable.

G, M, P

G goroutine a stack (starts at 2 KB), a program counter, and status. Cheap: millions are routine. M machine an OS thread. The only thing that actually executes code. Creating one is a syscall and costs ~8-64 KB of kernel stack. P processor a scheduling context holding a local run queue and an allocator cache. A goroutine needs a P to run. len(P) == GOMAXPROCS — this is what that knob sets. ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ global run queue [G][G][G] (checked 1 in 61 ticks) │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │ │ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ ┌────▼────┐ │ P0 │ │ P1 │ │ P2 │ │ runnext:G│ │ runnext:G│ │ runnext:-│ │ local: │ │ local: │ │ local: │ │ [G][G][G]│ │ [G] │ │ empty │──┐ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ │ │ │ │ │ work ┌────▼────┐ ┌─────▼───┐ ┌──────▼──┐ │ stealing │ M0 │ │ M1 │ │ M2 │◀────┘ │ running │ │ running │ │ steals │ takes HALF of │ G │ │ G │ │ from P0│ a victim's queue └─────────┘ └─────────┘ └─────────┘ Each P's local queue holds 256 goroutines plus one runnext slot — a fast path so a goroutine that just woke another runs it immediately (excellent for ping-pong channel patterns and cache locality). Overflow spills half the local queue to the global queue.

The scheduling loop

An M looking for work does, in order: 1 runnext on its P (the just-woken goroutine) 2 the P's local run queue (no lock needed) 3 the global queue (takes a lock) 4 the network poller (epoll/kqueue: any I/O that completed?) 5 steal half of a random P's local queue (4 attempts) 6 sleep Fairness: every 61st scheduling decision checks the global queue first, so goroutines there cannot starve behind a busy local queue.

What happens on a blocking call

The goroutine blocks on…What the runtime does
Channel, mutex, time.SleepG is parked and taken off the M. The M keeps its P and runs another G. Cost: a few hundred nanoseconds, no kernel involvement
Network I/OThe fd is registered with epoll/kqueue and the G parks. The M runs on. When data arrives the netpoller makes the G runnable again. This is why Go does not need async/await
A blocking syscall (file read, DNS via cgo)The M blocks in the kernel. After ~20 µs sysmon detaches the P and hands it to another M, so the other goroutines keep running. The blocked M returns later and parks
cgo callSame as a syscall — the P is released. Long cgo calls therefore cost a thread, which is why cgo-heavy programs grow thread counts
runtime.LockOSThreadThe G is pinned to that M for its lifetime. Needed for OpenGL and some C libraries with thread-local state
This is why a goroutine-per-connection scales

In a thread-per-connection server, 50,000 connections means 50,000 OS threads: gigabytes of stack and punishing context-switch cost. In Go it means 50,000 goroutines — about 100 MB of stack — multiplexed over GOMAXPROCS threads, with all the blocking I/O hidden behind epoll by the runtime. You write straight-line blocking code and get event-loop performance, which is the single biggest reason Go took over network services.

Preemption

Before Go 1.14 — cooperative only. A goroutine yielded at function calls, channel operations, and allocations. A tight loop with none of those never yielded: for {} // pinned a P forever for i := 0; i < 1e12; i++ {} // starved everything on that P Worse, the GC's stop-the-world could not start until every goroutine reached a safe point — so one such loop froze the whole program. Since Go 1.14 — asynchronous preemption. sysmon, a dedicated runtime thread that runs without a P, watches for a G running longer than 10 ms and sends the thread a SIGURG. The signal handler parks the goroutine at an asynchronous safe point. Consequences you can observe: · tight loops no longer starve other goroutines or block GC · Go programs show SIGURG traffic under strace — that is normal, not a bug · a debugger stepping through Go code sees these signals sysmon also: retakes Ps from long syscalls, forces a GC every 2 minutes if none has run, and scavenges unused memory back to the OS.

GOMAXPROCS

go · the container problem, and the fix
// GOMAXPROCS defaults to runtime.NumCPU(), which reads the number of CPUs
// visible to the process — NOT the cgroup CPU limit. In Kubernetes:
//
//   node has 64 cores, pod has `limits.cpu: 2`
//   → NumCPU() = 64  → GOMAXPROCS = 64  → 64 Ps for 2 cores' worth of quota
//
// Result: heavy context switching, GC workers oversubscribed, and CFS
// throttling — the pod is stopped hard at the end of every 100ms period.
// Latency p99 gets dramatically worse while CPU usage looks low.

import _ "go.uber.org/automaxprocs"   // reads the cgroup quota, sets it right

// Or set it explicitly from the limit you gave the pod:
//   env: [{name: GOMAXPROCS, value: "2"}]
// Go 1.25 makes the runtime cgroup-aware by default, but be explicit until
// every service in your fleet is on it.
This is the most common Go performance bug in Kubernetes

Symptoms: p99 latency several times p50, CPU throttling visible in container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total, and a goroutine profile showing far more runnable goroutines than the pod has cores. It is invisible on a developer laptop, where NumCPU() and the real core count agree. Check GOMAXPROCS before you profile anything else in a containerised Go service.

Reading a stuck goroutine dump

SIGQUIT, or /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2
goroutine 42 [chan send, 7 minutes]:
main.(*Pipeline).stage(0xc000112000, 0xc0001a2000)
	/app/pipe.go:88 +0x1a5
created by main.Run in goroutine 1
	/app/pipe.go:41 +0xd8

# The bracket is the state, and the duration is how long it has been
# there. These are the states you will see:

  running            on a CPU right now
  runnable           ready, waiting for a P  → many of these = starvation
  syscall            in the kernel
  IO wait            parked in the netpoller — normal for idle servers
  chan send/receive  blocked on a channel    → the classic leak
  select             blocked in a select
  semacquire         waiting on a mutex/WaitGroup → lock contention
  sync.Cond.Wait     waiting on a condition variable
  GC assist wait     the allocator is helping the GC → allocation pressure

# Send SIGQUIT to dump every goroutine and exit — the last resort on a
# hung process with no pprof endpoint:
$ kill -QUIT $(pidof app)
$ GOTRACEBACK=all ./app    # include runtime frames in the dump
Interview follow-up

“Why are goroutines cheaper than threads?” Three reasons, in order of weight. The stack: a goroutine starts at 2 KB and grows by copying, while an OS thread reserves a fixed 1–8 MB. The switch: moving between goroutines is a few register saves entirely in user space — no kernel transition, no TLB effects — roughly tens of nanoseconds against one to two microseconds. And the blocking model: the runtime turns blocking I/O into epoll registrations so a blocked goroutine costs nothing but its stack, whereas a blocked thread costs a thread. The honest caveat is that goroutines are not free — a leaked one holds its stack and everything it references forever.

R04

The garbage collector

Go's collector is concurrent, non-generational, non-compacting and tuned single-mindedly for short pauses. It trades throughput and memory for predictable latency — and knowing that trade tells you which knobs exist and which problems they cannot solve.

Tri-colour mark and sweep, running beside your code

Every object is conceptually one of three colours: white not yet proven reachable → swept (freed) at the end grey reachable, children not yet scanned → the work queue black reachable, children all scanned → done 1 Mark setup STOP THE WORLD (~10-100 µs) enable the write barrier, scan globals and the roots of every goroutine stack 2 Marking concurrent — GC workers use ~25% of GOMAXPROCS while your code keeps running. Drain the grey queue, colouring as it goes. If allocation outpaces marking, the allocating goroutine is drafted into GC assist — you pay for your own garbage, which is the backpressure. 3 Mark termination STOP THE WORLD (~10-100 µs) finish, disable the write barrier 4 Sweeping concurrent and lazy — spans are reclaimed as they are needed for allocation, not all at once Total STW per cycle: well under 1 ms, and it does not grow with heap size, because the marking that does scale is concurrent.
Why the write barrier exists

While marking runs concurrently, your code keeps mutating pointers — and it could hide a white object behind a black one, which the collector would then never revisit and would wrongly free. Go uses a hybrid Dijkstra/Yuasa write barrier that shades objects on pointer writes, preserving the invariant that no black object points to a white one. The cost is a few instructions on every pointer write during a GC cycle, which is why heavily pointer-mutating workloads slow slightly while a cycle is in progress.

What Go's collector deliberately does not do

Not doneConsequence
Not generationalEvery cycle scans the whole live heap. Go's bet is that escape analysis already keeps short-lived objects off the heap, so a nursery would buy less than it costs
Not compactingPointers never move, which makes cgo and unsafe workable — but the heap can fragment, and freed memory returns to the OS slowly
Not tunable per-generationThere are exactly two knobs: GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT. That is the whole interface, on purpose

Pacing: GOGC and GOMEMLIMIT

GOGC (default 100) sets the heap growth target: next GC when heap == live × (1 + GOGC/100) live heap 100 MB, GOGC=100 → collect at 200 MB live heap 100 MB, GOGC=200 → collect at 300 MB (fewer, bigger GCs) live heap 100 MB, GOGC=50 → collect at 150 MB (more, smaller) GOGC=off → never collect (only for batch jobs) GOMEMLIMIT (Go 1.19+) is a soft limit on total runtime memory. As the heap approaches it, the GC runs more aggressively — continuously if it has to — rather than exceeding it. GOMEMLIMIT=3GiB with a 4 GiB container limit The combination that works in production: GOGC=off + GOMEMLIMIT=<~80% of the container limit> The GC then runs only when memory pressure demands it: no wasted cycles while there is headroom, and no OOM kill when there is not. Leave ~20% for stacks, the allocator's own bookkeeping, and any cgo.
GOMEMLIMIT is soft, and that is not a bug

If the live heap genuinely exceeds the limit, the runtime cannot free memory that is still reachable — so it will exceed the limit rather than deadlock, while burning CPU in a near-continuous GC. That death spiral (high CPU, high memory, slow requests) is the signature of a real leak or of a limit set below the true working set. GOMEMLIMIT protects you from garbage accumulating past the container limit; it cannot protect you from live data doing so.

Watching it work

GODEBUG=gctrace=1
$ GODEBUG=gctrace=1 ./app
gc 14 @12.418s 3%: 0.082+41+0.11 ms clock, 0.65+12/40/0+0.92 ms cpu,
   412->418->209 MB, 425 MB goal, 0 MB stacks, 0 MB globals, 8 P

  14        cycle number
  @12.418s  time since start
  3%        cumulative % of CPU spent in GC since start  ← the headline
  0.082+41+0.11 ms   STW sweep-termination + concurrent mark + STW mark-term
                     ↑ the two STW numbers are your pause times
  412->418->209 MB   heap at start -> at end -> LIVE after collection
  425 MB goal        the pacer's target for this cycle
  8 P                GOMAXPROCS

# Healthy: GC CPU under ~5%, STW under 1 ms, and the live figure (209)
# flat over time. A live figure that climbs cycle after cycle is a leak.

$ GODEBUG=gctrace=1,scheddetail=1,schedtrace=1000 ./app   # plus scheduler
go · reading the same numbers from inside the program
import "runtime/metrics"

// runtime/metrics is the modern API — cheaper and more detailed than
// runtime.ReadMemStats, which stops the world briefly.
samples := []metrics.Sample{
	{Name: "/gc/heap/live:bytes"},
	{Name: "/gc/cycles/total:gc-cycles"},
	{Name: "/gc/pauses:seconds"},              // a histogram
	{Name: "/memory/classes/heap/objects:bytes"},
	{Name: "/memory/classes/total:bytes"},     // compare against GOMEMLIMIT
	{Name: "/sched/goroutines:goroutines"},
	{Name: "/sched/latencies:seconds"},        // time runnable→running
}
metrics.Read(samples)

// Export these to Prometheus. The four that matter on a dashboard:
//   goroutine count            — climbing means a leak
//   live heap                  — climbing means a leak
//   GC CPU fraction            — over ~10% means allocation pressure
//   scheduler latency p99      — high means GOMAXPROCS/CPU starvation

Reducing GC cost

LeverWhy it works
Allocate lessThe only fix that is always right. Preallocate, avoid Sprintf, reuse buffers (R02)
Fewer pointers per objectMarking cost is driven by pointers to trace, not bytes. []User beats []*User; an index beats a pointer; struct fields beat maps of pointers
GOMEMLIMIT + GOGC=offStops collecting while there is free memory — often a large CPU win for a service with a fixed container size
Raise GOGCTrades memory for fewer cycles. GOGC=400 can halve GC CPU if you have the RAM
sync.PoolFor proven large, frequent, short-lived buffers only
debug.SetGCPercentSame as GOGC, at runtime
runtime.GC()Almost never. Legitimate uses: before a benchmark, and after loading a large one-off dataset
A map[string]*Big with ten million entries is a GC problem

Each entry is at least two pointers the collector must trace every cycle, so mark time grows linearly with the number of pointers in the live heap — not with bytes. Large pointer-free structures are nearly free to collect: a []byte of 1 GB costs one object to mark. This is why high-cardinality in-process caches are a recurring cause of GC CPU in Go, and why the usual fixes are an off-heap or pointer-free representation, storing values rather than pointers, or moving the cache out of the process entirely.

Interview follow-up

“Go's GC has sub-millisecond pauses. What does it cost?” Throughput and memory. Because it is concurrent, GC workers consume roughly a quarter of available CPU while a cycle runs, and heavy allocators additionally pay GC assist time on their own allocation path. Because it is non-generational and non-compacting, every cycle scans the entire live heap and freed memory can fragment and returns to the OS slowly. And because GOGC targets heap growth, the steady-state footprint is roughly twice the live set. Those are exactly the right trades for a request-serving service with an SLO, and exactly the wrong ones for a batch job that would rather have throughput — which is what GOGC=off is for.

R05

Channels and select under the hood

A channel is one struct with a lock, a ring buffer and two wait queues. Knowing its layout explains the performance characteristics, the direct handoff optimisation, and why an unbuffered channel is not simply a buffered one with size zero.

The hchan struct

make(chan T, n) allocates one hchan on the heap: ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ qcount elements currently in the buffer │ │ dataqsiz buffer capacity (n) │ │ buf pointer to a ring buffer of n×sizeof(T)│ │ elemsize sizeof(T) │ │ closed 0 or 1 │ │ sendx next write index into the ring │ │ recvx next read index │ │ recvq queue of goroutines blocked receiving │ │ sendq queue of goroutines blocked sending │ │ lock a mutex — every operation takes it │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Every channel operation acquires that one lock. That is the whole story on channel throughput: a channel is a mutex-protected queue with a scheduler integration, not a lock-free structure. Entries in recvq/sendq are sudog records — a goroutine plus the address of the value it is waiting to send or receive.

The send path, in order

ch <- v 1 if the channel is nil → park forever 2 lock 3 if closed → unlock, panic 4 if a receiver is waiting in recvq: copy v DIRECTLY into the receiver's stack slot mark that goroutine runnable (into runnext — it runs next) unlock, return ← the fast path: no buffer touched 5 if the buffer has room: copy v into buf[sendx], advance, unlock, return 6 otherwise: build a sudog, push it onto sendq, park this goroutine (later, a receiver copies the value out and wakes it) Step 4 is the optimisation that makes Go channels fast. A value handed to a waiting receiver never touches the buffer and never allocates — it is memcpy'd straight from one stack to another, and the receiver is scheduled into the runnext slot for cache locality. The receive path is the mirror image: if a sender is parked on a full buffer, the receiver takes buf[recvx] and moves the parked sender's value into the freed slot, keeping FIFO order intact.
Why unbuffered is not "buffered with n=0"

With n == 0 there is no ring buffer at all, so every operation must take the direct-handoff path in step 4 or park. That is what makes the send a synchronisation point — the sender cannot proceed until a receiver has physically taken the value — and it is what the memory model's rule 4 formalises. It also means an unbuffered channel is often faster than a buffered one for ping-pong workloads: no buffer copy, and the wake-up lands in runnext.

Cost, measured

rough orders of magnitude — measure on your own hardware
BenchmarkChanUnbuffered-8        ~100 ns/op    two goroutines, ping-pong
BenchmarkChanBufferedSameG-8      ~25 ns/op    no contention, no park
BenchmarkMutexLockUnlock-8        ~15 ns/op
BenchmarkAtomicAddInt64-8          ~5 ns/op
BenchmarkFunctionCall-8            ~1 ns/op
goroutine park + unpark          ~200 ns     scheduler round trip
OS thread context switch         ~1-2 µs     what you are avoiding

# The lesson is not "channels are slow" — 100 ns is nothing next to any
# real work. The lesson is that a channel is the WRONG tool for a counter
# incremented a million times a second, and the right tool for handing a
# unit of work from one goroutine to another.

select is more expensive than it looks

A multi-case select must be atomic across several channels, so it: 1 evaluates every channel operand and its send values (all of them, in source order, even for cases that never fire) 2 builds a random polling order — this is the uniform choice among ready cases 3 builds a lock order sorted by address, to avoid deadlock 4 locks every channel involved 5 pass one: is any case ready? → run it, unlock, done 6 pass two: enqueue a sudog on every channel, park 7 on wake: dequeue from all the others, run the winner So an N-case select does O(N) work and, in the blocking path, O(N) sudog allocations and queue operations. Two practical consequences: · a select with a default never reaches step 6 — it is genuinely cheap, which is why non-blocking sends are the right shape for metrics and log shipping · a two-case select in a hot loop is fine; a twelve-case select in a hot loop is worth restructuring The single-case select with default is special-cased by the compiler into a direct non-blocking call — no ordering, no sudogs.
go · the operands are evaluated even when the case does not run
// expensive() is called EVERY time this select executes, whether or not
// that case is chosen — because the send value must exist before the
// runtime can decide. This surprises people.
select {
case ch <- expensive():
case <-ctx.Done():
	return
}

// If that matters, compute lazily:
select {
case <-ctx.Done():
	return
default:
}
v := expensive()
select {
case ch <- v:
case <-ctx.Done():
	return
}

Sizing a buffer

CapacityMeaning
0 (unbuffered)"I need to know you received this." Synchronisation, handoff, request/response
1A mailbox: one pending value. Also the correct size for a "result" channel a single goroutine writes once — it lets that goroutine exit even if nobody ever reads, which prevents a leak
N = worker countAbsorb a burst so producers do not stall on transient scheduling
Large (1000+)Usually a mistake. It hides backpressure: the producer runs ahead, latency grows invisibly, and a crash loses everything buffered
The unbuffered result channel that leaks

A goroutine doing resultCh <- v on an unbuffered channel blocks until someone receives. If the caller has already returned — a timeout fired, an errgroup sibling failed, the request was cancelled — nobody ever will, and that goroutine is parked forever holding everything it captured. Give such channels a buffer of 1 so the send always completes, or select on ctx.Done() alongside the send. This is the single most common goroutine leak in production Go.

Closed-channel semantics, restated precisely

go · why close is a broadcast, and who is allowed to call it
// close() wakes EVERY goroutine parked in recvq at once, each receiving
// the zero value with ok == false. That makes it the cheapest broadcast
// primitive in Go — and the reason `done := make(chan struct{})` +
// `close(done)` is the canonical cancellation signal.

// Buffered channels drain first: receives after close return the
// remaining buffered values, and only then start returning zero values.
ch := make(chan int, 2)
ch <- 1; ch <- 2
close(ch)
fmt.Println(<-ch)   // 1
fmt.Println(<-ch)   // 2
v, ok := <-ch       // 0, false

// Multiple senders? Nobody may close, because any sender closing races
// with the others' sends (which would panic). Use a separate done
// channel, or a sync.Once, or count the senders with a WaitGroup and
// close from a single coordinating goroutine after Wait.
var once sync.Once
stop := func() { once.Do(func() { close(done) }) }   // idempotent close
Interview follow-up

“Are channels lock-free?” No — every operation takes the channel's mutex. What makes them fast is not lock-freedom but the direct handoff: when a receiver is already waiting, the value is copied straight from the sender's stack to the receiver's with no buffer involved, and the woken goroutine goes into the scheduler's runnext slot so it runs immediately on the same P while the data is still in cache. A good follow-up is that this makes channels excellent for coordination and poor for high-frequency shared counters, where sync/atomic is roughly twenty times cheaper.

R06

Interfaces and maps in memory

Two data structures account for most of the surprising costs in ordinary Go code: the interface value, which sometimes allocates and always blocks inlining, and the map, which was rewritten from scratch in Go 1.24.

The interface value, and the itab

┌──────────────┬──────────────┐ │ tab │ data │ two words, always └──────┬───────┴──────┬───────┘ ▼ ▼ ┌───────────────┐ the VALUE, or a pointer to it │ itab │ │ inter *Shape│ the interface type │ _type *Circle│ the concrete type │ hash uint32│ for fast type switches │ fun[0] Area │ ← method pointers, resolved ONCE │ fun[1] Perim│ └───────────────┘ itabs are computed once and cached in a runtime hash table keyed by (interface type, concrete type). The first conversion of a given pair builds it; every later one is a lookup, and for statically known pairs the compiler emits it into the binary directly. any / interface{} has no methods, so it stores the _type pointer directly instead of an itab — an eface rather than an iface.
go · the two costs, and when they bite
// COST 1 — boxing. The data word is a POINTER. A value that is not
// already pointer-shaped must be copied to the heap to be stored.
var x any = 42          // allocates... except the runtime keeps a static
                        // table of small integers 0-255, so this one does not
var y any = 3.14        // allocates 8 bytes on the heap
var z any = myStruct    // allocates sizeof(myStruct)
var p any = &myStruct   // NO allocation — already a pointer

// This is why fmt.Println(i) allocates for an int outside 0-255, and why
// a []any of a million values is a million small heap objects.

// COST 2 — indirect calls cannot be inlined.
type Shape interface{ Area() float64 }

func totalConcrete(cs []Circle) float64 {   // Area() is INLINED, and the
	var t float64                           // loop may vectorise
	for _, c := range cs { t += c.Area() }
	return t
}

func totalIface(ss []Shape) float64 {       // indirect call through itab.fun[0]
	var t float64                           // every iteration: no inlining,
	for _, s := range ss { t += s.Area() }  // no escape analysis across it
	return t
}
// Typically 2-5× slower for a trivial method. Irrelevant when Area() does
// real work — which is almost always. Do not de-interface on instinct.
Devirtualisation happens when the compiler can prove the type

If the compiler can see that an interface variable can only ever hold one concrete type — a local created and used in the same function, or a call site where inlining revealed the assignment — it replaces the indirect call with a direct one and can then inline it. That is why microbenchmarks of interface dispatch are unreliable: the benchmark often devirtualises when the real call site cannot. Check with -gcflags='-m', which prints devirtualizing lines.

Maps: the classic bucket layout

Through Go 1.23, a map was an hmap pointing at 2^B buckets, each holding up to 8 key/value pairs: ┌─ hmap ──────────┐ │ count int │ len(m) │ B uint8 │ log2(number of buckets) │ buckets ptr ───┼──┐ │ oldbuckets ptr │ │ non-nil while growing └─────────────────┘ │ ▼ ┌─ bucket (bmap) ─────────────────────────────────────┐ │ tophash[8] top 8 bits of each key's hash │ │ keys[8] 8 keys, stored TOGETHER │ │ values[8] 8 values, stored together │ │ overflow ptr to another bucket if these 8 fill │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Keys and values are grouped separately, not interleaved, to avoid padding between a small key and a large value. Lookup: hash the key → low bits pick the bucket → compare the 8 tophash bytes (one byte each, so 8 candidates rejected almost free) → full key comparison only on a tophash match. Growth at load factor 6.5 per bucket: allocate 2× buckets, then migrate incrementally — each write evacuates one or two old buckets. This is why there is no single long pause on growth, and why an oldbuckets pointer exists.

Swiss tables, Go 1.24

Go 1.24 replaced the implementation with Swiss tables (the design from Abseil), keeping the language semantics identical: · groups of 8 slots with a 64-bit control word — one byte of hash metadata per slot, so a single SIMD/word comparison tests all 8 slots at once · open addressing with quadratic probing instead of overflow chains — fewer pointer dereferences, better cache behaviour · large maps are split into independent tables so growth work is bounded per operation Measured effect: roughly 30% faster lookups on large maps and lower memory for most shapes. No code change required. What did NOT change: iteration order is still randomised, maps are still not safe for concurrent use, elements are still not addressable, and maps still never shrink. Anything that depended on the old layout through unsafe broke — which is exactly what unsafe warns about.
go · what still costs money, in any implementation
// 1. Not preallocating. Growth rehashes everything, incrementally but
//    repeatedly: a map grown to 1M entries has gone through ~17 doublings.
m := make(map[string]int, 1_000_000)     // one allocation, zero rehashes

// 2. Pointer-heavy keys and values. The GC must trace every pointer in
//    the map on every cycle (R04).
map[string]*User      // 2 pointers per entry to trace
map[int32]User        // ZERO pointers to trace if User has none — the
                      // runtime marks the whole map as pointer-free

// 3. Large values stored by value. Every read and write copies them.
map[string]BigStruct     // copies BigStruct on each m[k] and m[k] = v
map[string]*BigStruct    // copies 8 bytes — but adds a pointer for the GC

// 4. Maps never shrink. After deleting 9M of 10M entries the buckets
//    remain. To actually release the memory, build a new map:
n := make(map[K]V, len(m))
maps.Copy(n, m)
m = n
Concurrent map access is a runtime crash, not a data race

The runtime maintains a write flag inside the map header and checks it on every operation. A concurrent read during a write reports fatal error: concurrent map read and map write and kills the process — it is not recoverable, and recover() cannot catch it, because a partially-grown map has no safe interpretation. This is a deliberate choice to make the bug loud. It is also only detected sometimes, so the absence of a crash is not evidence of correctness; use -race.

Where each structure's cost actually shows up

Symptom in a profileUsual cause
runtime.mapassign highMap built without a size hint, or used as a hot accumulator
runtime.mapaccess highLookup in an inner loop — hoist it, or switch to a slice index
runtime.convT64 / convTstringBoxing values into interfaces — usually fmt or a []any
runtime.growsliceMissing make([]T, 0, n)
runtime.typedmemmoveCopying large values — often a big struct in a map or a slice of big structs
runtime.gcDrain / scanobject highToo many pointers in the live heap (R04)
A slice often beats a map

Below roughly 10–20 elements, a linear scan over a slice is faster than a map lookup: no hashing, perfect cache locality, and no allocation. For small fixed sets — HTTP methods, enum names, a handful of feature flags — a sorted slice with slices.BinarySearch, or even a plain loop, measures better and allocates nothing. And for dense integer keys from zero, a slice indexed directly is not a micro-optimisation, it is the correct data structure.

Interview follow-up

“Why does putting an int into an any allocate?” Because an interface value's second word is a pointer, so any value that is not already pointer-shaped must be copied somewhere the pointer can point — the heap. The runtime shortcuts a few cases: small integers 0–255 come from a static array, and the zero value of any type points at a shared zero page. A good follow-up observation is that this is why fmt.Sprintf("%d", n) is much more expensive than strconv.Itoa(n) — the former boxes the argument, walks it with reflection, and parses a format string, while the latter is a straight integer-to-digits loop.

R07

Profiling with pprof

Profiling is built into the runtime and costs almost nothing, so the correct default for a Go service is to have it always available. The skill is not running the tool — it is knowing which of the six profiles answers the question you actually have.

The six profiles

ProfileAnswersCost
cpuWhere is on-CPU time going?~1-5%, sampled at 100 Hz per thread
heapWhat is allocated, and what is still live?Sampled every 512 KB. Effectively free
goroutineHow many, and where are they stuck?A brief stop-the-world to snapshot stacks
blockWhere do goroutines block on channels and locks?Off by default — must call SetBlockProfileRate
mutexWhere is lock contention?Off by default — SetMutexProfileFraction
threadcreateWhy are OS threads being created?Rarely useful; often broken
go · wiring it into a service, safely
import (
	"net/http"
	_ "net/http/pprof"      // registers handlers on http.DefaultServeMux
	"runtime"
)

func main() {
	// Block and mutex profiling are OFF by default because they add
	// overhead. These rates are cheap enough for production:
	runtime.SetBlockProfileRate(10_000)   // sample 1 blocking event per 10µs
	runtime.SetMutexProfileFraction(100)  // sample 1 in 100 contention events

	// CRITICAL: bind the debug endpoints to a SEPARATE listener that is
	// not exposed publicly. /debug/pprof on your main mux is a remote DoS
	// (a 30s CPU profile) and an information leak (heap contents, args).
	go func() {
		log.Println(http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:6060", nil))
	}()

	serveAPI()   // your real handler, on its own mux
}
Never expose /debug/pprof on a public listener

The blank import registers handlers on http.DefaultServeMux, so any service that serves DefaultServeMux publishes them to the internet. /debug/pprof/profile?seconds=300 then lets anyone pin a CPU for five minutes, and the heap and goroutine dumps expose stack contents, environment and argument values. Bind it to localhost and reach it through kubectl port-forward, or put it behind your internal auth. This is a recurring finding in real security audits of Go services.

Collecting

the commands you will actually type
# interactive, straight from a running process
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/allocs

# the flame-graph UI in a browser — start here, always
$ go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.pprof

# save first, analyse later (and attach it to the incident ticket)
$ curl -o cpu.pprof 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/profile?seconds=30'
$ curl -o heap.pprof 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/heap'

# goroutine dump as plain text — no pprof needed to read it
$ curl 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1'   # aggregated counts
$ curl 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=2'   # full stacks, one per G

# from a Kubernetes pod
$ kubectl port-forward pod/api-7d9f 6060:6060

# from a benchmark
$ go test -bench=. -cpuprofile=cpu.out -memprofile=mem.out -benchmem ./...

# DIFF two profiles — the single most underused pprof feature
$ go tool pprof -http=:8080 -base before.pprof after.pprof

Reading a CPU profile

flat vs cum is the whole skill
(pprof) top15 -cum
Showing nodes accounting for 27.3s, 91.0% of 30.0s total
      flat  flat%   sum%        cum   cum%
     0.01s  0.03%  0.03%     24.1s 80.3%  net/http.(*conn).serve
     0.02s  0.07%   0.1%     23.8s 79.3%  main.(*API).handleSearch
     0.05s  0.17%   0.3%     19.2s 64.0%  main.(*Index).Query
    11.4s 38.0% 38.3%     11.4s 38.0%  regexp.(*Regexp).doExecute
     6.20s 20.7% 59.0%      6.20s 20.7%  runtime.mallocgc
     3.10s 10.3% 69.3%      3.10s 10.3%  runtime.scanobject

  flat = time IN this function itself
  cum  = time in this function AND everything it called

  Sort by cum to find the expensive PATH (handleSearch → Query → regexp).
  Sort by flat to find the expensive CODE (doExecute, mallocgc).
  A high-cum/low-flat frame is a router, not a problem.

(pprof) list doExecute            # annotated source, line by line
(pprof) peek mallocgc             # who CALLS this?  ← the allocation source
(pprof) web                       # call graph as SVG
(pprof) traces                    # raw sample stacks
(pprof) granularity=lines; top20  # per-line instead of per-function
Three runtime frames and what they are telling you

runtime.mallocgc high means allocation pressure — use peek mallocgc to find the callers, then fix them with R02's techniques. runtime.gcDrain or scanobject high means the GC is spending its time marking — too many pointers in the live heap. runtime.selectgo, chansend or lock2 high means your program is coordinating rather than computing, and the block or mutex profile will say where.

The flame graph

go tool pprof -http=:8080 cpu.pprof → View → Flame Graph ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ runtime.main │ 100% ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ http.(*conn).serve │ 80% ├───────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┤ │ handleSearch 64% │ handleWrite 16% │ ├───────────────────┬───────────┼──────────────────────┤ │ regexp.doExecute │ json.Mar. │ db.Exec │ │ 38% │ 18% │ 14% │ └───────────────────┴───────────┴──────────────────────┘ Width is time. Depth is call stack. Order is alphabetical, not chronological — a flame graph is not a timeline. Read it top-down and look for wide plateaus. The widest box at the bottom of a stack is where time is actually spent; everything above it is just how you got there. A broad flat frame is a hotspot; a tall narrow tower is deep call structure, which is usually fine. Use the Peek and Source views next, and -base to diff a fix against the original — the diff view colours regressions red and improvements green, which is far easier to read than two top lists.

Continuous profiling, and labels

go · pprof labels let you slice a profile by tenant or endpoint
import "runtime/pprof"

func (a *API) handle(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	// Samples taken inside Do() carry these labels, so you can answer
	// "which endpoint is burning the CPU" from a single fleet-wide profile.
	pprof.Do(r.Context(), pprof.Labels(
		"endpoint", routePattern(r),
		"tenant", tenantFrom(r.Context()),
	), func(ctx context.Context) {
		a.route(ctx, w, r)
	})
}

// Then in pprof:  (pprof) tagfocus=endpoint:/v1/search
//                 (pprof) tagshow=tenant

// Labels propagate to goroutines started inside the Do block, which is
// what makes them useful for request-scoped work.
Always-on profiling beats reactive profiling

The moment you most want a CPU profile is during an incident that has already ended. Continuous profilers — Pyroscope, Parca, Datadog, Cloud Profiler — scrape the same pprof endpoints every minute and retain weeks of history, so you can compare today's flame graph with last Tuesday's and see exactly which deploy changed it. The overhead is the same 1–2% you already accept, and it converts profiling from an emergency skill into a routine one.

Interview follow-up

“A service's CPU has doubled since last week's deploy. Walk me through it.” Take a 30-second CPU profile from a live pod and, if you have one, a profile from before the deploy, then diff them with -base — that usually names the function outright. Without a baseline, sort by cum to find the hot path, then by flat to find the hot code, and check whether the top frames are yours or the runtime's: mallocgc and gcDrain mean the change added allocations rather than computation, which points at the heap profile instead. State the two-baseline habit explicitly; it is what separates people who have profiled in production from people who have read about it.

R08

The execution tracer and runtime metrics

A profile tells you where time is spent. The execution tracer tells you where time is not spent — the gaps, the waiting, the scheduling delays. It is the right tool for latency problems that a CPU profile says nothing about.

When to reach for the tracer instead of a profile

SymptomTool
High CPUCPU profile
High memoryHeap profile
High latency, low CPUExecution trace — you are waiting, not computing
p99 far above p50Execution trace — GC, scheduling, or lock convoy
Not using all coresExecution trace — serialisation or insufficient parallelism
Periodic latency spikesExecution trace — usually GC or a timer
Lock contentionMutex profile, then a trace to see the shape

Capturing and reading a trace

runtime/trace
$ curl -o trace.out 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/trace?seconds=5'
$ go tool trace trace.out
2026/09/14 10:22:01 Parsing trace...
2026/09/14 10:22:02 Splitting trace...
2026/09/14 10:22:02 Opening browser. Trace viewer is listening on
                    http://127.0.0.1:53421

# Keep it SHORT. A trace records every scheduling event, so 5 seconds of
# a busy service is already tens of megabytes and the viewer struggles
# past ~100 MB. 1-5 seconds is the useful range.

$ go test -trace=trace.out -bench=Handler ./...   # from a benchmark
The views, in the order you should use them: 1 Goroutine analysis ← start here, it is the most useful Per-goroutine totals broken into: execution, scheduler wait, sync block, GC assist, network wait, syscall. A goroutine spending 80% in "scheduler wait" is not slow — it is starved, and the fix is GOMAXPROCS or less contention, not code. 2 Synchronisation blocking profile Which channels and mutexes goroutines wait on, aggregated. 3 Scheduler latency profile Time between "became runnable" and "actually ran". Rising here means not enough Ps for the offered work. 4 The timeline (the trace viewer itself) ┌─ GC ▓▓░░░░░░▓▓░░░░░░▓▓░░░ ← regular bands = healthy pacing ├─ Heap ╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲╱╲ ← sawtooth = normal ├─ Threads ▁▁▂▂▁▁▂▂▁▁▂▂▁▁▂▂▁▁▂▂ ├─ Proc 0 ████░░████░░████░░██ ← gaps = idle cores ├─ Proc 1 ██░░░░░░██░░░░░░██░░ └─ Proc 2 ░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░ ← never used at all The picture above says the work is serialised: one P busy, two idle. Look for the channel or mutex everything funnels through. 5 User-defined tasks and regions ← your own annotations, below

Annotating your own code

go · tasks, regions and logs put your semantics into the trace
import "runtime/trace"

func (s *Server) handleOrder(ctx context.Context, req *Request) error {
	// A task spans a logical operation and can cross goroutines.
	ctx, task := trace.NewTask(ctx, "placeOrder")
	defer task.End()

	trace.Logf(ctx, "order", "id=%s items=%d", req.ID, len(req.Items))

	// A region is a span within one goroutine.
	var user *User
	func() {
		defer trace.StartRegion(ctx, "loadUser").End()
		user, _ = s.users.Get(ctx, req.UserID)
	}()

	func() {
		defer trace.StartRegion(ctx, "charge").End()
		s.payments.Charge(ctx, user, req.Total)
	}()

	return nil
}

// The "User-defined tasks" view then shows a latency distribution per
// task and, for any slow instance, exactly which region consumed the
// time and what the goroutine was doing during the gaps.
Go 1.21+ made tracing cheap enough to leave on

The tracer was rewritten to cut overhead from roughly 10–20% to around 1–2%, and trace.Start can now run continuously with a flight-recorder style buffer (runtime/trace.FlightRecorder in 1.25) that keeps the last few seconds in a ring and dumps them when something interesting happens. That inverts the usual problem: instead of trying to reproduce a latency spike while a trace is running, you arm the recorder and snapshot it from inside your own p99 alert.

GODEBUG: the runtime's own instrumentation

SettingPrints
gctrace=1One line per GC cycle: pauses, heap sizes, goal (R04)
schedtrace=1000Scheduler state every second: run-queue lengths per P
scheddetail=1With the above: every G, M and P individually
madvdontneed=1Return freed memory to the OS promptly (containers, RSS metrics)
inittrace=1Time spent in each package's init — for slow startup
allocfreetrace=1Every allocation with a stack. Enormously slow; last resort
http2debug=1|2HTTP/2 frame logging
tlsdebug=1TLS handshake details
invalidptr=1Crash on an invalid pointer — for debugging unsafe/cgo
cgocheck=2Thorough cgo pointer-passing checks (very slow)
panicnil=1Restore pre-1.21 panic(nil) behaviour
schedtrace: reading run-queue pressure
$ GODEBUG=schedtrace=1000 ./app
SCHED 1004ms: gomaxprocs=8 idleprocs=0 threads=14 spinningthreads=1
              idlethreads=3 runqueue=847 [102 98 110 95 88 104 91 99]

  gomaxprocs  number of Ps
  idleprocs   Ps with nothing to do  → 0 means saturated
  runqueue    GLOBAL queue length    → 847 waiting is very high
  [...]       per-P local queue lengths

  This program has ~1650 runnable goroutines and 8 Ps. Every one of them
  is waiting behind ~200 others. Latency here is queueing, not compute —
  a CPU profile would show nothing wrong. Either raise GOMAXPROCS (if the
  box has cores) or reduce concurrency (if it does not).

Exporting runtime metrics properly

go · the dashboard every Go service should have
import (
	"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus"
	"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/collectors"
)

func init() {
	// The modern collector reads runtime/metrics rather than MemStats, so
	// it does not stop the world, and it exposes the scheduler histograms.
	prometheus.MustRegister(collectors.NewGoCollector(
		collectors.WithGoCollectorRuntimeMetrics(
			collectors.MetricsScheduler,   // /sched/latencies:seconds
			collectors.MetricsGC,          // /gc/...
			collectors.MetricsMemory,      // /memory/classes/...
		),
	))
	prometheus.MustRegister(collectors.NewProcessCollector(
		collectors.ProcessCollectorOpts{}))
}

// Alert on these four, in this order of usefulness:
