//   go_goroutines                              rising without bound = leak
//   go_memstats_heap_inuse_bytes               rising without bound = leak
//   go_sched_latencies_seconds{quantile="0.99"} rising = CPU starvation
//   rate(go_gc_duration_seconds_count[5m])      spiking = allocation churn
Watch the live heap, not RSS

Go returns freed memory to the operating system lazily, so a container's RSS stays near the high-water mark long after the heap has shrunk — which makes RSS a poor leak indicator and a frequent source of false alarms. Alert on go_memstats_heap_inuse_bytes or /gc/heap/live:bytes instead, and treat RSS as the number the OOM killer watches, which is why you still set GOMEMLIMIT below the container limit. GODEBUG=madvdontneed=1 makes the release more eager if your platform's metrics depend on RSS.

Interview follow-up

“Your p50 is 20 ms and your p99 is 2 s, but CPU is at 30%. What is happening?” Low CPU with high tail latency means waiting, so a CPU profile is the wrong tool — take an execution trace. The usual four causes are: GC pauses or, more often, GC assist time charged to allocating goroutines; scheduler starvation from a GOMAXPROCS mismatch in a container; lock contention where a few requests queue behind a long critical section; and a downstream dependency whose own tail you are inheriting. The trace's goroutine analysis separates these directly — it attributes each goroutine's wall time to execution, scheduler wait, sync block, and GC assist, and whichever bucket is large names the cause.

R09

Benchmarking and optimisation

Go ships a benchmark runner, an allocation counter and a statistical comparison tool. Used together they turn "I think this is faster" into a number with a confidence interval — which is the only form of that claim worth acting on.

Writing a benchmark that measures something real

go · the anatomy, with the four mistakes marked
func BenchmarkEncode(b *testing.B) {
	// Setup is NOT timed if you reset afterwards — but ResetTimer is
	// easy to forget, so prefer doing setup before b.Loop / the loop
	// and calling ResetTimer explicitly.
	payload := makeLargePayload(1000)
	b.ResetTimer()
	b.ReportAllocs()               // or run with -benchmem

	for b.Loop() {                 // Go 1.24+: keeps args and results alive,
		encode(payload)            // so the compiler cannot elide the call
	}
}

// Before Go 1.24 you needed a sink to defeat dead-code elimination:
var sink []byte

func BenchmarkEncodeOld(b *testing.B) {
	payload := makeLargePayload(1000)
	b.ResetTimer()
	for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ {
		sink = encode(payload)     // assign to a package var, or the
	}                              // compiler may delete the whole call
}

// Parallel benchmarks measure contention — the thing that only appears
// under concurrency.
func BenchmarkCacheGet(b *testing.B) {
	c := newCache()
	b.RunParallel(func(pb *testing.PB) {
		for pb.Next() {
			c.Get("key")
		}
	})
}

// Sub-benchmarks over input sizes reveal the COMPLEXITY, which one
// number never can.
func BenchmarkSearch(b *testing.B) {
	for _, n := range []int{10, 100, 1_000, 10_000, 100_000} {
		b.Run(fmt.Sprintf("n=%d", n), func(b *testing.B) {
			data := generate(n)
			b.ResetTimer()
			for b.Loop() { search(data, target) }
		})
	}
}
The four ways a Go benchmark lies

1 · Dead-code elimination — nothing consumes the result, so the compiler deletes the work and you measure an empty loop (a suspiciously round 0.3 ns/op is the tell). 2 · Setup inside the timed loop — you are benchmarking makePayload. 3 · Unrealistic input — a ten-element slice when production sees ten thousand, so cache effects and algorithmic cost never appear. 4 · One run — machine noise on a laptop is routinely ±20%, which is larger than most optimisations.

Running and comparing

benchstat is the part people skip
$ go test -bench=Encode -benchmem -count=10 ./... | tee before.txt
BenchmarkEncode-8    18492    64821 ns/op    41216 B/op    1004 allocs/op
                       ↑        ↑              ↑              ↑
                   iterations  time         bytes        allocations
                               per op      per op         per op

# ...make the change...
$ go test -bench=Encode -benchmem -count=10 ./... | tee after.txt

$ go install golang.org/x/perf/cmd/benchstat@latest
$ benchstat before.txt after.txt
             │  before.txt  │             after.txt             │
             │    sec/op    │   sec/op     vs base              │
Encode-8       64.82µ ±  2%   21.31µ ± 1%  -67.12% (p=0.000 n=10)

             │   before.txt   │              after.txt              │
             │      B/op      │     B/op      vs base               │
Encode-8      41216.0 ±  0%    8192.0 ± 0%   -80.13% (p=0.000 n=10)

             │ before.txt  │            after.txt             │
             │ allocs/op   │ allocs/op   vs base              │
Encode-8       1004.0 ± 0%     3.0 ± 0%   -99.70% (p=0.000 n=10)

# p=0.000 means the difference is statistically significant.
# "~" in the vs base column means NO significant difference — which is
# the honest result of most "optimisations". Use -count=10 or more;
# benchstat cannot do statistics on a single sample.
Benchmark on hardware that resembles production

A laptop throttles thermally, has different cache sizes, and runs a browser. Results from it are fine for relative comparisons made back-to-back in the same session, and worthless as absolute numbers. For decisions that matter, run on a quiet machine matching production's CPU family, disable turbo if you can, and use -count high enough that benchstat reports a tight interval. In CI, compare against a baseline from the same runner type, never against a number recorded elsewhere.

The optimisation loop

1 Set a target. "p99 under 100 ms" — not "make it faster". Without a target you cannot know when to stop, and you will. 2 Measure in production. Which endpoint, which percentile, how often. Optimising a path that carries 2% of traffic is a hobby. 3 Profile. CPU for compute, heap for allocation, trace for waiting (R07, R08). Never optimise from a guess — every experienced engineer has a story about the week they spent on the wrong function. 4 Write a benchmark that reproduces it at realistic size. This is also your regression test. 5 Change ONE thing. Re-benchmark with benchstat. 6 Verify in production. Microbenchmarks routinely fail to transfer: cache behaviour, real input distributions and concurrency all differ. 7 Stop when you hit the target. Then write down what you did and why, because the next person will otherwise "clean up" the ugly fast version.

The wins, ranked by what they actually return

ChangeTypical effect
Fix the algorithm or the query10-1000×. An N+1 query or an O(n²) loop dwarfs everything below
Remove I/O from the hot path10-100×. Batch, cache, or make it concurrent
Preallocate slices and maps1.5-5×, and a large drop in GC pressure
Drop fmt for strconv/Builder3-10× on that line
A faster JSON library (sonic, go-json)2-5× on encode/decode, if JSON is genuinely hot
GOMEMLIMIT + GOGC=offOften 10-30% CPU back in a container (R04)
Fix GOMAXPROCS in a containerCan be dramatic for p99 (R03)
sync.Pool for large buffersMeaningful only when the heap profile already says so
Struct field reorderingMemory only, and only at high object counts (L05)
Removing bounds checks, unrollingSingle-digit %. Last resort, and fragile
Profile-guided optimisation is close to free

Since Go 1.21, dropping a CPU profile at default.pgo in your main package's directory makes the compiler use it automatically: hot functions get a larger inline budget, and hot interface call sites get devirtualised. Reported gains are 2–14% for no code change at all. Collect a profile from production, commit it, and refresh it when the workload shifts — a stale profile degrades gracefully rather than harming, but it stops helping.

When the answer is "do not"

Every optimisation is a permanent maintenance cost

The fast version is usually the harder one to read, so it is the one that gets a subtle bug during the next change. That is an acceptable trade when there is a measured problem and a target; it is a bad trade in a function that runs once per request against a 40 ms database call. The question to ask before any micro-optimisation is what fraction of total time this code accounts for — and if you cannot answer from a profile, the answer is that you should not be optimising it yet.

Interview follow-up

“How do you know an optimisation actually worked?” Run the benchmark at least ten times before and after and compare with benchstat, which reports a p-value — anything without statistical significance is noise, and a single before/after pair is almost always noise. Then say the part that matters more: verify in production, because microbenchmarks regularly fail to transfer once real input distributions, cache pressure and concurrency are involved. The strongest version of this answer includes having seen a benchmark improve and the service not.

R10

Races, deadlocks and production debugging

Concurrency bugs are the ones that pass code review, pass tests, and fail at 3am under load. Go gives you three instruments that find most of them — and a few habits that find the rest.

The race detector

go test -race
$ go test -race ./...
==================
WARNING: DATA RACE
Write at 0x00c0000b4010 by goroutine 8:
  main.(*Counter).Inc()
      /app/counter.go:14 +0x3c
  main.worker()
      /app/main.go:31 +0x5a

Previous read at 0x00c0000b4010 by goroutine 7:
  main.(*Counter).Value()
      /app/counter.go:19 +0x2f

Goroutine 8 (running) created at:
  main.main()
      /app/main.go:22 +0x104
==================
Found 1 data race(s)
FAIL

# Read it as four facts: the address, WHO wrote, WHO read, and where
# each goroutine was created. The creation stacks are the most useful
# part — they tell you which `go` statement to look at.

$ GORACE="halt_on_error=1 history_size=4" go test -race ./...
$ go build -race -o app-race .     # run this in staging, not prod
Race detector
FindsRaces that actually occurred during the run — it is dynamic, not static
False positivesNone. A reported race is always real
False negativesMany. Untested code paths and timing that did not happen are invisible
Cost~2-10× CPU, 5-10× memory, ~8 goroutine-created stacks retained per access
Where to run itAll of CI. A staging canary. Not production, except deliberately and briefly
Make the tests actually exercise concurrency

The race detector can only see what runs, so a test that calls a method once from one goroutine proves nothing. Write tests that hammer the type from several goroutines at once — t.Parallel(), a sync.WaitGroup with 100 writers and 100 readers, or a testing/quick-style loop — and run those under -race. A useful trick is go test -race -count=20, which reruns and reshuffles timing enough to surface races that one pass misses.

Deadlocks

Go detects exactly one case automatically: fatal error: all goroutines are asleep - deadlock! That fires only when every goroutine is blocked. A deadlock among two goroutines while an HTTP server keeps accepting connections is invisible to the runtime — the process looks healthy and quietly stops making progress. That is the realistic production case. The four classic shapes: 1 Lock ordering. A takes mu1 then mu2; B takes mu2 then mu1. → Fix: define a global lock order and never deviate. Document it next to the locks. 2 Re-entrant locking. A method holding mu calls another method that takes mu. Go's Mutex is not reentrant; this deadlocks instantly. → Fix: split into an exported locking wrapper and an unexported doSomethingLocked() that assumes the lock is held. 3 Channel with no counterparty. A send with no receiver, a range over a channel that is never closed, or a WaitGroup whose Done is skipped on an error path. → Fix: defer Done; close from the sender; select on ctx.Done(). 4 Lock held across a blocking call. Holding a mutex while doing network I/O turns a 2-second timeout into a 2-second global stall. → Fix: copy what you need, release the lock, then do the I/O.

Diagnosing a hung process

the order to try things
# 1. Goroutine counts by state — where are they all stuck?
$ curl -s localhost:6060/debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1 | head -30

# 2. If there is no pprof endpoint, SIGQUIT dumps every stack and exits.
$ kill -QUIT $(pidof app)
# or set GOTRACEBACK for more detail before it dies:
$ GOTRACEBACK=all ./app       # all user goroutines
$ GOTRACEBACK=system ./app    # plus runtime frames
$ GOTRACEBACK=crash ./app     # plus a core dump

# 3. Mutex profile: who is holding locks and for how long?
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/mutex

# 4. Block profile: what are goroutines waiting on?
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/block

# 5. Execution trace: the shape of the stall over time.
$ curl -o t.out 'localhost:6060/debug/pprof/trace?seconds=3' && go tool trace t.out

# 6. Last resort — attach a debugger to the live process.
$ dlv attach $(pidof app)
(dlv) goroutines -t           # every goroutine with its stack
(dlv) goroutine 42 bt
(dlv) print s.queue
Read the goroutine dump by state, not by count

Forty thousand goroutines in IO wait is a busy server. Forty thousand in chan send at the same line is a leak with an obvious address. Many in semacquire is lock contention. Many in runnable is CPU starvation — check GOMAXPROCS. ?debug=1 aggregates identical stacks with counts, which is what you want first; ?debug=2 gives every stack individually plus how long each has been blocked, which is what you want once you know where to look.

Delve

dlv — build with -gcflags='-N -l' or the debugger lies
$ dlv test ./internal/order -- -test.run TestPlaceOrder
$ dlv debug ./cmd/api -- --config=dev.yaml
$ dlv attach 4711
$ dlv core ./app /cores/core.4711      # post-mortem from a core dump

(dlv) break order.go:42
(dlv) condition 1 o.Total > 10000     # conditional breakpoint
(dlv) continue
(dlv) next / step / stepout
(dlv) print o
(dlv) locals -v
(dlv) goroutines                      # the killer feature vs gdb
(dlv) goroutine 17                    # switch to another goroutine
(dlv) stack
(dlv) set o.Total = 500               # mutate and continue

# Without -gcflags='-N -l', optimisation and inlining mean variables show
# as "optimized out" and single-stepping jumps around. `dlv debug` passes
# those flags for you; a manual `go build` does not.

Habits that prevent most of this

HabitCatches
go test -race ./... in CI, alwaysData races, before they ship
goleak.VerifyTestMain in every packageGoroutine leaks at build time
A comment naming what each mutex guardsLock-scope confusion in review
A documented global lock orderDeadlocks by ordering
Never hold a lock across I/OConvoys and cascading timeouts
context on every blocking callUnstoppable goroutines
Buffered result channels (cap 1)The most common leak (R05)
go vet + staticcheck in CIcopylocks, lostcancel, shadowed err
pprof on a private port in every serviceMakes the 3am investigation possible at all
Interview follow-up

“A production Go service stops responding but the process is alive and CPU is near zero. What do you do?” Zero CPU rules out a busy loop, so it is blocked — get the goroutine dump first, from /debug/pprof/goroutine?debug=1 or by sending SIGQUIT, and group by state. A large cluster in semacquire means a mutex is held by someone doing something slow; in chan send or chan receive means a channel with no counterparty; in IO wait on the same dependency means that dependency is hung and your timeouts are missing or too long. Mention that you would take the dump before restarting, because the restart destroys the only evidence and the bug will return.

B01

The net/http server

Go's HTTP server is production-grade standard library — TLS, HTTP/2, connection pooling and graceful shutdown are all in the box. The defaults, however, are wrong for the public internet, and that is where most of this chapter lives.

The default server will be taken down by a slow client

go · never ship http.ListenAndServe with nil timeouts
// http.ListenAndServe(":8080", mux) uses a zero-value Server: NO timeouts
// at all. One client that opens a connection and sends a byte a minute
// holds a goroutine and a file descriptor forever. A few thousand of
// those exhaust the process. This is Slowloris, and it still works.

srv := &http.Server{
	Addr:    ":8080",
	Handler: mux,

	// Headers must arrive within this window. The cheapest defence
	// against Slowloris, and it does not affect long request bodies.
	ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,

	// Whole request: headers + body. Set it if you accept uploads
	// with a known bound; leave it off and rely on per-handler
	// context deadlines if you stream.
	ReadTimeout: 15 * time.Second,

	// From the end of the request headers to the end of the response.
	// MUST exceed your slowest legitimate handler, or you truncate
	// responses with no error the client can interpret.
	WriteTimeout: 30 * time.Second,

	// How long an idle keep-alive connection is kept. Defaults to
	// ReadTimeout if unset, which is usually too short and causes
	// needless reconnects.
	IdleTimeout: 120 * time.Second,

	// Cap header size (default 1 MB). Protects against header bombs.
	MaxHeaderBytes: 1 << 20,

	// Route the server's own errors into your logger, not stderr.
	ErrorLog: slog.NewLogLogger(logger.Handler(), slog.LevelError),
}

log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServe())
Where each timeout applies on the connection timeline: accept ──▶ read headers ──▶ read body ──▶ handler ──▶ write ──▶ idle │ │ │ │ │ │ │◀── ReadHeaderTimeout ─────▶│ │ │ │ │◀──────── ReadTimeout ──────────────────▶│ │ │ │ │◀──── WriteTimeout ───▶│ │ │ │◀ Idle ▶│ WriteTimeout is the one that bites. It is measured from the end of the request headers, so it covers your handler's entire execution — a 30 s WriteTimeout with a 45 s report endpoint truncates the response mid-stream. For long or streaming handlers, set a generous WriteTimeout and enforce the real deadline with a per-route context.

Routing, since Go 1.22

go · ServeMux now does methods and path variables
mux := http.NewServeMux()

// "METHOD /path/{wildcard}" — the router most services no longer need
// a third-party package for.
mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/orders", h.listOrders)
mux.HandleFunc("POST /v1/orders", h.createOrder)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/orders/{id}", h.getOrder)
mux.HandleFunc("DELETE /v1/orders/{id}", h.deleteOrder)
mux.HandleFunc("GET /v1/files/{path...}", h.serveFile)   // trailing wildcard
mux.HandleFunc("GET /{$}", h.home)                        // EXACT "/" only

func (h *Handler) getOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	id := r.PathValue("id")                               // no third-party ctx
	...
}

// Precedence is by SPECIFICITY, not registration order: "/v1/orders/new"
// wins over "/v1/orders/{id}". Conflicting patterns panic at registration
// rather than silently shadowing — a real improvement over the old mux.

// Sub-routers by prefix stripping:
api := http.NewServeMux()
api.HandleFunc("GET /orders", h.listOrders)
mux.Handle("/v1/", http.StripPrefix("/v1", api))
When a third-party router still earns its place

The 1.22 mux covers method routing, path variables and precedence — which is what most services used chi or gorilla/mux for. Reach for chi when you want per-subtree middleware chains and route grouping as first-class features, or gin/echo if your team wants a batteries-included framework. Reach for httprouter-style radix routers only if routing genuinely shows up in your profile, which for almost everyone it does not. All of them implement http.Handler, so the choice is reversible.

Handlers and the two interfaces

type Handler interface { ServeHTTP(http.ResponseWriter, *http.Request) }
go · a handler with dependencies is a method on a struct
// HandlerFunc adapts a function to the Handler interface. These are
// equivalent; the struct form is what you want once there are deps.
type Handler struct {
	orders  *order.Service
	log     *slog.Logger
	metrics *Metrics
}

func (h *Handler) createOrder(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	// 1. Bound the body BEFORE decoding. Without this, a client can send
	//    a 10 GB JSON document and you will try to hold it.
	r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20)   // 1 MiB

	var req CreateOrderRequest
	dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
	dec.DisallowUnknownFields()        // reject typos instead of ignoring them
	if err := dec.Decode(&req); err != nil {
		writeError(w, http.StatusBadRequest, "invalid_json", err.Error())
		return
	}

	// 2. The request context is cancelled when the client disconnects.
	//    Pass it down so the database query stops too.
	o, err := h.orders.Place(r.Context(), req.UserID, req.Items)
	if err != nil {
		h.writeServiceError(w, r, err)
		return
	}

	// 3. Headers BEFORE WriteHeader; WriteHeader before Write.
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	w.Header().Set("Location", "/v1/orders/"+o.ID)
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusCreated)
	_ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(o)
}
Order of operations on ResponseWriter is strict

Set every header first, then call WriteHeader(status), then write the body. A header set after WriteHeader is silently dropped; the first Write implicitly calls WriteHeader(200), so an error path that writes then tries to set a 500 produces a 200 with an error body. And a second WriteHeader logs superfluous response.WriteHeader call and does nothing — if you see that in your logs, a handler is writing twice, usually because an error path forgot a return.

Streaming, flushing and hijacking

go · server-sent events, the simplest streaming shape
func (h *Handler) events(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
	w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-cache")
	w.Header().Set("Connection", "keep-alive")

	// Go 1.20+: ResponseController is the supported way to reach optional
	// capabilities through middleware wrappers, which used to break the
	// old `w.(http.Flusher)` type assertion.
	rc := http.NewResponseController(w)
	if err := rc.SetWriteDeadline(time.Time{}); err != nil {   // no deadline
		h.log.Warn("cannot clear write deadline", "err", err)
	}

	ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
	defer ticker.Stop()

	for {
		select {
		case <-r.Context().Done():        // client went away
			return
		case t := <-ticker.C:
			fmt.Fprintf(w, "data: %s\n\n", t.Format(time.RFC3339))
			if err := rc.Flush(); err != nil {
				return                     // connection gone
			}
		}
	}
}

Graceful shutdown, and what it does not do

go · drain in-flight requests, then exit
ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(),
	os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
defer stop()

go func() {
	if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
		log.Fatal(err)
	}
}()

<-ctx.Done()
log.Println("shutting down")

shutCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
defer cancel()

// Shutdown: stop accepting, close idle connections, WAIT for active
// handlers to return. It does NOT cancel their contexts.
if err := srv.Shutdown(shutCtx); err != nil {
	log.Printf("forced shutdown: %v", err)
	_ = srv.Close()              // hard close, drops connections
}
Shutdown waits; it does not interrupt

Shutdown returns when every in-flight handler has finished or the shutdown context expires — it never cancels a handler's own r.Context(). A handler with no internal deadline will run to completion, so a 60-second report blocks a 20-second shutdown and you fall through to Close(), cutting the connection anyway. Also note that Shutdown does not wait for hijacked connections (WebSockets) at all: you must track and close those yourself. And in Kubernetes, sleep a few seconds after SIGTERM before calling Shutdown, because endpoints propagate asynchronously and traffic can still arrive after the signal.

Interview follow-up

“What is wrong with http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil)?” Two things. There are no timeouts, so a slow client holds a goroutine and a descriptor indefinitely — Slowloris against the default configuration still works. And nil means http.DefaultServeMux, a package-level global that any imported package can register on, most notoriously net/http/pprof — so a blank import elsewhere in your dependency tree can publish heap dumps on your public port. The fix for both is one &http.Server{} literal with explicit timeouts and an explicit mux.

B02

Middleware and request context

Middleware in Go is a function that takes a handler and returns a handler. That is the entire abstraction — no framework, no registration API — and it composes into everything a real service needs.

The shape

type Middleware = func(http.Handler) http.Handler
go · one middleware, and a chain helper
func RequestID(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		id := r.Header.Get("X-Request-Id")
		if id == "" {
			id = uuid.NewString()
		}
		w.Header().Set("X-Request-Id", id)
		ctx := context.WithValue(r.Context(), ctxKeyRequestID{}, id)
		next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))   // r is immutable: rebuild it
	})
}

// Chain applies in READING order: Chain(a, b, c) runs a, then b, then c.
// (Naive composition reverses it, which surprises everyone once.)
func Chain(h http.Handler, ms ...func(http.Handler) http.Handler) http.Handler {
	for i := len(ms) - 1; i >= 0; i-- {
		h = ms[i](h)
	}
	return h
}

handler := Chain(mux,
	Recoverer,        // outermost: must catch panics from everything below
	RequestID,        // before logging, so the log line has the ID
	Logger,
	Metrics,
	Tracing,
	RateLimit,
	Authenticate,     // innermost: the cheap rejections happened already
)
Order matters, and the reasoning is always the same: cheap and universal on the outside, expensive and specific inside. request ─▶ Recoverer catches panics from all of the below ─▶ RequestID every later log line needs it ─▶ Logger must see the final status code, so it wraps the rest and reports on the way out ─▶ Metrics same reason ─▶ Tracing span covers real work, not the logger ─▶ CORS answer OPTIONS before doing any work ─▶ RateLimit reject before authenticating ─▶ Authenticate database or JWT work ─▶ Authorize needs the identity from the line above ─▶ handler Getting Recoverer inside Logger is the classic mistake: a panic then bypasses the log line entirely and the request vanishes from your logs.

Capturing the status code

go · ResponseWriter does not expose what was written
type recorder struct {
	http.ResponseWriter
	status int
	bytes  int
}

func (r *recorder) WriteHeader(code int) {
	if r.status == 0 {
		r.status = code
		r.ResponseWriter.WriteHeader(code)
	}
}

func (r *recorder) Write(b []byte) (int, error) {
	if r.status == 0 {
		r.status = http.StatusOK          // implicit 200 on first write
	}
	n, err := r.ResponseWriter.Write(b)
	r.bytes += n
	return n, err
}

// Unwrap lets http.ResponseController reach Flush/Hijack/SetDeadline
// through this wrapper. Without it, streaming handlers break behind
// your middleware — a subtle and very common bug.
func (r *recorder) Unwrap() http.ResponseWriter { return r.ResponseWriter }

func Logger(log *slog.Logger) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			start := time.Now()
			rec := &recorder{ResponseWriter: w}

			next.ServeHTTP(rec, r)

			log.LogAttrs(r.Context(), levelFor(rec.status), "http",
				slog.String("method", r.Method),
				slog.String("path", r.URL.Path),
				slog.String("route", routePattern(r)),   // NOT the raw path
				slog.Int("status", rec.status),
				slog.Int("bytes", rec.bytes),
				slog.Duration("dur", time.Since(start)),
				slog.String("request_id", RequestID(r.Context())),
			)
		})
	}
}
Log the route pattern, never the raw path

/v1/orders/8f2c-… as a metric label or log field produces unbounded cardinality: one time series per order ID, which will take down Prometheus and make your logs unsearchable. Use the matched pattern — /v1/orders/{id}, available from r.Pattern since Go 1.23 or from your router — for both metrics labels and the structured route field, and keep the concrete path in a separate high-cardinality-tolerant field if you need it.

Middleware you will write in every service

go · timeout, metrics, and authentication
// A per-request deadline that actually propagates to the database and
// to outbound calls, because everything downstream takes r.Context().
func Timeout(d time.Duration) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), d)
			defer cancel()
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))
		})
	}
}

func Metrics(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		rec := &recorder{ResponseWriter: w}
		start := time.Now()
		inflight.Inc()
		defer inflight.Dec()

		next.ServeHTTP(rec, r)

		// RED: Rate, Errors, Duration — labelled by ROUTE and method only.
		lbl := prometheus.Labels{
			"route":  routePattern(r),
			"method": r.Method,
			"status": strconv.Itoa(rec.status),
		}
		requests.With(lbl).Inc()
		duration.With(lbl).Observe(time.Since(start).Seconds())
	})
}

func Authenticate(v *TokenVerifier) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			tok, ok := strings.CutPrefix(r.Header.Get("Authorization"), "Bearer ")
			if !ok {
				writeError(w, http.StatusUnauthorized, "missing_token", "")
				return
			}
			claims, err := v.Verify(r.Context(), tok)
			if err != nil {
				writeError(w, http.StatusUnauthorized, "invalid_token", "")
				return
			}
			ctx := context.WithValue(r.Context(), ctxKeyUser{}, claims)
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r.WithContext(ctx))
		})
	}
}

Typed context accessors

go · one small file that makes context values safe to use
package reqctx

// Unexported struct keys: no other package can collide, and no string
// constant can be typo'd. Never use a plain string as a context key.
type (
	userKey      struct{}
	requestIDKey struct{}
)

func WithUser(ctx context.Context, u *User) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, userKey{}, u)
}

// Two forms: one that returns ok for callers that can cope without it,
// and one that must not fail. Do NOT return (nil, nil) and hope.
func User(ctx context.Context) (*User, bool) {
	u, ok := ctx.Value(userKey{}).(*User)
	return u, ok
}

func MustUser(ctx context.Context) *User {
	u, ok := User(ctx)
	if !ok {
		panic("reqctx: no user in context — Authenticate middleware missing")
	}
	return u
}
Keep the context payload small and request-scoped

Request ID, trace span, authenticated principal, locale, tenant — these are cross-cutting and genuinely belong there. A database handle, a logger with no request fields, a config struct or a feature-flag client do not: they are dependencies, and putting them in the context hides them from every function signature, defeats the compiler, and makes the code untestable without constructing a context by hand. If a reviewer cannot tell what a function needs by reading its signature, the context is being used as a service locator.

Per-route middleware

go · apply only where it belongs
// Global chain: everything.
root := Chain(mux, Recoverer, RequestID, Logger, Metrics)

// Per-route: wrap the individual handler before registering it.
mux.Handle("POST /v1/admin/reindex",
	Chain(http.HandlerFunc(h.reindex), Authenticate(v), RequireRole("admin")))

// Health checks must NOT go through auth, rate limiting or heavy logging —
// register them on the bare mux so a probe cannot be rate-limited into
// failing and restarting a healthy pod.
mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
})
mux.HandleFunc("GET /readyz", h.ready)      // this one DOES check dependencies
Interview follow-up

“How would you add request tracing to an existing Go service?” Middleware, and the answer should mention two specifics. First, it must wrap the handler and observe on the way out, because the status code and duration only exist after the handler returns — which requires a ResponseWriter wrapper that also implements Unwrap so streaming and hijacking still work through it. Second, the span and request ID go into the request context via r.WithContext, so every downstream call that already takes a context — database, HTTP client, queue publish — is correlated with no further changes. That is the whole reason context.Context is the first parameter everywhere.

B03

JSON, validation and API shape

encoding/json is reflection-based, permissive by default, and has a handful of behaviours that produce real bugs in APIs. Knowing them — and designing your request and response types deliberately — removes most of the friction.

Tags, and the defaults that surprise

go · every tag option that matters
type Order struct {
	ID       string    `json:"id"`
	Total    int64     `json:"total_cents,string"` // encode as a JSON STRING —
	                                               // JS loses precision past 2^53
	Note     string    `json:"note,omitempty"`     // omit if ""
	Tags     []string  `json:"tags,omitempty"`     // omit if nil OR empty
	Internal string    `json:"-"`                  // never marshalled
	Dash     string    `json:"-,"`                 // a field literally named "-"
	Created  time.Time `json:"created_at"`         // RFC 3339 automatically
	Meta     any       `json:"meta,omitzero"`      // Go 1.24: omit if ZERO,
	                                               // which omitempty does not do
	secret   string                                // unexported: invisible
}

// Decoding is CASE-INSENSITIVE and matches the tag first, then the field
// name. So {"ID":...}, {"id":...} and {"Id":...} all populate ID. This
// is occasionally useful and frequently astonishing.

// Unknown fields are SILENTLY IGNORED unless you opt out:
dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
dec.DisallowUnknownFields()        // a typo'd field is now a 400, not a no-op
Four encoding/json behaviours that cause production bugs

1 · A nil slice marshals to null, an empty slice to [] — clients that do for (const x of res.items) break on null. Initialise response slices. 2 · omitempty omits zero values, so false, 0 and "" disappear — which silently breaks a "set this flag to false" API. 3 · Unmarshalling into a non-empty struct leaves absent fields at their previous value, not the zero value. 4 · Numbers decode into any as float64, so a large int64 ID loses precision; use dec.UseNumber() or a concrete type.

Telling "absent" from "null" from "zero"

go · the PATCH problem, and the two solutions
// PATCH {"note": ""}   → set note to empty
// PATCH {"note": null} → clear note
// PATCH {}             → leave note alone
// A plain `Note string` cannot distinguish any of these.

// Solution 1 — pointers. Simple, and enough for "absent vs present".
type PatchOrder struct {
	Note   *string `json:"note"`     // nil = absent, &"" = set to empty
	Status *string `json:"status"`
}

func (s *Service) Patch(ctx context.Context, id string, p PatchOrder) error {
	o, err := s.store.Get(ctx, id)
	if err != nil { return err }
	if p.Note != nil   { o.Note = *p.Note }
	if p.Status != nil { o.Status = *p.Status }
	return s.store.Update(ctx, o)
}

// Solution 2 — an explicit three-state wrapper when null must differ
// from absent.
type Optional[T any] struct {
	Set   bool
	Null  bool
	Value T
}

func (o *Optional[T]) UnmarshalJSON(b []byte) error {
	o.Set = true
	if string(b) == "null" {
		o.Null = true
		return nil
	}
	return json.Unmarshal(b, &o.Value)
}

Custom marshalling

go · a money type that is correct on the wire
type Money struct {
	Cents    int64
	Currency string
}

// Value receiver: works for both Money and *Money. A POINTER receiver
// here would silently not fire for a Money value inside a struct —
// a classic and very confusing bug.
func (m Money) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) {
	return json.Marshal(struct {
		Amount   string `json:"amount"`
		Currency string `json:"currency"`
	}{
		Amount:   fmt.Sprintf("%d.%02d", m.Cents/100, m.Cents%100),
		Currency: m.Currency,
	})
}

// Unmarshal ALWAYS needs a pointer receiver — it mutates.
func (m *Money) UnmarshalJSON(b []byte) error {
	var raw struct {
		Amount   string `json:"amount"`
		Currency string `json:"currency"`
	}
	if err := json.Unmarshal(b, &raw); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	cents, err := parseDecimalToCents(raw.Amount)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("money: %q: %w", raw.Amount, err)
	}
	m.Cents, m.Currency = cents, raw.Currency
	return nil
}
Receiver type decides whether your marshaller runs

MarshalJSON on a pointer receiver is in *T's method set only, so json.Marshal(v) where v is a T value — including a T field inside another struct, or an element of a []T — will not call it and you get the default field-by-field encoding instead. Use a value receiver for MarshalJSON, a pointer receiver for UnmarshalJSON, and assert both at compile time with var _ json.Marshaler = Money{} and var _ json.Unmarshaler = (*Money)(nil).

Separate wire types from domain types

Validation

go · a Validate method beats a tag DSL for anything conditional
type CreateOrderRequest struct {
	UserID   string `json:"user_id"`
	Items    []Item `json:"items"`
	Currency string `json:"currency"`
	Coupon   string `json:"coupon,omitempty"`
}

// Collect ALL errors — returning only the first makes an API that clients
// have to call five times to fill in a form correctly.
func (r CreateOrderRequest) Validate() error {
	var errs []error
	if r.UserID == "" {
		errs = append(errs, &FieldError{"user_id", "required"})
	}
	if len(r.Items) == 0 {
		errs = append(errs, &FieldError{"items", "at least one item required"})
	}
	if len(r.Items) > 100 {
		errs = append(errs, &FieldError{"items", "at most 100 items"})
	}
	if !slices.Contains([]string{"EUR", "USD", "GBP"}, r.Currency) {
		errs = append(errs, &FieldError{"currency", "must be EUR, USD or GBP"})
	}
	for i, it := range r.Items {
		if it.Qty <= 0 {
			errs = append(errs, &FieldError{
				fmt.Sprintf("items[%d].qty", i), "must be positive"})
		}
	}
	return errors.Join(errs...)     // nil if errs is empty
}
Tag-based validators are fine for the boring 80%

go-playground/validator (validate:"required,email,max=100") removes a lot of repetitive code and is well worth using for field-level rules. Where it falls down is conditional logic — "shipping address required only when delivery is physical", "end must be after start" — which becomes an unreadable tag or a custom validator registered far from the type. The pragmatic split is tags for field shape, a Validate() method for anything involving two fields or the domain.

One error envelope, everywhere

go · consistent errors are an API feature
type ErrorResponse struct {
	Error struct {
		Code      string       `json:"code"`               // stable, machine-readable
		Message   string       `json:"message"`            // human, safe to display
		Fields    []FieldError `json:"fields,omitempty"`   // for 422
		RequestID string       `json:"request_id"`         // for support tickets
	} `json:"error"`
}

func (h *Handler) writeServiceError(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, err error) {
	status, code := http.StatusInternalServerError, "internal_error"
	msg := "something went wrong"       // NEVER leak err.Error() on a 500

	var ve *ValidationError
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, order.ErrNotFound):
		status, code, msg = http.StatusNotFound, "order_not_found", "order not found"
	case errors.Is(err, order.ErrConflict):
		status, code, msg = http.StatusConflict, "version_conflict", "resource changed"
	case errors.As(err, &ve):
		status, code, msg = http.StatusUnprocessableEntity, "validation_failed", ve.Error()
	case errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded):
		status, code, msg = http.StatusGatewayTimeout, "timeout", "upstream timed out"
	case errors.Is(err, context.Canceled):
		return                           // client hung up: nobody to answer
	}

	if status >= 500 {
		h.log.ErrorContext(r.Context(), "request failed", "err", err)
	}
	writeJSON(w, status, envelope(code, msg, reqctx.RequestID(r.Context())))
}
Never put err.Error() in a 5xx response body

Internal error strings routinely contain table names, SQL fragments, internal hostnames, file paths and occasionally connection strings — all of which are free reconnaissance for an attacker and meaningless to a legitimate client. Log the full wrapped chain server-side with the request ID, and return a generic message plus that same request ID. Support can then find the exact log line, and nobody learns your schema from a 500.

Interview follow-up

“Is encoding/json fast enough?” For most services, yes — it is rarely the bottleneck next to a database round trip. When it genuinely is, the reason is reflection: every field is discovered at runtime and every value boxed. The options in order are to shrink the payload, generate code with easyjson or ffjson, use a SIMD implementation like bytedance/sonic, or move off JSON to protobuf. Worth adding: Go 1.25 introduced encoding/json/v2 behind GOEXPERIMENT=jsonv2, which is substantially faster and fixes several of the behaviours above — but it is not yet the default and should not be assumed in production.

B04

Project architecture and wiring

Go has no dependency-injection framework in general use, and does not need one. Dependencies are struct fields, wiring is a function in main, and the entire architecture question reduces to which package is allowed to import which.

The dependency rule

Dependencies point inward. The domain imports nothing. ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ cmd/api — wiring only. Imports everything; nothing │ │ imports it. │ └───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │ transport internal/http, internal/grpc │ │ decode → call the service → encode │ │ knows about HTTP; knows nothing about SQL │ └───────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘ │ ┌───────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────┐ │ domain internal/order, internal/billing │ │ types, business rules, and the INTERFACES it │ │ needs (Store, Payments, Publisher) │ │ imports no database, no http, no framework │ └───────────────────────▲──────────────────────────────────┘ │ implements the interfaces above ┌───────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────┐ │ adapters internal/postgres, internal/stripe, │ │ internal/kafka, internal/redis │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ The inversion is the whole point: the domain declares what it needs, the adapters satisfy it, and main connects them. Swap Postgres for an in-memory fake in a test and the domain package does not notice.

The domain package

go · internal/order/order.go — types and rules, no I/O
package order

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"time"
)

var (
	ErrNotFound = errors.New("order not found")
	ErrConflict = errors.New("order was modified")
	ErrEmpty    = errors.New("order has no items")
)

type Order struct {
	ID        string
	UserID    string
	Items     []Item
	Status    Status
	Version   int          // optimistic locking
	CreatedAt time.Time
}

// Business rules live on the type, and are unit-testable with no
// database, no HTTP, and no mocks.
func (o *Order) Total() int64 {
	var t int64
	for _, it := range o.Items { t += it.Price * int64(it.Qty) }
	return t
}

func (o *Order) Cancel(now time.Time) error {
	switch o.Status {
	case StatusShipped:
		return errors.New("cannot cancel a shipped order")
	case StatusCancelled:
		return nil                        // idempotent
	}
	if now.Sub(o.CreatedAt) > 24*time.Hour {
		return errors.New("cancellation window has closed")
	}
	o.Status = StatusCancelled
	return nil
}

// The interfaces this package needs, declared HERE — narrow, and named
// for what the domain wants rather than what the adapter is.
type Store interface {
	Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (*Order, error)
	Save(ctx context.Context, o *Order) error
}

type Payments interface {
	Charge(ctx context.Context, userID string, cents int64) (string, error)
}

type Publisher interface {
	Publish(ctx context.Context, event Event) error
}

The service: orchestration, not logic

go · internal/order/service.go
type Service struct {
	store    Store
	payments Payments
	events   Publisher
	log      *slog.Logger
	clock    func() time.Time     // injected: makes time testable
}

// Constructor takes dependencies explicitly. No globals, no init(), no
// service locator — the compiler enforces that everything is provided.
func NewService(s Store, p Payments, e Publisher, log *slog.Logger) *Service {
	return &Service{store: s, payments: p, events: e, log: log, clock: time.Now}
}

func (s *Service) Place(ctx context.Context, userID string, items []Item) (*Order, error) {
	if len(items) == 0 {
		return nil, ErrEmpty
	}
	o := &Order{
		ID: newID(), UserID: userID, Items: items,
		Status: StatusPending, CreatedAt: s.clock(),
	}

	chargeID, err := s.payments.Charge(ctx, userID, o.Total())
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("charge: %w", err)
	}
	o.ChargeID = chargeID
	o.Status = StatusPaid

	if err := s.store.Save(ctx, o); err != nil {
		// The charge succeeded and the save failed. This is the hard case:
		// compensate, or write to an outbox so a worker reconciles later.
		s.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "saved failed after charge",
			"order", o.ID, "charge", chargeID, "err", err)
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("save order: %w", err)
	}

	// Best effort: a failed event must not fail the order. In a system
	// that cares, this is a transactional outbox row instead (B12).
	if err := s.events.Publish(ctx, OrderPlaced{OrderID: o.ID}); err != nil {
		s.log.WarnContext(ctx, "publish failed", "order", o.ID, "err", err)
	}
	return o, nil
}

Wiring in main

go · cmd/api/main.go — the only place that knows every package
func main() {
	if err := run(); err != nil {
		slog.Error("fatal", "err", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}

// run returns an error instead of calling log.Fatal, so every defer in
// it actually executes and the whole thing is testable.
func run() error {
	cfg, err := config.Load()
	if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("config: %w", err) }

	log := slog.New(slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, &slog.HandlerOptions{
		Level: cfg.LogLevel,
	}))

	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(),
		os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	// --- adapters ---
	pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, cfg.DatabaseURL)
	if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("database: %w", err) }
	defer pool.Close()

	if err := pool.Ping(ctx); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("database ping: %w", err)   // fail fast at startup
	}

	store := postgres.NewOrderStore(pool)
	payments := stripe.New(cfg.StripeKey, stripe.WithTimeout(5*time.Second))
	events := kafka.NewPublisher(cfg.Brokers, "orders")
	defer events.Close()

	// --- domain ---
	orders := order.NewService(store, payments, events, log)

	// --- transport ---
	h := httpapi.New(orders, log)
	srv := &http.Server{
		Addr:              cfg.Addr,
		Handler:           h.Routes(),
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
		IdleTimeout:       120 * time.Second,
	}

	g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
	g.Go(func() error {
		if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})
	g.Go(func() error {
		<-gctx.Done()
		sc, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 20*time.Second)
		defer cancel()
		return srv.Shutdown(sc)
	})
	return g.Wait()
}
The func run() error pattern

log.Fatal and os.Exit skip every deferred function, so a main full of them leaks connections, never flushes traces, and never closes files. Putting everything in a run() that returns an error means defer pool.Close() actually runs, and it makes the whole startup path callable from a test. It costs four lines and is the single highest-value structural habit in Go main functions.

When wiring gets big

ApproachWhen
Manual wiring in run()The default. Explicit, greppable, compiler-checked. Fine well past 50 dependencies
Group into an app structWhen run() passes 150 lines — bundle related adapters into sub-structs
google/wireCode generation at build time. Real value only in very large graphs; adds a generate step
uber-go/fx, digRuntime reflection DI. Moves wiring errors from compile time to startup — a poor trade for most Go teams
Do not build a layer you cannot justify

Hexagonal architecture earns its keep when there are genuinely multiple adapters, several transports, or domain logic complex enough to deserve isolation. A CRUD service with one database and one HTTP API does not need a repository interface, a service layer and a DTO for every entity — that is four files and three mapping functions to move a string. Start with handler plus store, and introduce the interface at the moment you have a second implementation or a test that demands it. Layers are easy to add later and painful to remove.

Interview follow-up

“Why does Go not use dependency-injection frameworks?” Because the language already gives you what they provide. Dependencies are struct fields set by a constructor, interfaces are satisfied implicitly so the concrete type never declares a binding, and the wiring is one function whose correctness the compiler checks completely. A reflection-based container converts those compile-time guarantees into startup-time panics and makes the dependency graph invisible to go to definition — which is a bad trade in a language whose main selling point is that you can read unfamiliar code and know what it does.

B05

Configuration and secrets

Configuration is the code path most likely to be wrong in an environment you cannot see. The fix is to load it once, validate it completely at startup, and refuse to start when it is invalid — not to discover a missing variable when the first request arrives.

The precedence order

defaults ◀ config file ◀ environment ◀ flags (in code) (optional) (deployment) (operator override) Each layer overrides the one to its left. Two consequences worth designing around: · every setting must have a sensible default, so a new deployment starts without a twelve-variable checklist · the flag layer exists so an operator can override one thing during an incident without redeploying What goes where: defaults timeouts, pool sizes, log level, feature flags off file per-environment structure (routes, limits, tiers) environment everything that differs per deployment, and everything secret flags operational overrides, and one-off tooling
go · one struct, one Load, validated once
package config

type Config struct {
	Addr            string        `env:"ADDR"             default:":8080"`
	LogLevel        slog.Level    `env:"LOG_LEVEL"        default:"info"`
	Env             string        `env:"ENV"              default:"development"`

	DatabaseURL     string        `env:"DATABASE_URL,required"`
	DBMaxConns      int32         `env:"DB_MAX_CONNS"     default:"25"`
	DBConnLifetime  time.Duration `env:"DB_CONN_LIFETIME" default:"30m"`

	RedisURL        string        `env:"REDIS_URL"`
	StripeKey       Secret        `env:"STRIPE_KEY,required"`
	JWTSigningKey   Secret        `env:"JWT_SIGNING_KEY,required"`

	RequestTimeout  time.Duration `env:"REQUEST_TIMEOUT"  default:"15s"`
	ShutdownTimeout time.Duration `env:"SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT" default:"20s"`
	OTLPEndpoint    string        `env:"OTLP_ENDPOINT"`
}

func Load() (*Config, error) {
	var c Config
	if err := env.Parse(&c); err != nil {        // caarlos0/env, or your own
		return nil, err
	}
	if err := c.validate(); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return &c, nil
}

// Validate EVERYTHING here. A service that starts with a bad config and
// fails on the first request has turned a deploy-time error into an
// incident — and the rollback signal is much weaker.
func (c *Config) validate() error {
	var errs []error
	if _, err := url.Parse(c.DatabaseURL); err != nil {
		errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf("DATABASE_URL: %w", err))
	}
	if c.DBMaxConns < 1 || c.DBMaxConns > 500 {
		errs = append(errs, errors.New("DB_MAX_CONNS must be 1..500"))
	}
	if c.RequestTimeout >= c.ShutdownTimeout {
		errs = append(errs, errors.New(
			"SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT must exceed REQUEST_TIMEOUT or requests are cut off"))
	}
	if c.Env == "production" {
		if len(c.JWTSigningKey) < 32 {
			errs = append(errs, errors.New("JWT_SIGNING_KEY too short for production"))
		}
		if c.OTLPEndpoint == "" {
			errs = append(errs, errors.New("OTLP_ENDPOINT required in production"))
		}
	}
	return errors.Join(errs...)
}
Fail fast, and say exactly what is wrong

The best configuration error names the variable, the value it received, and what it expected: SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT (10s) must exceed REQUEST_TIMEOUT (15s). Collect every problem with errors.Join rather than returning the first, so an operator fixes all five in one deploy instead of five. And validate cross-field relationships, not just individual values — most genuinely broken configurations are internally inconsistent rather than syntactically wrong.

A secret type that cannot be logged by accident

go · redaction enforced by the type system
type Secret string

// Covers fmt.Println, %v, %s, slog, and anything else that formats.
func (s Secret) String() string        { return "[REDACTED]" }
func (s Secret) GoString() string      { return "[REDACTED]" }
func (s Secret) LogValue() slog.Value  { return slog.StringValue("[REDACTED]") }
func (s Secret) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) { return []byte(`"[REDACTED]"`), nil }
func (s Secret) MarshalText() ([]byte, error) { return []byte("[REDACTED]"), nil }

// Reveal is the one deliberate escape hatch. It is greppable, which is
// the entire point: `grep -rn '.Reveal()'` audits every use.
func (s Secret) Reveal() string { return string(s) }

// Now this is safe:
log.Info("starting", "config", cfg)     // StripeKey prints as [REDACTED]
fmt.Printf("%+v\n", cfg)                // same
// And this is a deliberate, reviewable act:
client := stripe.New(cfg.StripeKey.Reveal())
Secrets leak through logs far more often than through breaches

The realistic path is: someone adds log.Info("config loaded", "cfg", cfg) for debugging, it ships, and the API key is now in your log aggregator — retained for 90 days, searchable by everyone with log access, and probably replicated to a third-party SaaS. A Secret type makes that impossible by construction rather than by review discipline. The same applies to error messages: a connection string in a wrapped error ends up in a 500 response body unless you are careful (B03).

Where secrets come from

SourceVerdict
Hardcoded in sourceNever. Git history is forever, and rotation means a deploy
.env committed to the repoNever. Same problem with extra steps
.env in .gitignore, local onlyFine for development
Environment variables from the orchestratorThe baseline. Visible in /proc/pid/environ and pod specs, so not perfect
Mounted files from a secret storeBetter — supports rotation without a restart, and is not in the process environment
Fetched at startup via workload identityBest. Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, GCP Secret Manager — no static credential exists at all
go · reading a mounted secret, with rotation support
// Kubernetes updates the file in place when the Secret changes, so a
// value read once at startup goes stale. Read through an atomic pointer
// and reload on change.
type RotatingSecret struct {
	path string
	v    atomic.Pointer[string]
}

func NewRotatingSecret(ctx context.Context, path string) (*RotatingSecret, error) {
	r := &RotatingSecret{path: path}
	if err := r.reload(); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	go func() {
		t := time.NewTicker(30 * time.Second)
		defer t.Stop()
		for {
			select {
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return
			case <-t.C:
				if err := r.reload(); err != nil {
					slog.Warn("secret reload failed", "path", path, "err", err)
				}
			}
		}
	}()
	return r, nil
}

func (r *RotatingSecret) reload() error {
	b, err := os.ReadFile(r.path)
	if err != nil { return err }
	s := strings.TrimSpace(string(b))
	r.v.Store(&s)
	return nil
}

func (r *RotatingSecret) Get() string { return *r.v.Load() }

Flags, for the operational layer

go · the standard library is enough for most binaries
func main() {
	var (
		addr    = flag.String("addr", ":8080", "listen address")
		level   = flag.String("log-level", "info", "debug|info|warn|error")
		dryRun  = flag.Bool("dry-run", false, "do not write anything")
		version = flag.Bool("version", false, "print version and exit")
	)
	flag.Parse()

	if *version {
		fmt.Println(buildinfo.String())
		return
	}
	...
}

// For multi-command tools (serve / migrate / worker), spf13/cobra is the
// convention. For a single binary, flag is fine and adds no dependency.

// Version information without a flag: the toolchain embeds VCS data.
import "runtime/debug"

func buildVersion() string {
	bi, ok := debug.ReadBuildInfo()
	if !ok { return "unknown" }
	var rev, dirty string
	for _, s := range bi.Settings {
		switch s.Key {
		case "vcs.revision": rev = s.Value
		case "vcs.modified": if s.Value == "true" { dirty = "-dirty" }
		}
	}
	return rev + dirty
}

Feature flags

Separate deploy from release

A feature flag lets you ship code dark, enable it for 1% of traffic, and turn it off in seconds without a rollback — which turns a risky release into a reversible experiment. Keep the evaluation cheap and local (an in-process cache refreshed in the background, never a network call per request), give every flag an owner and a removal date, and treat a flag that has been at 100% for a quarter as technical debt. The failure mode of flags is not the mechanism; it is a codebase with 200 of them and no idea which are live.

Interview follow-up

“How do you handle configuration across environments?” One Config struct with defaults, populated from the environment, validated completely at startup, and the process refuses to start if anything is wrong or missing. Environment variables rather than files for anything that differs per deployment, because that is what every orchestrator injects natively; secrets from a secret manager or a mounted file rather than baked into an image. The detail that signals experience is validating relationships between settings — a shutdown timeout shorter than the request timeout, a connection pool larger than the database's max_connections divided by the replica count — because those are the misconfigurations that pass a syntax check and cause an outage.

B06

Structured logging with slog

Go 1.21 added structured logging to the standard library, which ended a decade of every service picking a different logger. slog is fast enough, has a pluggable backend, and — most importantly — takes a context, which is what makes request correlation automatic.

Setup

go · JSON in production, text for humans
func newLogger(cfg *config.Config) *slog.Logger {
	opts := &slog.HandlerOptions{
		Level:     cfg.LogLevel,
		AddSource: cfg.Env != "production",    // file:line — useful, not free

		// Rewrite attributes globally: rename keys, redact, reformat.
		ReplaceAttr: func(groups []string, a slog.Attr) slog.Attr {
			switch a.Key {
			case slog.TimeKey:
				a.Key = "ts"                    // match your log platform
			case slog.MessageKey:
				a.Key = "msg"
			case "password", "token", "authorization", "set-cookie":
				return slog.String(a.Key, "[REDACTED]")
			}
			return a
		},
	}

	var h slog.Handler
	if cfg.Env == "production" {
		h = slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, opts)     // one JSON object per line
	} else {
		h = slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stdout, opts)     // or tint/devslog for colour
	}

	// Fields on EVERY line — this is what makes fleet-wide queries possible.
	log := slog.New(h).With(
		"service", "orders-api",
		"version", buildVersion(),
		"env", cfg.Env,
	)

	slog.SetDefault(log)    // so libraries using the package-level API agree
	return log
}

The API, and the one call you should prefer

go · three forms, increasing in both speed and verbosity
// 1. Alternating key/value — convenient, and allocates via `any`.
//    An odd number of arguments produces a "!BADKEY" entry rather than
//    a compile error, which is the price of the ergonomics.
log.Info("order placed", "order_id", o.ID, "total", o.Total())

// 2. Typed attributes — no boxing for the common types.
log.LogAttrs(ctx, slog.LevelInfo, "order placed",
	slog.String("order_id", o.ID),
	slog.Int64("total_cents", o.Total()),
	slog.Duration("took", elapsed),
)

// 3. Context-aware shorthands — ALWAYS prefer these in request code,
//    because the handler can pull the trace ID out of the context.
log.InfoContext(ctx, "order placed", "order_id", o.ID)
log.ErrorContext(ctx, "charge failed", "err", err, "order_id", o.ID)

// Grouping keeps related fields together in the output:
log.Info("request",
	slog.Group("http",
		slog.String("method", r.Method),
		slog.Int("status", status),
	),
)   // → {"http":{"method":"POST","status":201}}
LogValuer is how a type controls its own logging

Implement LogValue() slog.Value and the type decides what appears in every log line — redacting a secret, flattening a struct to an ID, or expanding into a group. It is also lazy: the method is only called if the record is actually emitted, so an expensive representation costs nothing at a level that is filtered out. This is the mechanism behind the Secret type in B05, and the right place to put "log a User as just its ID".

Request correlation, which is the whole point

go · a Handler that pulls trace and request IDs from the context
type ContextHandler struct{ slog.Handler }

func (h ContextHandler) Handle(ctx context.Context, r slog.Record) error {
	if id := reqctx.RequestID(ctx); id != "" {
		r.AddAttrs(slog.String("request_id", id))
	}
	// OpenTelemetry correlation: now every log line joins to its trace.
	if sc := trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx); sc.IsValid() {
		r.AddAttrs(
			slog.String("trace_id", sc.TraceID().String()),
			slog.String("span_id", sc.SpanID().String()),
		)
	}
	if u, ok := reqctx.User(ctx); ok {
		r.AddAttrs(slog.String("user_id", u.ID))
	}
	return h.Handler.Handle(ctx, r)
}

// Wrap it once at construction:
log := slog.New(ContextHandler{slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, opts)})

// Now every *Context call anywhere in the call graph is correlated,
// with no logger threading and no explicit fields at the call site.
What one request looks like in the aggregator: {"ts":"...","level":"INFO","msg":"http","request_id":"a3f…", "trace_id":"4bf92f…","route":"/v1/orders/{id}","status":200,"dur":"14ms"} {"ts":"...","level":"DEBUG","msg":"cache miss","request_id":"a3f…","key":"o:88"} {"ts":"...","level":"WARN","msg":"slow query","request_id":"a3f…","ms":412} One field — request_id — turns three unrelated lines into a story. One field — trace_id — joins those logs to the distributed trace and to the spans in your APM. Everything else in this chapter exists to make those two fields appear without anyone remembering to add them.

What to log, and at which level

LevelMeaningIn production
DebugDetail useful while diagnosingOff, or sampled. Enable per-request with a header if you can
InfoA thing happened that you would want in an auditOn. This is the default level
WarnDegraded but handled: a retry, a fallback, a stale cacheOn, and worth a dashboard
ErrorThe request failed and a human may need to knowOn, and alert on the rate, not on individual lines
Three logging mistakes that cost real money

1 · Logging in a hot loop. One line per iteration over ten thousand rows is ten thousand lines, and log ingestion is billed per gigabyte — logging bills exceeding compute bills is common and usually traceable to one such loop. 2 · Logging the same error at every layer. Handle it or return it, never both (L09). 3 · Logging personal data. Email addresses, full request bodies and authorisation headers in a 90-day-retention system is a GDPR problem and a breach waiting to be someone else's. Log IDs, not contents.

Making debug logs usable in production

go · per-request level override, and sampling
// A LevelVar can be changed at runtime — expose it on an admin endpoint
// so you can raise the level for five minutes during an incident and
// lower it again without a deploy.
var logLevel = new(slog.LevelVar)

mux.HandleFunc("PUT /admin/log-level", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	var lv slog.Level
	if err := lv.UnmarshalText([]byte(r.FormValue("level"))); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "bad level", http.StatusBadRequest); return
	}
	logLevel.Set(lv)
	slog.Warn("log level changed", "level", lv)
})

// Sampling: log the first N per second at full detail, then one in M.
// Essential for a high-volume warn that you still want some visibility of.
type SamplingHandler struct {
	slog.Handler
	limiter *rate.Limiter
}

func (h SamplingHandler) Handle(ctx context.Context, r slog.Record) error {
	if r.Level >= slog.LevelError || h.limiter.Allow() {
		return h.Handler.Handle(ctx, r)
	}
	return nil
}
Write to stdout and stop there

In a container, the platform collects stdout — so log rotation, file paths, and shipping agents inside your image are all solved problems you should not re-solve. A service writing to /var/log/app.log inside a container is writing into the ephemeral filesystem, will fill the node's disk, and loses everything on restart. The twelve-factor rule holds: treat logs as an event stream, write to stdout, and let the platform route them.

Interview follow-up

“Why structured logging rather than formatted strings?” Because a log line is data, not prose. log.Printf("order %s failed for user %s: %v", …) can only be searched with a regular expression that breaks the moment someone reorders the format, while {"order_id":"o_1","user_id":"u_9"} can be filtered, grouped and aggregated — "error rate by tenant for this endpoint over the last hour" becomes a query rather than an impossibility. The second reason is correlation: structured fields let you join logs to traces and metrics by ID, which is what turns three observability tools into one investigation.

B07

Databases: database/sql, pools and transactions

Go's database layer is a thin, honest wrapper around a connection pool. There is no ORM in the standard library and no magic — which means the pool settings, the context plumbing and the rows.Close discipline are yours, and all three are places services break under load.

The pool is the whole story

go · sql.DB is a POOL, not a connection
db, err := sql.Open("pgx", cfg.DatabaseURL)
if err != nil { return err }          // does NOT connect — it only validates the DSN
defer db.Close()

// Verify connectivity explicitly at startup, so a bad DSN fails the deploy.
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
defer cancel()
if err := db.PingContext(ctx); err != nil {
	return fmt.Errorf("database unreachable: %w", err)
}

db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)                 // hard ceiling; 0 = UNLIMITED (dangerous)
db.SetMaxIdleConns(25)                 // keep them warm — match MaxOpen
db.SetConnMaxLifetime(30 * time.Minute) // recycle: helps failover and LB rebalancing
db.SetConnMaxIdleTime(5 * time.Minute)  // release idle connections

// sql.DB is safe for concurrent use and is meant to be a long-lived
// singleton. Creating one per request is a common and expensive bug.
Sizing the pool — arithmetic, not intuition Postgres max_connections = 200 reserved for superuser + tooling = −20 ──── available to applications = 180 pods running = 12 other services sharing this database = 2 pools of 20 ──── per-pod budget = (180 − 40) / 12 ≈ 11 Bigger is not better. Postgres forks a process per connection; past a few hundred, context switching and lock contention make everything slower. A pool of 10 with queries queueing briefly beats a pool of 100 thrashing the server. The formula that matters: throughput = pool_size / query_latency. 25 connections × 5 ms queries = 5,000 queries/second per pod. If that is not enough, make the queries faster before making the pool bigger. And remember the multiplier: a HorizontalPodAutoscaler that scales to 60 pods silently multiplies your connection count by 5. Put a connection pooler (PgBouncer, transaction mode) in front, or cap the replica count against the database's limit.

Querying

go · the three shapes, with the mistakes marked
// ── one row ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
func (s *Store) Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (*Order, error) {
	var o Order
	err := s.db.QueryRowContext(ctx,
		`SELECT id, user_id, total_cents, status, version
		   FROM orders WHERE id = $1`, id,
	).Scan(&o.ID, &o.UserID, &o.Total, &o.Status, &o.Version)

	if errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) {
		return nil, order.ErrNotFound       // translate at the boundary
	}
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("get order %s: %w", id, err)
	}
	return &o, nil
}

// ── many rows ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
func (s *Store) List(ctx context.Context, userID string, limit int) ([]Order, error) {
	rows, err := s.db.QueryContext(ctx,
		`SELECT id, total_cents, status FROM orders
		  WHERE user_id = $1 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT $2`, userID, limit)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("list orders: %w", err)
	}
	defer rows.Close()          // MANDATORY — otherwise the connection leaks

	out := make([]Order, 0, limit)               // preallocate
	for rows.Next() {
		var o Order
		if err := rows.Scan(&o.ID, &o.Total, &o.Status); err != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("scan order: %w", err)
		}
		out = append(out, o)
	}
	// THE LINE EVERYONE FORGETS: rows.Next() returns false both at the
	// end and on error. Without this check, a mid-iteration failure
	// silently returns a partial result set as if it were complete.
	if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("iterate orders: %w", err)
	}
	return out, nil
}

// ── write ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
res, err := s.db.ExecContext(ctx,
	`UPDATE orders SET status = $1, version = version + 1
	  WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3`, status, id, expectedVersion)
if err != nil { return err }
n, _ := res.RowsAffected()
if n == 0 {
	return order.ErrConflict      // optimistic lock lost, or row is gone
}
Three leaks that look identical in production

A missing defer rows.Close(), a QueryRow whose Scan is skipped on an early return, and a transaction with no defer tx.Rollback() all hold a pooled connection forever. The symptom is always the same: requests start hanging in sql.(*DB).conn once the pool is exhausted, while the database itself looks idle. Watch db.Stats().WaitCount and WaitDuration — a rising wait count with low database CPU is this bug, not a slow database.

Transactions

go · the closure pattern makes rollback impossible to forget
func (s *Store) InTx(ctx context.Context, fn func(*sql.Tx) error) error {
	tx, err := s.db.BeginTx(ctx, &sql.TxOptions{
		Isolation: sql.LevelReadCommitted,
	})
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("begin: %w", err)
	}
	// Rollback after a successful Commit is a no-op returning ErrTxDone,
	// so this defer is safe on every path — including a panic.
	defer func() { _ = tx.Rollback() }()

	if err := fn(tx); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if err := tx.Commit(); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("commit: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

// Callers cannot get it wrong:
err := s.InTx(ctx, func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
	if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
		`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - $1 WHERE id = $2`, amt, from); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
		`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + $1 WHERE id = $2`, amt, to); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return nil
})
A transaction holds one connection for its entire lifetime

So a transaction that makes an HTTP call, waits on a lock, or loops over rows doing per-row work occupies a pool slot for that whole duration — and at a pool size of 25, twenty-five slow transactions stall every other query in the process. Keep transactions short and purely database-bound: gather data before Begin, call external systems after Commit, and never hold a transaction across a network call you do not control. This is also why SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a long transaction is such a reliable way to cause a production incident.

pgx, and why most Postgres services use it directly

database/sql + pgx stdlibpgx native
InterfacePortable across driversPostgres-specific
ProtocolFalls back to text for many typesBinary — faster, and type-exact
Postgres typesArrays, jsonb, ranges need wrappersNative
COPY bulk loadAwkwardCopyFrom, dramatically faster
LISTEN/NOTIFYNoYes
BatchingNoSendBatch — one round trip for many statements
Scanning into structsManualpgx.CollectRows + RowToStructByName
go · pgx native, with the ergonomics that justify it
pool, err := pgxpool.New(ctx, cfg.DatabaseURL)

// Struct scanning without a mapping layer:
rows, _ := pool.Query(ctx,
	`SELECT id, user_id, total_cents FROM orders WHERE user_id = $1`, userID)
orders, err := pgx.CollectRows(rows, pgx.RowToStructByName[Order])

// Bulk insert via COPY — orders of magnitude faster than looped INSERTs.
_, err = pool.CopyFrom(ctx,
	pgx.Identifier{"order_items"},
	[]string{"order_id", "sku", "qty"},
	pgx.CopyFromSlice(len(items), func(i int) ([]any, error) {
		return []any{orderID, items[i].SKU, items[i].Qty}, nil
	}),
)

// One round trip for a batch of statements:
batch := &pgx.Batch{}
for _, it := range items {
	batch.Queue(`INSERT INTO order_items (order_id, sku, qty) VALUES ($1,$2,$3)`,
		orderID, it.SKU, it.Qty)
}
if err := pool.SendBatch(ctx, batch).Close(); err != nil { return err }

Always use placeholders

Identifiers cannot be parameterised — allowlist them

Placeholders bind values, not table or column names, so dynamic ORDER BY $1 does not work. Never interpolate a user-supplied sort column or direction into the SQL string; map it through a fixed allowlist (map[string]string{"created": "created_at", "total": "total_cents"}) and reject anything absent. The same applies to dynamic IN lists — build the placeholder list from the slice length, not from the values.

Interview follow-up

“Your service starts timing out under load but the database CPU is low. What is happening?” Almost certainly connection-pool exhaustion rather than a slow database. Check db.Stats(): a high WaitCount and WaitDuration with InUse pinned at MaxOpenConns confirms it. The causes, in order of frequency: a leaked connection from a missing rows.Close() or an un-rolled-back transaction; a transaction held open across an external call; a pool sized too small for the concurrency; or an N+1 query pattern issuing hundreds of round trips per request. The goroutine dump makes it obvious — everything parked in database/sql.(*DB).conn.

B08

Data modelling, migrations and the repository

Go has no dominant ORM, and the community mostly regards that as a feature. This chapter covers the spectrum from hand-written SQL to full ORM, how to run migrations safely against a live service, and what a repository should and should not be.

The spectrum

ToolModelGood when
database/sql / pgxYou write SQL and scan manuallyFull control, no magic. Verbose for large structs
sqlcSQL → generated type-safe GoThe community default. Real SQL, compile-time-checked, zero runtime reflection
sqlxThin helpers over database/sqlStructScan and named parameters without generation
squirrel, goquQuery buildersGenuinely dynamic queries — filters that vary per request
entSchema-as-code, generated graph APIComplex relationship traversal; a large opinionated framework
GORMFull ORM, reflection-drivenRapid CRUD. Obscures the SQL, which is where the N+1s hide
sql · sqlc — write the query, get the Go
-- query.sql
-- name: GetOrder :one
SELECT id, user_id, total_cents, status, version, created_at
  FROM orders WHERE id = $1;

-- name: ListOrdersByUser :many
SELECT id, total_cents, status, created_at
  FROM orders
 WHERE user_id = $1 AND created_at > $2
 ORDER BY created_at DESC
 LIMIT $3;

-- name: UpdateOrderStatus :execrows
UPDATE orders SET status = $1, version = version + 1
 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3;
go · what sqlc generates, and why it is the sweet spot
// Generated — do not edit. Types come from the actual schema, so a
// renamed column is a COMPILE error rather than a runtime scan failure.
func (q *Queries) GetOrder(ctx context.Context, id string) (Order, error)
func (q *Queries) ListOrdersByUser(ctx context.Context, arg ListOrdersByUserParams) ([]ListOrdersByUserRow, error)
func (q *Queries) UpdateOrderStatus(ctx context.Context, arg UpdateOrderStatusParams) (int64, error)

// sqlc connects to your database (or reads the migrations) at generation
// time and verifies every query against the real schema. The result:
//   · you write and review real SQL — no query-builder dialect to learn
//   · no reflection at runtime, so it is as fast as hand-written code
//   · schema drift breaks `go build`, which is where you want it
//
// The cost is a generation step in the build, and dynamic queries still
// need a builder or hand-written SQL alongside.

Migrations

sql · one directory, numbered, forward and back
-- migrations/000004_add_order_currency.up.sql
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN currency text;
UPDATE orders SET currency = 'EUR' WHERE currency IS NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN currency SET NOT NULL;
ALTER TABLE orders ALTER COLUMN currency SET DEFAULT 'EUR';

-- migrations/000004_add_order_currency.down.sql
ALTER TABLE orders DROP COLUMN currency;
Expand / contract — the only safe way to change a live schema You cannot deploy code and schema at the same instant: during a rolling deploy, old and new code run simultaneously against one database. So every change is split across releases. Renaming a column, correctly: R1 Expand ADD COLUMN currency (nullable, no default rewrite — instant) deploy code that writes both old and new, reads old R2 Backfill batched UPDATE in the background never one statement over 50M rows R3 Switch deploy code that writes both, reads new R4 Contract deploy code that uses only new then DROP COLUMN old Four deploys to rename a column. That is the price of not having downtime, and every shortcut has taken someone's site down. Instant vs rewriting, in Postgres: ADD COLUMN nullable, no default instant ADD COLUMN with a constant default (11+) instant ADD COLUMN NOT NULL with no default rewrites the table CREATE INDEX locks writes CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY no write lock, slower, cannot run in a transaction ALTER COLUMN TYPE usually rewrites + locks
Never run migrations from an application's init or startup

With N replicas rolling out, N processes race to apply the same migration; most migration tools take an advisory lock, so N−1 pods block on startup, fail their readiness probe, and get killed — a self-inflicted outage during what should be a routine deploy. Run migrations as a separate step: a Kubernetes Job or Helm pre-upgrade hook, or an explicit CI step, that completes before the new pods roll. The application should verify the schema version at startup and refuse to run against an unexpected one, not apply it.

go · embedded migrations, applied by a separate command
import (
	"embed"
	"github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4"
	"github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4/source/iofs"
)

//go:embed migrations/*.sql
var migrationsFS embed.FS

// cmd/migrate/main.go — its own binary, built from the same image.
func migrateUp(dsn string) error {
	src, err := iofs.New(migrationsFS, "migrations")
