	if err != nil { return err }

	m, err := migrate.NewWithSourceInstance("iofs", src, dsn)
	if err != nil { return err }
	defer m.Close()

	if err := m.Up(); err != nil && !errors.Is(err, migrate.ErrNoChange) {
		return fmt.Errorf("migrate up: %w", err)
	}
	v, dirty, _ := m.Version()
	slog.Info("migrations applied", "version", v, "dirty", dirty)
	return nil
}

// Alternatives worth knowing: pressly/goose (Go migrations as well as
// SQL), atlas (declarative schema, diffs and lint rules for exactly the
// locking hazards above).

The repository, kept honest

go · translate at the boundary; leak nothing upward
package postgres

type OrderStore struct{ q *db.Queries }

var _ order.Store = (*OrderStore)(nil)     // compile-time conformance

func (s *OrderStore) Get(ctx context.Context, id string) (*order.Order, error) {
	row, err := s.q.GetOrder(ctx, id)
	if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
		return nil, order.ErrNotFound       // domain error, not a driver error
	}
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("get order: %w", err)
	}
	return toDomain(row), nil               // db row → domain type
}

func (s *OrderStore) Save(ctx context.Context, o *order.Order) error {
	n, err := s.q.UpdateOrderStatus(ctx, db.UpdateOrderStatusParams{
		Status: string(o.Status), ID: o.ID, Version: int32(o.Version),
	})
	if err != nil {
		var pgErr *pgconn.PgError
		if errors.As(err, &pgErr) && pgErr.Code == "23505" {
			return order.ErrConflict        // unique violation → domain meaning
		}
		return fmt.Errorf("save order: %w", err)
	}
	if n == 0 {
		return order.ErrConflict            // optimistic lock lost
	}
	return nil
}
A repository that returns *sql.Rows is not a repository

The point of the boundary is that nothing above it knows which database you use. Returning driver types, exposing a Query(sql string) method, or letting pgx.ErrNoRows travel into the HTTP handler all defeat that — and you discover it the day you try to write an in-memory fake and find you have to implement a SQL parser. Return domain types and domain errors, and keep every pgconn import inside one package.

Testing against a real database

go · testcontainers — the fake that cannot lie about SQL
func TestMain(m *testing.M) {
	ctx := context.Background()
	pg, err := postgres.Run(ctx, "postgres:16-alpine",
		postgres.WithDatabase("test"),
		testcontainers.WithWaitStrategy(
			wait.ForLog("database system is ready to accept connections").
				WithOccurrence(2).WithStartupTimeout(30*time.Second)),
	)
	if err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }

	dsn, _ := pg.ConnectionString(ctx, "sslmode=disable")
	if err := migrateUp(dsn); err != nil { log.Fatal(err) }
	testDSN = dsn

	code := m.Run()
	_ = pg.Terminate(ctx)
	os.Exit(code)
}

// Each test in its own transaction, rolled back — fast, and fully isolated
// so tests can run in parallel without interfering.
func withTx(t *testing.T) *sql.Tx {
	t.Helper()
	tx, err := testDB.BeginTx(context.Background(), nil)
	if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }
	t.Cleanup(func() { _ = tx.Rollback() })
	return tx
}
Mock the database only for the layers above it

An in-memory fake store is the right tool for testing business logic in the domain package — it is fast, deterministic, and you can make it return any error you want. It is the wrong tool for testing the SQL itself, because a fake that happily accepts your query proves nothing about whether Postgres will. Split it: fakes above the repository interface, a real containerised database at and below it.

Interview follow-up

“How do you add a NOT NULL column to a 100-million-row table with no downtime?” Never in one statement. Add it nullable with a constant default — instant in Postgres 11+ because the default is stored in the catalogue rather than written to every row — then deploy code that populates it on write, then backfill the existing rows in throttled batches of a few thousand with a pause between them so replication does not fall behind, then add the NOT NULL constraint (using NOT VALID plus VALIDATE CONSTRAINT to avoid a long exclusive lock). The signal an interviewer listens for is that you split it across multiple deploys because old and new code run at the same time.

B09

Caching, Redis and rate limiting

A cache is a correctness problem disguised as a performance problem. This chapter covers the three cache layers, the invalidation strategies that actually work, and rate limiting — which is the same machinery pointed at protecting yourself rather than speeding yourself up.

Three layers, three failure modes

1 In-process a map or an LRU in your own memory latency ~50 ns problem every replica has a different copy, so invalidation is a distributed problem and stale data differs per pod use for config, feature flags, small reference data, and anything where a few seconds of staleness is fine 2 Distributed Redis, Memcached latency ~0.5-2 ms (one network round trip) problem it is a dependency: it can be down, slow, or full, and your code must work when it is use for sessions, rendered pages, expensive query results, anything that must be consistent across replicas 3 CDN / HTTP Cache-Control, ETag, a reverse proxy latency 0 — the request never reaches you problem invalidation is someone else's API, and you cannot see what is cached use for static assets, public GET responses Always measure before adding one. A cache in front of a 2 ms query adds a dependency and a class of staleness bug to save 1.5 ms. A cache in front of a 400 ms aggregation earns its keep on the first request.

An in-process cache with TTL and singleflight

go · generic, bounded, and stampede-proof
type entry[V any] struct {
	val     V
	expires time.Time
}

type Cache[K comparable, V any] struct {
	mu    sync.RWMutex
	m     map[K]entry[V]
	ttl   time.Duration
	group singleflight.Group
	hits, misses atomic.Int64
}

func (c *Cache[K, V]) Get(ctx context.Context, k K,
	load func(context.Context) (V, error)) (V, error) {

	c.mu.RLock()
	e, ok := c.m[k]
	c.mu.RUnlock()
	if ok && time.Now().Before(e.expires) {
		c.hits.Add(1)
		return e.val, nil
	}
	c.misses.Add(1)

	// singleflight collapses N concurrent misses on the same key into
	// ONE call to load — without it, a popular key expiring sends every
	// in-flight request to the database at once (L14).
	v, err, _ := c.group.Do(fmt.Sprint(k), func() (any, error) {
		val, err := load(ctx)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		c.mu.Lock()
		c.m[k] = entry[V]{val: val, expires: time.Now().Add(c.jitteredTTL())}
		c.mu.Unlock()
		return val, nil
	})
	if err != nil {
		var zero V
		return zero, err
	}
	return v.(V), nil
}

// Jitter the TTL by ±10%. Without it, everything cached during a deploy
// expires in the same second and you get a synchronised stampede an
// hour later — a real and recurring production pattern.
func (c *Cache[K, V]) jitteredTTL() time.Duration {
	j := float64(c.ttl) * (0.9 + 0.2*rand.Float64())
	return time.Duration(j)
}
Use a real LRU for anything unbounded

The map above grows forever unless you evict. hashicorp/golang-lru/v2 gives you a size-bounded, generic, thread-safe cache in one line, and dgraph-io/ristretto adds admission control and per-item cost accounting for high-throughput use. An in-process cache with no size bound is a memory leak with a nicer name, and it usually surfaces as an OOM kill two weeks after launch.

Redis

go · cache-aside, with the failure path that matters
rdb := redis.NewClient(&redis.Options{
	Addr:         cfg.RedisAddr,
	PoolSize:     20,
	MinIdleConns: 5,
	DialTimeout:  2 * time.Second,
	ReadTimeout:  200 * time.Millisecond,   // AGGRESSIVE: a slow cache is
	WriteTimeout: 200 * time.Millisecond,   // worse than no cache
	MaxRetries:   2,
})

func (s *Service) GetUser(ctx context.Context, id string) (*User, error) {
	key := "user:" + id

	b, err := s.rdb.Get(ctx, key).Bytes()
	switch {
	case err == nil:
		var u User
		if json.Unmarshal(b, &u) == nil {
			return &u, nil
		}
		// Corrupt entry — fall through and reload rather than failing.
	case errors.Is(err, redis.Nil):
		// Normal miss.
	default:
		// CACHE IS DOWN. Log it, count it, and CONTINUE to the database.
		// A cache outage must degrade latency, never availability.
		s.metrics.cacheErrors.Inc()
		s.log.WarnContext(ctx, "redis get failed", "key", key, "err", err)
	}

	u, err := s.store.GetUser(ctx, id)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// Write-back is best effort, and must not block the response or
	// inherit the request's cancellation.
	go func() {
		bg, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.WithoutCancel(ctx), time.Second)
		defer cancel()
		if b, err := json.Marshal(u); err == nil {
			s.rdb.Set(bg, key, b, 10*time.Minute)
		}
	}()
	return u, nil
}
A cache must never be on the critical path for availability

If Redis being down makes your service return errors, you have not added a cache — you have added a single point of failure and made your uptime the product of two systems'. Every read path needs a fallback to the origin, every write to the cache needs to be best-effort, and the timeouts need to be short enough that a hung Redis costs milliseconds rather than the request. Test this deliberately: kill Redis in staging and confirm the service still serves, slower.

Invalidation

StrategyHowTrade
TTL onlyLet it expireSimplest and most robust. Stale for up to the TTL
Delete on writeDEL key after the database commitFresh, but a failed delete leaves it stale forever
Write-throughUpdate cache and database togetherNo miss after a write; two systems to keep consistent
Versioned keysuser:{id}:v{version}No invalidation at all — old versions just expire. Excellent
Tag / group flushTrack key sets, flush togetherPowerful, and the bookkeeping is where bugs live
Delete after the commit, not before — and accept the race

Deleting before the write means a concurrent reader can repopulate the cache from the old row before your transaction commits, leaving stale data with no TTL-independent way to notice. Deleting after narrows the window but does not close it. If correctness genuinely matters, use versioned keys so no invalidation is needed, or accept a short TTL as the backstop. There is no lock-free scheme that makes a cache and a database atomically consistent, and designs that claim to are usually hiding the race rather than removing it.

Rate limiting

go · per-key token bucket, in process
import "golang.org/x/time/rate"

type Limiter struct {
	mu       sync.Mutex
	limiters map[string]*rate.Limiter
	r        rate.Limit
	burst    int
}

func (l *Limiter) Allow(key string) bool {
	l.mu.Lock()
	lim, ok := l.limiters[key]
	if !ok {
		lim = rate.NewLimiter(l.r, l.burst)
		l.limiters[key] = lim        // NOTE: evict these, or it grows forever
	}
	l.mu.Unlock()
	return lim.Allow()
}

func RateLimit(l *Limiter) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			key := tenantOrIP(r)
			if !l.Allow(key) {
				w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "1")
				w.Header().Set("X-RateLimit-Limit", strconv.Itoa(l.burst))
				writeError(w, http.StatusTooManyRequests, "rate_limited",
					"too many requests")
				return
			}
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		})
	}
}
go · distributed limiting: the whole decision must be atomic
// In-process limiting with N replicas means the real limit is N × your
// configured rate, and it changes when the HPA scales. For a limit that
// is actually a limit, keep the counter in Redis — and do the read,
// compute and write in ONE round trip, or two requests race.
var tokenBucket = redis.NewScript(`
local key    = KEYS[1]
local rate   = tonumber(ARGV[1])   -- tokens per second
local burst  = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local cost   = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local b = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or burst
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now

tokens = math.min(burst, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= cost then
  tokens  = tokens - cost
  allowed = 1
end

redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, math.ceil(burst / rate) * 2)
return allowed
`)

func (l *RedisLimiter) Allow(ctx context.Context, key string) (bool, error) {
	n, err := tokenBucket.Run(ctx, l.rdb, []string{"rl:" + key},
		l.rate, l.burst, float64(time.Now().UnixNano())/1e9, 1).Int()
	if err != nil {
		return true, err     // FAIL OPEN: a broken limiter must not
	}                        // take down the service it protects
	return n == 1, nil
}
Rate limit by tenant, not by IP

IP-based limiting punishes everyone behind a corporate NAT or a mobile carrier and is trivially evaded by anyone who matters. Limit by the authenticated principal — API key, tenant, user — and keep IP limiting only for unauthenticated endpoints such as login and signup, where it is a brute-force defence rather than a fairness mechanism. And always return Retry-After: a 429 without it teaches clients to retry immediately, which is how a rate limit turns into a retry storm.

Interview follow-up

“A popular cache key expires and a thousand requests hit the database at once. What do you do?” That is a cache stampede, and there are three layers of defence. singleflight collapses concurrent misses for the same key into one origin call — the immediate fix, and one line. TTL jitter stops many keys expiring in the same second, which is what turns one stampede into a periodic one. And probabilistic early refresh — recomputing a value shortly before it expires, with a probability that rises as expiry approaches — means the key is usually already warm when it would have expired. Mention that the first is nearly free and the last is what large caches actually run.

B10

Authentication and authorization

Authentication answers "who are you"; authorization answers "may you". Go's standard library gives you the cryptography and leaves the policy to you — which is correct, and means the decisions in this chapter are yours to get right.

Passwords

go · hash with a memory-hard function, compare in constant time
import (
	"golang.org/x/crypto/argon2"
	"crypto/subtle"
	"crypto/rand"
)

// Argon2id is the current recommendation; bcrypt remains acceptable and
// is simpler. NEVER use SHA-256, MD5, or any fast hash: GPUs compute
// billions of those per second, so a leaked table is cracked in hours.
type params struct{ memory, iterations uint32; parallelism uint8; keyLen uint32 }

var defaultParams = params{memory: 64 * 1024, iterations: 3, parallelism: 2, keyLen: 32}

func HashPassword(pw string) (string, error) {
	salt := make([]byte, 16)
	if _, err := rand.Read(salt); err != nil {     // crypto/rand, never math/rand
		return "", err
	}
	k := argon2.IDKey([]byte(pw), salt, defaultParams.iterations,
		defaultParams.memory, defaultParams.parallelism, defaultParams.keyLen)

	// Store the parameters WITH the hash so they can be raised later
	// without invalidating existing passwords.
	return fmt.Sprintf("$argon2id$v=%d$m=%d,t=%d,p=%d$%s$%s",
		argon2.Version, defaultParams.memory, defaultParams.iterations,
		defaultParams.parallelism,
		base64.RawStdEncoding.EncodeToString(salt),
		base64.RawStdEncoding.EncodeToString(k)), nil
}

func VerifyPassword(pw, encoded string) (bool, error) {
	p, salt, want, err := decodeHash(encoded)
	if err != nil { return false, err }
	got := argon2.IDKey([]byte(pw), salt, p.iterations, p.memory, p.parallelism, p.keyLen)
	// Constant time: a byte-by-byte == leaks how many bytes matched
	// through timing, which is a real attack on remote services.
	return subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(got, want) == 1, nil
}
Four rules, and they are not negotiable

1 · Never store a password, only a hash from bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2id. 2 · Never use math/rand for anything security-related — it is deterministic and seedable; use crypto/rand. 3 · Compare secrets with subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, never ==. 4 · Return the same error and take roughly the same time for "unknown user" and "wrong password", or the login endpoint becomes a user-enumeration oracle — which means hashing a dummy password even when the user does not exist.

Sessions or tokens

Server-side sessionJWT
StateIn Redis or a databaseIn the token itself
RevocationImmediate — delete the rowHard — valid until expiry unless you keep a denylist
VerificationOne lookup per requestSignature check, no I/O
SizeA short opaque IDHundreds of bytes on every request
Best forBrowser apps, anything needing logoutService-to-service, short-lived access tokens
JWTs are overused, and the reason is revocation

"Stateless" sounds like a benefit until a user changes their password, an employee is offboarded, or a token leaks — and the token stays valid until it expires because nothing checks a server. The usual fix is a revocation list, at which point you are doing a lookup per request and have a session with extra cryptography. The design that actually works is a short-lived access token (5–15 minutes, stateless, no revocation needed because it expires fast) plus a long-lived refresh token that is stored server-side and can be revoked. For a plain browser app with a single backend, a server-side session cookie is simpler and better.

Verifying a JWT without shooting yourself

go · the algorithm check is the part people omit
import "github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v5"

func (v *Verifier) Verify(ctx context.Context, raw string) (*Claims, error) {
	var claims Claims
	tok, err := jwt.ParseWithClaims(raw, &claims,
		func(t *jwt.Token) (any, error) {
			// CRITICAL: pin the algorithm. Without this check an attacker
			// can present alg:"none", or hand you an HMAC token signed
			// with your PUBLIC key while you expected RS256.
			if _, ok := t.Method.(*jwt.SigningMethodRSA); !ok {
				return nil, fmt.Errorf("unexpected alg %v", t.Header["alg"])
			}
			kid, _ := t.Header["kid"].(string)
			return v.keys.PublicKey(ctx, kid)     // JWKS, cached with a TTL
		},
		jwt.WithValidMethods([]string{"RS256"}),  // belt and braces
		jwt.WithIssuer(v.issuer),                 // check iss
		jwt.WithAudience(v.audience),             // check aud
		jwt.WithLeeway(30*time.Second),           // clock skew
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("verify token: %w", err)
	}
	if !tok.Valid {
		return nil, errors.New("invalid token")
	}
	return &claims, nil
}
The two classic JWT vulnerabilities

The none algorithm: a token whose header says {"alg":"none"} with an empty signature, accepted by libraries that trust the header. Algorithm confusion: a service expecting RS256 receives an HS256 token signed with the RSA public key as the HMAC secret — and since the public key is public, anyone can mint valid tokens. Both are prevented by refusing to let the token choose its own verification method: pin the expected algorithm in code, and validate iss, aud and exp explicitly rather than assuming the library does.

Session cookies, set correctly

go · every flag here is load-bearing
func setSession(w http.ResponseWriter, id string, ttl time.Duration) {
	http.SetCookie(w, &http.Cookie{
		Name:     "session",
		Value:    id,                       // opaque random ID, not data
		Path:     "/",
		MaxAge:   int(ttl.Seconds()),
		HttpOnly: true,                     // JavaScript cannot read it → XSS
		Secure:   true,                     // HTTPS only → no network capture
		SameSite: http.SameSiteLaxMode,     // CSRF defence for cross-site POSTs
	})
}

func newSessionID() string {
	b := make([]byte, 32)
	_, _ = rand.Read(b)                     // crypto/rand
	return base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(b)
}

// Rotate the session ID on privilege change (login, role elevation) so a
// fixed session cannot be used to ride the upgrade — session fixation.
func login(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, u *User) error {
	_ = store.Delete(r.Context(), currentSessionID(r))
	id := newSessionID()
	if err := store.Create(r.Context(), id, u.ID, 24*time.Hour); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	setSession(w, id, 24*time.Hour)
	return nil
}

Authorization

go · check ownership at the data layer, not only in middleware
// Role checks in middleware handle the coarse cases:
func RequireRole(roles ...string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			u := reqctx.MustUser(r.Context())
			if !slices.Contains(roles, u.Role) {
				writeError(w, http.StatusForbidden, "forbidden", "")
				return
			}
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		})
	}
}

// But the dangerous bug is object-level: an authenticated user asking
// for someone ELSE's resource. Middleware cannot see that — only the
// query can. Scope every lookup by the principal:
func (s *Store) GetOrderForUser(ctx context.Context, orderID, userID string) (*Order, error) {
	// NOT: SELECT ... WHERE id = $1   then compare in Go and forget once.
	row := s.db.QueryRowContext(ctx,
		`SELECT id, total_cents FROM orders WHERE id = $1 AND user_id = $2`,
		orderID, userID)
	...
}

// Better still, make it structurally impossible: put the tenant in the
// connection (Postgres RLS with SET LOCAL app.tenant_id) so a query
// that forgets the filter returns nothing rather than everything.
Broken object-level authorization is the most common real API vulnerability

It is number one on the OWASP API list, and it is always the same shape: the endpoint authenticates correctly, then fetches by an ID taken from the URL without checking that the ID belongs to the caller. Changing /v1/orders/1042 to /v1/orders/1043 returns someone else's data. The defences that survive contact with a growing codebase are structural rather than disciplinary — scope every query by the principal, or enforce it in the database with row-level security — because a rule that relies on every future developer remembering will eventually be forgotten.

OAuth / OIDC, briefly

Authorization Code flow with PKCE — the only one you should use for a new application. Implicit is deprecated; password grant is dead. browser ──▶ /authorize (+ code_challenge) ──▶ identity provider user authenticates browser ◀── redirect with ?code=…&state=… ◀── your backend ──▶ /token (code + code_verifier + client_secret) your backend ◀── access_token, id_token, refresh_token What your code must check, every time: · state matches what you generated — this is the CSRF defence · the id_token signature, iss, aud, exp and nonce · the redirect URI is an exact match from an allowlist — never a prefix match, which open-redirects to an attacker Use golang.org/x/oauth2 plus coreos/go-oidc. Do not hand-roll the token exchange; the specification's sharp edges are all in the parts that look optional.
Interview follow-up

“How do you revoke a JWT?” Honestly: you cannot, which is the point of the design — a JWT is valid until it expires because verification involves no server. The workable answers are to keep access tokens short-lived (5–15 minutes) so the exposure window is small, and to hold the refresh token server-side where it can be revoked; or to maintain a denylist of revoked token IDs checked on every request, which reintroduces the lookup you were avoiding. A strong answer names the trade explicitly and adds that for a first-party browser application a server-side session is usually the better fit, because logout is a requirement, not a nicety.

B11

gRPC, protobuf and outbound HTTP

Two ways to call another service. gRPC gives you a schema, code generation and streaming; HTTP gives you universal reach. Both have defaults that will hurt you, and the client side is where most of the damage happens.

Protobuf and the service definition

protobuf · orders/v1/orders.proto
syntax = "proto3";
package orders.v1;
option go_package = "github.com/acme/service/gen/orders/v1;ordersv1";

import "google/protobuf/timestamp.proto";

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder   (GetOrderRequest)   returns (Order);
  rpc ListOrders (ListOrdersRequest) returns (stream Order);      // server stream
  rpc Ingest     (stream Event)      returns (IngestSummary);     // client stream
  rpc Sync       (stream Event)      returns (stream Ack);        // bidirectional
}

message Order {
  string id = 1;
  string user_id = 2;
  int64  total_cents = 3;
  Status status = 4;
  google.protobuf.Timestamp created_at = 5;
  repeated Item items = 6;
  reserved 7, 8;                  // never reuse a deleted field's number
  reserved "legacy_note";
}

enum Status {
  STATUS_UNSPECIFIED = 0;         // proto3 REQUIRES a zero value; make it
  STATUS_PENDING     = 1;         // "unspecified" so you can tell "not set"
  STATUS_PAID        = 2;         // from a real value
}
Wire compatibility: the rules that keep old clients working SAFE · add a new field with a new number · add a new method or a new service · add a new enum value (old clients see the zero value) · rename a field (the NUMBER is the identity, not the name) · rename a message or an enum BREAKING · change a field's number or its type · reuse a number that was ever used for something else ← use reserved · move a field into or out of a oneof · change a method's request or response type · rename a package or a service (these are on the wire) Enforce it in CI: buf breaking --against '.git#branch=main'. A broken proto in a monorepo of twenty services is not a code review problem, it is an outage across all twenty.

A gRPC server with the interceptors that matter

go · interceptors are gRPC's middleware
srv := grpc.NewServer(
	grpc.ChainUnaryInterceptor(
		recovery.UnaryServerInterceptor(),              // panic → codes.Internal
		otelgrpc.UnaryServerInterceptor(),              // tracing
		logging.UnaryServerInterceptor(interceptorLogger(log)),
		ratelimit.UnaryServerInterceptor(limiter),
		auth.UnaryServerInterceptor(authFunc),
		validator.UnaryServerInterceptor(),             // protoc-gen-validate
	),
	grpc.KeepaliveParams(keepalive.ServerParameters{
		MaxConnectionIdle: 5 * time.Minute,
		Time:              30 * time.Second,   // ping an idle client
		Timeout:           10 * time.Second,
	}),
	grpc.KeepaliveEnforcementPolicy(keepalive.EnforcementPolicy{
		MinTime:             10 * time.Second,  // reject clients pinging faster
		PermitWithoutStream: true,
	}),
	grpc.MaxRecvMsgSize(8<<20),                 // default is only 4 MiB
)

ordersv1.RegisterOrderServiceServer(srv, &orderServer{svc: orders})
reflection.Register(srv)        // enables grpcurl — remove in production,
                                // or gate it behind an internal port

// Errors carry a CODE, which is the whole point over HTTP status guessing.
func (s *orderServer) GetOrder(ctx context.Context, req *ordersv1.GetOrderRequest) (*ordersv1.Order, error) {
	o, err := s.svc.Get(ctx, req.GetId())
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, order.ErrNotFound):
		return nil, status.Errorf(codes.NotFound, "order %s not found", req.GetId())
	case errors.Is(err, order.ErrPermission):
		return nil, status.Error(codes.PermissionDenied, "forbidden")
	case err != nil:
		s.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "get order", "err", err)
		return nil, status.Error(codes.Internal, "internal error")
	}
	return toProto(o), nil
}

// Graceful shutdown: stop accepting, let in-flight RPCs finish.
go func() { <-ctx.Done(); srv.GracefulStop() }()
gRPC codeMeaningRetry?
InvalidArgumentThe request is malformedNo
NotFound, AlreadyExistsResource stateNo
PermissionDenied, UnauthenticatedAuthorizationNo
FailedPreconditionSystem state is wrong for this callNo
AbortedConcurrency conflictYes, at a higher level
ResourceExhaustedRate limited or out of quotaYes, with backoff
UnavailableTransient — the server is down or restartingYes
DeadlineExceededTimed outOnly if idempotent
Internal, UnknownA bugNo

The gRPC client

go · one connection, reused, with retry policy in config
// A ClientConn is a long-lived, concurrency-safe, multiplexed connection.
// Create it once at startup — NOT per request.
conn, err := grpc.NewClient(cfg.OrdersAddr,
	grpc.WithTransportCredentials(creds),
	grpc.WithChainUnaryInterceptor(otelgrpc.UnaryClientInterceptor()),
	grpc.WithDefaultServiceConfig(`{
	  "loadBalancingConfig": [{"round_robin":{}}],
	  "methodConfig": [{
	    "name": [{"service": "orders.v1.OrderService"}],
	    "timeout": "3s",
	    "retryPolicy": {
	      "maxAttempts": 4,
	      "initialBackoff": "0.1s",
	      "maxBackoff": "2s",
	      "backoffMultiplier": 2,
	      "retryableStatusCodes": ["UNAVAILABLE", "RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED"]
	    }
	  }]
	}`),
	grpc.WithKeepaliveParams(keepalive.ClientParameters{
		Time: 30 * time.Second, Timeout: 10 * time.Second, PermitWithoutStream: true,
	}),
)
defer conn.Close()

client := ordersv1.NewOrderServiceClient(conn)

// Deadlines propagate: the server sees the remaining budget in its
// context and stops work when the caller has given up.
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
defer cancel()
o, err := client.GetOrder(ctx, &ordersv1.GetOrderRequest{Id: id})
gRPC through a plain L4 load balancer breaks balancing

gRPC runs over HTTP/2 with long-lived multiplexed connections, so a TCP load balancer picks a backend once and every subsequent RPC on that connection goes to the same pod. New replicas receive no traffic, and one pod ends up carrying a client's entire load. The fixes are client-side load balancing with DNS or xDS resolution (the round_robin config above plus a headless service), an L7 proxy that understands HTTP/2 (Envoy, a service mesh, a gRPC-aware ingress), or MAX_CONNECTION_AGE on the server to force periodic reconnection.

Outbound HTTP: the default client is unsafe

go · never use http.DefaultClient in a service
// http.DefaultClient has NO TIMEOUT. One unresponsive upstream and your
// goroutines accumulate until the process dies. And http.DefaultTransport
// allows only 2 idle connections per host, so a busy client opens and
// closes TCP+TLS connections constantly.

var transport = &http.Transport{
	Proxy: http.ProxyFromEnvironment,
	DialContext: (&net.Dialer{
		Timeout:   3 * time.Second,
		KeepAlive: 30 * time.Second,
	}).DialContext,
	MaxIdleConns:          200,
	MaxIdleConnsPerHost:   100,     // default 2 — raise it for a hot upstream
	MaxConnsPerHost:       200,     // a ceiling, so you cannot flood a dependency
	IdleConnTimeout:       90 * time.Second,
	TLSHandshakeTimeout:   3 * time.Second,
	ExpectContinueTimeout: 1 * time.Second,
	ForceAttemptHTTP2:     true,
}

var client = &http.Client{
	Transport: transport,
	Timeout:   10 * time.Second,     // whole request, including body read
	CheckRedirect: func(r *http.Request, via []*http.Request) error {
		if len(via) >= 3 { return http.ErrUseLastResponse }
		return nil
	},
}

func (c *Client) GetUser(ctx context.Context, id string) (*User, error) {
	req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodGet, c.base+"/users/"+id, nil)
	if err != nil { return nil, err }
	req.Header.Set("Accept", "application/json")

	resp, err := c.http.Do(req)
	if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("get user: %w", err) }

	// MANDATORY: drain and close, or the connection cannot be reused and
	// you leak a descriptor per call.
	defer func() {
		_, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<10))
		_ = resp.Body.Close()
	}()

	if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusOK {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("get user: unexpected status %d", resp.StatusCode)
	}
	var u User
	if err := json.NewDecoder(io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 1<<20)).Decode(&u); err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("decode user: %w", err)
	}
	return &u, nil
}
Not closing the response body is the most common Go client bug

The body must be closed on every path including non-2xx responses, or the underlying connection is never returned to the pool — the symptom is a slowly climbing file-descriptor count and eventually dial tcp: too many open files. And closing without reading to the end also prevents reuse for keep-alive, so drain it first (bounded, so a huge error body cannot be used against you). One defer immediately after the error check covers both.

Interview follow-up

“When would you choose gRPC over REST?” For internal service-to-service traffic where both sides are yours: you get a schema enforced at compile time, generated clients in every language, binary encoding that is meaningfully smaller and faster, first-class streaming, deadline propagation across hops, and a status-code vocabulary that says whether a failure is retryable. For a public API, REST over JSON, because every client on earth can call it without tooling and it is debuggable with curl. The pragmatic middle ground worth mentioning is Connect or gRPC-Gateway, which serve the same protobuf definition over both.

B12

Background jobs, queues and the outbox

Anything slow, retryable, or not needed before the response belongs off the request path. The mechanics are easy; the correctness — exactly-once semantics that do not exist, and the dual-write problem — is what this chapter is about.

What belongs in the background

Move it off the request whenExample
It is slow and the user does not need the resultSending email, generating a PDF, resizing an image
It can fail independently and should be retriedWebhook delivery, third-party sync
It is scheduledNightly reports, expiring trials, cleanup
It fans outOne order → inventory, billing, analytics, search index
It would couple you to a dependency's uptimeAnything that must survive the other system being down
go doSomething() in a handler is not a background job

It has no retry, no persistence, no visibility and no backpressure — and the moment the pod is rescheduled, scaled down, or simply restarted during a deploy, every in-flight goroutine is destroyed silently. The email is never sent, and nothing anywhere records that. A background job must survive process death, which means it must be written down somewhere durable before the request returns. If losing the work is genuinely acceptable, say so in a comment; otherwise it needs a queue.

Picking a queue

BackendGood forWatch
Postgres table (SKIP LOCKED)Start here. Transactional with your data, no new infrastructure, easy to inspectTops out around a few thousand jobs/second
Redis (asynq, river)Fast, scheduling and retries built inDurability depends on Redis persistence config
NATS JetStreamLightweight streaming, at-least-onceLess ecosystem than Kafka
KafkaHigh throughput, replay, event sourcing, many consumersReal operational weight; ordering only within a partition
SQS / Pub-SubManaged, scales itselfAt-least-once; SQS standard does not preserve order
sql · a Postgres queue that is genuinely correct
CREATE TABLE jobs (
  id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  kind        text        NOT NULL,
  payload     jsonb       NOT NULL,
  run_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  attempts    int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  max_attempts int        NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,
  locked_at   timestamptz,
  last_error  text
);

-- Partial index: only pending rows are indexed, so it stays small even
-- when the table holds millions of completed jobs.
CREATE INDEX jobs_pending ON jobs (run_at) WHERE locked_at IS NULL;

-- FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is what makes this safe with N workers: each
-- worker takes different rows instead of blocking on the same one.
UPDATE jobs SET locked_at = now(), attempts = attempts + 1
 WHERE id = (
   SELECT id FROM jobs
    WHERE locked_at IS NULL AND run_at <= now() AND attempts < max_attempts
    ORDER BY run_at
    FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
    LIMIT 1
 )
RETURNING id, kind, payload, attempts;

The dual-write problem, and the outbox

The bug: two writes to two systems cannot be atomic. tx.Commit() order saved ✓ kafka.Publish(OrderPlaced) process dies ✗ → the order exists and nobody downstream knows Reverse the order and you get the opposite failure: an event for an order that was never saved. There is no ordering that fixes this. The transactional outbox: write the event to the SAME database, in the SAME transaction, and let a separate process publish it. ┌─────────────────── one transaction ───────────────────┐ │ INSERT INTO orders (…) │ │ INSERT INTO outbox (topic, payload) │ └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ relay (a goroutine, or Debezium/CDC) ▼ ┌─────────────┐ │ Kafka/NATS │ ──▶ consumers └─────────────┘ │ mark outbox row published Now the order and the intent to publish commit together or not at all. The relay can crash and retry; the worst case is publishing an event twice, which is why consumers must be idempotent — see below.
go · writing to the outbox, and relaying from it
func (s *Service) Place(ctx context.Context, o *Order) error {
	return s.store.InTx(ctx, func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
		if err := insertOrder(ctx, tx, o); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		payload, _ := json.Marshal(OrderPlaced{OrderID: o.ID, Total: o.Total()})
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
			`INSERT INTO outbox (topic, key, payload) VALUES ($1,$2,$3)`,
			"orders.placed", o.ID, payload)
		return err            // both rows commit together, or neither does
	})
}

func (r *Relay) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	t := time.NewTicker(200 * time.Millisecond)
	defer t.Stop()
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return ctx.Err()
		case <-t.C:
			if err := r.flush(ctx); err != nil {
				r.log.Error("outbox flush", "err", err)
			}
		}
	}
}

func (r *Relay) flush(ctx context.Context) error {
	rows, err := r.db.QueryContext(ctx,
		`SELECT id, topic, key, payload FROM outbox
		  WHERE published_at IS NULL ORDER BY id
		  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 100`)
	// ... publish each, then UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() ...
	// If the publish succeeds and the UPDATE fails, the event is sent
	// twice. That is the accepted trade: at-least-once, never zero.
	_ = rows
	return err
}

Exactly-once does not exist. Idempotency does.

go · make the consumer safe to run twice
// Every delivery system is at-least-once in the presence of failure.
// So the question is never "how do I deliver once" — it is "how do I
// make processing twice indistinguishable from processing once".

// 1. A dedupe table, written in the same transaction as the effect.
func (w *Worker) Handle(ctx context.Context, msg Message) error {
	return w.db.InTx(ctx, func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
			`INSERT INTO processed_messages (id) VALUES ($1)`, msg.ID)
		var pg *pgconn.PgError
		if errors.As(err, &pg) && pg.Code == "23505" {
			return nil                 // already handled — silently succeed
		}
		if err != nil { return err }
		return w.apply(ctx, tx, msg)   // the effect commits with the marker
	})
}

// 2. Natural idempotency — an upsert or a set is inherently safe.
//    UPDATE orders SET status = 'paid' WHERE id = $1
//    is fine to run a hundred times. `balance = balance + $1` is not.

// 3. An idempotency key supplied by the caller, for HTTP APIs:
//    POST /v1/payments with header `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>`
//    Store key → response. A repeat returns the ORIGINAL response
//    rather than charging again. This is how Stripe's API works, and
//    it is the right pattern for any endpoint that moves money.
Ordering is weaker than people assume

Kafka guarantees order only within a partition, so events for one aggregate must share a partition key — usually the entity ID. SQS standard queues do not preserve order at all (FIFO queues do, at much lower throughput). And even with ordered delivery, retries reorder things: message 1 fails and is redelivered after message 2 succeeds. Design consumers so that out-of-order arrival is survivable — carry a version or a timestamp in the event and ignore anything older than what you have already applied.

Retries, backoff and the dead-letter queue

go · exponential backoff with full jitter
func backoff(attempt int) time.Duration {
	const base, max = 500 * time.Millisecond, 5 * time.Minute
	d := min(time.Duration(float64(base)*math.Pow(2, float64(attempt))), max)
	// FULL jitter: a random point in [0, d). Without it, everything that
	// failed during an outage retries in the same millisecond when the
	// dependency recovers — and knocks it straight back over.
	return time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(d)))
}

// A job that has failed max_attempts times goes to a dead-letter queue
// rather than retrying forever or being dropped. The DLQ is not a
// graveyard: alert on its depth, because a non-empty DLQ means work
// that a customer expected to happen has not happened.
func (w *Worker) run(ctx context.Context, j Job) {
	err := w.handlers[j.Kind](ctx, j.Payload)
	switch {
	case err == nil:
		w.complete(ctx, j.ID)
	case errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent) || j.Attempts >= j.MaxAttempts:
		w.deadLetter(ctx, j, err)      // stop retrying; alert
	default:
		w.reschedule(ctx, j.ID, backoff(j.Attempts), err)
	}
}
Distinguish permanent failures from transient ones

Retrying a malformed payload five times with exponential backoff wastes twenty minutes and then dead-letters it anyway — it was never going to succeed. Have handlers return a typed ErrPermanent (or wrap one) for validation failures, 4xx responses from upstreams, and anything where the input is the problem; retry only genuine transients such as timeouts, 5xx, and connection errors. The metric that tells you whether you got this right is the ratio of retries to successes.

Interview follow-up

“You save an order to Postgres and publish an event to Kafka. The process dies between them. What happens?” That is the dual-write problem, and no ordering of the two operations fixes it — you either lose the event or publish an event for an order that does not exist. The standard answer is a transactional outbox: insert the event into an outbox table inside the same database transaction as the order, then have a relay (a polling goroutine, or change-data-capture with Debezium) publish rows and mark them sent. That converts an impossible atomicity problem into at-least-once delivery, which is solvable — provided consumers are idempotent, which you should say in the same breath.

B13

Testing

Go's testing story is deliberately minimal: no assertion library, no mocking framework, no BDD syntax. What you get is a runner, subtests, coverage, benchmarks, fuzzing and httptest — and the community convention of writing tests as ordinary Go with table-driven cases.

Table-driven tests

go · the dominant Go test shape, and why
func TestParseDuration(t *testing.T) {
	tests := []struct {
		name    string
		in      string
		want    time.Duration
		wantErr bool
	}{
		{"seconds",      "30s",  30 * time.Second, false},
		{"minutes",      "5m",   5 * time.Minute,  false},
		{"compound",     "1h30m", 90 * time.Minute, false},
		{"zero",         "0",    0,                false},
		{"empty",        "",     0,                true},
		{"no unit",      "30",   0,                true},
		{"negative",     "-5s",  -5 * time.Second, false},
		{"overflow",     "9999999999h", 0,         true},
	}

	for _, tt := range tests {
		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			t.Parallel()                       // subtests run concurrently
			got, err := ParseDuration(tt.in)
			if (err != nil) != tt.wantErr {
				t.Fatalf("ParseDuration(%q) error = %v, wantErr %v", tt.in, err, tt.wantErr)
			}
			if got != tt.want {
				t.Errorf("ParseDuration(%q) = %v, want %v", tt.in, got, tt.want)
			}
		})
	}
}

// Adding a case is one line. Each subtest is independently named,
// runnable (-run 'TestParseDuration/overflow') and reported.

// t.Error  — record a failure, CONTINUE (check several things)
// t.Fatal  — record and STOP this test (nothing after makes sense)
// t.Skip   — skip, with a reason
// t.Helper — exclude this function from the reported line number
// t.Cleanup— run at the end of THIS test, even on failure — better than defer
//            because it also fires for subtests and parallel tests
t.Parallel() and shared state

A parallel subtest pauses, lets the parent return, and resumes once the parent's sequential work is done — which means any defer in the parent runs before the parallel subtests execute. Use t.Cleanup instead, which is ordered correctly. Also note that before Go 1.22 the loop variable was shared, so tt had to be copied (tt := tt) or every parallel subtest saw the last case; in a module declaring go 1.22 or later that copy is unnecessary — but you will still see it in existing code.

Fakes, not mocks

A fake is thirty lines and you write it once

Because Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly and the ones you define are small (L06), a fake is usually a map plus a mutex plus an error-injection hook. It is real Go — you can put invariant checks inside it, it works for concurrent tests, and it does not break when you reorder calls. Reach for gomock or mockery when an interface is genuinely large and third-party, or when the interaction is the thing under test ("did we call Charge exactly once?"). For everything else, the fake is less code and a better test.

Testing HTTP handlers

go · httptest, both directions
// ── your handler, with no server ──────────────────────────────────────
func TestCreateOrder(t *testing.T) {
	h := NewHandler(order.NewService(&fakeStore{}, &fakePayments{}, …))

	body := strings.NewReader(`{"user_id":"u_1","items":[{"sku":"a","qty":2}]}`)
	req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, "/v1/orders", body)
	req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
	rec := httptest.NewRecorder()

	h.Routes().ServeHTTP(rec, req)

	if rec.Code != http.StatusCreated {
		t.Fatalf("status = %d, want 201; body = %s", rec.Code, rec.Body)
	}
	var got Order
	if err := json.Unmarshal(rec.Body.Bytes(), &got); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("decode: %v", err)
	}
	if got.ID == "" {
		t.Error("expected an order ID")
	}
}

// ── a fake UPSTREAM, for testing your client ──────────────────────────
func TestPaymentsClient(t *testing.T) {
	srv := httptest.NewServer(http.HandlerFunc(
		func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			if got := r.Header.Get("Authorization"); got != "Bearer test" {
				t.Errorf("auth header = %q", got)
			}
			w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
			_, _ = w.Write([]byte(`{"id":"ch_1","status":"succeeded"}`))
		}))
	defer srv.Close()

	c := payments.New(srv.URL, "test")     // point the client at the fake
	ch, err := c.Charge(context.Background(), "u_1", 4999)
	...
}

// httptest.NewTLSServer + srv.Client() gives you a TLS upstream with a
// client already configured to trust its certificate.

Golden files

go · for anything whose expected output is large
var update = flag.Bool("update", false, "update golden files")

func TestRenderInvoice(t *testing.T) {
	got := RenderInvoice(testInvoice)
	golden := filepath.Join("testdata", t.Name()+".golden")

	if *update {
		if err := os.WriteFile(golden, got, 0o644); err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }
		return
	}
	want, err := os.ReadFile(golden)
	if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }
	if diff := cmp.Diff(string(want), string(got)); diff != "" {
		t.Errorf("mismatch (-want +got):\n%s", diff)
	}
}

// go test ./... -update    regenerates. REVIEW the diff before committing —
// the whole value of a golden file is that an unexpected change is visible
// in code review, and blindly regenerating destroys that.
//
// testdata/ is special: the go tool ignores it, so anything in there is
// never compiled or treated as a package.

Fuzzing

go · coverage-guided fuzzing, built in since 1.18
func FuzzParseOrder(f *testing.F) {
	// Seeds: known-interesting inputs, including past bug reports.
	f.Add([]byte(`{"id":"o_1","total":100}`))
	f.Add([]byte(`{}`))
	f.Add([]byte(`{"total":-1}`))

	f.Fuzz(func(t *testing.T, data []byte) {
		o, err := ParseOrder(data)
		if err != nil {
			return              // rejecting bad input is correct
		}
		// Properties that must hold for ANY accepted input:
		if o.Total < 0 {
			t.Errorf("accepted a negative total: %d", o.Total)
		}
		// Round-trip: encode(decode(x)) must decode identically.
		b, err := json.Marshal(o)
		if err != nil { t.Fatal(err) }
		o2, err := ParseOrder(b)
		if err != nil { t.Fatalf("re-parse failed: %v", err) }
		if !reflect.DeepEqual(o, o2) {
			t.Errorf("round-trip mismatch")
		}
	})
}

// go test -fuzz=FuzzParseOrder -fuzztime=60s ./...
// A crash is written to testdata/fuzz/ and becomes a permanent regression
// test that runs in the normal `go test` from then on.
Fuzz anything that parses untrusted bytes

Protocol decoders, JSON and YAML handling, URL and header parsing, template rendering, decompression, image handling. Fuzzing finds the inputs no human writes a test case for — deeply nested structures, integer overflow at boundaries, slices of length zero — and in Go it costs one function and a minute in CI. The properties worth asserting are usually "does not panic", "round-trips", and "never produces an invalid internal state".

The test pyramid, and running it

the commands
$ go test ./...                            # everything
$ go test -run 'TestOrder/create' ./internal/order   # one subtest
$ go test -race ./...                      # ALWAYS in CI
$ go test -count=1 ./...                   # defeat the test cache
$ go test -short ./...                     # skip slow ones (testing.Short())
$ go test -tags=integration ./...          # build-tag gated
$ go test -timeout=60s ./...               # panic with all stacks on hang
$ go test -v ./... 2>&1 | go tool test2json # machine-readable

# coverage
$ go test -coverprofile=c.out ./... && go tool cover -html=c.out
$ go test -coverprofile=c.out -covermode=atomic ./...   # with -race
$ go tool cover -func=c.out | tail -1
total:    (statements)    78.4%

# flaky-test hunting: run it twenty times with shuffled order
$ go test -count=20 -shuffle=on -race ./internal/order
Coverage is a diagnostic, not a target

A line is "covered" if it executed, not if its behaviour was checked — a test with no assertions gives 100% coverage and zero confidence. Mandating a number produces tests written to satisfy the number: trivial getters tested, error paths ignored because they are hard to reach. The useful ways to read coverage are as a map of what is untested (open the HTML and look for red in the error handling) and as a ratchet (fail the build if coverage drops on changed files), not as a KPI.

Interview follow-up

“How do you test code that depends on time?” Never with time.Sleep — that makes the test slow and flaky simultaneously. Inject the clock: a clock func() time.Time field, or a small Clock interface with Now and After, defaulting to the real implementation and replaced with a controllable fake in tests. Then "the token expires after an hour" is an instant, deterministic assertion rather than an hour-long test. The same pattern — inject the dependency, default to the real thing — is the answer for randomness, UUIDs and anything else nondeterministic, and Go 1.25's testing/synctest now does it for the whole runtime clock in concurrent tests.

B14

Observability: metrics, traces and health

Logs tell you what happened to one request. Metrics tell you what is happening to all of them. Traces tell you where the time went across services. A production Go service needs all three, and OpenTelemetry now provides a single way to emit them.

Metrics: RED and USE

RED — for anything that serves requests Rate requests per second, by route and method Errors failed requests per second, by route and status class Duration a HISTOGRAM, so you can compute p50/p95/p99 USE — for anything that is a resource Utilisation how busy: CPU %, pool in-use / pool size Saturation the queue: pool WaitCount, run-queue depth, lag Errors failures: connection errors, timeouts Saturation is the one people omit and the one that predicts outages. Utilisation at 80% is information; a connection-pool wait count that just became non-zero is a warning that arrives before the latency does. Four golden signals (Google's phrasing) = latency, traffic, errors, saturation — the same list with different names.
go · Prometheus metrics, with the cardinality rules obeyed
var (
	httpRequests = promauto.NewCounterVec(prometheus.CounterOpts{
		Name: "http_requests_total",
		Help: "Total HTTP requests.",
	}, []string{"route", "method", "status"})        // BOUNDED labels only

	httpDuration = promauto.NewHistogramVec(prometheus.HistogramOpts{
		Name: "http_request_duration_seconds",
		Help: "HTTP request latency.",
		// Buckets must bracket your SLO. Default buckets top out at 10s,
		// which is useless for a service with a 200ms target.
		Buckets: []float64{.005, .01, .025, .05, .1, .25, .5, 1, 2.5, 5},
	}, []string{"route", "method"})

	dbPoolInUse = promauto.NewGaugeFunc(prometheus.GaugeOpts{
		Name: "db_pool_in_use",
	}, func() float64 { return float64(db.Stats().InUse) })

	dbPoolWaits = promauto.NewCounterFunc(prometheus.CounterOpts{
		Name: "db_pool_wait_total",             // SATURATION — alert on this
	}, func() float64 { return float64(db.Stats().WaitCount) })
)

// Serve /metrics on the INTERNAL port, next to pprof (R07).
internal := http.NewServeMux()
internal.Handle("/metrics", promhttp.Handler())
go http.ListenAndServe("127.0.0.1:6060", internal)
Cardinality is how you take down your monitoring system

Every distinct label-value combination is a separate time series, stored and indexed forever. A user_id label with a million users is a million series; a raw URL path with IDs in it is unbounded. A histogram multiplies that by its bucket count — so ten buckets and three label values each is not 3 series but 3 × 10 × 3. Labels must come from a small, closed set: route pattern, method, status class, region, queue name. Anything unbounded belongs in a log or a trace, which are built for high cardinality.

OpenTelemetry tracing

go · setup, and the shape of an instrumented call
func initTracing(ctx context.Context, cfg *config.Config) (func(context.Context) error, error) {
	exp, err := otlptracegrpc.New(ctx,
		otlptracegrpc.WithEndpoint(cfg.OTLPEndpoint),
		otlptracegrpc.WithInsecure(),
	)
	if err != nil { return nil, err }

	tp := sdktrace.NewTracerProvider(
		sdktrace.WithBatcher(exp),                  // batch, never sync
		sdktrace.WithResource(resource.NewWithAttributes(
			semconv.SchemaURL,
			semconv.ServiceName("orders-api"),
			semconv.ServiceVersion(buildVersion()),
			semconv.DeploymentEnvironment(cfg.Env),
		)),
		// ParentBased keeps a trace whole: if the caller sampled it, we do
		// too. Sampling independently per service produces broken traces.
		sdktrace.WithSampler(sdktrace.ParentBased(
			sdktrace.TraceIDRatioBased(cfg.TraceSampleRate))),
	)
	otel.SetTracerProvider(tp)
	// W3C tracecontext is what propagates the trace across HTTP and gRPC.
	otel.SetTextMapPropagator(propagation.NewCompositeTextMapPropagator(
		propagation.TraceContext{}, propagation.Baggage{}))
	return tp.Shutdown, nil        // flush on exit, or you lose the last spans
}

var tracer = otel.Tracer("github.com/acme/service/internal/order")

func (s *Service) Place(ctx context.Context, userID string, items []Item) (*Order, error) {
	ctx, span := tracer.Start(ctx, "order.Place",
		trace.WithAttributes(
			attribute.String("user.id", userID),
			attribute.Int("order.item_count", len(items)),
		))
	defer span.End()

	o, err := s.doPlace(ctx, userID, items)
	if err != nil {
		span.RecordError(err)
		span.SetStatus(codes.Error, err.Error())   // marks the span as failed
		return nil, err
	}
	span.SetAttributes(attribute.String("order.id", o.ID))
	return o, nil
}
What a trace buys you that metrics cannot POST /v1/orders 412 ms ├─ auth.verify 2 ms ├─ order.Place 408 ms │ ├─ payments.Charge 380 ms ◀── here it is │ │ └─ HTTP POST api.stripe.com 375 ms │ ├─ postgres INSERT orders 6 ms │ └─ kafka publish 3 ms (async, links to a consumer span) └─ encode response 1 ms Metrics told you p99 went from 90 ms to 400 ms. The trace tells you which of eleven downstream calls caused it, on which request, with the arguments attached. That is the difference between knowing you have a problem and knowing where it is. Instrument the boundaries first — inbound HTTP/gRPC, outbound HTTP, database, cache, queue. The libraries do this for you: otelhttp.NewHandler · otelhttp.NewTransport otelgrpc interceptors · otelpgx · otelsql · otelredis Hand-written spans are for your own domain operations, not plumbing.
Sample by trace, and keep the errors

Tracing every request at scale is expensive to store and rarely more informative than tracing 1–10%. Use ParentBased head sampling so the decision is made once at the edge and respected by every downstream service — independent per-service sampling produces traces with holes in them. Better still, if your backend supports it, use tail sampling at the collector: buffer complete traces and keep 100% of the ones containing an error or exceeding a latency threshold, plus a small random sample of the rest. That is the configuration that makes traces useful during incidents.

Health checks

go · liveness and readiness are different questions
// LIVENESS: "is this process wedged?" — must check NOTHING external.
// A liveness probe that pings the database restarts every pod in the
// fleet when the database has a blip, turning a degradation into an
// outage. This is a genuinely common and very damaging misconfiguration.
mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
})

// READINESS: "should this pod receive traffic right now?" — checks the
// dependencies it cannot serve without. Failing readiness removes the
// pod from the load balancer; it does not restart it.
mux.HandleFunc("GET /readyz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second)
	defer cancel()

	if shuttingDown.Load() {
		http.Error(w, "shutting down", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
		return
	}
	if err := db.PingContext(ctx); err != nil {
		http.Error(w, "database unavailable", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
		return
	}
	// Redis is a CACHE: its absence degrades, it does not disqualify.
	// Do not fail readiness on an optional dependency.
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
})

// STARTUP: for slow boots — caches to warm, migrations to verify.
// Kubernetes disables liveness and readiness until this passes.
mux.HandleFunc("GET /startupz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	if !initialised.Load() {
		http.Error(w, "starting", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
		return
	}
	w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
})

Alert on symptoms

Alert onNot on
Error rate above the SLO budget burnA single 500
p99 latency above target for 5 minutesOne slow request
Goroutine count rising for 30 minutesA goroutine spike
Connection-pool waits becoming non-zeroCPU at 70%
Queue lag or DLQ depth growingA single retry
Certificate expiring in 14 daysDisk at 60%
Every alert must be actionable at 3am

If the runbook says "check whether it recovers", it is a dashboard, not an alert. Page on user-visible symptoms — requests failing, latency above the SLO, work not being processed — and leave causes to the investigation. The reason is practical rather than philosophical: cause-based alerts multiply (there are fifty ways to make requests slow) and they fire during events that users never notice, which is how a team learns to ignore the pager.

Interview follow-up

“What is the difference between liveness and readiness, and why does it matter?” Liveness asks whether the process should be killed and restarted; readiness asks whether it should receive traffic right now. The consequence of confusing them is severe: a liveness probe that checks the database means a thirty-second database blip restarts every pod simultaneously, and the resulting cold caches and reconnect storm turn a brief degradation into a full outage. Liveness should check only that the process itself is responsive — no dependencies — while readiness checks the things the pod genuinely cannot serve without, and must also start failing at the beginning of shutdown so traffic drains before the server stops accepting.

P01

Building and shipping

A Go build is one command, which makes it easy to ship something subtly wrong: an unversioned binary, a build that differs between your machine and CI, or a 30 MB artefact with debug symbols. This chapter is the build you actually want in a pipeline.

The production build command

bash · every flag here earns its place
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

VERSION=${VERSION:-$(git describe --tags --always --dirty)}
COMMIT=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
DATE=$(git show -s --format=%cI HEAD)      # commit date, NOT `date` —
                                            # `date` makes builds unreproducible

CGO_ENABLED=0 \
GOOS=linux GOARCH=amd64 \
go build \
  -trimpath \
  -buildvcs=true \
  -ldflags="-s -w \
    -X main.version=${VERSION} \
    -X main.commit=${COMMIT} \
    -X main.date=${DATE}" \
  -o bin/app ./cmd/api

#  -trimpath        strip absolute paths from the binary: smaller, no
#                   /Users/you/ leaked, and REQUIRED for reproducibility
#  -s -w            drop the symbol table and DWARF: ~25-30% smaller.
#                   Panics still show function names (that is pclntab,
#                   not DWARF) but you lose debugger support.
#  -buildvcs        embed the VCS revision and dirty state
#  CGO_ENABLED=0    fully static: runs on scratch, alpine, anywhere
go · reading version info back out, with and without ldflags
package main

// Set by -ldflags. Must be package-level STRING vars; the linker cannot
// set a const, a struct field, or anything typed.
var (
	version = "dev"
	commit  = "none"
	date    = "unknown"
)

// Or skip ldflags entirely: the toolchain embeds VCS data automatically.
func buildInfo() string {
	bi, ok := debug.ReadBuildInfo()
	if !ok {
		return version
	}
	var rev, t, dirty string
	for _, s := range bi.Settings {
		switch s.Key {
		case "vcs.revision": rev = s.Value[:min(12, len(s.Value))]
		case "vcs.time":     t = s.Value
		case "vcs.modified": if s.Value == "true" { dirty = "+dirty" }
		}
	}
	return fmt.Sprintf("%s (%s%s, %s, %s)", bi.Main.Version, rev, dirty, t, bi.GoVersion)
}

// Expose it. Every service should answer "what version are you?" three
// ways: a flag, an endpoint, and a metric with a constant value of 1.
mux.HandleFunc("GET /version", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	_ = json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(map[string]string{
		"version": version, "commit": commit, "date": date, "go": runtime.Version(),
	})
})
A build_info metric is worth more than it looks

promauto.NewGaugeFunc with labels version, commit and go_version, always set to 1, lets you answer "which version is each pod running?" from the same dashboard as your error rate — and it makes "the error rate rose at 14:03" and "the deploy landed at 14:02" the same graph. Grafana joins on it with * on(instance) group_left(version) build_info.

Reproducible builds

A reproducible build produces a byte-identical binary from the same source, on any machine, at any time. That matters because it is what lets a third party verify that the artefact in your registry was built from the commit it claims. What breaks it, and the fix: absolute paths in the binary → -trimpath a timestamp from date → use the commit date a different Go toolchain → pin it (toolchain go1.24.2 in go.mod, and in the Dockerfile) a different module version → go.sum already guarantees this CGO linking against system libs → CGO_ENABLED=0 embedded hostname / user / env → do not Verify it: go build -trimpath -o a ./cmd/api go build -trimpath -o b ./cmd/api sha256sum a b → the two hashes must match Then go further: sign the artefact and publish provenance. cosign sign --yes ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:… cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp … Keyless signing via OIDC ties the signature to the GitHub Actions workflow that produced it, with no key to leak.

An SBOM and a vulnerability gate

the supply-chain steps that belong in every pipeline
$ go install golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest
$ govulncheck ./...
Scanning your code and 412 packages across 38 dependent modules...

Vulnerability #1: GO-2024-2687
    HTTP/2 CONTINUATION flood in net/http
  More info: https://pkg.go.dev/vuln/GO-2024-2687
  Standard library
    Found in: net/http@go1.22.0
    Fixed in: net/http@go1.22.2
    Example traces found:
      #1: internal/http/server.go:41:23: httpapi.Routes calls http.Server

# govulncheck is better than a generic scanner because it does REACHABILITY
# analysis: it reports a CVE only if your code can actually reach the
# vulnerable function. That turns a wall of 200 findings into the three
# that matter, which is the difference between a gate people respect and
# one they disable.

$ syft dir:. -o spdx-json=sbom.json       # software bill of materials
$ grype sbom:sbom.json --fail-on high     # scan the SBOM
$ cosign attest --predicate sbom.json --type spdxjson $IMAGE

The CI pipeline for a Go service

yaml · .github/workflows/ci.yml — the stages that matter
name: ci
on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-go@v5
        with:
          go-version-file: go.mod      # single source of truth for the version
          cache: true                  # caches GOMODCACHE and GOCACHE

      # Fail on anything that would change a committed file.
      - run: go mod tidy && git diff --exit-code go.mod go.sum
      - run: test -z "$(gofmt -l .)" || { gofmt -l .; exit 1; }
      - run: go vet ./...
      - uses: golangci/golangci-lint-action@v6

      - run: go build ./...
      - run: go test -race -coverprofile=cover.out -covermode=atomic ./...
      - run: go test -tags=integration ./...

      - run: go run golang.org/x/vuln/cmd/govulncheck@latest ./...

  build:
    needs: test
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write
      id-token: write                  # required for keyless cosign signing
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with: { fetch-depth: 0 }       # so `git describe` sees tags
      - uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          platforms: linux/amd64,linux/arm64
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/acme/api:${{ github.sha }}
          provenance: true
          sbom: true
Tag images by digest, never by latest

A mutable tag means the thing you tested and the thing that runs can differ — a rollback to v1.4.0 can pull a different image than the one that was there before, and "it works in staging" stops being evidence. Deploy by immutable digest (ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:…), keep the semantic tag as a human-readable alias, and make the deployment manifest record the digest. This is also what makes signature verification meaningful: a signature covers a digest, not a tag.

Multiple binaries, one module

makefile · the Makefile most Go services end up with
VERSION ?= $(shell git describe --tags --always --dirty)
LDFLAGS := -s -w -X main.version=$(VERSION)
BINARIES := api worker migrate

.PHONY: all test lint build clean

all: lint test build

build: $(BINARIES)

$(BINARIES):
	CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" \
		-o bin/$@ ./cmd/$@

test:
	go test -race -count=1 ./...

lint:
	gofmt -l . | tee /dev/stderr | (! read)
	go vet ./...
	golangci-lint run

generate:
	go generate ./...
	sqlc generate
	buf generate

clean:
	rm -rf bin/
Pin your tools the same way you pin your dependencies

A tools.go file with a build tag and blank imports of sqlc, mockgen, buf and the rest puts those tools in go.mod, so every developer and every CI run uses the same version — instead of whatever go install …@latest happened to fetch that day. Go 1.24 formalised this with a tool directive in go.mod and go get -tool, which is now the preferred spelling. A generated file that differs between machines is almost always an unpinned generator.

Interview follow-up

“Why would you set CGO_ENABLED=0?” To get a fully static binary with no libc dependency, which means it runs on scratch and on Alpine, cross-compiles without a C toolchain, and cannot break because the base image's glibc version changed. The costs are worth naming: you lose any package that needs cgo, and Go's pure-Go DNS resolver is used instead of the system one — which behaves differently for some /etc/nsswitch.conf configurations and for certain corporate DNS setups. For a typical containerised service, it is the right default; for something linking SQLite or a C library, it is not available and you use a distroless base with the matching libc instead.

P02

Containerising Go

Go containers should be small, static and boring. A correct Dockerfile is about fifteen lines — and the ways people get it wrong (a 900 MB image, a missing CA bundle, PID 1 that ignores SIGTERM) are all avoidable with the same template.

The Dockerfile

dockerfile · multi-stage, cached, minimal
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1

# ---- build ----------------------------------------------------------
FROM golang:1.24-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src

# Copy the manifests FIRST. This layer is cached until a dependency
# changes, so an ordinary code edit skips the download entirely.
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod go mod download

COPY . .

ARG VERSION=dev
ARG TARGETOS TARGETARCH          # supplied automatically by buildx

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/go/pkg/mod \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/go-build \
    CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=$TARGETOS GOARCH=$TARGETARCH \
    go build -trimpath -ldflags="-s -w -X main.version=${VERSION}" \
      -o /out/app ./cmd/api

# ---- runtime --------------------------------------------------------
FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian12:nonroot
COPY --from=build /out/app /app

USER nonroot:nonroot             # UID 65532 — never run as root
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["/app"]              # EXEC form: the binary is PID 1 and
                                 # receives SIGTERM directly
Base imageSizeContainsUse when
scratch0Nothing at allStatic binary, no TLS, no timezones, no user database
distroless/static~2 MBCA certs, tzdata, /etc/passwd, nonroot userThe default for a static Go binary
distroless/base~20 MB+ glibcCGO_ENABLED=1 against glibc
alpine~8 MB+ a shell and busyboxWhen you genuinely need to exec into it. musl, not glibc
debian:slim~80 MBA real distributionComplex native dependencies
Three things scratch does not have, and the symptoms

1 · CA certificates — every outbound HTTPS call fails with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. 2 · /etc/passwd — os/user lookups fail, and USER nonroot has no name to resolve. 3 · tzdata — time.LoadLocation("Europe/Berlin") returns an error, so anything rendering local times silently falls back to UTC. Distroless static includes all three, which is why it is the better default. If you must use scratch, copy the certs in explicitly and import _ "time/tzdata" to embed the timezone database in the binary.

Layer caching, in the right order

Docker caches per layer and invalidates everything after the first changed one. So order instructions least- to most-frequently changed: FROM golang:1.24-alpine changes monthly WORKDIR /src COPY go.mod go.sum ./ changes weekly RUN go mod download ◀── cached across every code edit COPY . . changes constantly RUN go build … Putting COPY . . before go mod download re-downloads every dependency on every single build. It is the most common Dockerfile mistake in any language, and in Go it costs a minute per build. BuildKit cache mounts go further: --mount=type=cache on /go/pkg/mod and /root/.cache/go-build persists the module cache and the compilation cache between builds, even when the layer is invalidated. A rebuild after a one-line change goes from ~90 s to ~10 s. .dockerignore matters too — without it, COPY . . ships your .git directory, local binaries and node_modules into the build context, invalidating the cache whenever any of them change: .git bin/ *.pprof .env

PID 1, signals and shutdown

dockerfile · the exec form is not a style preference
# SHELL form — Docker wraps this in `/bin/sh -c`. The shell becomes PID 1,
# it does NOT forward SIGTERM to your binary, and Kubernetes ends up
# SIGKILLing your process after the grace period. In-flight requests die.
ENTRYPOINT /app --config /etc/app.yaml        # WRONG

# EXEC form — your binary is PID 1 and receives signals directly.
ENTRYPOINT ["/app", "--config", "/etc/app.yaml"]    # RIGHT

# If you genuinely need a shell wrapper, exec into the binary so it
# REPLACES the shell rather than running as a child:
#   #!/bin/sh
#   exec /app "$@"
A Go binary as PID 1 has no zombie reaper

PID 1 is normally responsible for reaping orphaned child processes, and a plain Go binary does not do that. This only matters if your service spawns subprocesses — most do not — but if it does, defunct entries accumulate until the process table fills. The fix is a minimal init: tini as the entrypoint, or shareProcessNamespace / the pause container in Kubernetes, which already reaps for you in most configurations.

Kubernetes: the manifest a Go service wants

yaml · every field here fixes a specific Go failure mode
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45     # MUST exceed preStop + Shutdown
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api@sha256:9f2c...   # digest, not a tag
          ports: [{containerPort: 8080}]

          env:
            # The single most important Go setting in Kubernetes (R03).
            - name: GOMAXPROCS
              valueFrom:
                resourceFieldRef: {resource: limits.cpu}
            # Soft memory ceiling below the hard limit (R04).
            - name: GOMEMLIMIT
              value: "450MiB"

          resources:
            requests: {cpu: "500m", memory: "256Mi"}
            limits:   {memory: "512Mi"}      # NOTE: no CPU limit — see below

          # Liveness checks NOTHING external.
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
            periodSeconds: 10
            failureThreshold: 3

          # Readiness checks required dependencies, and starts failing
          # the moment shutdown begins.
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /readyz, port: 8080}
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 2

          startupProbe:
            httpGet: {path: /healthz, port: 8080}
            failureThreshold: 30
            periodSeconds: 2                 # up to 60s to boot

          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              # Endpoint removal is ASYNCHRONOUS. Without this sleep, the
              # server stops accepting while the load balancer is still
              # sending traffic — visible to users as 502s on every deploy.
              exec: {command: ["/bin/sleep", "10"]}

          securityContext:
            runAsNonRoot: true
            runAsUser: 65532
            readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
            allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
            capabilities: {drop: ["ALL"]}
The shutdown sequence, and why the numbers must line up t=0 kubectl delete / rollout ├─▶ pod marked Terminating ├─▶ preStop hook runs (sleep 10) └─▶ endpoint removal starts ← asynchronous, and slower than you expect t=10 preStop returns → SIGTERM sent └─▶ your signal.NotifyContext fires ├─▶ readiness starts failing └─▶ srv.Shutdown(ctx) drains in-flight requests t=30 Shutdown completes, process exits 0 t=45 SIGKILL if still alive (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) The invariant: preStop + Shutdown timeout < terminationGracePeriodSeconds Get it wrong and Kubernetes kills the process mid-request. The preStop sleep is not a hack — it is the documented way to wait out the race between endpoint propagation and SIGTERM.
Do not set a CPU limit on a latency-sensitive Go service

CPU limits are enforced by CFS quota: the container gets N milliseconds of CPU per 100 ms period and is then hard-stopped until the next period, even if the node is idle. For a Go service this is brutal — a GC cycle or a burst of goroutines exhausts the quota and every in-flight request stalls for the rest of the period, producing a p99 many times the p50 with CPU utilisation that looks low. Set CPU requests for scheduling and leave limits off; use GOMAXPROCS matched to the request to keep the runtime honest. Memory limits, by contrast, you absolutely do set — there is no graceful throttling for memory, only the OOM killer.

Interview follow-up

“Your Go service returns 502s during every deploy. Why?” Almost always the shutdown race. When a pod is deleted, SIGTERM and endpoint removal happen in parallel, and endpoint propagation to every kube-proxy and ingress takes a second or more — so the server stops accepting while traffic is still being routed to it. The fix has three parts: a preStop sleep long enough to cover propagation, a readiness probe that starts failing immediately on SIGTERM, and srv.Shutdown to drain in-flight requests, with the grace period set longer than the two combined. Mentioning that the preStop sleep exists specifically because endpoint removal is asynchronous is the detail that shows you have debugged this rather than read about it.

P03

Runtime tuning in production

Go has few knobs, which is a feature — but the three that exist matter enormously in a container, and their defaults are wrong there. This chapter is the settings checklist and the numbers to watch afterwards.

The three settings, and what each fixes

SettingDefaultIn a container, set it toFixes
GOMAXPROCSNumCPU() — the node's coresthe pod's CPU limit or requestContext-switch thrash, CFS throttling, p99 blowout
GOMEMLIMITunset (∞)~75-80% of the memory limitOOM kills from GC running too late
GOGC100off when GOMEMLIMIT is set, else 200-400GC CPU burned while memory is free
The combination that works, for a 512 MiB / 2-core pod: resources: requests: {cpu: "2", memory: "512Mi"} limits: {memory: "512Mi"} no CPU limit env: GOMAXPROCS: "2" from limits.cpu, or automaxprocs GOMEMLIMIT: "400MiB" ~78% of the memory limit GOGC: "off" Why GOGC=off with a memory limit is the right pairing: GOGC=100 alone collects every time the heap doubles, even with 300 MB free. Wasted CPU. GOMEMLIMIT alone GOGC still fires at 2× live heap first, so the limit rarely engages. GOGC=off + GOMEMLIMIT collects only under memory pressure. Uses the memory you paid for; never exceeds it. Typically 10-30% CPU back. The headroom matters. GOMEMLIMIT covers the Go heap, stacks and runtime structures — but not cgo allocations, not memory-mapped files, and not the kernel's page cache for your process. 20-25% below the container limit is the safe margin.
go · setting them from inside the program, when env vars are not available
import (
	"runtime/debug"
	_ "go.uber.org/automaxprocs"      // reads the cgroup quota at init
)

func init() {
	// If you cannot use automaxprocs, read the cgroup v2 quota yourself:
	//   /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max  →  "200000 100000" = 2 cores
	// Go 1.25 makes the runtime cgroup-aware by default; until every
	// service is on it, be explicit.

	// Derive GOMEMLIMIT from the container limit rather than hardcoding,
	// so resizing the pod does not require a code change.
	if lim, err := cgroupMemoryLimit(); err == nil && lim > 0 {
		debug.SetMemoryLimit(int64(float64(lim) * 0.78))
		debug.SetGCPercent(-1)        // equivalent to GOGC=off
	}
}

func cgroupMemoryLimit() (uint64, error) {
	b, err := os.ReadFile("/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max")     // cgroup v2
	if err != nil {
		b, err = os.ReadFile("/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes")
		if err != nil { return 0, err }
	}
	s := strings.TrimSpace(string(b))
	if s == "max" { return 0, errors.New("no limit set") }
	return strconv.ParseUint(s, 10, 64)
}
Verify, do not assume — log the effective values at startup

The number of services running with GOMAXPROCS=64 on a two-core pod because someone assumed the orchestrator handled it is very large.
