Log runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0), debug.SetMemoryLimit(-1) (which reads without setting) and runtime.NumCPU() on the first line of every service, and put go_sched_gomaxprocs_threads on your dashboard. It costs one log line and it is the first thing you will want during a latency investigation.

The numbers to watch after tuning

a healthy Go service, and what "unhealthy" looks like in each
go_goroutines                          ~2-5 per concurrent request
   rising monotonically for >30 min  → leak (L14, R10)

go_memstats_heap_inuse_bytes           sawtooth, flat trend
   rising trend across sawteeth      → leak. Watch THIS, not RSS.

go_gc_duration_seconds{quantile="1"}   < 1 ms
   > 10 ms                           → huge live heap, or swapping

rate(go_gc_cycles_total[5m])           < 1/s under steady load
   many per second                    → allocation churn (R02)

GC CPU fraction (gctrace "3%")         < 5%
   > 10%                             → allocation pressure or GOGC too low

go_sched_latencies_seconds p99         < 1 ms
   > 10 ms                            → CPU starvation / GOMAXPROCS wrong

container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds    0
   anything non-zero                  → a CPU limit is hurting you

go_threads                             ≈ GOMAXPROCS + a few
   hundreds                           → blocking syscalls or cgo (R03)

Memory that looks like a leak but is not

RSS stays high after the heap shrinks. Go returns freed pages to the OS lazily, via the background scavenger. RSS is therefore a poor leak signal and a good OOM-killer signal — which is why you alert on the live heap but still set GOMEMLIMIT below the container limit. GODEBUG=madvdontneed=1 release more eagerly (Linux) debug.FreeOSMemory() force it now — expensive; use after a large one-off load, not on a timer The four real leak shapes in Go, and how each looks: 1 Goroutine leak go_goroutines rises; heap rises with it (each holds a 2 KB+ stack and its captures) → pprof goroutine, group by state 2 Unbounded cache heap rises smoothly, goroutines flat → pprof heap -inuse_space; look for a map 3 Slice/substring pin heap much larger than the data you think you hold → a small slice pinning a big array (L07). slices.Clone fixes it. 4 Fragmentation heap in-use flat, RSS high, many size classes → rare, and usually means variable large allocations. Pool or normalise sizes.

Stacks, threads and file descriptors

go · the limits that bite at scale, and how to raise them
// Goroutine stacks start at 2 KB and GROW by copying, doubling as
// needed, up to 1 GB (debug.SetMaxStack). Deep recursion in a service
// with 100k goroutines is a memory problem long before it is a crash.

// Thread limit: 10,000 by default. Hitting it is fatal and the message
// is explicit. It means blocking syscalls or cgo calls are holding Ms.
debug.SetMaxThreads(15000)       // raise ONLY after understanding why

// File descriptors: the usual production ceiling. Each connection,
// each open file and each pooled database connection is one.
//   ulimit -n                    → often 1024 by default; 65536 is sane
//   /proc/<pid>/limits           → what the process actually has
//   ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l    → what it is using
// In Kubernetes, set it in the pod spec or the container runtime config;
// `too many open files` under load is almost always this plus a leaked
// response body (B11).

// Watch all three as metrics:
//   process_open_fds / process_max_fds
//   go_threads
//   go_memstats_stack_inuse_bytes
Profile-guided optimisation belongs in this chapter too

Once the runtime settings are right, PGO is the cheapest remaining win: collect a 30-second CPU profile from a production pod, commit it as default.pgo next to main.go, and the compiler uses it automatically — more aggressive inlining of hot functions and devirtualisation of hot interface calls, typically 2–14% CPU for no code change (R09). Refresh it when the workload shifts meaningfully; a stale profile degrades to no benefit rather than harm.

A tuning checklist

plaintext · in order, because each step changes the next
1  GOMAXPROCS matches the pod's CPU allocation          ← do this FIRST
2  No CPU limit on latency-sensitive services
3  GOMEMLIMIT at ~78% of the memory limit, GOGC=off
4  Effective values logged at startup and exported as metrics
5  pprof + /metrics on a private port in every environment
6  Baseline profile captured while healthy, and stored
7  Alert on: goroutines, live heap, sched latency p99, CFS throttling
8  Load test to the knee; record requests-per-pod capacity
9  PGO profile committed and refreshed quarterly
10 Re-measure after every one of the above — in that order
Interview follow-up

“A Go service in Kubernetes has p50 of 15 ms and p99 of 900 ms, at 25% CPU. Where do you start?” With GOMAXPROCS and CFS throttling, before touching any code. Low average CPU with a huge tail is the signature of the container mismatch: the runtime sees the node's 64 cores, creates 64 Ps for a two-core quota, and the pod is hard-stopped at the end of each CFS period — so requests unlucky enough to be running then stall for the remainder. Confirm it with container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total and the scheduler-latency histogram, fix it with GOMAXPROCS from the limit and by removing the CPU limit, and only then take an execution trace if the tail persists.

P04

Resilience in Go

Every network call fails eventually. Resilience is the set of decisions you make in advance about what happens then — and in Go those decisions are mostly about contexts, bounded concurrency, and knowing when not to retry.

Timeouts: a budget, spent downward

Every call gets a deadline, and every deadline is smaller than its caller's. Context makes this automatic — WithTimeout on a context that already has a shorter deadline keeps the shorter one. client ─── 30 s ────────────────────────────────────▶ your API ─── 10 s ──────────────────────────────▶ auth check ─ 500 ms ─▶ database query ──── 3 s ──────▶ payments API ──────── 5 s ───────────▶ ↳ retry 1 ── 2 s ──▶ ↳ retry 2 ── 2 s ──▶ The budget must leave room for the retries. A 5 s deadline with three 2 s attempts means attempt three never runs — you configured three retries and get two. Size the outer deadline as attempts × (attempt_timeout + backoff), or use a per-attempt timeout derived from the remaining budget. And a timeout you cannot enforce is not a timeout. A handler with a 10 s context that calls a library ignoring contexts will run as long as it likes; the context only stops what checks it.
go · per-attempt deadlines carved from the remaining budget
func (c *Client) callWithRetry(ctx context.Context, req *Request) (*Response, error) {
	const maxAttempts = 3
	var lastErr error

	for attempt := 0; attempt < maxAttempts; attempt++ {
		if attempt > 0 {
			d := backoff(attempt)
			// Wait, but give up immediately if the parent is done —
			// never time.Sleep in a retry loop.
			select {
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return nil, fmt.Errorf("after %d attempts: %w", attempt, ctx.Err())
			case <-time.After(d):
			}
		}

		// Per-attempt timeout, capped by what is left of the budget.
		attemptCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, c.perAttempt)
		resp, err := c.do(attemptCtx, req)
		cancel()

		if err == nil {
			return resp, nil
		}
		lastErr = err
		if !retryable(err) {
			return nil, err           // 4xx, validation — retrying cannot help
		}
	}
	return nil, fmt.Errorf("after %d attempts: %w", maxAttempts, lastErr)
}

func retryable(err error) bool {
	// Never retry a cancelled parent, and never retry a permanent error.
	if errors.Is(err, context.Canceled) { return false }

	var ne net.Error
	if errors.As(err, &ne) && ne.Timeout() { return true }

	var he *HTTPError
	if errors.As(err, &he) {
		return he.Status == 429 || he.Status == 502 ||
			he.Status == 503 || he.Status == 504
	}
	return errors.Is(err, syscall.ECONNRESET) || errors.Is(err, io.ErrUnexpectedEOF)
}
Only retry idempotent operations, and add a retry budget

A POST /payments that times out may well have succeeded — the response was lost, not the charge. Retrying double-charges. Make such calls idempotent with a client-supplied idempotency key (B12) and retry safely, or do not retry at all. Separately, cap retries fleet-wide: a retry budget that allows retries only while they are under ~10% of total requests means that when a dependency is genuinely down, retries stop instead of tripling the load on a system already failing. Retry storms turn partial outages into total ones more reliably than almost anything else.

Circuit breakers

A breaker stops you hammering something that is already down, and — just as importantly — fails fast so your own latency does not collapse while waiting on it. ┌──────────┐ failure rate > threshold ┌──────────┐ │ CLOSED │ ─────────────────────────▶ │ OPEN │ │ let all │ │ reject │ │ through │ ◀───────────────────────────│ instantly│ └──────────┘ probe succeeded └────┬─────┘ ▲ │ after │ │ cool-off │ ┌──────────────┐ │ └─────────│ HALF-OPEN │◀──────────────┘ │ allow a few │ │ probe calls │──▶ still failing → OPEN └──────────────┘ Tune on a RATE over a window, not a raw count. "5 failures" trips on a quiet service after five requests; "50% of at least 20 requests in 10 seconds" does not. Per dependency, not per process. One breaker for "the payments API" — not one shared breaker that opens for everything when one upstream has a bad minute.
go · sony/gobreaker, with a fallback that degrades rather than fails
cb := gobreaker.NewCircuitBreaker[*Recommendations](gobreaker.Settings{
	Name:        "recommendations",
	MaxRequests: 3,                    // probes allowed in half-open
	Interval:    60 * time.Second,     // counter reset window when closed
	Timeout:     30 * time.Second,     // how long to stay open
	ReadyToTrip: func(c gobreaker.Counts) bool {
		return c.Requests >= 20 &&
			float64(c.TotalFailures)/float64(c.Requests) >= 0.5
	},
	OnStateChange: func(name string, from, to gobreaker.State) {
		// ALWAYS alert on this. A breaker opening is a real event, and
		// it is often your earliest signal that a dependency is sick.
		slog.Warn("breaker state change", "name", name, "from", from, "to", to)
		breakerState.WithLabelValues(name).Set(float64(to))
	},
})

func (s *Service) Recommend(ctx context.Context, userID string) *Recommendations {
	recs, err := cb.Execute(func() (*Recommendations, error) {
		return s.client.Fetch(ctx, userID)
	})
	if err != nil {
		// A non-critical feature MUST degrade, not fail the request.
		s.metrics.recsDegraded.Inc()
		return s.popularFallback()          // stale, cached, or generic
	}
	return recs
}

Bulkheads: isolate the failure

go · a separate concurrency budget per dependency
// Without isolation, one slow dependency consumes every goroutine,
// every connection and every pool slot — and requests that do not even
// touch it start failing. That is a bulkhead breach.
type Bulkhead struct{ sem chan struct{} }

func NewBulkhead(n int) *Bulkhead { return &Bulkhead{sem: make(chan struct{}, n)} }

func (b *Bulkhead) Do(ctx context.Context, f func(context.Context) error) error {
	select {
	case b.sem <- struct{}{}:
		defer func() { <-b.sem }()
		return f(ctx)
	case <-ctx.Done():
		return ctx.Err()
	default:
		// Full: reject IMMEDIATELY rather than queueing. Queueing here
		// just converts a capacity problem into a latency problem.
		return ErrOverloaded
	}
}

// One per dependency, sized by that dependency's capacity:
var (
	paymentsBulkhead = NewBulkhead(20)
	searchBulkhead   = NewBulkhead(50)
	recsBulkhead     = NewBulkhead(10)   // non-critical: a small budget
)

Load shedding and backpressure

go · reject early, by priority, before you fall over
// Under overload, the worst outcome is accepting everything and serving
// nothing. Shed deliberately: a fast 503 lets the caller retry elsewhere
// or degrade, while a 30-second timeout wastes both sides' capacity.
func Shed(maxInflight int64, priority func(*http.Request) int) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	var inflight atomic.Int64
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			n := inflight.Add(1)
			defer inflight.Add(-1)

			// Shed low-priority work first, at a lower threshold.
			threshold := maxInflight
			if p := priority(r); p > 2 {
				threshold = maxInflight / 2
			}
			if n > threshold {
				shed.WithLabelValues(routePattern(r)).Inc()
				w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "2")
				http.Error(w, "overloaded", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
				return
			}
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		})
	}
}
Backpressure is the version of this that does not lose work

Shedding drops requests; backpressure slows the producer down. In Go the mechanism is simply a bounded channel — a full buffer blocks the producer, which is exactly the signal you want travelling upstream. That is why an unbounded queue is dangerous: it converts overload into unbounded memory growth and latency that nobody can see, right up to the OOM kill. Bound every queue, and decide explicitly what happens when it is full: block (backpressure), drop (shed), or reject (fail fast).

Putting it in order

LayerProtects againstWithout it
TimeoutA hung dependencyGoroutines accumulate until the process dies
Retry + jitterA transient blipAvoidable errors reach users
Retry budgetYour own retriesA retry storm amplifies an outage
Circuit breakerA sustained outageYou wait on something already down
BulkheadOne dependency taking everythingUnrelated requests fail too
Load sheddingMore traffic than you can serveYou accept everything and complete nothing
FallbackA non-critical feature failingA recommendations outage becomes a checkout outage
Interview follow-up

“A downstream service starts responding in 30 seconds instead of 50 milliseconds. What happens to your Go service, and what should have been in place?” Without protection: every request waiting on it holds a goroutine and a connection, in-flight count climbs, memory and file descriptors follow, and requests that never touch that dependency start failing too — a total outage caused by one partial one. What should be there, in order: a per-call context deadline far below the caller's, so you fail in 500 ms instead of 30 seconds; a bulkhead capping concurrent calls to that dependency; a circuit breaker so you stop calling it at all once the failure rate is sustained; and a fallback if the feature is non-critical. The insight worth stating is that the timeout is doing most of the work — everything else is refinement.

P05

Scaling a Go service

Go removes the concurrency ceiling that limits most runtimes, which means the bottleneck moves somewhere else — almost always to a connection pool, a single writer, or a lock. This chapter is about finding which, in order.

The order things saturate

In a Go service this sequence is remarkably consistent: 1 Nothing Go handles 10k+ concurrent connections on one pod without trying. The goroutine-per-request model is not the constraint. 2 The database connection pool pods × pool_size hits the database's max_connections, or requests queue on db.Stats().WaitCount. → fix: fewer queries per request, a pooler, or a bigger database 3 A single writer one Postgres primary, one Redis master, one partition leader. → fix: read replicas, caching, sharding, moving work async 4 A lock in your own code a global mutex, a shared map, a singleflight group everything passes through. → fix: shard it, or make it atomic 5 GC / allocation only after the above, and only if the profile says so (R02, R04) 6 CPU the one people assume is first. It rarely is. Diagnose in this order. Every step you skip is a day spent optimising something that was not the problem.
the three queries that identify the bottleneck
# 1. Is the pool the constraint? (saturation, not utilisation)
db_pool_wait_total          0      ← healthy
                          rising    ← requests are QUEUEING for a connection
db_pool_in_use / max        < 0.8

# 2. Is the scheduler the constraint?
go_sched_latencies_seconds{quantile="0.99"}   < 1ms healthy
                                              > 10ms CPU starvation

# 3. Is a lock the constraint?
$ go tool pprof http://localhost:6060/debug/pprof/mutex
(pprof) top
      flat  flat%   cum   cum%
    4.2min 91.3%  4.2min 91.3%  main.(*Registry).Get
                                   ↑ one RWMutex, every request

# and confirm with the trace's goroutine analysis (R08): a large
# "sync block" bucket names the lock directly.

Reducing per-request database work

A request-scoped dataloader batches without restructuring callers

When the N+1 is spread across a call graph — common with GraphQL resolvers, or a service layer that fetches lazily — collect the keys and flush once per tick. graph-gophers/dataloader or a hand-rolled version using a channel plus a 1 ms window turns hundreds of individual lookups into one WHERE id = ANY($1), with no change to the code doing the asking. The other half of the win is caching within the request: the same user fetched five times per request should cost one query.

Read replicas and routing

go · route reads away from the primary, carefully
type DB struct {
	primary  *pgxpool.Pool
	replicas []*pgxpool.Pool
	next     atomic.Uint64
}

func (d *DB) Read(ctx context.Context) *pgxpool.Pool {
	// Read-your-own-writes: after a write in this request, reads MUST go
	// to the primary or the user will not see what they just saved.
	// This is the number one replica bug, and it always looks like a
	// caching bug at first.
	if wroteInThisRequest(ctx) {
		return d.primary
	}
	if len(d.replicas) == 0 {
		return d.primary
	}
	i := d.next.Add(1) % uint64(len(d.replicas))
	return d.replicas[i]
}

func (d *DB) Write(ctx context.Context) *pgxpool.Pool {
	markWrote(ctx)
	return d.primary
}

// Replicas are ASYNCHRONOUS by default: lag of milliseconds normally,
// seconds under load, minutes during a large migration. Export the lag
// as a metric and alert on it — and never route a read that must be
// consistent to a replica.

Sharding a lock

go · when one mutex becomes the bottleneck
// One RWMutex over a hot map serialises every writer and, under
// contention, readers too. Sharding by key hash turns one point of
// contention into N.
const shards = 64

type ShardedMap[V any] struct {
	s [shards]struct {
		mu sync.RWMutex
		m  map[string]V
		_  [40]byte        // pad to avoid FALSE SHARING: two mutexes in
	}                      // the same 64-byte cache line ping-pong
}                          // between cores even when logically unrelated

func (s *ShardedMap[V]) shard(k string) int {
	return int(maphash.String(seed, k) % shards)
}

func (s *ShardedMap[V]) Get(k string) (V, bool) {
	sh := &s.s[s.shard(k)]
	sh.mu.RLock()
	defer sh.mu.RUnlock()
	v, ok := sh.m[k]
	return v, ok
}

// Before reaching for this: check whether the value is really shared.
// An atomic.Pointer swap for a whole immutable snapshot is lock-free
// for readers and is usually the better answer for read-mostly config.
Measure contention before sharding anything

Sharding multiplies memory, complicates iteration (which now needs every shard's lock, in a fixed order, or it deadlocks), and buys nothing if the lock was never contended. The mutex profile tells you: a lock that appears with minutes of cumulative wait across a 30-second window is contended; one that does not appear is not. And prefer removing the sharing entirely — per-goroutine accumulation merged at the end, an atomic snapshot pointer, or a channel to a single owner goroutine — over making the shared thing faster.

Horizontal scaling: what breaks

Adding replicas multiplies…Which breaksFix
Database connectionsmax_connectionsPgBouncer in transaction mode; smaller per-pod pools
In-process rate limitsThe effective limit becomes N × configuredMove the counter to Redis (B09)
In-process cachesHit rate falls; N copies to invalidateA shared cache, or accept per-pod staleness
Scheduled jobsThe cron runs N timesA leader lease, or an external scheduler
Outbound connectionsYou flood the upstreamMaxConnsPerHost, and bulkheads (P04)
Kafka consumersIdle consumers past the partition countMore partitions — decided in advance
go · a leader lease, so a periodic job runs once across the fleet
// Postgres advisory lock: no new infrastructure, and it releases
// automatically if the holder's connection dies.
func (w *Worker) runIfLeader(ctx context.Context, key int64, f func(context.Context) error) error {
	conn, err := w.pool.Acquire(ctx)
	if err != nil { return err }
	defer conn.Release()

	var got bool
	if err := conn.QueryRow(ctx,
		`SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock($1)`, key).Scan(&got); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if !got {
		return nil                 // another pod is doing it
	}
	defer conn.Exec(ctx, `SELECT pg_advisory_unlock($1)`, key)
	return f(ctx)
}

// Alternatives: a Kubernetes Lease object via client-go's leaderelection
// package, or a Redis SET NX with a TTL and a renewal goroutine.
// Whichever you pick, the job must be idempotent anyway — leases can
// overlap during a network partition, and every one of them says so in
// the documentation.
Interview follow-up

“Traffic is doubling next quarter. How do you prepare a Go service for it?” Measure first: load test to the knee with production-shaped data and record requests-per-pod capacity, then identify which resource saturates — pool waits, scheduler latency, mutex contention, database CPU — because that determines everything else. Then the arithmetic: doubling pods doubles database connections, so check that against max_connections and put a pooler in front if needed; doubling pods also multiplies any in-process rate limit and any cron job, so those move to shared state and a leader lease. Finally, the cheapest capacity is usually latency: halving per-request time halves the concurrency needed for the same throughput, and an N+1 query is frequently sitting right there.

P06

Security

Go removes whole vulnerability classes — no buffer overflows, no use-after-free, memory-safe by construction. What remains is everything above the memory layer: input handling, dependencies, TLS, and the code you wrote.

Dependencies

the supply-chain toolkit
$ govulncheck ./...          # reachability-aware; the one that matters
$ go list -m -u all          # what is outdated
$ go mod why -m github.com/x/y  # who pulled this in?
$ go mod graph | grep vulnerable
$ go mod verify              # cache matches go.sum

# Lock down where modules come from:
$ go env -w GOPROXY=https://proxy.golang.org,direct
$ go env -w GOSUMDB=sum.golang.org
$ go env -w GOPRIVATE=github.com/acme/*   # private: skip proxy + sumdb
$ go env -w GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly         # CI must not edit go.mod

# In CI, fail the build — a scanner whose output nobody reads is theatre.
$ govulncheck -format sarif ./... > results.sarif
Go's dependency story is genuinely safer than most

Three properties help: go.sum verifies the exact bytes of every module, so a re-tagged or tampered dependency fails the build; the checksum database provides an independent, append-only attestation; and there are no install-time scripts — adding a Go dependency cannot execute code on your machine, which removes the entire npm-style postinstall attack. The remaining risk is the code itself running in your process, which is what govulncheck and a small dependency count address. Prefer the standard library: it is the most-audited Go code in existence.

Input handling

go · the four injection classes and their Go-specific fixes
// ── SQL ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
db.QueryContext(ctx, `SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1`, email)  // ✓
// Identifiers cannot be parameterised — allowlist them (B07).

// ── Command ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
exec.CommandContext(ctx, "convert", "-resize", size, input, output)  // ✓
// Go's exec does NOT use a shell, so there is no shell metacharacter
// injection — unless you reintroduce one:
exec.Command("sh", "-c", "convert "+userInput)                        // ✗

// ── Path traversal ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
// filepath.Join CLEANS but does not CONFINE: "../../etc/passwd" escapes.
func safeJoin(root, name string) (string, error) {
	p := filepath.Join(root, filepath.Clean("/"+name))    // strip leading ../
	if !strings.HasPrefix(p, filepath.Clean(root)+string(os.PathSeparator)) {
		return "", errors.New("path escapes root")
	}
	return p, nil
}
// Go 1.24's os.Root does this properly — an fd-scoped directory that
// cannot be escaped even via symlinks:
root, _ := os.OpenRoot("/srv/uploads")
f, err := root.Open(userSuppliedName)                                 // ✓

// ── XSS ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// html/template escapes CONTEXTUALLY — differently inside an attribute,
// a URL, a <script> block and CSS. text/template does NOT escape at all.
import "html/template"                                                // ✓
// import "text/template"  for HTML                                   // ✗

// And template.HTML(userInput) disables escaping for that value. Every
// use of template.HTML, template.JS or template.URL on non-constant
// data is a potential XSS — grep for them in review.

// ── SSRF ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// A user-supplied URL fetched by your server can reach 169.254.169.254
// (cloud metadata), localhost, and your internal network. Validate the
// resolved IP, not the hostname — and re-check after redirects.
Bound every input before you process it

http.MaxBytesReader on every request body, io.LimitReader on every response body you read, a cap on JSON nesting depth if you accept arbitrary documents, a limit on multipart form size and file count, a maximum on any user-supplied limit or page size, and a timeout on every regular expression evaluated against user input. Unbounded input is how a memory-safe language still gets taken down: not a buffer overflow, just an allocation big enough to OOM the pod.

TLS

go · defaults are good; these are the deliberate deviations
srv := &http.Server{
	Addr: ":8443",
	TLSConfig: &tls.Config{
		MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12,     // 1.3 if every client supports it
		// Go chooses good cipher suites and orders them by hardware
		// support. Do NOT hand-pick a list you copied from a blog in
		// 2016 — you will end up worse than the default.
		CurvePreferences: []tls.CurveID{tls.X25519, tls.CurveP256},
	},
}
log.Fatal(srv.ListenAndServeTLS(certFile, keyFile))

// NEVER in production, and grep for it in review:
tls.Config{InsecureSkipVerify: true}    // disables ALL certificate
                                        // validation — the connection is
                                        // encrypted but unauthenticated,
                                        // so a MITM is undetectable

// mTLS: verify the client too.
pool := x509.NewCertPool()
pool.AppendCertsFromPEM(caPEM)
tlsCfg := &tls.Config{
	ClientCAs:  pool,
	ClientAuth: tls.RequireAndVerifyClientCert,
	MinVersion: tls.VersionTLS12,
}

Security headers

go · one middleware, and what each header actually prevents
func SecurityHeaders(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		h := w.Header()
		// Force HTTPS for a year, including subdomains.
		h.Set("Strict-Transport-Security", "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains")
		// Stop the browser guessing a response's type (MIME sniffing).
		h.Set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
		// Block framing → clickjacking.
		h.Set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY")
		// The strongest XSS defence, and the hardest to retrofit.
		h.Set("Content-Security-Policy",
			"default-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; "+
				"frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'")
		// Do not leak the full URL (which may contain IDs) cross-origin.
		h.Set("Referrer-Policy", "strict-origin-when-cross-origin")
		h.Set("Permissions-Policy", "geolocation=(), microphone=(), camera=()")
		next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
	})
}

// CORS: an allowlist, never a reflection of the Origin header.
func CORS(allowed []string) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	set := make(map[string]struct{}, len(allowed))
	for _, o := range allowed { set[o] = struct{}{} }
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			origin := r.Header.Get("Origin")
			if _, ok := set[origin]; ok {
				w.Header().Set("Access-Control-Allow-Origin", origin)
				w.Header().Set("Vary", "Origin")     // or caches poison this
				w.Header().Set("Access-Control-Allow-Credentials", "true")
			}
			if r.Method == http.MethodOptions {
				w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNoContent)
				return
			}
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		})
	}
}
Allow-Origin: * with credentials is rejected by browsers — and reflecting the origin is worse

Echoing back whatever Origin the request carried, together with Allow-Credentials: true, means any website can make authenticated requests to your API as a logged-in user. It is functionally the same as having no same-origin policy. Use an explicit allowlist, and remember the Vary: Origin header or a shared cache will serve one origin's CORS response to another.

Cryptography

NeedUseNever
Random tokens, salts, keyscrypto/randmath/rand — deterministic and seedable
Password hashingargon2.IDKey, bcryptSHA-256, MD5, any fast hash
Comparing secretssubtle.ConstantTimeCompare== — leaks via timing
Symmetric encryptioncrypto/cipher AES-GCM, or chacha20poly1305AES-CBC without a MAC; any mode without authentication
Signing a payloadcrypto/hmac with SHA-256Appending a secret and hashing (length-extension)
A general-purpose hashsha256, or maphash for mapsMD5, SHA-1
All of the above, simplyfilippo.io/age, golang.org/x/crypto/naclComposing primitives yourself
Never reuse a nonce with AES-GCM

GCM's security collapses completely if the same key and nonce encrypt two different messages — an attacker recovers the authentication key and can forge arbitrary ciphertexts. Generate the 12-byte nonce from crypto/rand for every single encryption and prepend it to the ciphertext; never derive it from a counter you might restart, and never from a timestamp. If that makes you uncomfortable, that is the correct reaction: use a higher-level library like nacl/secretbox or age that does not expose the nonce at all.

Static analysis in CI

yaml · .golangci.yml — the security-relevant linters
linters:
  enable:
    - gosec          # hardcoded credentials, weak crypto, unsafe permissions
    - errcheck       # unchecked errors — including a missed Close or Verify
    - bodyclose      # unclosed HTTP response bodies (B11)
    - sqlclosecheck  # unclosed rows (B07)
    - noctx          # HTTP requests built without a context
    - rowserrcheck   # missing rows.Err()
    - contextcheck   # a context that should have been propagated
    - staticcheck
    - govet

linters-settings:
  gosec:
    excludes:
      - G404          # math/rand — exclude only if you audit each use
issues:
  exclude-rules:
    - path: _test\.go
      linters: [gosec, errcheck]
Interview follow-up

“What security advantages does Go give you, and what does it not?” Memory safety removes buffer overflows, use-after-free and most of the CVE classes that dominate C and C++, and the module system removes install-time script execution while verifying every dependency's bytes against go.sum and a public checksum log. What it does not touch is everything semantic: SQL injection if you concatenate, SSRF if you fetch user-supplied URLs, broken object-level authorization if you fetch by ID without scoping to the caller, secrets in logs, and misconfigured TLS. Go makes the memory layer safe and leaves the application layer entirely to you — which is where essentially all modern breaches happen anyway.

P07

A complete service, end to end

Everything in this book, assembled into one shape. This is a reference you can copy: the layout, the wiring, the request path, and the deployment — small enough to read in one sitting and complete enough to run.

Layout

orders/ ├── go.mod go.sum Makefile Dockerfile .golangci.yml ├── cmd/ │ ├── api/main.go wiring — the only package that imports │ │ every other one │ ├── worker/main.go outbox relay + job consumer │ └── migrate/main.go schema, run as a Job before rollout ├── internal/ │ ├── order/ domain — types, rules, interfaces │ │ ├── order.go Order, Status, Total(), Cancel() │ │ ├── service.go Service: orchestration │ │ ├── errors.go ErrNotFound, ErrConflict, … │ │ └── service_test.go table-driven, uses fakes │ ├── postgres/ adapter — implements order.Store │ │ ├── store.go sqlc-generated queries + translation │ │ └── store_test.go testcontainers, real Postgres │ ├── stripe/ adapter — implements order.Payments │ ├── outbox/ adapter — implements order.Publisher │ ├── httpapi/ transport │ │ ├── routes.go mux + middleware chain │ │ ├── orders.go handlers: decode → call → encode │ │ ├── errors.go error → status + envelope │ │ └── middleware.go │ ├── config/config.go │ ├── observability/ slog, OTel, Prometheus setup │ └── reqctx/ typed context accessors ├── migrations/ 000001_init.up.sql, … ├── query.sql sqlc.yaml └── deploy/ deployment.yaml service.yaml hpa.yaml Dependency direction: cmd → httpapi → order ← postgres/stripe/outbox The domain imports nothing but the standard library.

The request path, traced

POST /v1/orders 1 Recoverer panic → 500, stack logged, request survives 2 RequestID generate or accept X-Request-Id 3 otelhttp extract traceparent, start the server span 4 Logger wrap the ResponseWriter; log on the way out 5 Metrics RED counters + duration histogram 6 Timeout(10s) context deadline every layer inherits 7 RateLimit by tenant; 429 + Retry-After 8 Authenticate verify JWT → user into the context 9 handler MaxBytesReader(1 MiB) → decode → DisallowUnknownFields → Validate() 10 order.Service business rules ├─ payments.Charge 3 s deadline, bulkhead(20), breaker, │ retry only with an idempotency key └─ one transaction ├─ INSERT orders └─ INSERT outbox ← atomic with the order (B12) 11 encode 201, Location, JSON of a RESPONSE type 12 unwinding metrics observed, log line written with status + duration + request_id + trace_id, span ended Asynchronously, in cmd/worker: the relay polls outbox with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, publishes orders.placed, marks the row published. At-least-once, so every consumer dedupes on the event ID.

cmd/api/main.go

go · the whole wiring, with nothing elided
func main() {
	if err := run(); err != nil {
		slog.Error("fatal", "err", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}

func run() error {
	cfg, err := config.Load()
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("config: %w", err)
	}

	log := observability.NewLogger(cfg)
	slog.SetDefault(log)
	log.Info("starting",
		"version", buildVersion(),
		"gomaxprocs", runtime.GOMAXPROCS(0),      // verify the tuning (P03)
		"gomemlimit", debug.SetMemoryLimit(-1),
	)

	ctx, stop := signal.NotifyContext(context.Background(),
		os.Interrupt, syscall.SIGTERM)
	defer stop()

	shutdownTracing, err := observability.InitTracing(ctx, cfg)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("tracing: %w", err)
	}
	defer func() {
		sc, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 5*time.Second)
		defer cancel()
		_ = shutdownTracing(sc)                   // flush the last spans
	}()

	// --- adapters ---------------------------------------------------
	poolCfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(cfg.DatabaseURL.Reveal())
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("parse dsn: %w", err)
	}
	poolCfg.MaxConns = cfg.DBMaxConns
	poolCfg.MaxConnLifetime = cfg.DBConnLifetime
	poolCfg.ConnConfig.Tracer = otelpgx.NewTracer()

	pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, poolCfg)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("database: %w", err)
	}
	defer pool.Close()
	if err := pool.Ping(ctx); err != nil {        // fail fast
		return fmt.Errorf("database ping: %w", err)
	}

	store := postgres.NewOrderStore(pool)
	payments := stripe.New(cfg.StripeKey.Reveal(),
		stripe.WithTimeout(3*time.Second),
		stripe.WithBreaker(breakerSettings),
		stripe.WithBulkhead(20),
	)
	publisher := outbox.New(pool)

	// --- domain -----------------------------------------------------
	orders := order.NewService(store, payments, publisher, log)

	// --- transport --------------------------------------------------
	api := httpapi.New(orders, log, cfg)
	srv := &http.Server{
		Addr:              cfg.Addr,
		Handler:           api.Routes(),
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
		ReadTimeout:       15 * time.Second,
		WriteTimeout:      30 * time.Second,
		IdleTimeout:       120 * time.Second,
		MaxHeaderBytes:    1 << 20,
		ErrorLog:          slog.NewLogLogger(log.Handler(), slog.LevelError),
	}

	// Private port: metrics, pprof, and nothing public (R07, B14).
	internal := &http.Server{
		Addr:              "127.0.0.1:6060",
		Handler:           observability.InternalMux(pool),
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
	}

	g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)

	g.Go(func() error {
		log.Info("http listening", "addr", srv.Addr)
		if err := srv.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})
	g.Go(func() error {
		if err := internal.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})
	g.Go(func() error {
		<-gctx.Done()
		log.Info("draining")
		api.SetNotReady()                          // /readyz starts failing
		sc, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), cfg.ShutdownTimeout)
		defer cancel()
		_ = internal.Shutdown(sc)
		return srv.Shutdown(sc)
	})

	err = g.Wait()
	log.Info("stopped")
	return err
}

internal/httpapi/routes.go

go · routing, probes, and the middleware order that matters
func (a *API) Routes() http.Handler {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()

	// Probes: NO auth, NO rate limiting, NO heavy middleware (B14).
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", a.healthz)      // liveness: checks nothing
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /readyz", a.readyz)        // readiness: checks the DB
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /version", a.version)

	// Business routes, Go 1.22 method+wildcard patterns (B01).
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/orders",
		a.authed(http.HandlerFunc(a.createOrder)))
	mux.Handle("GET /v1/orders/{id}",
		a.authed(http.HandlerFunc(a.getOrder)))
	mux.Handle("DELETE /v1/orders/{id}",
		a.authed(http.HandlerFunc(a.cancelOrder)))

	return Chain(mux,
		Recoverer(a.log),
		RequestID,
		func(h http.Handler) http.Handler {
			return otelhttp.NewHandler(h, "api",
				otelhttp.WithSpanNameFormatter(func(_ string, r *http.Request) string {
					return r.Method + " " + routePattern(r)   // low cardinality
				}))
		},
		Logger(a.log),
		Metrics,
		SecurityHeaders,
		CORS(a.cfg.AllowedOrigins),
		Timeout(a.cfg.RequestTimeout),
	)
}

func (a *API) authed(h http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return Chain(h, RateLimit(a.limiter), Authenticate(a.verifier))
}

What this service does when things go wrong

FailureBehaviourMechanism
A handler panics500 for that request; process survives; stack loggedRecoverer (L04)
The client disconnectsContext cancels; the database query is cancelled toor.Context() (L13)
Stripe is slow3 s timeout, then a bulkhead rejection, then the breaker opensP04
Postgres restartsReadiness fails, traffic drains, pool reconnects, readiness recoversB14
Redis is downLatency rises; requests still succeed from the originB09
Kafka is downOrders still commit; the outbox backs up and drains laterB12
Traffic triplesLoad shedding returns 503 + Retry-After before collapseP04
SIGTERM during a deploypreStop → readiness fails → in-flight requests drain → exit 0P02
A memory leak is introducedGOMEMLIMIT keeps the pod alive; the heap metric alertsP03
Build it in this order

Handler plus store plus main first — get one endpoint serving real data end to end. Then structured logging and the two probes, because you cannot deploy without them. Then metrics and the timeout middleware. Then the domain/adapter split, at the moment you write your second adapter or your first test that needs a fake. Then tracing, then resilience, then tuning. Every one of those is easy to add later and hard to justify before there is anything to protect — building the full structure on day one is how a CRUD service ends up with twelve packages and one endpoint.

Interview follow-up

“Walk me through the architecture of a Go service you have built.” Give the dependency direction first — cmd wires, transport decodes, the domain holds rules and declares the interfaces it needs, adapters implement them — and say explicitly that the domain package imports no database and no HTTP. Then trace one request through the middleware chain and name what each layer does. Then the operational answer: how it shuts down, what happens when each dependency fails, and which four metrics you would put on the dashboard. Architecture questions are really asking whether you have operated the thing you designed, so the failure table is the part that lands.

P08

The standard library, in one chapter

Go's standard library is unusually complete and unusually stable, and reaching for a dependency before checking it is the most common avoidable mistake in a Go codebase. This is the map: what is in the box, and the one thing worth knowing about each.

The packages a backend service actually uses

PackageForWorth knowing
net/httpServer and clientProduction-grade; the defaults are not (B01, B11)
contextCancellation, deadlinesFirst parameter, never a struct field (L13)
encoding/jsonJSONReflection-based; case-insensitive decode (B03)
database/sqlSQL, driver-agnosticIt is a pool; always defer rows.Close() (B07)
log/slogStructured loggingUse the *Context variants (B06)
errorsWrapping, Is, As, JoinAs takes a pointer to the target (L09)
sync, sync/atomicMutexes, once, typed atomicsNever copy a lock (L13)
timeClocks, durations, timersInject the clock for tests; Stop() your tickers
ioReader, Writer, Copy, LimitReaderThe most-implemented interfaces in Go
os, os/execFiles, env, processesexec uses no shell — that is a security feature (P06)
slices, maps, cmpGeneric helpersReplaced most hand-written loops (L11)
strings, bytes, strconvTextBuilder, Cut, and strconv over fmt (L08)
testingTests, benchmarks, fuzzingNo assertion library needed (B13)
net/http/httptestHandler and upstream testingBoth directions (B13)
html/templateHTML renderingContextually auto-escaping; text/template is not
crypto/*TLS, hashing, randomnesscrypto/rand, never math/rand (P06)
embedFiles into the binaryMigrations, templates, static assets (R01)
runtime/pprof, runtime/traceProfilingAlways wire it up (R07, R08)

io: the interfaces everything speaks

go · composition, streaming, and never loading it all into memory
// Stream through a pipeline instead of buffering: gzip → hash → upload,
// with constant memory regardless of size.
func upload(ctx context.Context, src io.Reader, dst io.Writer) (string, error) {
	h := sha256.New()
	tee := io.TeeReader(src, h)        // hash as the bytes flow past

	gz := gzip.NewWriter(dst)
	if _, err := io.Copy(gz, tee); err != nil {   // uses ReadFrom/WriteTo
		return "", err                            // when available: zero-copy
	}
	if err := gz.Close(); err != nil {            // Close FLUSHES — check it
		return "", err
	}
	return hex.EncodeToString(h.Sum(nil)), nil
}

io.LimitReader(r, n)      // bound untrusted input — always (P06)
io.MultiReader(a, b, c)   // concatenate
io.MultiWriter(f, os.Stdout)
io.Discard                // a /dev/null writer; drain a body into it (B11)
io.ReadAll(r)             // convenient, unbounded — wrap in LimitReader
io.Pipe()                 // connect a writer to a reader across goroutines
io.NopCloser(r)           // give a Reader a no-op Close

// fs.FS is the abstraction over "a filesystem": os.DirFS, embed.FS and
// zip archives all satisfy it, so code written against fs.FS works on
// all three without knowing which it has.
func loadTemplates(fsys fs.FS) (*template.Template, error) {
	return template.ParseFS(fsys, "templates/*.html")
}

time: the three traps

go · durations, monotonic clocks, and leaking timers
// 1. A Duration is an int64 of NANOSECONDS. `5` is five nanoseconds,
//    not five seconds — and it compiles.
time.Sleep(5)                     // 5 ns. Almost certainly a bug.
time.Sleep(5 * time.Second)       // correct

// 2. time.Time carries BOTH a wall clock and a monotonic reading.
//    Subtraction uses the monotonic one, so it is immune to NTP steps
//    and DST — but any operation that strips it (Round, Truncate,
//    marshalling, UTC()) loses that. Measure with Since, never by
//    subtracting two round-tripped timestamps.
start := time.Now()
elapsed := time.Since(start)      // monotonic: correct even if the clock jumps

// 3. Tickers and timers must be stopped, or they leak.
t := time.NewTicker(time.Second)
defer t.Stop()                    // ALWAYS
// time.Tick() has no Stop at all — never use it outside main.

// AfterFunc is the cheap way to schedule one-off work:
timer := time.AfterFunc(30*time.Second, func() { cleanup() })
defer timer.Stop()

// Parsing uses a reference layout, not format codes. The reference is
// Mon Jan 2 15:04:05 MST 2006  (1 2 3 4 5 6 7 if you order the fields).
t2, err := time.Parse(time.RFC3339, "2026-09-14T10:00:00Z")
s := t2.Format("2006-01-02 15:04:05")

// Store and compare in UTC; convert to a location only for display.
loc, _ := time.LoadLocation("Europe/Berlin")   // needs tzdata (P02)
fmt.Println(t2.In(loc))
Never compare times with ==

Two time.Time values are equal under == only if their wall clock, monotonic reading and location all match — so a timestamp that has been through JSON and back will never equal the original, even for the same instant. Use t1.Equal(t2), which compares the instant. The same applies to putting a time.Time in a map key or a struct you compare with ==: it will behave unpredictably, and reflect.DeepEqual on structs containing times is a recurring source of flaky tests.

os/exec, and net

go · running a process, and the details that matter
cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "ffmpeg", "-i", in, "-vf", filter, out)
cmd.Env = append(os.Environ(), "TMPDIR=/scratch")
var stderr bytes.Buffer
cmd.Stderr = &stderr                 // capture it — you will want it
cmd.WaitDelay = 5 * time.Second      // Go 1.20+: SIGKILL if it ignores the
                                     // context cancellation's SIGKILL... and
                                     // still holds a pipe open
out, err := cmd.Output()
if err != nil {
	var ee *exec.ExitError
	if errors.As(err, &ee) {
		return fmt.Errorf("ffmpeg exit %d: %s", ee.ExitCode(), stderr.String())
	}
	return err
}

// net: DNS, dialers, and the pieces under net/http.
ips, err := net.DefaultResolver.LookupIPAddr(ctx, host)
conn, err := (&net.Dialer{Timeout: 3 * time.Second}).DialContext(ctx, "tcp", addr)
_, port, _ := net.SplitHostPort(addr)
ip := net.ParseIP(s)
_, cidr, _ := net.ParseCIDR("10.0.0.0/8")
cidr.Contains(ip)                    // the SSRF check (P06)

// net/netip is the modern, allocation-free, comparable address type —
// prefer it for anything storing or comparing addresses at volume.
addrp, _ := netip.ParseAddr("2001:db8::1")
pfx := netip.MustParsePrefix("10.0.0.0/8")
pfx.Contains(addrp)

regexp, and when not to use it

go · RE2: linear time, no backtracking, no lookahead
// Compile ONCE, at package level. Compiling in a handler is a common
// and entirely unnecessary cost.
var emailRe = regexp.MustCompile(`^[^@\s]+@[^@\s]+\.[a-z]{2,}$`)

// Go's regexp is RE2: guaranteed linear time, so it is immune to
// catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS) — a real advantage over PCRE. The
// price is no backreferences and no lookahead/lookbehind.

// For simple cases, strings is 10-100× faster and clearer:
strings.HasPrefix(s, "v1/")            // not `^v1/`
strings.Contains(s, "error")           // not `error`
before, after, ok := strings.Cut(s, "=")  // not a capture group

// Use regexp when the pattern is genuinely a pattern, and prefer the
// indexed forms to avoid allocating:
if m := emailRe.FindStringSubmatchIndex(s); m != nil { … }

The golang.org/x packages worth treating as standard

PackageGives you
x/sync/errgroupWaitGroup + first error + cancellation + SetLimit (L14)
x/sync/singleflightDuplicate-call collapsing (B09)
x/sync/semaphoreA weighted semaphore that respects context
x/time/rateToken-bucket rate limiting (B09)
x/cryptoargon2, bcrypt, chacha20poly1305, ssh, acme/autocert
x/expThe staging ground for future standard packages
x/textCollation, normalisation, transliteration, language matching
x/nethttp2 internals, websocket, publicsuffix, proxy
x/vulngovulncheck (P06)
x/perfbenchstat (R09)
x/toolsgoimports, stringer, analysis framework
Check the standard library before adding a dependency

A very large share of Go dependencies exist to provide something the standard library already does, or now does: routing with method matching (1.22), structured logging (1.21), generic slice and map helpers (1.21), embedded files (1.16), and — coming — a faster JSON. Every dependency is code you run, a supply-chain surface, and something to keep upgraded. The counter-balance is that hand-rolling cryptography, a database driver, or a protocol implementation is a far worse idea than importing one; the rule is to prefer the standard library, then a well-maintained single-purpose package, and to be suspicious of frameworks.

Interview follow-up

“Which third-party libraries would you add to a new Go service?” A short, defensible list is the right answer: a database driver (pgx) and possibly sqlc; golang.org/x/sync for errgroup and singleflight; a metrics client and the OpenTelemetry SDK; and a migration tool. Everything else — routing, logging, JSON, HTTP client, testing — is in the standard library and has been since 1.21 or 1.22. Naming what you would not add, and why, says more than a longer list: it shows you know the surface area each dependency costs and that you have checked what shipped recently.

P09

Common mistakes and the review checklist

Every mistake below has been found in production Go by someone competent. They cluster into five areas, and most are caught by a linter, a habit, or one line in a review.

The top ten, in order of how much damage they do

#MistakeConsequenceFix
1http.ListenAndServe with no timeoutsSlowloris; goroutine and fd exhaustionAn explicit &http.Server{} (B01)
2Goroutine sending on a channel nobody readsSilent leak until OOMBuffer of 1, or select on ctx.Done() (R05)
3GOMAXPROCS left at the node's core countp99 many times p50; CFS throttlingSet it from the pod limit (R03, P03)
4Missing defer rows.Close() / resp.Body.Close()Pool exhaustion; too many open filessqlclosecheck, bodyclose (B07, B11)
5Returning a typed nil as an errorerr != nil for a successDeclare the return type as error (L06)
6No rows.Err() after the loopPartial results returned as completerowserrcheck (B07)
7Shadowed err via := inside a blockErrors silently swallowedThe shadow linter (L02)
8Unbounded fan-out (go f() per item)You take down a dependencyerrgroup.SetLimit (L14)
9A value receiver on a type containing a mutexThe lock protects nothinggo vet copylocks (L05)
10High-cardinality metric labelsMonitoring falls overRoute pattern, not raw path (B14)

Concurrency

go · the five that recur
// 1. WaitGroup.Add inside the goroutine — Wait can return before it runs.
for _, x := range xs {
	go func() { wg.Add(1); defer wg.Done(); f(x) }()   // ✗ race
}
// Add BEFORE `go`.                                     // ✓

// 2. `break` inside a select breaks the select, not the loop (L03).
for { select { case <-ch: break } }                     // ✗ spins
loop: for { select { case <-ch: break loop } }          // ✓

// 3. Closing a channel from multiple senders → panic.
// Only the sole sender closes; with many, use a done channel or Once.

// 4. time.After in a loop leaks a timer per iteration (L12).
for { select { case <-ch: case <-time.After(time.Minute): } }  // ✗
// Reuse a Timer, or use context.WithTimeout.                   // ✓

// 5. Holding a lock across I/O — one slow call stalls every goroutine.
mu.Lock()
resp, _ := http.Get(url)      // ✗ 2s with the lock held
mu.Unlock()
// Gather under the lock, release, then do the I/O.   // ✓

Errors and nil

go · four shapes that pass review and fail in production
// 1. Comparing with == across a wrap.
if err == ErrNotFound { }                  // ✗ fails once anything wraps it
if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) { }         // ✓

// 2. errors.As with the wrong pointer depth — compiles, panics.
var ve *ValidationError
errors.As(err, ve)                         // ✗ panic
errors.As(err, &ve)                        // ✓

// 3. Logging AND returning — one failure, six log lines (L09).
if err != nil { log.Error(err); return err }              // ✗
if err != nil { return fmt.Errorf("get %s: %w", id, err) } // ✓

// 4. Ignoring an error from something that can genuinely fail.
defer f.Close()                            // ✗ on a WRITER: loses data
defer func() {                             // ✓
	if cerr := f.Close(); cerr != nil && err == nil { err = cerr }
}()

// And the nil-map write, which panics rather than failing quietly:
var m map[string]int
m["k"] = 1                                 // ✗ panic
m := make(map[string]int)                  // ✓

Slices, strings and allocation

go · the aliasing and O(n²) traps
// 1. make with a LENGTH when you meant a CAPACITY.
out := make([]T, len(in))                  // ✗ len(in) zero values, then
for _, x := range in { out = append(out, f(x)) }   //   append after them
out := make([]T, 0, len(in))               // ✓

// 2. Appending to a sub-slice overwrites the parent (L07).
head := all[:2]; head = append(head, x)    // ✗ clobbers all[2]
head := all[:2:2]                          // ✓ capped, so append copies

// 3. A small slice pinning a large array.
prefix := hugeBody[:100]                   // ✗ keeps all 10 MB alive
prefix := bytes.Clone(hugeBody[:100])      // ✓

// 4. String concatenation in a loop.
for _, s := range xs { out += s }          // ✗ O(n²)
var b strings.Builder                      // ✓ O(n)

// 5. fmt.Sprintf where strconv does.
fmt.Sprintf("%d", n)                       // ✗ reflection + boxing
strconv.Itoa(n)                            // ✓ ~10× faster

// 6. Indexing a string expecting a character.
s[0]                                       // ✗ a BYTE
[]rune(s)[0]                               // ✓ a rune (and it allocates)

HTTP and the database

go · the client and server mistakes that cost availability
http.Get(url)                              // ✗ DefaultClient: NO timeout
client.Do(reqWithContext)                  // ✓ timeout + context

// Body not drained → the connection cannot be reused (B11).
defer resp.Body.Close()                    // ✗ incomplete
defer func() {                             // ✓
	_, _ = io.Copy(io.Discard, io.LimitReader(resp.Body, 4<<10))
	_ = resp.Body.Close()
}()

json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req)       // ✗ unbounded body
r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 1<<20)   // ✓

w.WriteHeader(500); w.Header().Set("X", "y")     // ✗ header dropped
// Headers first, then WriteHeader, then Write.  // ✓

sql.Open(...)                              // per request  ✗ — it is a POOL
// One *sql.DB for the process lifetime.               ✓

db.SetMaxOpenConns(0)                      // ✗ unlimited: floods Postgres
db.SetMaxOpenConns(25)                     // ✓ and do the arithmetic (B07)

"SELECT * FROM t WHERE x = '" + v + "'"    // ✗ injection
"SELECT * FROM t WHERE x = $1", v          // ✓

The review checklist

Correctness □ every error is handled or wrapped with context — not both □ no err == Err…; errors.Is / errors.As instead □ error-returning functions declare error, not a concrete type □ rows.Err() checked after every row loop □ Close deferred for every body, row set, file and transaction □ nil map / nil slice semantics considered Concurrency □ every goroutine has a defined exit path and an owner □ ctx.Done() in every long-lived loop and every blocking select □ fan-out is bounded (SetLimit, a pool, or a semaphore) □ result channels are buffered or selected with cancellation □ no lock held across I/O; no lock copied by value □ shared state is guarded, and a comment says by what HTTP □ server timeouts set explicitly □ request bodies bounded with MaxBytesReader □ r.Context() threaded to every downstream call □ outbound calls use a configured client with a deadline □ no err.Error() in a 5xx response body Observability □ structured logging with request/trace IDs, at one layer □ metric labels are low-cardinality (route pattern, not path) □ liveness checks nothing external; readiness checks what matters Security □ all SQL parameterised; identifiers allowlisted □ secrets are a redacting type, and not in logs or errors □ every lookup scoped to the authenticated principal □ crypto/rand, constant-time comparison, no InsecureSkipVerify Tests & build □ table-driven, with the error cases present □ -race in CI; goleak in packages that spawn goroutines □ no time.Sleep as synchronisation □ gofmt, go vet, golangci-lint, govulncheck all gate the build

Make the machine do it

yaml · .golangci.yml — the set that pays for itself
linters:
  enable:
    - errcheck        # unchecked errors                          → #4, #6
    - govet           # copylocks, lostcancel, printf             → #9
    - staticcheck     # the broadest correctness analyser
    - bodyclose       # unclosed response bodies                  → #4
    - sqlclosecheck   # unclosed rows                             → #4
    - rowserrcheck    # missing rows.Err()                        → #6
    - noctx           # HTTP requests without a context
    - contextcheck    # a context that should have propagated
    - nilerr          # `return nil` when err is non-nil
    - errorlint       # == on errors instead of errors.Is         → #5
    - gosec           # security issues
    - goconst         # repeated string literals
    - unconvert
    - wastedassign
    - makezero        # make([]T, n) then append                  → slices

run:
  timeout: 5m
issues:
  exclude-rules:
    - path: _test\.go
      linters: [errcheck, gosec]
Every rule a linter can enforce should not be a review comment

Human review is expensive and inconsistent; a linter is neither. Spend review attention on the things a tool cannot check — whether the abstraction is right, whether the failure mode is acceptable, whether the error message will help someone at 3am — and let CI catch unclosed bodies and shadowed variables. When you find a bug in review that a linter could have caught, enable the linter in the same pull request; that is how the checklist above shrinks over time instead of growing.

Interview follow-up

“What do you look for when reviewing Go code?” Lead with the operational questions, because they are what distinguish a Go review from a general one: does every goroutine have a defined exit path, does every network call have a deadline that propagates, is every Close deferred, and is each error either handled or wrapped but never both. Then the design question — is the interface defined where it is used and is it as small as that use requires. Mentioning that formatting, unused variables and unchecked errors never come up because CI already rejects them is a good signal in itself.

P10

Interviews and the road on

Three things: how Go interviews are actually structured, the questions that separate a confident answer from a memorised one, and an honest map of where to go next.

What the rounds are testing

RoundLooks likeActually assessing
Language“What happens when you append to a slice in a function?”Whether you know the semantics, not the syntax
Concurrency“Write a worker pool.” “Find the bug in this code.”Exit paths and cancellation — everyone can start a goroutine
Runtime“How does the scheduler work?” “Stack or heap?”Whether you have debugged Go or only written it
Design“Design a rate-limited API gateway in Go.”Interfaces, boundaries, failure modes
Debugging“Memory is climbing in production. Go.”A method: measure, narrow, confirm
Code reviewA diff with four planted bugsWhether you spot the leak and the missing Close
The habit that marks a senior answer

Say what you would measure before saying what you would change. “I would take a goroutine profile and group by state” beats “I would add a mutex”; “I would check GOMAXPROCS and CFS throttling first” beats “I would optimise the handler”. Interviewers cannot verify your experience directly, but they can hear whether your first instinct is evidence or guessing — and that instinct is the difference the role is hiring for.

Twenty-five questions, one line each

Slice vs array?
An array's length is part of its type and it copies on assignment; a slice is a three-word view (pointer, len, cap) onto a shared backing array.
Nil vs empty slice?
Behaviourally identical for len, range and append; nil marshals to null, empty to [].
Why does append sometimes not affect the caller?
The callee has a copy of the header; if capacity is exceeded it points at a new array. Always return the slice.
Why is map iteration random?
Deliberately randomised so nobody depends on an order that was never guaranteed.
Why is a map element not addressable?
Growth can move entries, so a pointer into a map could dangle. Use map[K]*V.
Value or pointer receiver?
Pointer for mutation, large structs, or anything containing a lock. Pick one and use it for every method on the type.
Why does my type not satisfy the interface?
The method has a pointer receiver, so only *T is in the method set — you passed a T.
Why is err != nil true when I returned nil?
Typed nil: a non-nil concrete type in the interface's type word. Declare the return as error.
Is embedding inheritance?
No. There is no virtual dispatch — the embedded method calls the embedded type's own methods.
What does defer cost?
Near zero since open-coded defers in 1.13, except inside loops or conditionals.
When do defer arguments evaluate?
At the defer statement. Wrap in a closure to capture the later value.
Buffered vs unbuffered channel?
Unbuffered rendezvouses — the send completes only when a receiver takes it; buffered decouples.
What happens on a closed channel?
Receive returns the zero value immediately with ok=false; send and close panic.
Who closes a channel?
The sender, and only when there is exactly one. Never the receiver.
How do you stop a goroutine?
You ask: pass a context and select on ctx.Done(). There is no kill.
Mutex or channel?
Mutex to protect state; channel to transfer ownership or orchestrate.
What is a data race?
Two goroutines touching the same memory, one writing, with no happens-before edge between them.
What does -race guarantee?
No false positives, many false negatives — it only sees races that actually occurred.
Stack or heap?
The compiler decides by escape analysis. Read it with -gcflags='-m'.
G, M and P?
Goroutine, OS thread, scheduling context. len(P) == GOMAXPROCS, and a G needs a P to run.
Why are goroutines cheap?
2 KB growable stacks, user-space switches, and blocking I/O turned into epoll registrations.
How does the GC work?
Concurrent tri-colour mark and sweep, non-generational, non-compacting, two sub-millisecond stop-the-world phases.
GOGC vs GOMEMLIMIT?
Heap-growth ratio vs a soft total-memory ceiling. In a container, GOGC=off plus GOMEMLIMIT.
Why set GOMAXPROCS in Kubernetes?
The runtime sees the node's cores, not the cgroup quota — the single most common Go performance bug in containers.
When do you use generics?
Containers and algorithms over any element type. Not where a small interface would do.

The live-coding questions, and what a good answer contains

“Write a worker pool.” They are checking: bounded workers, a closed jobs channel so the range ends, a WaitGroup, close(results) exactly once after Wait, and a ctx.Done() case so a departing consumer does not deadlock the workers. Getting the close right is the whole question. “Find the bug.” It will be one of: a goroutine sending to a channel nobody reads · WaitGroup.Add inside the goroutine · break inside a select · a loop variable captured pre-1.22 · a missing rows.Close · a mutex copied by value. “Implement a rate limiter.” Token bucket. Then the follow-up that matters: “now make it work across ten replicas” — the counter moves to Redis, and the read-compute-write must be atomic (a Lua script), or two requests race. “Fan out these N calls.” errgroup.WithContext + SetLimit. Write results into a pre-sized slice by index — no mutex needed, and they will ask why. “Add a cache.” Say what invalidates it before you write a line, add singleflight for the stampede, jitter the TTL, and make the origin path work when the cache is down.

Where to go next

To go deeper onRead / do
The language itselfThe Go spec — it is short, readable, and settles arguments. Then Effective Go and the Code Review Comments wiki
The runtimego/src/runtime is well-commented Go; start with proc.go, chan.go, mgc.go. Then the design docs in go/design
PerformanceDave Cheney's High Performance Go workshop; the compiler's -m output on your own hot paths
ConcurrencyConcurrency in Go (Cox-Buday); the Go memory model document; errgroup's source
API and service designThe Google API Improvement Proposals; gRPC's own guides; read the standard library's net/http as a design example
Distributed systemsDesigning Data-Intensive Applications; then implement Raft — hashicorp/raft is readable Go
Real codebasesKubernetes (enormous, mixed quality), CockroachDB (excellent), Caddy, Prometheus, Grafana Loki, pgx
Staying currentThe release notes for every version — they are short, and most of this book's "since 1.2x" notes came from them

The part that does not go out of date

Six habits worth more than any API

Read the errors. Go's compiler and runtime tell you exactly what is wrong; most confusion is a message that was skimmed. Read the source. The standard library is on your disk, it is well written, and go doc plus jump-to-definition answers most questions faster than a search. Measure before you change. Profiles over intuition, always. Make the zero value useful. It removes constructors and initialisation bugs. Give every goroutine an owner. If you cannot say how it exits, it leaks. Prefer boring. The Go community's strong preference for the obvious implementation over the clever one is not conservatism — it is what makes a codebase that ten people can maintain for five years.

Last interview follow-up

“What do you like and dislike about Go?” Answer honestly and specifically, because a candidate with no criticisms has not used the language seriously. The genuine strengths: predictable latency, cheap concurrency with a readable blocking style, a single static binary, a standard library that covers a service end to end, and a compiler fast enough that the edit-test loop stays tight. The genuine frustrations: if err != nil is verbose even when you accept why; generics arrived late and remain limited; the lack of sum types or an Option makes some invariants unexpressible; and nil interfaces holding typed nils is a sharp edge the type system could have prevented. Naming those, and then saying which you would trade away, is a better answer than praising it.

D01

Quill: what we are building, and why it is shaped this way

Sixteen chapters, one system. Quill is a collaborative notebook: you write notes offline, they sync when you reconnect, you share a notebook with a colleague by email or by link, and you can publish a single note to the public web. Everything in Parts I–IV appears here doing a job.

The requirements, written as constraints

RequirementWhat it forces on the design
Secure authenticationArgon2id, short-lived access tokens, rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection, optional TOTP, enumeration-resistant flows
Offline-first, instantly responsiveA local SQLite replica, optimistic local writes, an operation log, and a conflict policy that converges — this is the hardest part of the system
Private, shared and public notesThree visibility states, an ACL evaluated on every read, plus Postgres row-level security as a second wall
Sharing by email and by linkTwo invitation shapes with different threat models: one bound to an address and single-use, one unbound with a TTL and a use cap
Production-readyValidation at the edge, RFC 9457 problem responses, migrations that survive rolling deploys, observability, graceful shutdown, and a runbook
MicroservicesSix deployables with strict data ownership, an event backbone, and — importantly — a local read model so authorization does not become a synchronous network hop
An honest note about microservices, before we build six of them

For a product at this stage, a single Go binary with the same package boundaries would be simpler, faster, and cheaper to operate — and that is what I would ship first in real life. We are building the distributed version because you asked to learn it and because the failure modes only appear when the boundaries are real: a permission check that becomes a network call, an ACL that goes stale, an event that arrives twice. Chapter D16 closes with the honest assessment of what this decomposition bought and what it cost, and how to collapse it back if you do not need it.

The services

┌──────────────┐ browser / desktop ──────▶│ gateway │ :8080 public edge (local SQLite replica) │ │ │ · TLS, CORS, CSRF │ │ · JWT verify (JWKS cache)│ │ · rate limit (Redis) │ │ · request id + tracing │ │ · problem-details errors │ └──┬───┬───┬───┬───┬───────┘ ┌─────────────────────┘ │ │ │ └───────────────┐ ▼ ▼ │ ▼ ▼ ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌─────────────┐ ┌──────────┐ │ identity │ │ notes │ │ collab │ │ realtime │ │ :8081 │ │ :8082 │ │ :8083 │ │ :8084 │ ├─────────────┤ ├──────────────┤ ├─────────────┤ ├──────────┤ │ users │ │ notebooks │ │ memberships │ │ WS hub │ │ credentials │ │ notes │ │ invitations │ │ presence │ │ sessions │ │ note_ops │ │ roles │ │ fan-out │ │ JWKS │ │ search index │ │ audit log │ │ │ │ │ │ acl_replica │ │ │ │ │ └──────┬──────┘ └──────┬───────┘ └──────┬──────┘ └────┬─────┘ │ │ │ │ └──────────────┬───────┴─────────┬───────┴──────────────┘ ▼ ▼ ┌────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ NATS │ │ mailer │ :8085 │ JetStream │───▶│ outbox relay│ │ (events) │ │ SMTP / API │ └────────────┘ └──────────────┘ Each service owns its own Postgres schema and nobody reads anyone else's tables. Redis holds rate-limit counters, the JWKS cache and short-lived public-page caches. Nothing else is shared.

Who owns what

ServiceOwnsNever touches
identityusers, credentials, sessions, refresh-token families, TOTP secrets, the signing keysnotes, permissions
notesnotebooks, notes, the operation log, the search index, public slugs, a replica of the ACLwho a user is beyond an ID; who granted access
collabmemberships, roles, invitations, the audit log — the source of truth for authorizationnote content
realtimeWebSocket connections, subscriptions, presence. Stateless and disposableany persistent data at all
mailerthe delivery outbox, templates, provider credentials, bounce handlinganything it was not sent in an event
gatewaynothing. It is routing, auth verification and translationevery database
The one rule that makes a decomposition survive

A service may only read data it owns. If notes needs to know whether a user may read a notebook, it does not query collab's tables and it does not make a synchronous call on every read. collab publishes membership changes as events and notes maintains a local replica table it owns — a read model. That is CQRS in its least ceremonious form, and it is what keeps a read path at 3 ms instead of 30. Chapter D10 covers what to do about the staleness window that buys you.

How the pieces talk

Client → gateway HTTPS + JSON. One public surface, versioned at /v1. RFC 9457 problem documents on failure. gateway → service HTTP + JSON over the cluster network, with the verified subject forwarded in a signed internal header. Timeouts and a circuit breaker per route. service → service gRPC, and only where a synchronous answer is genuinely required: collab.CheckPermission (the strong path) identity.GetUsers (batch display names) Everything else is an event. service ⇄ service NATS JetStream, at-least-once, consumers idempotent by event id. Published through a transactional outbox so the database write and the event commit together (B12). server → client WebSocket, but only as a doorbell: the server says "notebook N has changes past seq S" and the client pulls the delta over HTTP. The socket never carries authoritative data, which is what makes a dropped connection harmless.
Why the WebSocket carries no data

If live updates arrive only over the socket, then every reconnect, every proxy timeout and every missed frame becomes a correctness problem — the client has a gap it cannot detect. Making the socket a notification and the HTTP change-feed the source of truth means a client that misses every message still converges the moment it polls, and the socket becomes a latency optimisation you can lose without consequence. This is the single most important design decision in the sync layer and it is why D11 spends a whole chapter on the protocol before any code.

The request you should be able to trace by the end

A user edits a note's title while offline, then reconnects. 1 local write SQLite notes row updated, plus a row in pending_ops with a client ULID and a Lamport stamp. The UI re-renders from SQLite. Zero network. 2 reconnect the sync loop drains pending_ops: POST/v1/sync/push {ops:[…]} 3 gateway verify access JWT (local, JWKS-cached) → forward with X-Quill-Subject, signed, plus request id and trace. 4 notes check the ACL replica: is this user an editor of that notebook? → dedupe by op_id (unique index) → apply per-field last-writer-wins → append to note_ops, which assigns a monotonic server_seq → write an outbox row. All in one transaction. 5 outbox relay publishes notes.changed to NATS. 6 realtime fan-out to every socket subscribed to that notebook: {"type":"changed","notebook_id":"…","server_seq":8842} 7 other clients GET/v1/sync/changes?since=8791 → apply → render. 8 the editor's own client receives the push response, marks those ops acked, deletes them from pending_ops, advances its cursor. Every numbered step is a chapter. By D13 you will have written all of them, including the failure branches: a rejected op, a permission revoked between steps 1 and 4, a duplicate push after a timeout, and a client that has been offline for a month.

The technology choices, and the reason for each

ChoiceWhy, in one line
Go workspace monorepoSix modules developed together with no replace directives and one make test
Postgres 16, schema per serviceOne operational surface while we are small; the schemas are the seam to split on later
pgx/v5 + sqlcReal SQL, checked against the real schema at generation time, no runtime reflection (B08)
golang-migrate, embeddedMigrations ship inside the binary and run as a separate Job, never at startup
Ed25519 JWTs + JWKSSmall tokens, fast verification, and the gateway needs no network call per request
Opaque refresh tokensRevocable, rotatable, and reuse-detectable — which a JWT refresh token is not
NATS JetStreamDurable at-least-once with a fraction of Kafka's operational weight at this size
RedisRate-limit counters that must be shared across replicas, and public-page caching
SQLite on the clientThe local replica; embedded, transactional, and the same SQL the server speaks
ULIDs for every idClient-generatable (so offline writes get real ids), lexicographically time-sortable, index-friendly
Why ULIDs rather than UUIDv4 or a sequence

An offline client must be able to create a note and give it a permanent identity with no server round trip, which rules out a database sequence. UUIDv4 would work but is random, so inserts scatter across the B-tree and index locality collapses at scale. A ULID is 48 bits of millisecond timestamp followed by 80 bits of randomness, so it sorts by creation time, keeps inserts at the right-hand edge of the index, and is still collision-safe across clients. UUIDv7 is the standardised equivalent and would be an equally good choice.

quill/ ├── go.work ties the modules together ├── Makefile ├── docker-compose.yml local: postgres, redis, nats, mailhog ├── platform/ module: shared libraries (D02) │ ├── go.mod │ ├── config/ httpx/ problem/ validate/ idgen/ │ ├── pg/ outbox/ eventbus/ obs/ authn/ │ └── testsupport/ ├── proto/ module: generated gRPC contracts │ ├── collab/v1/collab.proto │ └── identity/v1/identity.proto ├── services/ │ ├── gateway/ D06 │ ├── identity/ D04, D05 │ ├── notes/ D07, D08, D11, D12 │ ├── collab/ D09, D10 │ ├── realtime/ D14 │ └── mailer/ D14 ├── clients/ │ └── syncd/ the local sync daemon — D13 └── deploy/ ├── k8s/ D16 └── grafana/ Every service module has the same internal shape, so moving between them costs nothing: services/notes/ ├── go.mod ├── cmd/api/main.go wiring only ├── internal/ │ ├── config/config.go │ ├── domain/ types + rules, imports nothing │ ├── app/ use cases, orchestration │ ├── store/ postgres adapter, sqlc output │ ├── transport/http/ handlers, DTOs, routing │ └── events/ publishers and consumers ├── migrations/ ├── query.sql └── sqlc.yaml

What we will deliberately not build

OmittedBecause
A front endThis is a Go book. The syncd client in D13 is the interesting half and it is Go
A full text CRDTReal collaborative text editing needs Yjs or Automerge. D11 explains the boundary precisely and implements per-field LWW with conflict copies, which is what most note apps actually ship
Billing, teams, adminThey add surface without adding a new lesson
A service meshSix services do not need one, and it would hide the resilience code we are writing on purpose
Interview follow-up

“Walk me through how you would design a collaborative note-taking app.” Lead with the two decisions that constrain everything else: where the source of truth lives (server, with clients holding a replica) and how conflicts resolve (an operation log with a total order assigned server-side, plus a deterministic merge rule). Then say the thing most candidates miss — that the realtime channel must be a notification rather than a data channel, so a dropped socket is a latency problem instead of a correctness problem. Only then talk about services, and be ready to justify why any of them are separate.

D02

The monorepo and the platform module

Six services that each reinvent configuration, logging, error responses and server bootstrap will drift apart within a month. Everything shared lives in one module, platform/, and every service imports it. This chapter writes all of it.

The workspace

go.work
go 1.24

use (
	./platform
	./proto
	./services/gateway
	./services/identity
	./services/notes
	./services/collab
	./services/realtime
	./services/mailer
	./clients/syncd
)
Workspace, not replace

go.work makes the toolchain resolve these modules locally across every go command, without a single replace directive in any go.mod. That matters because a replace lives in a committed file and shipping one to a release build is a classic mistake — the module then cannot be fetched by anyone else. Add go.work and go.work.sum to .gitignore only if your team disagrees about layout; in a monorepo, committing it is usually right.

Makefile
SERVICES := gateway identity notes collab realtime mailer
VERSION  ?= $(shell git describe --tags --always --dirty)
LDFLAGS  := -s -w -X main.version=$(VERSION)

.PHONY: all lint test build generate migrate up down

all: lint test build

generate:
	go generate ./...
	cd services/identity && sqlc generate
	cd services/notes    && sqlc generate
