	cd services/collab   && sqlc generate
	buf generate

lint:
	gofmt -l . | tee /dev/stderr | (! read)
	go vet ./...
	golangci-lint run

test:
	go test -race -count=1 ./...

test-integration:
	go test -race -tags=integration -count=1 ./...

build: $(SERVICES)

$(SERVICES):
	CGO_ENABLED=0 go build -trimpath -ldflags="$(LDFLAGS)" \
		-o bin/$@ ./services/$@/cmd/api

up:
	docker compose up -d
	$(MAKE) migrate

migrate:
	@for s in identity notes collab mailer; do \
		echo "--- $$s"; \
		go run ./services/$$s/cmd/migrate up; \
	done

down:
	docker compose down -v

Configuration

platform/config/config.go
// Package config loads and validates service configuration from the
// environment. Every service embeds Base and adds its own fields.
package config

import (
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"os"
	"strconv"
	"time"
)

// Base is the configuration every Quill service needs.
type Base struct {
	ServiceName     string
	Env             string        // development | staging | production
	Addr            string        // public/api listen address
	InternalAddr    string        // metrics + pprof, bound to loopback
	LogLevel        slog.Level
	RequestTimeout  time.Duration
	ShutdownTimeout time.Duration
	OTLPEndpoint    string
}

func LoadBase(service string) (Base, error) {
	b := Base{
		ServiceName:     service,
		Env:             str("QUILL_ENV", "development"),
		Addr:            str("ADDR", ":8080"),
		InternalAddr:    str("INTERNAL_ADDR", "127.0.0.1:9090"),
		RequestTimeout:  dur("REQUEST_TIMEOUT", 15*time.Second),
		ShutdownTimeout: dur("SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT", 25*time.Second),
		OTLPEndpoint:    str("OTLP_ENDPOINT", ""),
	}
	if err := b.LogLevel.UnmarshalText([]byte(str("LOG_LEVEL", "info"))); err != nil {
		return b, fmt.Errorf("LOG_LEVEL: %w", err)
	}

	var errs []error
	// Validate RELATIONSHIPS, not just values. A shutdown budget shorter
	// than a request budget means in-flight requests get cut off on every
	// deploy — a misconfiguration that passes any per-field check.
	if b.ShutdownTimeout <= b.RequestTimeout {
		errs = append(errs, fmt.Errorf(
			"SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT (%s) must exceed REQUEST_TIMEOUT (%s)",
			b.ShutdownTimeout, b.RequestTimeout))
	}
	if b.Env == "production" && b.OTLPEndpoint == "" {
		errs = append(errs, errors.New("OTLP_ENDPOINT is required in production"))
	}
	return b, errors.Join(errs...)
}

func (b Base) IsProd() bool { return b.Env == "production" }

// ---- typed readers -------------------------------------------------

func str(key, def string) string {
	if v, ok := os.LookupEnv(key); ok && v != "" {
		return v
	}
	return def
}

func Req(key string) (string, error) {
	v := os.Getenv(key)
	if v == "" {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("%s is required", key)
	}
	return v, nil
}

func dur(key string, def time.Duration) time.Duration {
	v, ok := os.LookupEnv(key)
	if !ok {
		return def
	}
	d, err := time.ParseDuration(v)
	if err != nil {
		return def // surfaced by validation in the caller if it matters
	}
	return d
}

func Int(key string, def int) int {
	v, ok := os.LookupEnv(key)
	if !ok {
		return def
	}
	n, err := strconv.Atoi(v)
	if err != nil {
		return def
	}
	return n
}
platform/config/secret.go
package config

import "log/slog"

// Secret is a string that refuses to print itself. Every credential in
// Quill is this type, so logging a whole config struct is safe by
// construction rather than by review discipline.
type Secret string

func (s Secret) String() string                { return "[REDACTED]" }
func (s Secret) GoString() string              { return "[REDACTED]" }
func (s Secret) LogValue() slog.Value          { return slog.StringValue("[REDACTED]") }
func (s Secret) MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error)  { return []byte(`"[REDACTED]"`), nil }
func (s Secret) MarshalText() ([]byte, error)  { return []byte("[REDACTED]"), nil }

// Reveal is the single deliberate escape hatch. It is greppable on
// purpose: `grep -rn '.Reveal()'` audits every use in the repository.
func (s Secret) Reveal() string { return string(s) }

func ReqSecret(key string) (Secret, error) {
	v, err := Req(key)
	return Secret(v), err
}

Errors on the wire: RFC 9457 problem details

platform/problem/problem.go
// Package problem implements RFC 9457 "Problem Details for HTTP APIs".
// One envelope for every error in every service, so clients write one
// error handler instead of six.
package problem

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"log/slog"
	"net/http"
)

type Problem struct {
	Type     string  `json:"type"`               // stable URI identifying the class
	Title    string  `json:"title"`              // short, human, stable
	Status   int     `json:"status"`
	Detail   string  `json:"detail,omitempty"`   // instance-specific, SAFE to display
	Instance string  `json:"instance,omitempty"` // the request id
	Errors   []Field `json:"errors,omitempty"`   // field-level validation
}

type Field struct {
	Field  string `json:"field"`
	Code   string `json:"code"`   // machine-readable: "required", "too_long"
	Detail string `json:"detail"` // human
}

const base = "https://errors.quill.app/"

func New(status int, kind, title, detail string) *Problem {
	return &Problem{Type: base + kind, Title: title, Status: status, Detail: detail}
}

// The catalogue. Keeping every error here means the set is reviewable
// and clients can rely on `type` never changing for a given condition.
func BadRequest(detail string) *Problem {
	return New(http.StatusBadRequest, "bad-request", "Malformed request", detail)
}
func Unauthorized(detail string) *Problem {
	return New(http.StatusUnauthorized, "unauthorized", "Authentication required", detail)
}
func Forbidden(detail string) *Problem {
	return New(http.StatusForbidden, "forbidden", "Not permitted", detail)
}
func NotFound(resource string) *Problem {
	return New(http.StatusNotFound, "not-found", "Not found", resource+" does not exist")
}
func Conflict(detail string) *Problem {
	return New(http.StatusConflict, "conflict", "Conflict", detail)
}
func Validation(fields []Field) *Problem {
	p := New(http.StatusUnprocessableEntity, "validation-failed",
		"Validation failed", "one or more fields are invalid")
	p.Errors = fields
	return p
}
func TooManyRequests(retryAfter int) *Problem {
	p := New(http.StatusTooManyRequests, "rate-limited", "Too many requests", "")
	p.Detail = "retry after " + itoa(retryAfter) + "s"
	return p
}
func Internal() *Problem {
	// NEVER carries err.Error(). Internal strings leak table names, SQL,
	// hostnames and occasionally connection strings (B03).
	return New(http.StatusInternalServerError, "internal",
		"Something went wrong", "the failure has been logged")
}

func (p *Problem) Error() string { return p.Title + ": " + p.Detail }

// Write renders the problem. It takes the context so the request id can
// be attached without the caller remembering to.
func Write(ctx context.Context, w http.ResponseWriter, p *Problem) {
	p.Instance = RequestIDFromContext(ctx)
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/problem+json; charset=utf-8")
	w.Header().Set("Cache-Control", "no-store")
	if p.Status == http.StatusTooManyRequests && w.Header().Get("Retry-After") == "" {
		w.Header().Set("Retry-After", "1")
	}
	w.WriteHeader(p.Status)
	if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(p); err != nil {
		slog.ErrorContext(ctx, "write problem", "err", err)
	}
}
Why a catalogue rather than ad-hoc errors

Every problem the API can produce is a function in one file, so the whole error surface is reviewable in a single screen and a client can branch on type forever. The alternative — constructing status codes and messages at each call site — produces an API where the same logical failure is a 400 in one handler and a 422 in another, and where nobody can enumerate what a client must handle. It also gives you one place to enforce that 5xx bodies never contain internal detail.

Validation

platform/validate/validate.go
// Package validate builds field-level validation errors that map
// directly onto problem.Field, so a request DTO's Validate method and
// the HTTP response share one vocabulary.
package validate

import (
	"net/mail"
	"strings"
	"unicode/utf8"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/problem"
)

type V struct{ errs []problem.Field }

func New() *V { return &V{} }

func (v *V) add(field, code, detail string) { v.errs = append(v.errs, problem.Field{Field: field, Code: code, Detail: detail}) }

// Problem returns nil when everything passed, so callers can write
// `if p := v.Problem(); p != nil { return p }`.
func (v *V) Problem() *problem.Problem {
	if len(v.errs) == 0 {
		return nil
	}
	return problem.Validation(v.errs)
}

func (v *V) Required(field, value string) *V {
	if strings.TrimSpace(value) == "" {
		v.add(field, "required", "must not be empty")
	}
	return v
}

// Length counts RUNES, not bytes — otherwise a 50-character limit
// rejects a 30-character name written in Japanese (L08).
func (v *V) Length(field, value string, min, max int) *V {
	n := utf8.RuneCountInString(value)
	switch {
	case n < min:
		v.add(field, "too_short", "must be at least "+itoa(min)+" characters")
	case n > max:
		v.add(field, "too_long", "must be at most "+itoa(max)+" characters")
	}
	return v
}

func (v *V) Email(field, value string) *V {
	addr, err := mail.ParseAddress(value)
	if err != nil || addr.Address != value {
		v.add(field, "invalid_email", "must be a valid email address")
		return v
	}
	if len(value) > 254 { // RFC 5321 maximum path length
		v.add(field, "too_long", "must be at most 254 characters")
	}
	return v
}

func (v *V) OneOf(field, value string, allowed ...string) *V {
	for _, a := range allowed {
		if value == a {
			return v
		}
	}
	v.add(field, "invalid_choice", "must be one of: "+strings.Join(allowed, ", "))
	return v
}

func (v *V) Max(field string, value, max int) *V {
	if value > max {
		v.add(field, "too_large", "must be at most "+itoa(max))
	}
	return v
}

func (v *V) UTF8(field, value string) *V {
	if !utf8.ValidString(value) {
		v.add(field, "invalid_encoding", "must be valid UTF-8")
	}
	return v
}

// Custom lets a domain rule participate without importing this package's
// internals — used for cross-field checks like "expires_at must be future".
func (v *V) Custom(ok bool, field, code, detail string) *V {
	if !ok {
		v.add(field, code, detail)
	}
	return v
}
Collect every error, not the first

An API that returns one validation error at a time forces a client to submit a form five times to discover five problems. Accumulating into a slice and returning them together costs nothing and is the difference between an API that is pleasant to integrate against and one that is not. The same reasoning applies to configuration (errors.Join above) and to bulk operations, where a per-item result array beats failing the whole batch on the first bad row.

The HTTP toolkit

platform/httpx/server.go
// Package httpx is the server bootstrap every Quill service shares:
// correct timeouts, an internal port for metrics and pprof, and a
// shutdown sequence that drains before exiting.
package httpx

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"log/slog"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/pprof"
	"sync/atomic"
	"time"

	"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promhttp"
	"golang.org/x/sync/errgroup"
)

type Server struct {
	public   *http.Server
	internal *http.Server
	log      *slog.Logger
	ready    atomic.Bool
	shutdown time.Duration
}

type Options struct {
	Addr            string
	InternalAddr    string
	Handler         http.Handler
	Log             *slog.Logger
	ShutdownTimeout time.Duration
	ReadinessCheck  func(context.Context) error
}

func NewServer(o Options) *Server {
	s := &Server{log: o.Log, shutdown: o.ShutdownTimeout}
	s.ready.Store(true)

	s.public = &http.Server{
		Addr:    o.Addr,
		Handler: o.Handler,
		// The defaults are unsafe on a public network (B01). Every one
		// of these is load-bearing:
		ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,  // Slowloris
		ReadTimeout:       20 * time.Second,
		WriteTimeout:      40 * time.Second, // must exceed the slowest handler
		IdleTimeout:       120 * time.Second,
		MaxHeaderBytes:    1 << 20,
		ErrorLog:          slog.NewLogLogger(o.Log.Handler(), slog.LevelWarn),
	}

	// /metrics, /debug/pprof and the probes live on a SEPARATE listener
	// bound to loopback. Exposing pprof publicly is a remote DoS and an
	// information leak (R07).
	mux := http.NewServeMux()
	mux.Handle("GET /metrics", promhttp.Handler())
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /debug/pprof/", pprof.Index)
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /debug/pprof/cmdline", pprof.Cmdline)
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /debug/pprof/profile", pprof.Profile)
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /debug/pprof/symbol", pprof.Symbol)
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /debug/pprof/trace", pprof.Trace)

	// Liveness checks NOTHING external. A liveness probe that pings the
	// database restarts every pod when the database blips (B14).
	mux.HandleFunc("GET /healthz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
	})

	mux.HandleFunc("GET /readyz", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		if !s.ready.Load() {
			http.Error(w, "draining", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
			return
		}
		if o.ReadinessCheck != nil {
			ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(r.Context(), 2*time.Second)
			defer cancel()
			if err := o.ReadinessCheck(ctx); err != nil {
				http.Error(w, "not ready", http.StatusServiceUnavailable)
				return
			}
		}
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
	})

	s.internal = &http.Server{
		Addr: o.InternalAddr, Handler: mux, ReadHeaderTimeout: 5 * time.Second,
	}
	return s
}

// Run blocks until ctx is cancelled, then drains. It returns nil on a
// clean shutdown so main can distinguish "asked to stop" from "crashed".
func (s *Server) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)

	g.Go(func() error {
		s.log.Info("listening", "addr", s.public.Addr)
		if err := s.public.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})
	g.Go(func() error {
		if err := s.internal.ListenAndServe(); !errors.Is(err, http.ErrServerClosed) {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})
	g.Go(func() error {
		<-gctx.Done()
		// Fail readiness FIRST so the load balancer stops sending work,
		// then give in-flight requests time to finish (P02).
		s.ready.Store(false)
		s.log.Info("draining", "for", s.shutdown)

		sctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), s.shutdown)
		defer cancel()
		_ = s.internal.Shutdown(sctx)
		return s.public.Shutdown(sctx)
	})

	return g.Wait()
}
platform/httpx/json.go
package httpx

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"errors"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"strings"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/problem"
)

const maxBody = 1 << 20 // 1 MiB

// Decode reads and validates a JSON request body. It is deliberately
// strict: bounded, no unknown fields, no trailing data.
func Decode[T any](w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) (T, *problem.Problem) {
	var v T

	if ct := r.Header.Get("Content-Type"); ct != "" &&
		!strings.HasPrefix(ct, "application/json") {
		return v, problem.New(http.StatusUnsupportedMediaType, "unsupported-media-type",
			"Unsupported media type", "expected application/json")
	}

	// Bound the body BEFORE decoding, or a client can send 10 GB (B01).
	r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxBody)

	dec := json.NewDecoder(r.Body)
	dec.DisallowUnknownFields() // a typo'd field is a 400, not a silent no-op

	if err := dec.Decode(&v); err != nil {
		var maxErr *http.MaxBytesError
		var syntaxErr *json.SyntaxError
		var typeErr *json.UnmarshalTypeError
		switch {
		case errors.As(err, &maxErr):
			return v, problem.New(http.StatusRequestEntityTooLarge, "body-too-large",
				"Request too large", "body must be under 1 MiB")
		case errors.As(err, &syntaxErr):
			return v, problem.BadRequest("malformed JSON at byte " + itoa(int(syntaxErr.Offset)))
		case errors.As(err, &typeErr):
			return v, problem.Validation([]problem.Field{{
				Field: typeErr.Field, Code: "invalid_type",
				Detail: "expected " + typeErr.Type.String(),
			}})
		case errors.Is(err, io.EOF):
			return v, problem.BadRequest("a JSON body is required")
		default:
			// DisallowUnknownFields produces an untyped error; surface it
			// verbatim because it names the offending field and is safe.
			return v, problem.BadRequest(err.Error())
		}
	}
	// Reject trailing content: {"a":1}{"b":2} must not silently succeed.
	if dec.More() {
		return v, problem.BadRequest("body must contain a single JSON object")
	}
	return v, nil
}

// JSON writes a success response. Headers first, then status, then body
// — in that order, always (B01).
func JSON(ctx context.Context, w http.ResponseWriter, status int, v any) {
	w.Header().Set("Content-Type", "application/json; charset=utf-8")
	w.WriteHeader(status)
	if v == nil || status == http.StatusNoContent {
		return
	}
	if err := json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v); err != nil {
		// The status is already written; all we can do is record it.
		logFromContext(ctx).ErrorContext(ctx, "encode response", "err", err)
	}
}

Identifiers

platform/idgen/id.go
// Package idgen produces ULIDs: 48 bits of millisecond timestamp plus
// 80 bits of cryptographic randomness, Crockford base32, 26 characters.
//
// Why ULIDs and not UUIDv4 or a sequence:
//   · an OFFLINE client must create a note and give it a permanent id
//     with no round trip, which rules out a database sequence
//   · they sort by creation time, so inserts stay at the right-hand edge
//     of the index instead of scattering like UUIDv4
//   · 80 random bits per millisecond is collision-safe across clients
package idgen

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"database/sql/driver"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	"github.com/oklog/ulid/v2"
)

type ID string

func New() ID { return ID(ulid.MustNew(ulid.Now(), rand.Reader).String()) }

func Parse(s string) (ID, error) {
	u, err := ulid.ParseStrict(s)
	if err != nil {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("invalid id %q: %w", s, err)
	}
	return ID(u.String()), nil
}

func (id ID) Valid() bool { _, err := ulid.ParseStrict(string(id)); return err == nil }
func (id ID) String() string { return string(id) }

// Time extracts the creation instant — useful for debugging and for
// cheap "created before X" filters without touching a timestamp column.
func (id ID) Time() time.Time {
	u, err := ulid.ParseStrict(string(id))
	if err != nil {
		return time.Time{}
	}
	return ulid.Time(u.Time())
}

// database/sql plumbing so ID can be scanned and bound directly.
func (id ID) Value() (driver.Value, error) { return string(id), nil }

func (id *ID) Scan(src any) error {
	switch v := src.(type) {
	case string:
		*id = ID(v)
	case []byte:
		*id = ID(v)
	case nil:
		*id = ""
	default:
		return fmt.Errorf("idgen: cannot scan %T", src)
	}
	return nil
}

Request context

platform/httpx/reqctx.go
package httpx

import (
	"context"
	"log/slog"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
)

// Unexported struct keys: no other package can collide, and no string
// constant can be typo'd (L13).
type (
	ctxRequestID struct{}
	ctxSubject   struct{}
	ctxLogger    struct{}
)

// Subject is the authenticated principal, put here by the gateway's auth
// middleware and forwarded to every service.
type Subject struct {
	UserID    idgen.ID
	SessionID idgen.ID
	Email     string
	Scopes    []string
	MFA       bool // did this session complete a second factor?
}

func WithRequestID(ctx context.Context, id string) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, ctxRequestID{}, id)
}

func RequestID(ctx context.Context) string {
	id, _ := ctx.Value(ctxRequestID{}).(string)
	return id
}

func WithSubject(ctx context.Context, s Subject) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, ctxSubject{}, s)
}

func SubjectFrom(ctx context.Context) (Subject, bool) {
	s, ok := ctx.Value(ctxSubject{}).(Subject)
	return s, ok
}

// MustSubject is for handlers registered behind the auth middleware.
// Panicking is correct here: reaching it without a subject is a routing
// bug, not a runtime condition, and the recovery middleware turns it
// into a 500 with a stack (L04).
func MustSubject(ctx context.Context) Subject {
	s, ok := SubjectFrom(ctx)
	if !ok {
		panic("httpx: no subject in context — route registered outside RequireAuth")
	}
	return s
}

func WithLogger(ctx context.Context, l *slog.Logger) context.Context {
	return context.WithValue(ctx, ctxLogger{}, l)
}

func logFromContext(ctx context.Context) *slog.Logger {
	if l, ok := ctx.Value(ctxLogger{}).(*slog.Logger); ok {
		return l
	}
	return slog.Default()
}

Observability

platform/obs/log.go
// Package obs wires logging, metrics and tracing so that a single
// request is correlated across all three by request_id and trace_id.
package obs

import (
	"context"
	"log/slog"
	"os"

	"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/config"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/httpx"
)

// contextHandler pulls correlation fields out of the context so no call
// site ever has to remember them (B06).
type contextHandler struct{ slog.Handler }

func (h contextHandler) Handle(ctx context.Context, r slog.Record) error {
	if id := httpx.RequestID(ctx); id != "" {
		r.AddAttrs(slog.String("request_id", id))
	}
	if sc := trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx); sc.IsValid() {
		r.AddAttrs(
			slog.String("trace_id", sc.TraceID().String()),
			slog.String("span_id", sc.SpanID().String()),
		)
	}
	if s, ok := httpx.SubjectFrom(ctx); ok {
		r.AddAttrs(slog.String("user_id", s.UserID.String()))
	}
	return h.Handler.Handle(ctx, r)
}

// Level is exported so an admin endpoint can raise it during an incident
// without a redeploy.
var Level = new(slog.LevelVar)

func NewLogger(cfg config.Base) *slog.Logger {
	Level.Set(cfg.LogLevel)

	opts := &slog.HandlerOptions{
		Level:     Level,
		AddSource: !cfg.IsProd(),
		ReplaceAttr: func(_ []string, a slog.Attr) slog.Attr {
			switch a.Key {
			case slog.TimeKey:
				a.Key = "ts"
			case slog.MessageKey:
				a.Key = "msg"
			case "password", "token", "authorization", "cookie", "set-cookie":
				return slog.String(a.Key, "[REDACTED]")
			}
			return a
		},
	}

	var h slog.Handler = slog.NewJSONHandler(os.Stdout, opts)
	if !cfg.IsProd() {
		h = slog.NewTextHandler(os.Stdout, opts)
	}

	log := slog.New(contextHandler{h}).With(
		"service", cfg.ServiceName,
		"env", cfg.Env,
		"version", Version(),
	)
	slog.SetDefault(log)
	return log
}
platform/obs/version.go
package obs

import (
	"runtime/debug"
	"sync"

	"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus"
	"github.com/prometheus/client_golang/prometheus/promauto"
)

// Version is read from the VCS data the toolchain embeds — no ldflags
// required, though we set them too so a tag shows up (P01).
var Version = sync.OnceValue(func() string {
	bi, ok := debug.ReadBuildInfo()
	if !ok {
		return "unknown"
	}
	var rev, dirty string
	for _, s := range bi.Settings {
		switch s.Key {
		case "vcs.revision":
			if len(s.Value) >= 12 {
				rev = s.Value[:12]
			}
		case "vcs.modified":
			if s.Value == "true" {
				dirty = "+dirty"
			}
		}
	}
	if rev == "" {
		return bi.Main.Version
	}
	return rev + dirty
})

// A constant-1 gauge labelled with the version turns "the error rate rose
// at 14:03" and "the deploy landed at 14:02" into the same graph.
func init() {
	promauto.NewGaugeFunc(prometheus.GaugeOpts{
		Name:        "quill_build_info",
		Help:        "Build information; always 1.",
		ConstLabels: prometheus.Labels{"version": Version()},
	}, func() float64 { return 1 })
}
Where this pays off

Six services now log identically, fail identically, validate identically and shut down identically — and a fix to any of it is one pull request rather than six. The risk of a shared platform module is that it becomes a dumping ground with a dependency on everything; the discipline that prevents it is that platform/ may import third-party libraries and the standard library, but never a service. If something needs a service's type, it is not platform code.

Interview follow-up

“How do you keep multiple services consistent without coupling them?” A shared library for cross-cutting mechanics — configuration, logging, error envelope, server bootstrap, database helpers — versioned with the services in a monorepo so a change lands everywhere at once. The rule that keeps it healthy is a strict dependency direction: the platform module may not import any service, which mechanically prevents it accumulating domain logic. And the things that must not be shared are domain types and database access, because sharing those is how you build a distributed monolith where one schema change breaks four deployments.

D03

The data model, migrations and the database layer

Four schemas, one Postgres instance, and a hard rule that nobody reads across a schema boundary. This chapter writes every table, every index with its justification, the row-level security policies that act as a second wall, and the shared database and outbox packages.

One instance, four schemas

postgres://quill ├── schema identity owned by role identity_svc ├── schema notes owned by role notes_svc ├── schema collab owned by role collab_svc └── schema mailer owned by role mailer_svc Each service connects with its own role, and that role has no grants at all on the other schemas. The isolation is enforced by Postgres, not by convention — so "just join across" is not merely discouraged, it fails with a permission error at development time. Why one instance rather than four databases? Because at this size four instances quadruple the operational surface — four backup schedules, four failovers, four connection budgets — to buy isolation we already get from grants. The schemas are the seam: splitting one out later is a pg_dump of a schema, a new DSN, and nothing else, precisely because nothing joins across them.

Migrations: the rules before the SQL

RuleWhy
Never run from application startupN replicas race for the advisory lock; N−1 block, fail readiness, and get killed — a self-inflicted outage during a routine deploy (B08)
A separate binary, run as a Jobcmd/migrate per service, same image, completes before the new pods roll
Migrations are embedded//go:embed migrations/*.sql — nothing to mount, nothing to version separately
Every change is expand/contractOld and new code run simultaneously during a rolling deploy; schema and code can never change at the same instant
Indexes are built CONCURRENTLYWhich means that migration cannot run inside a transaction — the tool needs telling
The app verifies, never appliesOn boot it checks the schema version and refuses to start on a mismatch

Identity

services/identity/migrations/000001_init.up.sql
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS identity;
SET search_path TO identity;

CREATE TABLE users (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,               -- ULID
    email           citext      NOT NULL,                  -- case-insensitive
    email_verified  boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
    display_name    text        NOT NULL,
    status          text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                    CHECK (status IN ('active','suspended','deleted')),
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Partial unique index, not a plain UNIQUE constraint: a deleted user's
-- address must become reusable, and a soft delete must not block signup.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_active_key
    ON users (email) WHERE status <> 'deleted';

CREATE TABLE credentials (
    user_id         text        PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    password_hash   text        NOT NULL,   -- full PHC string: $argon2id$v=19$m=...
    algo_version    smallint    NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
    updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE totp_secrets (
    user_id         text        PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    secret_enc      bytea       NOT NULL,   -- AES-GCM, key from the KMS/env
    confirmed_at    timestamptz,
    recovery_hashes text[]      NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- A "family" is one login. Rotating a refresh token creates a new row in
-- the same family; presenting a token that has already been rotated
-- means it leaked, and the WHOLE family is revoked (D05).
CREATE TABLE token_families (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id         text        NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    user_agent      text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    ip_prefix       inet,                    -- /24 or /64 only: enough to spot
                                             -- a change, not enough to track
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    last_used_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    revoked_at      timestamptz,
    revoked_reason  text
);
CREATE INDEX token_families_user_idx ON token_families (user_id, created_at DESC);

CREATE TABLE refresh_tokens (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,
    family_id       text        NOT NULL REFERENCES token_families(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    token_hash      bytea       NOT NULL,   -- sha256 of the token; NEVER the token
    expires_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
    used_at         timestamptz,            -- non-null once rotated
    replaced_by     text        REFERENCES refresh_tokens(id),
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX refresh_tokens_hash_key ON refresh_tokens (token_hash);
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_family_idx     ON refresh_tokens (family_id);
CREATE INDEX refresh_tokens_expiry_idx     ON refresh_tokens (expires_at)
    WHERE used_at IS NULL;

-- One table for every single-use, time-limited, emailed token. Keeping
-- them together means one expiry sweep and one set of security rules.
CREATE TABLE action_tokens (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,
    user_id         text        NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    purpose         text        NOT NULL
                    CHECK (purpose IN ('verify_email','reset_password','change_email')),
    token_hash      bytea       NOT NULL,
    payload         jsonb       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',  -- e.g. the new email
    expires_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
    consumed_at     timestamptz,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX action_tokens_hash_key ON action_tokens (token_hash);
-- At most one live token per purpose per user: re-requesting a reset
-- invalidates the previous link rather than leaving both valid.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX action_tokens_live_key
    ON action_tokens (user_id, purpose) WHERE consumed_at IS NULL;

-- Signing keys live in the database so every replica agrees and rotation
-- is a row insert. The private half is encrypted at rest.
CREATE TABLE signing_keys (
    kid             text        PRIMARY KEY,
    algorithm       text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'EdDSA',
    public_key      bytea       NOT NULL,
    private_key_enc bytea       NOT NULL,
    active          boolean     NOT NULL DEFAULT true,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    retired_at      timestamptz
);
-- Exactly one active signing key at a time, enforced by the database.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX signing_keys_one_active ON signing_keys ((true)) WHERE active;

CREATE TABLE login_attempts (
    id              bigserial   PRIMARY KEY,
    email           citext      NOT NULL,
    ip_prefix       inet        NOT NULL,
    succeeded       boolean     NOT NULL,
    at              timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX login_attempts_email_idx ON login_attempts (email, at DESC);
CREATE INDEX login_attempts_ip_idx    ON login_attempts (ip_prefix, at DESC);
Three details in that schema that are security decisions, not style

1 · token_hash bytea, never the token itself — a database dump must not yield working credentials, exactly as with passwords. 2 · ip_prefix inet storing a /24 or /64 rather than a full address: enough to notice a session moving continents, not enough to be a tracking log you have to explain to a regulator. 3 · the partial unique index on action_tokens means requesting a second password reset invalidates the first, so a leaked email from last week cannot be replayed after the user requests a new one.

Notes

services/notes/migrations/000001_init.up.sql
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS notes;
SET search_path TO notes;

CREATE TABLE notebooks (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,
    owner_id        text        NOT NULL,          -- identity.users.id, NOT an FK:
                                                   -- cross-schema FKs would couple
                                                   -- the two services' deploys
    title           text        NOT NULL,
    icon            text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deleted_at      timestamptz
);
CREATE INDEX notebooks_owner_idx ON notebooks (owner_id) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

CREATE TABLE notes (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,
    notebook_id     text        NOT NULL REFERENCES notebooks(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    title           text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    body            text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    visibility      text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'private'
                    CHECK (visibility IN ('private','shared','public')),

    -- Per-FIELD logical clocks. The sync merge is last-writer-wins per
    -- field, so each mergeable field carries its own (lamport, actor)
    -- pair rather than one timestamp for the whole row (D11).
    title_lamport   bigint      NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    title_actor     text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    body_lamport    bigint      NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    body_actor      text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',

    version         bigint      NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,   -- optimistic concurrency
    created_by      text        NOT NULL,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    deleted_at      timestamptz                       -- tombstone, never a DELETE:
                                                      -- offline clients must be
                                                      -- able to learn about it
);
CREATE INDEX notes_notebook_idx ON notes (notebook_id, updated_at DESC)
    WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- Public publishing. A separate table because it has a different
-- lifecycle, a different access pattern, and a unique slug that must not
-- be reused after unpublishing.
CREATE TABLE public_notes (
    slug            text        PRIMARY KEY,          -- short, unguessable
    note_id         text        NOT NULL UNIQUE REFERENCES notes(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    password_hash   text,                             -- optional link password
    published_at    timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    revoked_at      timestamptz,
    view_count      bigint      NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX public_notes_live_idx ON public_notes (slug) WHERE revoked_at IS NULL;

-- ── the operation log: the heart of sync ──────────────────────────────
-- Append-only. server_seq gives a TOTAL ORDER per notebook, which is
-- what lets a client say "give me everything after 8791" and converge.
CREATE TABLE note_ops (
    op_id           text        PRIMARY KEY,          -- CLIENT-generated ULID
    notebook_id     text        NOT NULL REFERENCES notebooks(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    note_id         text        NOT NULL,
    server_seq      bigint      NOT NULL,
    actor_id        text        NOT NULL,
    device_id       text        NOT NULL,
    kind            text        NOT NULL
                    CHECK (kind IN ('create','set_field','delete','restore')),
    field           text,                             -- 'title' | 'body' | 'visibility'
    value           text,
    lamport         bigint      NOT NULL,
    applied         boolean     NOT NULL,             -- false = lost the merge,
                                                      -- still logged for audit
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- THE critical index: the change feed is always "this notebook, after
-- this sequence, in order". It also enforces per-notebook uniqueness of
-- the sequence, which is the invariant the whole protocol rests on.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX note_ops_feed_key ON note_ops (notebook_id, server_seq);
CREATE INDEX note_ops_note_idx ON note_ops (note_id, lamport DESC);

-- One sequence generator per notebook, so two notebooks never contend
-- and a hot notebook cannot stall a quiet one.
CREATE TABLE notebook_seq (
    notebook_id     text        PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES notebooks(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    last_seq        bigint      NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);

-- ── the ACL replica ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
-- collab owns permissions. notes keeps a LOCAL COPY, updated by events,
-- so a read is an index lookup instead of a network hop (D10).
CREATE TABLE acl_replica (
    notebook_id     text        NOT NULL,
    user_id         text        NOT NULL,
    role            text        NOT NULL
                    CHECK (role IN ('owner','editor','commenter','viewer')),
    revision        bigint      NOT NULL,   -- monotonic per (notebook,user):
                                            -- lets us ignore out-of-order events
    updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (notebook_id, user_id)
);
CREATE INDEX acl_replica_user_idx ON acl_replica (user_id);

-- Full-text search, maintained by a trigger so it cannot drift.
ALTER TABLE notes ADD COLUMN search tsvector
    GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title,'')), 'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body,'')),  'B')
    ) STORED;
CREATE INDEX notes_search_idx ON notes USING gin (search);
Why owner_id is not a foreign key

A foreign key from notes.notebooks to identity.users would be lovely for integrity and fatal for independence: the two services could no longer be deployed, migrated, backed up or split apart separately, and deleting a user would take a lock in another service's schema. Cross-service references are IDs with no constraint, and consistency is maintained by events plus a periodic reconciliation job. Inside a schema, use foreign keys everywhere — notes.id → notebooks.id is a real FK because one service owns both.

Collaboration

services/collab/migrations/000001_init.up.sql
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS collab;
SET search_path TO collab;

CREATE TABLE memberships (
    notebook_id     text        NOT NULL,
    user_id         text        NOT NULL,
    role            text        NOT NULL
                    CHECK (role IN ('owner','editor','commenter','viewer')),
    granted_by      text        NOT NULL,
    granted_via     text        NOT NULL
                    CHECK (granted_via IN ('owner','email_invite','link_invite')),
    revision        bigint      NOT NULL,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    PRIMARY KEY (notebook_id, user_id)
);
CREATE INDEX memberships_user_idx ON memberships (user_id);

-- Exactly one owner per notebook, enforced by the database rather than
-- by application logic that someone will eventually forget.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX memberships_one_owner
    ON memberships (notebook_id) WHERE role = 'owner';

CREATE TABLE invitations (
    id              text        PRIMARY KEY,
    notebook_id     text        NOT NULL,
    inviter_id      text        NOT NULL,
    kind            text        NOT NULL CHECK (kind IN ('email','link')),

    -- email invites: bound to an address, single use
    email           citext,
    -- link invites: unbound, capped uses, always time-limited
    max_uses        integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 1 CHECK (max_uses BETWEEN 1 AND 500),
    used_count      integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,

    role            text        NOT NULL
                    CHECK (role IN ('editor','commenter','viewer')),  -- never owner
    token_hash      bytea       NOT NULL,
    expires_at      timestamptz NOT NULL,
    revoked_at      timestamptz,
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),

    -- The two shapes have different required fields; the database
    -- enforces the distinction so a malformed invite cannot be stored.
    CONSTRAINT email_invite_shape CHECK (
        (kind = 'email' AND email IS NOT NULL AND max_uses = 1) OR
        (kind = 'link'  AND email IS NULL)
    ),
    CONSTRAINT uses_within_cap CHECK (used_count <= max_uses)
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX invitations_token_key ON invitations (token_hash);
CREATE INDEX invitations_notebook_idx ON invitations (notebook_id, created_at DESC);
-- One live email invite per (notebook, address): re-inviting replaces.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX invitations_live_email_key
    ON invitations (notebook_id, email)
    WHERE kind = 'email' AND revoked_at IS NULL AND used_count = 0;

CREATE TABLE invitation_redemptions (
    invitation_id   text        NOT NULL REFERENCES invitations(id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
    user_id         text        NOT NULL,
    redeemed_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    ip_prefix       inet,
    PRIMARY KEY (invitation_id, user_id)   -- one redemption per user per link
);

-- Append-only audit. Every permission change is a row, forever.
CREATE TABLE audit_log (
    id              bigserial   PRIMARY KEY,
    notebook_id     text        NOT NULL,
    actor_id        text        NOT NULL,
    action          text        NOT NULL,
    target_user_id  text,
    detail          jsonb       NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
    at              timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX audit_log_notebook_idx ON audit_log (notebook_id, at DESC);

CREATE SEQUENCE membership_revision_seq;
The two invitation shapes have genuinely different threat models

An email invite is bound to an address and single-use, so possession of the link is not sufficient — the accepting account's verified email must match. A link invite is a bearer token: anyone who has it gets in, so it must always have a TTL, a use cap, and a visible revoke button, and it must never be able to grant owner. The CHECK constraint encodes that distinction in the database, which means a bug in the service cannot produce an unbounded email invite or an address-bound link.

Row-level security as the second wall

services/notes/migrations/000002_rls.up.sql
SET search_path TO notes;

-- Defence in depth. The application already scopes every query by the
-- caller (D10) — this makes a query that FORGETS to return nothing
-- instead of everything. It is the difference between a code review
-- miss and a data breach.
ALTER TABLE notes     ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE notebooks ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE note_ops  ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- The service sets this per transaction: SET LOCAL quill.user_id = '...'
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION current_user_id() RETURNS text
LANGUAGE sql STABLE AS $$
    SELECT nullif(current_setting('quill.user_id', true), '')
$$;

CREATE POLICY notebooks_member ON notebooks
    USING (
        owner_id = current_user_id()
        OR EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 FROM acl_replica a
             WHERE a.notebook_id = notebooks.id
               AND a.user_id = current_user_id()
        )
    );

CREATE POLICY notes_member ON notes
    USING (
        EXISTS (
            SELECT 1 FROM notebooks nb
             WHERE nb.id = notes.notebook_id
               AND (nb.owner_id = current_user_id()
                    OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM acl_replica a
                                WHERE a.notebook_id = nb.id
                                  AND a.user_id = current_user_id()))
        )
    );

CREATE POLICY note_ops_member ON note_ops
    USING (
        EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM notebooks nb
                 WHERE nb.id = note_ops.notebook_id
                   AND (nb.owner_id = current_user_id()
                        OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM acl_replica a
                                    WHERE a.notebook_id = nb.id
                                      AND a.user_id = current_user_id())))
    );

-- The service role is subject to RLS; only the migration role bypasses.
ALTER TABLE notes     FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE notebooks FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE note_ops  FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- Public reads run as a DIFFERENT role with a narrow policy, so the
-- public page cannot see anything but published notes.
CREATE ROLE notes_public NOLOGIN;
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA notes TO notes_public;
GRANT SELECT ON notes, public_notes TO notes_public;
CREATE POLICY notes_public_read ON notes TO notes_public
    USING (
        visibility = 'public' AND deleted_at IS NULL
        AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM public_notes p
                     WHERE p.note_id = notes.id AND p.revoked_at IS NULL)
    );
RLS is a safety net, not the authorization model

It is a second wall behind an application that already filters correctly, and it has real costs: every policy predicate runs per row, so a badly written policy turns an index scan into a sequential one, and the planner's choices change in ways that surprise people. Measure the queries that matter with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) both ways. What RLS buys is that the failure mode of a forgotten WHERE clause becomes “returns nothing” rather than “returns everyone's notes” — and that trade is worth it for anything multi-tenant.

The shared database package

platform/pg/pg.go
// Package pg is the shared Postgres layer: a correctly configured pool,
// a transaction helper that cannot leak, and the RLS session variable.
package pg

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgconn"
	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
	"github.com/exaring/otelpgx"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/config"
)

type Config struct {
	DSN             config.Secret
	MaxConns        int32
	MinConns        int32
	MaxConnLifetime time.Duration
	MaxConnIdleTime time.Duration
	SearchPath      string // the service's own schema, and only that
}

func Open(ctx context.Context, c Config) (*pgxpool.Pool, error) {
	cfg, err := pgxpool.ParseConfig(c.DSN.Reveal())
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("parse dsn: %w", err)
	}

	// Sizing is arithmetic, not taste: max_connections, minus a reserve,
	// divided by replicas, divided by services sharing the instance (B07).
	cfg.MaxConns = c.MaxConns
	cfg.MinConns = c.MinConns
	// Recycling helps failover and lets a load balancer rebalance.
	cfg.MaxConnLifetime = c.MaxConnLifetime
	cfg.MaxConnIdleTime = c.MaxConnIdleTime
	cfg.ConnConfig.Tracer = otelpgx.NewTracer()

	// Pin the search path so a service physically cannot resolve another
	// service's tables by accident.
	cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams["search_path"] = c.SearchPath
	cfg.ConnConfig.RuntimeParams["application_name"] = "quill-" + c.SearchPath

	pool, err := pgxpool.NewWithConfig(ctx, cfg)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("connect: %w", err)
	}

	// sql.Open-style lazy connection hides a bad DSN until the first
	// request. Ping so a misconfiguration fails the deploy instead.
	pingCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
	defer cancel()
	if err := pool.Ping(pingCtx); err != nil {
		pool.Close()
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("ping: %w", err)
	}
	return pool, nil
}

// InTx runs fn inside a transaction. Rollback after a successful commit
// is a no-op, so the defer is correct on every path including a panic.
func InTx(ctx context.Context, pool *pgxpool.Pool, fn func(pgx.Tx) error) error {
	tx, err := pool.BeginTx(ctx, pgx.TxOptions{IsoLevel: pgx.ReadCommitted})
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("begin: %w", err)
	}
	defer func() { _ = tx.Rollback(ctx) }()

	if err := fn(tx); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if err := tx.Commit(ctx); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("commit: %w", err)
	}
	return nil
}

// InTxAs is InTx with the RLS session variable set. SET LOCAL is scoped
// to the transaction, so it cannot leak to the next borrower of this
// pooled connection — which a plain SET absolutely would.
func InTxAs(ctx context.Context, pool *pgxpool.Pool, userID string, fn func(pgx.Tx) error) error {
	return InTx(ctx, pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		if _, err := tx.Exec(ctx, "SELECT set_config('quill.user_id', $1, true)", userID); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("set rls subject: %w", err)
		}
		return fn(tx)
	})
}

// ---- error translation ---------------------------------------------

const (
	uniqueViolation     = "23505"
	foreignKeyViolation = "23503"
	checkViolation      = "23514"
	serializationFail   = "40001"
	deadlockDetected    = "40P01"
)

var (
	ErrNotFound  = errors.New("not found")
	ErrConflict  = errors.New("conflict")
	ErrViolation = errors.New("constraint violation")
	ErrRetryable = errors.New("retryable")
)

// Translate turns driver errors into domain-shaped ones at the boundary,
// so nothing above the store package ever imports pgx (B08).
func Translate(err error) error {
	if err == nil {
		return nil
	}
	if errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
		return ErrNotFound
	}
	var pe *pgconn.PgError
	if errors.As(err, &pe) {
		switch pe.Code {
		case uniqueViolation:
			return fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrConflict, pe.ConstraintName)
		case foreignKeyViolation, checkViolation:
			return fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrViolation, pe.ConstraintName)
		case serializationFail, deadlockDetected:
			return fmt.Errorf("%w: %s", ErrRetryable, pe.Code)
		}
	}
	return err
}

The transactional outbox

services/notes/migrations/000003_outbox.up.sql
SET search_path TO notes;

-- Identical in every service. The event and the business write commit
-- together or not at all, which is the only correct answer to the
-- dual-write problem (B12).
CREATE TABLE outbox (
    id              bigserial   PRIMARY KEY,
    event_id        text        NOT NULL UNIQUE,   -- ULID; consumers dedupe on it
    subject         text        NOT NULL,          -- "notes.changed"
    payload         jsonb       NOT NULL,
    trace_id        text        NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    published_at    timestamptz,
    attempts        integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_error      text
);

-- Partial index: only unpublished rows are indexed, so the relay's query
-- stays fast even when the table holds ten million published rows.
CREATE INDEX outbox_pending_idx ON outbox (id) WHERE published_at IS NULL;
platform/outbox/outbox.go
// Package outbox implements the transactional outbox: Enqueue writes an
// event row inside the caller's transaction, and Relay publishes it.
package outbox

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"
	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/pgxpool"
	"go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
)

type Event struct {
	ID      idgen.ID        `json:"id"`
	Subject string          `json:"subject"`
	Payload json.RawMessage `json:"payload"`
	TraceID string          `json:"trace_id"`
}

// Enqueue takes the CALLER'S transaction. That is the whole point: the
// business write and this insert share a commit.
func Enqueue(ctx context.Context, tx pgx.Tx, subject string, payload any) (idgen.ID, error) {
	b, err := json.Marshal(payload)
	if err != nil {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("marshal %s: %w", subject, err)
	}
	id := idgen.New()

	var traceID string
	if sc := trace.SpanContextFromContext(ctx); sc.IsValid() {
		traceID = sc.TraceID().String() // so the consumer's span links back
	}

	_, err = tx.Exec(ctx,
		`INSERT INTO outbox (event_id, subject, payload, trace_id) VALUES ($1,$2,$3,$4)`,
		id, subject, b, traceID)
	return id, err
}

type Publisher interface {
	Publish(ctx context.Context, e Event) error
}

type Relay struct {
	pool  *pgxpool.Pool
	pub   Publisher
	log   *slog.Logger
	batch int
	tick  time.Duration
}

func NewRelay(pool *pgxpool.Pool, pub Publisher, log *slog.Logger) *Relay {
	return &Relay{pool: pool, pub: pub, log: log, batch: 200, tick: 250 * time.Millisecond}
}

func (r *Relay) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	t := time.NewTicker(r.tick)
	defer t.Stop()
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return nil
		case <-t.C:
			n, err := r.flush(ctx)
			if err != nil {
				r.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "outbox flush", "err", err)
				continue
			}
			// Drain eagerly when we filled a batch, so a backlog after an
			// outage clears in seconds rather than at one batch per tick.
			for n == r.batch {
				if n, err = r.flush(ctx); err != nil {
					break
				}
			}
		}
	}
}

func (r *Relay) flush(ctx context.Context) (int, error) {
	var published int

	err := pgx.BeginFunc(ctx, r.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		// FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED: several relay replicas can run without
		// blocking on each other or double-publishing within a batch.
		rows, err := tx.Query(ctx, `
			SELECT id, event_id, subject, payload, trace_id
			  FROM outbox
			 WHERE published_at IS NULL
			 ORDER BY id
			 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
			 LIMIT $1`, r.batch)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		type row struct {
			id int64
			ev Event
		}
		var batch []row
		for rows.Next() {
			var x row
			if err := rows.Scan(&x.id, &x.ev.ID, &x.ev.Subject,
				&x.ev.Payload, &x.ev.TraceID); err != nil {
				rows.Close()
				return err
			}
			batch = append(batch, x)
		}
		rows.Close()
		if err := rows.Err(); err != nil { // the line everyone forgets (B07)
			return err
		}

		for _, x := range batch {
			if err := r.pub.Publish(ctx, x.ev); err != nil {
				// Stop at the first failure: order within a subject is
				// worth preserving, and the rest stay locked until the
				// transaction ends.
				_, _ = tx.Exec(ctx,
					`UPDATE outbox SET attempts = attempts + 1, last_error = $2 WHERE id = $1`,
					x.id, err.Error())
				return fmt.Errorf("publish %s: %w", x.ev.Subject, err)
			}
			if _, err := tx.Exec(ctx,
				`UPDATE outbox SET published_at = now() WHERE id = $1`, x.id); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			published++
		}
		return nil
	})

	// A publish that succeeded followed by a failed commit republishes on
	// the next pass. That is at-least-once, which is why every consumer
	// dedupes on event_id (B12) — there is no third option.
	return published, err
}
Keeping the outbox from becoming the biggest table in the database

Published rows are worth keeping briefly — they are an audit trail and they let you replay after a consumer bug — but not forever. A nightly job deleting published_at < now() - interval '7 days' in batches of ten thousand keeps it bounded without a long lock, and the partial index means the relay's own query never touches the dead rows anyway. Alert on the count of unpublished rows older than a minute: a growing backlog is your earliest signal that the event bus is unhappy.

The migration runner

services/notes/cmd/migrate/main.go
// A separate binary from the same image, run as a Kubernetes Job before
// the new pods roll. Never called from the API's startup path (B08).
package main

import (
	"embed"
	"errors"
	"flag"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"os"

	"github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4"
	"github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4/database/postgres"
	"github.com/golang-migrate/migrate/v4/source/iofs"
	_ "github.com/jackc/pgx/v5/stdlib"
	"database/sql"
)

//go:embed all:../../migrations/*.sql
var migrationsFS embed.FS

func main() {
	cmd := flag.String("cmd", "up", "up | down | version | force")
	to := flag.Int("to", 0, "target version for force")
	flag.Parse()

	if err := run(*cmd, *to); err != nil {
		slog.Error("migrate", "err", err)
		os.Exit(1)
	}
}

func run(cmd string, to int) error {
	dsn := os.Getenv("DATABASE_URL")
	if dsn == "" {
		return errors.New("DATABASE_URL is required")
	}

	db, err := sql.Open("pgx", dsn)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer db.Close()

	// The migration role is separate from the service role: it owns the
	// schema and bypasses RLS; the service role does neither.
	driver, err := postgres.WithInstance(db, &postgres.Config{
		SchemaName:      "notes",
		MigrationsTable: "schema_migrations",
		// Advisory lock so concurrent runners serialise instead of
		// corrupting each other — the reason this must not be N pods.
		DatabaseName: "quill",
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	src, err := iofs.New(migrationsFS, "../../migrations")
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	m, err := migrate.NewWithInstance("iofs", src, "postgres", driver)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer m.Close()

	switch cmd {
	case "up":
		err = m.Up()
	case "down":
		err = m.Steps(-1)
	case "force":
		err = m.Force(to)
	case "version":
		v, dirty, verr := m.Version()
		fmt.Printf("version=%d dirty=%v\n", v, dirty)
		return verr
	default:
		return fmt.Errorf("unknown command %q", cmd)
	}

	if err != nil && !errors.Is(err, migrate.ErrNoChange) {
		return err
	}
	v, dirty, _ := m.Version()
	slog.Info("migrations applied", "version", v, "dirty", dirty)
	if dirty {
		return fmt.Errorf("schema is DIRTY at version %d — a migration failed "+
			"partway; inspect, fix, then `-cmd=force -to=N`", v)
	}
	return nil
}
What “dirty” means and why it needs a human

golang-migrate marks the schema dirty when a migration fails partway, and it refuses to proceed afterwards. That is correct: the database is in a state neither version describes, and guessing which statements ran would be worse than stopping. The recovery is to inspect what actually happened, finish or undo it by hand, then force the version number. The way to avoid ever needing that is to keep each migration to one logical change and to run CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in its own file, outside a transaction.

Interview follow-up

“How do you handle data ownership across microservices?” One service owns each table and nobody else reads it — enforced by database roles and separate schemas, not by convention, so a cross-schema query fails at development time rather than surviving to production. Cross-service references are plain IDs with no foreign key, because an FK across a boundary re-couples the deployments it was supposed to separate. Where a service genuinely needs another's data on a hot path, it subscribes to events and maintains a read model it owns — which is what makes an authorization check an index lookup instead of a network call, at the price of a staleness window you must then handle deliberately.

D04

Identity I: registration, passwords and verification

The signup and login paths are where a product gets breached. This chapter builds them properly: Argon2id with tunable parameters stored alongside the hash, timing-equalised lookups so the endpoint is not a user-enumeration oracle, single-use email tokens, and rate limits that count both address and network. Part VI rebuilds this as a full authenticator model — passkeys, social sign-in, email codes — of which the password is then only one case.

Password hashing

services/identity/internal/domain/password.go
package domain

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/subtle"
	"encoding/base64"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"runtime"
	"strings"

	"golang.org/x/crypto/argon2"
)

// Params are stored INSIDE the encoded hash, so they can be raised later
// without invalidating a single existing password: a user logging in
// with an old hash is verified with its own parameters and transparently
// re-hashed with the new ones.
type Params struct {
	Memory      uint32 // KiB
	Iterations  uint32
	Parallelism uint8
	SaltLen     uint32
	KeyLen      uint32
}

// OWASP's 2024 floor is m=19456,t=2,p=1. We use more memory because a
// notebook app's login rate is low and memory is the parameter that
// actually costs an attacker with GPUs.
func DefaultParams() Params {
	p := Params{Memory: 64 * 1024, Iterations: 3, Parallelism: 2, SaltLen: 16, KeyLen: 32}
	if n := runtime.NumCPU(); n < int(p.Parallelism) {
		p.Parallelism = uint8(n)
	}
	return p
}

var (
	ErrInvalidHash  = errors.New("invalid password hash format")
	ErrIncompatible = errors.New("incompatible argon2 version")
)

func HashPassword(password string, p Params) (string, error) {
	salt := make([]byte, p.SaltLen)
	if _, err := rand.Read(salt); err != nil { // crypto/rand, never math/rand
		return "", fmt.Errorf("salt: %w", err)
	}
	key := argon2.IDKey([]byte(password), salt, p.Iterations, p.Memory, p.Parallelism, p.KeyLen)

	// PHC string format — the same encoding every other language's
	// argon2 library understands, so this is not a lock-in.
	return fmt.Sprintf("$argon2id$v=%d$m=%d,t=%d,p=%d$%s$%s",
		argon2.Version, p.Memory, p.Iterations, p.Parallelism,
		base64.RawStdEncoding.EncodeToString(salt),
		base64.RawStdEncoding.EncodeToString(key)), nil
}

// VerifyPassword reports whether the password matches, and whether the
// stored hash uses weaker parameters than the current default — the
// caller re-hashes on a successful login when needsRehash is true.
func VerifyPassword(password, encoded string) (ok bool, needsRehash bool, err error) {
	p, salt, want, err := decodeHash(encoded)
	if err != nil {
		return false, false, err
	}
	got := argon2.IDKey([]byte(password), salt, p.Iterations, p.Memory, p.Parallelism, p.KeyLen)

	// Constant time. A byte-by-byte == leaks how many bytes matched
	// through timing, which is a practical attack against a remote
	// service given enough samples.
	if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(got, want) != 1 {
		return false, false, nil
	}
	cur := DefaultParams()
	needsRehash = p.Memory < cur.Memory || p.Iterations < cur.Iterations
	return true, needsRehash, nil
}

func decodeHash(encoded string) (p Params, salt, key []byte, err error) {
	parts := strings.Split(encoded, "$")
	if len(parts) != 6 || parts[1] != "argon2id" {
		return p, nil, nil, ErrInvalidHash
	}
	var version int
	if _, err = fmt.Sscanf(parts[2], "v=%d", &version); err != nil {
		return p, nil, nil, ErrInvalidHash
	}
	if version != argon2.Version {
		return p, nil, nil, ErrIncompatible
	}
	if _, err = fmt.Sscanf(parts[3], "m=%d,t=%d,p=%d",
		&p.Memory, &p.Iterations, &p.Parallelism); err != nil {
		return p, nil, nil, ErrInvalidHash
	}
	if salt, err = base64.RawStdEncoding.DecodeString(parts[4]); err != nil {
		return p, nil, nil, ErrInvalidHash
	}
	if key, err = base64.RawStdEncoding.DecodeString(parts[5]); err != nil {
		return p, nil, nil, ErrInvalidHash
	}
	p.SaltLen, p.KeyLen = uint32(len(salt)), uint32(len(key))
	return p, salt, key, nil
}

// dummyHash is verified against when the email does not exist, so the
// unknown-user path costs the same CPU as the wrong-password path. See
// the note on enumeration below.
var dummyHash = func() string {
	h, err := HashPassword("quill-dummy-password-do-not-use", DefaultParams())
	if err != nil {
		panic(err) // at init, with a constant input — a bug, not a condition
	}
	return h
}()

func BurnPasswordTime(password string) { _, _, _ = VerifyPassword(password, dummyHash) }
The four password rules, and why each one is not optional

1 · A memory-hard hash — Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt — never SHA-256, because a GPU computes billions of those per second and a leaked table is cracked in hours. 2 · crypto/rand for the salt; math/rand is deterministic and seedable. 3 · subtle.ConstantTimeCompare, because == short-circuits on the first differing byte. 4 · Parameters stored with the hash, so raising the cost in 2027 does not log out every user.

Password policy

services/identity/internal/domain/policy.go
package domain

import (
	"strings"
	"unicode/utf8"
)

// Modern guidance (NIST SP 800-63B) is: length, a breach-corpus check,
// and nothing else. Composition rules — "one uppercase, one symbol" —
// measurably reduce entropy because users satisfy them predictably
// (Password1!), and they train people to write passwords down.
const (
	MinPasswordRunes = 12
	MaxPasswordBytes = 128 // argon2 cost is bounded; also stops a 10 MB body
)

type PasswordProblem string

const (
	PasswordTooShort   PasswordProblem = "too_short"
	PasswordTooLong    PasswordProblem = "too_long"
	PasswordBreached   PasswordProblem = "breached"
	PasswordSimilar    PasswordProblem = "similar_to_email"
	PasswordNotUTF8    PasswordProblem = "invalid_encoding"
)

type BreachChecker interface {
	// Breached reports whether the password appears in a known corpus.
	// The implementation uses k-anonymity: it sends the first five hex
	// characters of the SHA-1 and matches the suffix locally, so the
	// password never leaves the process.
	Breached(password string) (bool, error)
}

func CheckPassword(password, email string, bc BreachChecker) []PasswordProblem {
	var out []PasswordProblem

	if !utf8.ValidString(password) {
		return []PasswordProblem{PasswordNotUTF8}
	}
	// Count RUNES for the minimum and BYTES for the maximum: a 12-rune
	// Japanese passphrase is fine, and a 128-byte cap bounds hash cost.
	if utf8.RuneCountInString(password) < MinPasswordRunes {
		out = append(out, PasswordTooShort)
	}
	if len(password) > MaxPasswordBytes {
		out = append(out, PasswordTooLong)
	}
	if local, _, ok := strings.Cut(email, "@"); ok && len(local) >= 4 &&
		strings.Contains(strings.ToLower(password), strings.ToLower(local)) {
		out = append(out, PasswordSimilar)
	}
	if bc != nil && len(out) == 0 {
		// Fail OPEN on a checker error: a down third party must not stop
		// people signing up. Log it and count it instead.
		if breached, err := bc.Breached(password); err == nil && breached {
			out = append(out, PasswordBreached)
		}
	}
	return out
}

Registration

services/identity/internal/app/register.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"strings"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
)

type RegisterInput struct {
	Email       string
	Password    string
	DisplayName string
}

type RegisterOutput struct {
	UserID idgen.ID
	// Deliberately no token, no session, no "already registered" flag:
	// the response is identical whether or not the address was taken.
}

func (s *Service) Register(ctx context.Context, in RegisterInput) (RegisterOutput, error) {
	email := domain.NormaliseEmail(in.Email)

	if probs := domain.CheckPassword(in.Password, email, s.breaches); len(probs) > 0 {
		return RegisterOutput{}, domain.PasswordRejected(probs)
	}

	hash, err := domain.HashPassword(in.Password, domain.DefaultParams())
	if err != nil {
		return RegisterOutput{}, fmt.Errorf("hash password: %w", err)
	}

	userID := idgen.New()
	plainToken, tokenHash := domain.NewActionToken()

	err = pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		created, err := q.InsertUserIfAbsent(ctx, InsertUserIfAbsentParams{
			ID:          userID,
			Email:       email,
			DisplayName: strings.TrimSpace(in.DisplayName),
		})
		if err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}

		// The address is already registered. We do NOT return an error —
		// that would make this endpoint an enumeration oracle. Instead we
		// send a "someone tried to sign up with your address" email and
		// return the same success shape. The attacker learns nothing; the
		// real owner learns something useful.
		if !created {
			if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.signup_attempted",
				map[string]any{"email": email}); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			return nil
		}

		if err := q.InsertCredentials(ctx, InsertCredentialsParams{
			UserID: userID, PasswordHash: hash,
		}); err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}

		if err := q.InsertActionToken(ctx, InsertActionTokenParams{
			ID:        idgen.New(),
			UserID:    userID,
			Purpose:   "verify_email",
			TokenHash: tokenHash,
			ExpiresAt: time.Now().Add(24 * time.Hour),
		}); err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}

		// The email is an EVENT in the same transaction, not an SMTP call.
		// If the commit fails, no email is sent; if it succeeds, the
		// email is guaranteed to go out even if the mailer is down (B12).
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.user_registered",
			UserRegistered{
				UserID: userID, Email: email,
				DisplayName: in.DisplayName, VerifyToken: plainToken,
			})
		return err
	})
	if err != nil {
		return RegisterOutput{}, err
	}

	return RegisterOutput{UserID: userID}, nil
}
services/identity/query.sql — excerpt
-- name: InsertUserIfAbsent :one
-- ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING plus a RETURNING trick: the boolean tells the
-- caller whether a row was actually created, in one round trip and with
-- no race between a SELECT and an INSERT.
INSERT INTO users (id, email, display_name)
VALUES (@id, @email, @display_name)
ON CONFLICT (email) WHERE status <> 'deleted' DO NOTHING
RETURNING true AS created;

-- name: InsertCredentials :exec
INSERT INTO credentials (user_id, password_hash) VALUES (@user_id, @password_hash);

-- name: InsertActionToken :exec
-- The partial unique index means re-requesting supersedes: consume any
-- live token for this purpose first, so an old emailed link dies.
WITH superseded AS (
    UPDATE action_tokens SET consumed_at = now()
     WHERE user_id = @user_id AND purpose = @purpose AND consumed_at IS NULL
)
INSERT INTO action_tokens (id, user_id, purpose, token_hash, expires_at)
VALUES (@id, @user_id, @purpose, @token_hash, @expires_at);

-- name: ConsumeActionToken :one
-- Single use, enforced atomically: the UPDATE both checks and consumes,
-- so two concurrent redemptions cannot both succeed.
UPDATE action_tokens
   SET consumed_at = now()
 WHERE token_hash = @token_hash
   AND purpose    = @purpose
   AND consumed_at IS NULL
   AND expires_at > now()
RETURNING user_id, payload;

-- name: FindCredentialsByEmail :one
SELECT u.id, u.email, u.email_verified, u.status, c.password_hash
  FROM users u
  JOIN credentials c ON c.user_id = u.id
 WHERE u.email = @email AND u.status = 'active';

Tokens sent by email

services/identity/internal/domain/token.go
package domain

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/base64"
)

// 32 bytes of entropy, URL-safe. We return the plaintext (to email) and
// the hash (to store). The plaintext is never persisted anywhere — a
// database dump must not yield working password-reset links.
func NewActionToken() (plain string, hash []byte) {
	b := make([]byte, 32)
	if _, err := rand.Read(b); err != nil {
		panic("crypto/rand failed: " + err.Error()) // unrecoverable
	}
	plain = base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(b)
	return plain, HashToken(plain)
}

// SHA-256 rather than Argon2: these tokens are already 256 bits of
// uniform randomness, so there is nothing to brute-force and no reason
// to pay a memory-hard cost on every verification. That reasoning does
// NOT transfer to passwords, which are low-entropy by nature.
func HashToken(plain string) []byte {
	sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(plain))
	return sum[:]
}

Login

services/identity/internal/app/login.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"net/netip"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
)

type LoginInput struct {
	Email     string
	Password  string
	TOTPCode  string
	UserAgent string
	IP        netip.Addr
}

type LoginOutput struct {
	Tokens      TokenPair
	MFARequired bool
	MFAToken    string // short-lived, only valid for the TOTP step
}

// One error for every failure reason. The caller cannot distinguish
// "no such user" from "wrong password" from "unverified" from "locked",
// which is the whole point.
var ErrInvalidCredentials = errors.New("invalid credentials")

func (s *Service) Login(ctx context.Context, in LoginInput) (LoginOutput, error) {
	email := domain.NormaliseEmail(in.Email)
	prefix := domain.IPPrefix(in.IP) // /24 or /64

	// Two independent limits. Per-account stops credential stuffing
	// against one victim; per-network stops spraying across many
	// accounts from one source. Either alone is trivially bypassed.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "login:email:"+email, 10, time.Minute); err != nil {
		return LoginOutput{}, err
	}
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "login:ip:"+prefix.String(), 60, time.Minute); err != nil {
		return LoginOutput{}, err
	}

	cred, err := s.q.FindCredentialsByEmail(ctx, email)
	switch {
	case errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound):
		// Burn the same CPU the real path would, so the response time
		// does not reveal whether the address exists. Without this, the
		// endpoint is an enumeration oracle measurable over the network.
		domain.BurnPasswordTime(in.Password)
		s.recordAttempt(ctx, email, prefix, false)
		return LoginOutput{}, ErrInvalidCredentials
	case err != nil:
		return LoginOutput{}, err
	}

	ok, needsRehash, err := domain.VerifyPassword(in.Password, cred.PasswordHash)
	if err != nil {
		// A corrupt stored hash is our bug, not the user's. Log it as an
		// error and still return the generic failure to the caller.
		s.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "corrupt password hash", "user_id", cred.ID, "err", err)
		return LoginOutput{}, ErrInvalidCredentials
	}
	if !ok {
		s.recordAttempt(ctx, email, prefix, false)
		return LoginOutput{}, ErrInvalidCredentials
	}

	// Unverified accounts fail with the SAME error, so signing up with
	// someone else's address tells you nothing about whether they have
	// an account already.
	if !cred.EmailVerified {
		s.recordAttempt(ctx, email, prefix, false)
		return LoginOutput{}, ErrInvalidCredentials
	}

	// Transparent upgrade: the password was correct, so we have the
	// plaintext exactly once and can re-hash at current parameters.
	if needsRehash {
		if newHash, herr := domain.HashPassword(in.Password, domain.DefaultParams()); herr == nil {
			if uerr := s.q.UpdatePasswordHash(ctx, cred.ID, newHash); uerr != nil {
				s.log.WarnContext(ctx, "rehash failed", "user_id", cred.ID, "err", uerr)
			}
		}
	}

	s.recordAttempt(ctx, email, prefix, true)

	if s.hasConfirmedTOTP(ctx, cred.ID) {
		if in.TOTPCode == "" {
			tok, err := s.issueMFAChallenge(ctx, cred.ID)
			return LoginOutput{MFARequired: true, MFAToken: tok}, err
		}
		if err := s.verifyTOTP(ctx, cred.ID, in.TOTPCode); err != nil {
			s.recordAttempt(ctx, email, prefix, false)
			return LoginOutput{}, ErrInvalidCredentials
		}
	}

	pair, err := s.issueSession(ctx, cred.ID, in.UserAgent, prefix, true)
	return LoginOutput{Tokens: pair}, err
}
Enumeration resistance costs three lines and is almost always missing

If “no such user” returns in 3 ms and “wrong password” takes 60 ms because it ran Argon2, an attacker can enumerate your entire user base over the network with a stopwatch — and then target those addresses with phishing or credential stuffing. Hashing a dummy password on the unknown-user path equalises the cost. The same principle governs the response body (one generic error), the registration endpoint (same response whether or not the address exists), and password reset (“if that address exists, we sent a link”).

Rate limiting

platform/authn/limiter.go
package authn

import (
	"context"
	"time"

	"github.com/redis/go-redis/v9"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/problem"
)

// An in-process limiter would mean the real limit is N × configured and
// changes whenever the autoscaler moves, so the counter lives in Redis.
// The whole decision must be ONE round trip or two requests race.
var tokenBucket = redis.NewScript(`
local key    = KEYS[1]
local rate   = tonumber(ARGV[1])   -- tokens per second
local burst  = tonumber(ARGV[2])
local now    = tonumber(ARGV[3])
local ttl    = tonumber(ARGV[4])

local b      = redis.call('HMGET', key, 'tokens', 'ts')
local tokens = tonumber(b[1]) or burst
local ts     = tonumber(b[2]) or now

tokens = math.min(burst, tokens + (now - ts) * rate)

local allowed = 0
if tokens >= 1 then
  tokens  = tokens - 1
  allowed = 1
end

redis.call('HMSET', key, 'tokens', tokens, 'ts', now)
redis.call('EXPIRE', key, ttl)
return {allowed, math.floor(tokens)}
`)

type Limiter struct {
	rdb *redis.Client
}

func NewLimiter(rdb *redis.Client) *Limiter { return &Limiter{rdb: rdb} }

// Check allows `burst` requests per `window`, refilling smoothly.
func (l *Limiter) Check(ctx context.Context, key string, burst int, window time.Duration) error {
	rate := float64(burst) / window.Seconds()
	now := float64(time.Now().UnixNano()) / 1e9
	ttl := int(window.Seconds()*2) + 1

	res, err := tokenBucket.Run(ctx, l.rdb, []string{"rl:" + key},
		rate, burst, now, ttl).Slice()
	if err != nil {
		// FAIL OPEN. A limiter outage must not become a login outage —
		// but count it, because failing open silently is how you
		// discover Redis has been down for a week during an incident.
		limiterErrors.Inc()
		return nil
	}
	if allowed, _ := res[0].(int64); allowed == 1 {
		return nil
	}
	return problem.TooManyRequests(int(window.Seconds()))
}
Fail open on the limiter, fail closed on authentication

The directions are opposite and both are deliberate. A rate limiter exists to protect availability, so when the limiter itself is unavailable, enforcing it would cause the outage it was meant to prevent — allow the request and alert. Authentication exists to protect data, so when the verifier is unavailable the only safe answer is to reject. Getting these the wrong way round produces either a service that falls over when Redis hiccups, or one that lets everyone in when the key server is slow.

Email verification and password reset

services/identity/internal/app/verify.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
)

var ErrTokenInvalid = errors.New("token is invalid or has expired")

func (s *Service) VerifyEmail(ctx context.Context, plainToken string) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// ConsumeActionToken checks purpose, expiry and single-use in one
		// atomic UPDATE, so two concurrent clicks cannot both win.
		row, err := q.ConsumeActionToken(ctx, ConsumeActionTokenParams{
			TokenHash: domain.HashToken(plainToken),
			Purpose:   "verify_email",
		})
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return ErrTokenInvalid
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.MarkEmailVerified(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.email_verified",
			map[string]any{"user_id": row.UserID})
		return err
	})
}

// RequestPasswordReset always reports success. The response, the status
// code and the timing are identical whether or not the address exists.
func (s *Service) RequestPasswordReset(ctx context.Context, email string) error {
	email = domain.NormaliseEmail(email)

	// Rate limit BEFORE the lookup, so this cannot be used as an
	// enumeration oracle by watching which addresses get limited.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "reset:"+email, 3, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return nil // still report success
	}

	user, err := s.q.FindActiveUserByEmail(ctx, email)
	if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
		return nil
	}
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	plain, hash := domain.NewActionToken()
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.InsertActionToken(ctx, InsertActionTokenParams{
			ID: idgen.New(), UserID: user.ID, Purpose: "reset_password",
			TokenHash: hash,
			// Short TTL: a reset link sitting in an inbox is a standing
			// credential, and 30 minutes is plenty for a real user.
			ExpiresAt: time.Now().Add(30 * time.Minute),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.password_reset_requested",
			map[string]any{"user_id": user.ID, "email": email, "token": plain})
		return err
	})
}

func (s *Service) ResetPassword(ctx context.Context, plainToken, newPassword string) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		row, err := q.ConsumeActionToken(ctx, ConsumeActionTokenParams{
