		// the point of having roles at all.
		role, err := s.roleFor(ctx, q, note.NotebookID, in.UserID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if !role.CanPublish() {
			return domain.ErrForbidden
		}

		slug = newSlug()

		var pwHash *string
		if in.Password != "" {
			h, err := domain.HashLinkPassword(in.Password)
			if err != nil {
				return err
			}
			pwHash = &h
		}

		if err := q.InsertPublicNote(ctx, InsertPublicNoteParams{
			Slug: slug, NoteID: in.NoteID, PasswordHash: pwHash,
		}); err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}
		if err := q.SetVisibility(ctx, SetVisibilityParams{
			ID: in.NoteID, Visibility: string(domain.Public),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Publishing is an auditable security event, not a content edit.
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "notes.published", NotePublished{
			NoteID: in.NoteID, NotebookID: note.NotebookID,
			ActorID: in.UserID, Slug: slug, HasPassword: pwHash != nil,
		})
		return err
	})
	return slug, err
}

// The slug IS the access control for a public note, so it must be
// unguessable: 20 bytes of crypto/rand is 160 bits, which no amount of
// enumeration will find. A sequential id or a title-derived slug would
// let anyone walk the corpus.
func newSlug() string {
	b := make([]byte, 20)
	if _, err := rand.Read(b); err != nil {
		panic("crypto/rand failed: " + err.Error())
	}
	return strings.ToLower(base32.StdEncoding.
		WithPadding(base32.NoPadding).EncodeToString(b))
}

// Unpublish revokes rather than deletes, so the slug is never reused —
// a link that was shared and then revoked must stay dead forever, not
// start resolving to someone else's note.
func (s *Service) Unpublish(ctx context.Context, userID, noteID idgen.ID) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		note, err := q.GetNoteForUpdate(ctx, noteID)
		if err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}
		role, err := s.roleFor(ctx, q, note.NotebookID, userID)
		if err != nil || !role.CanPublish() {
			return domain.ErrForbidden
		}
		if err := q.RevokePublicNote(ctx, noteID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.SetVisibility(ctx, SetVisibilityParams{
			ID: noteID, Visibility: string(domain.Private),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// The cache must be purged NOW. A revoked note still served from
		// an edge cache for an hour is the user's data still public for
		// an hour, and they were told it was private.
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "notes.unpublished",
			map[string]any{"note_id": noteID, "slug": note.Slug})
		return err
	})
}
An unguessable URL is a capability, and it behaves like one

160 bits of randomness means the slug cannot be found by enumeration — but it can be forwarded, pasted into a chat, indexed by a browser extension, or leaked in a Referer header when the reader clicks an outbound link. Treat it as a bearer token: send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer on the public page, set X-Robots-Tag: noindex unless the owner opts in, offer the optional link password for anything sensitive, and make revocation instant and cache-purging. Never tell a user that an unguessable link is “private”.

Rendering untrusted markdown

services/notes/internal/render/markdown.go
// Package render turns a note body into HTML that is safe to serve to a
// browser. Every note body is UNTRUSTED input written by one user and
// displayed to another, so this is a security boundary, not a
// presentation detail.
package render

import (
	"bytes"
	"sync"

	"github.com/microcosm-cc/bluemonday"
	"github.com/yuin/goldmark"
	"github.com/yuin/goldmark/extension"
	"github.com/yuin/goldmark/renderer/html"
)

var (
	md = goldmark.New(
		goldmark.WithExtensions(extension.GFM, extension.Typographer),
		goldmark.WithRendererOptions(
			// Raw HTML in the source is NOT rendered. Even with the
			// sanitiser behind it, not parsing it at all removes a whole
			// class of parser-differential bug where goldmark and
			// bluemonday disagree about what a construct means.
			html.WithXHTML(),
		),
	)

	// The policy is an allowlist: anything not named is stripped. Built
	// once because compiling it is not free and it is immutable after.
	policy = sync.OnceValue(func() *bluemonday.Policy {
		p := bluemonday.UGCPolicy()

		// Links open in a new tab, and rel prevents the opener attack
		// where the target page can rewrite window.opener.location.
		p.AllowAttrs("target").Matching(bluemonday.Paragraph).OnElements("a")
		p.RequireNoFollowOnLinks(true)
		p.RequireNoReferrerOnLinks(true)
		p.AddTargetBlankToFullyQualifiedLinks(true)

		// Only http(s) and mailto. Without this, `[click](javascript:…)`
		// is a stored XSS, and `data:text/html,…` is the same thing
		// wearing a hat.
		p.AllowURLSchemes("http", "https", "mailto")

		// Images by URL only, and no dimensions an attacker can use to
		// probe the reader's network by timing.
		p.AllowAttrs("src", "alt", "title").OnElements("img")
		p.AllowAttrs("class").Matching(
			regexp.MustCompile(`^language-[a-z0-9]+$`)).OnElements("code")

		p.AllowElements("table", "thead", "tbody", "tr", "th", "td")
		return p
	})
)

func ToSafeHTML(markdown string) (string, error) {
	var buf bytes.Buffer
	if err := md.Convert([]byte(markdown), &buf); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}
	// Sanitise AFTER rendering. Sanitising the markdown first does not
	// work: the renderer can produce HTML from constructs the sanitiser
	// never saw, and the sanitiser's own output is not markdown.
	return policy().Sanitize(buf.String()), nil
}
Sanitise the output, never the input

Sanitising markdown before rendering is a recurring and subtle mistake: the two stages disagree about syntax, so a construct the sanitiser reads as text can become a tag after rendering. Render first, then run an allowlist sanitiser over the resulting HTML, and do it at read time rather than storing sanitised HTML — because when a sanitiser CVE lands you want to fix it by deploying, not by reprocessing every row you ever stored. Store the markdown; sanitise on the way out; add a CSP as the layer behind both.

The public page

services/gateway/internal/transport/http/public.go
package http

import (
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/hex"
	"net/http"
	"strconv"
	"time"
)

func (g *Gateway) publicPage() http.Handler {
	return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
		ctx := r.Context()
		slug := r.PathValue("slug")

		// A short Redis cache in front of the notes service. Public pages
		// are the only genuinely cacheable thing in Quill, and they are
		// also the only thing that can be hit by a crowd.
		if page, ok := g.pageCache.Get(ctx, slug); ok {
			g.writePublicPage(w, r, page)
			return
		}

		// singleflight: a link going viral must produce ONE origin
		// request per gateway pod, not ten thousand (B09).
		v, err, _ := g.pageGroup.Do(slug, func() (any, error) {
			return g.fetchPublicPage(ctx, slug)
		})
		if err != nil {
			g.writePublicError(w, r, err)
			return
		}
		page := v.(*PublicPage)

		// Do NOT cache a password-protected page at the edge: the cached
		// copy would be served to someone who never supplied the
		// password.
		if !page.RequiresPassword {
			g.pageCache.Set(ctx, slug, page, 60*time.Second)
		}
		g.writePublicPage(w, r, page)
	})
}

func (g *Gateway) writePublicPage(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, p *PublicPage) {
	h := w.Header()
	h.Set("Content-Type", "text/html; charset=utf-8")

	// A much stricter CSP than the app's, because this page renders
	// content written by a stranger. No inline script at all; styles are
	// a single hashed inline block.
	h.Set("Content-Security-Policy",
		"default-src 'none'; img-src https: data:; "+
			"style-src 'sha256-"+styleHash+"'; "+
			"font-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'none'; "+
			"form-action 'none'")
	h.Set("X-Content-Type-Options", "nosniff")
	h.Set("X-Frame-Options", "DENY")
	// The slug is a capability; do not leak it to sites the reader
	// navigates to from here.
	h.Set("Referrer-Policy", "no-referrer")
	if !p.Indexable {
		h.Set("X-Robots-Tag", "noindex, nofollow, noarchive")
	}

	if p.RequiresPassword {
		// Never cache the challenge page, and never let a shared cache
		// hold anything about this slug.
		h.Set("Cache-Control", "no-store, private")
		g.renderPasswordPrompt(w, p)
		return
	}

	// Conditional requests: an unchanged page costs a 304 with no body,
	// which is most of the benefit of a CDN without needing one.
	etag := `"` + p.Version + `"`
	h.Set("ETag", etag)
	h.Set("Last-Modified", p.UpdatedAt.UTC().Format(http.TimeFormat))
	// `public` is safe ONLY because this response contains no
	// user-specific data at all. Getting this wrong on an authenticated
	// route puts one user's notes in a shared cache.
	h.Set("Cache-Control", "public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300")
	h.Add("Vary", "Accept-Encoding")

	if match := r.Header.Get("If-None-Match"); match == etag {
		w.WriteHeader(http.StatusNotModified)
		return
	}
	_ = publicTemplate.Execute(w, p)
}
services/notes/internal/transport/http/templates/public.gohtml
{{/*
  html/template escapes CONTEXTUALLY — differently inside an attribute,
  a URL, a script block and CSS. text/template escapes nothing, and
  using it here would be a stored XSS (P06).

  .BodyHTML is template.HTML, which DISABLES escaping for that value.
  That is only acceptable because render.ToSafeHTML sanitised it with an
  allowlist immediately before. Every other use of template.HTML on
  non-constant data in this repository is a bug.
*/}}
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>{{ .Title }} · Quill</title>
  <meta property="og:title" content="{{ .Title }}">
  <meta property="og:description" content="{{ .Excerpt }}">
  {{ if not .Indexable }}<meta name="robots" content="noindex, nofollow">{{ end }}
  <style>{{ .InlineCSS }}</style>
</head>
<body>
  <article>
    <h1>{{ .Title }}</h1>
    <p class="meta">
      Published {{ .PublishedAt.Format "2 January 2006" }}
    </p>
    {{ .BodyHTML }}
  </article>
  <footer><a href="https://quill.app">Published with Quill</a></footer>
</body>
</html>

Cache invalidation on unpublish

services/gateway/internal/events/purge.go
package events

// The gateway subscribes to notes.unpublished and notes.changed so a
// revoked or edited page stops being served immediately. This is the
// piece people forget, and it is the difference between "I made it
// private" and "it was private an hour later".
func (c *Consumer) handleUnpublished(ctx context.Context, e outbox.Event) error {
	var p struct {
		Slug string `json:"slug"`
	}
	if err := json.Unmarshal(e.Payload, &p); err != nil {
		// A malformed payload is permanent: retrying cannot fix it, so
		// acknowledge and dead-letter rather than looping forever (B12).
		return fmt.Errorf("%w: unmarshal: %v", ErrPermanent, err)
	}
	if p.Slug == "" {
		return nil
	}

	// Purge every gateway replica's local cache, not just this one.
	// A NATS broadcast subject with a per-pod ephemeral consumer is the
	// simplest mechanism that reaches all of them.
	if err := c.pageCache.Delete(ctx, p.Slug); err != nil {
		return err // transient: let the retry handle it
	}
	// And the CDN, if there is one in front. This call is idempotent and
	// safe to repeat, which is why at-least-once delivery is fine.
	return c.cdn.PurgeTag(ctx, "note:"+p.Slug)
}
Cache keys, and the header that makes them safe

Every cached response must be keyed on everything that varies it. The public page varies on nothing but the slug — which is exactly why it can be Cache-Control: public. The moment a response depends on who is asking, public becomes a data leak through any shared cache, and you need private or no-store plus a Vary that names every input. The gateway sets no-store by default on every proxied response and only the public page opts out, which makes the dangerous case the one you have to write down deliberately.

Search

services/notes/query.sql — search
-- name: SearchNotes :many
-- websearch_to_tsquery accepts what a user actually types — quoted
-- phrases, OR, a leading minus for exclusion — and never errors on
-- malformed input. plainto_tsquery ignores operators; to_tsquery throws
-- a syntax error on a stray apostrophe, which becomes a 500 the first
-- time someone searches for "don't".
SELECT n.id, n.notebook_id, n.title, n.updated_at,
       ts_rank_cd(n.search, q.query) AS rank,
       ts_headline('english', n.body, q.query,
                   'MaxFragments=2, MaxWords=18, MinWords=6, '
                   'StartSel=<mark>, StopSel=</mark>') AS snippet
  FROM notes n,
       websearch_to_tsquery('english', @q) AS q(query)
 WHERE n.search @@ q.query
   AND n.deleted_at IS NULL
   -- The same ACL scope as every other read. A search endpoint that
   -- forgets it is the most damaging possible place to forget it,
   -- because it returns content rather than just existence.
   AND EXISTS (
       SELECT 1 FROM notebooks nb
        WHERE nb.id = n.notebook_id
          AND nb.deleted_at IS NULL
          AND (nb.owner_id = @user_id
               OR EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM acl_replica a
                           WHERE a.notebook_id = nb.id AND a.user_id = @user_id))
   )
 ORDER BY rank DESC, n.updated_at DESC
 LIMIT @page_size;
services/notes/internal/app/search.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"html"
	"strings"
	"time"
	"unicode/utf8"
)

const (
	maxQueryRunes = 200
	searchTimeout = 3 * time.Second
)

func (s *Service) Search(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	q string, pageSize int) ([]SearchHit, error) {

	q = strings.TrimSpace(q)
	if q == "" {
		return nil, nil // an empty query is not an error; it is no results
	}
	if utf8.RuneCountInString(q) > maxQueryRunes {
		return nil, domain.ErrQueryTooLong
	}
	pageSize = clamp(pageSize, 1, 50) // never trust a client-supplied limit

	// Search is the query most likely to go pathological on a large
	// corpus, so it gets a tighter deadline than the route default. The
	// user sees "search timed out" instead of the whole page hanging.
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, searchTimeout)
	defer cancel()

	rows, err := s.q.SearchNotes(ctx, SearchNotesParams{
		Q: q, UserID: userID, PageSize: int32(pageSize),
	})
	if err != nil {
		if errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded) {
			searchTimeouts.Inc()
			return nil, domain.ErrSearchTimeout
		}
		return nil, err
	}

	hits := make([]SearchHit, 0, len(rows)) // preallocate (R02)
	for _, r := range rows {
		hits = append(hits, SearchHit{
			NoteID: r.ID, NotebookID: r.NotebookID,
			Title: r.Title, UpdatedAt: r.UpdatedAt,
			// ts_headline emits our <mark> tags around matches and
			// escapes nothing else, so the snippet is passed to the
			// client as structured data and the CLIENT decides how to
			// render it. We never inject it into HTML server-side.
			Snippet: r.Snippet,
		})
	}
	return hits, nil
}
When Postgres full-text search stops being enough

It is genuinely good to a few million documents: one tsvector column, one GIN index, no extra infrastructure, and it participates in the same transaction and the same ACL as everything else — which is the property that matters most, because a separate search cluster is where permission checks get forgotten. You outgrow it when you need typo tolerance, multi-language analysis, faceting, or relevance tuning beyond ts_rank_cd. At that point the move is to OpenSearch or Typesense with a projection kept current by the same event stream — and the first thing to get right is that the search index must carry the ACL, or it becomes a way to read other people's notes.

The generated column, and why it is not a trigger

ALTER TABLE notes ADD COLUMN search tsvector GENERATED ALWAYS AS ( setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(title,'')), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector('english', coalesce(body, '')), 'B') ) STORED; GENERATED ALWAYS rather than a trigger, for three reasons: · it cannot drift — there is no path that writes a row without updating the vector, including a direct psql UPDATE during an incident · it is declarative, so the definition is visible in \d notes instead of hidden in a function · the planner knows it is deterministic setweight makes a title match rank above a body match, which is what a user expects: searching "budget" should surface the note called Budget before one that mentions the word in passing. The cost: every write recomputes the vector, so a 1 MiB body costs real CPU on each save. For Quill that is fine — notes are saved at human speed. For a high-write table, the answer is a separate index table updated asynchronously from the op log.

Caching layers, and what each is for

LayerHoldsInvalidated by
Client SQLiteEverything the user can seeThe sync protocol itself (D11) — not a TTL
Browser / CDNPublic pages onlyETag revalidation, plus an explicit purge on unpublish
Redis, gatewayRendered public pages, 60 sTTL plus an event-driven delete
Redis, JWKSPublic signing keys, 5 minTTL, plus refetch on an unknown kid
In-process ACL replicaPermissions, in PostgresEvents from collab (D10)
NothingAuthenticated note readsThey come from the client's local replica, which is faster than any server cache could be
The best cache is the one on the client

Quill deliberately does not cache authenticated note reads server-side, and the reason is architectural rather than lazy: the client already holds a complete local replica, so a read is a SQLite query at tens of microseconds. A server-side cache would sit behind a network round trip and could only ever be slower, while adding an invalidation problem and a staleness bug class. This is the payoff of local-first design — you get the cache-hit path for free and you get it correct, because the sync protocol is what keeps it fresh.

Interview follow-up

“A user publishes a note publicly, then unpublishes it. What has to happen?” Revoke rather than delete, so the slug is permanently dead and can never resolve to different content. Flip the visibility. Then — the part that is usually missed — purge every cache that could still serve it: the gateway's Redis copy, every gateway replica's local copy, and the CDN, driven by an event rather than a best-effort call, so it still happens if the purge fails the first time. Until that purge completes the note is still public, and the user has been told it is not, so the time-to-purge is a number worth measuring and alerting on.

D09

Collaboration: invitations by email and by link

Two ways to invite someone, with genuinely different threat models. An email invite is bound to an address and single-use; a link invite is a bearer token anyone can forward. This chapter builds both, plus membership management, revocation and the audit trail that makes all of it defensible.

The two shapes, side by side

Email inviteLink invite
Bound toA specific verified addressNobody — whoever holds it
UsesExactly one1 to 500, capped
Expiry7 daysMandatory, max 30 days
Possession sufficient?No — the accepting account's email must matchYes. It is a capability
Can granteditor, commenter, viewereditor, commenter, viewer
Never grantsowner — ownership transfer is a separate, re-authenticated flow
Leaked link meansNothing, unless the attacker also controls that mailboxAccess, until revoked
RevocationPer invitePer invite, and it must be one click
Why an invitation may never grant ownership

Ownership carries the right to delete the notebook, to publish it to the internet, and to remove every other member — including the current owner. An invite link that grants it turns a forwarded URL into a total account-level compromise of that notebook. Transfer is therefore a distinct flow: the current owner initiates it, the recipient must already be a member, both parties are notified, and the initiating owner re-authenticates. The CHECK constraint in the schema (D03) means even a bug in this service cannot produce an owner-granting invite.

Creating an invitation

services/collab/internal/domain/invitation.go
package domain

import (
	"errors"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
)

type InviteKind string

const (
	InviteEmail InviteKind = "email"
	InviteLink  InviteKind = "link"
)

var (
	ErrInviteInvalid   = errors.New("invitation is invalid, expired or used up")
	ErrInviteWrongUser = errors.New("this invitation was sent to a different address")
	ErrInviteEmailUnverified = errors.New("verify your email address first")
	ErrAlreadyMember   = errors.New("already a member")
	ErrCannotGrantOwner = errors.New("invitations cannot grant ownership")
	ErrSelfInvite      = errors.New("you cannot invite yourself")
)

const (
	MaxEmailInviteTTL = 7 * 24 * time.Hour
	MaxLinkInviteTTL  = 30 * 24 * time.Hour
	MaxLinkUses       = 500
)

type Invitation struct {
	ID         idgen.ID
	NotebookID idgen.ID
	InviterID  idgen.ID
	Kind       InviteKind
	Email      string // email invites only
	Role       Role
	MaxUses    int
	UsedCount  int
	ExpiresAt  time.Time
	RevokedAt  *time.Time
}

// Usable is the single place that decides whether an invitation can be
// redeemed. Having one function rather than four scattered checks means
// a new condition is added once and applies everywhere.
func (i *Invitation) Usable(now time.Time) error {
	switch {
	case i.RevokedAt != nil:
		return ErrInviteInvalid
	case now.After(i.ExpiresAt):
		return ErrInviteInvalid
	case i.UsedCount >= i.MaxUses:
		return ErrInviteInvalid
	}
	return nil
}

func ValidateNewInvite(kind InviteKind, role Role, ttl time.Duration, maxUses int) error {
	if role == RoleOwner {
		return ErrCannotGrantOwner
	}
	if !role.Valid() {
		return errors.New("unknown role")
	}
	switch kind {
	case InviteEmail:
		if ttl <= 0 || ttl > MaxEmailInviteTTL {
			return errors.New("email invitations expire within 7 days")
		}
		if maxUses != 1 {
			return errors.New("email invitations are single use")
		}
	case InviteLink:
		// A link with no expiry is a permanent credential in whatever
		// chat it was pasted into. Mandatory, no exceptions.
		if ttl <= 0 || ttl > MaxLinkInviteTTL {
			return errors.New("link invitations must expire within 30 days")
		}
		if maxUses < 1 || maxUses > MaxLinkUses {
			return errors.New("link invitations allow 1 to 500 uses")
		}
	default:
		return errors.New("unknown invitation kind")
	}
	return nil
}
services/collab/internal/app/invite.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"strings"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/collab/internal/domain"
)

type CreateInviteInput struct {
	ActorID    idgen.ID
	NotebookID idgen.ID
	Kind       domain.InviteKind
	Email      string
	Role       domain.Role
	TTL        time.Duration
	MaxUses    int
}

type CreateInviteOutput struct {
	InvitationID idgen.ID
	URL          string // returned ONCE; never retrievable afterwards
	ExpiresAt    time.Time
}

func (s *Service) CreateInvite(ctx context.Context, in CreateInviteInput) (CreateInviteOutput, error) {
	if err := domain.ValidateNewInvite(in.Kind, in.Role, in.TTL, in.MaxUses); err != nil {
		return CreateInviteOutput{}, err
	}

	// Only an owner may invite. An editor with sharing rights would let
	// anyone who gains edit access escalate to granting access — a
	// privilege-escalation path that is easy to create by accident.
	role, err := s.roleOf(ctx, in.NotebookID, in.ActorID)
	if err != nil {
		return CreateInviteOutput{}, err
	}
	if !role.CanShare() {
		return CreateInviteOutput{}, domain.ErrForbidden
	}

	email := strings.ToLower(strings.TrimSpace(in.Email))
	if in.Kind == domain.InviteEmail {
		if email == "" {
			return CreateInviteOutput{}, errors.New("email is required")
		}
		// Rate limit per notebook, not per user: an owner who can send
		// a thousand invites is a spam relay wearing your domain's
		// reputation.
		if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx,
			"invite:"+in.NotebookID.String(), 50, time.Hour); err != nil {
			return CreateInviteOutput{}, err
		}
	}

	plain, hash := domain.NewInviteToken()
	id := idgen.New()
	expires := time.Now().Add(in.TTL)

	err = pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// Re-inviting an address supersedes the previous live invite, so
		// an old emailed link stops working. Without this, every resend
		// leaves another valid credential in another inbox.
		if in.Kind == domain.InviteEmail {
			if err := q.RevokeLiveEmailInvites(ctx, RevokeLiveEmailInvitesParams{
				NotebookID: in.NotebookID, Email: email,
			}); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		if err := q.InsertInvitation(ctx, InsertInvitationParams{
			ID: id, NotebookID: in.NotebookID, InviterID: in.ActorID,
			Kind: string(in.Kind), Email: nullIfEmpty(email),
			Role: string(in.Role), MaxUses: int32(in.MaxUses),
			TokenHash: hash, ExpiresAt: expires,
		}); err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}

		if err := q.InsertAudit(ctx, InsertAuditParams{
			NotebookID: in.NotebookID, ActorID: in.ActorID,
			Action: "invitation.created",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{
				"kind": in.Kind, "role": in.Role, "email": email,
				"max_uses": in.MaxUses, "expires_at": expires,
			}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Only email invites produce an email. A link invite is handed
		// to the creator to distribute however they like.
		if in.Kind == domain.InviteEmail {
			_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "collab.invitation_created",
				InvitationCreated{
					InvitationID: id, NotebookID: in.NotebookID,
					InviterID: in.ActorID, Email: email,
					Role: string(in.Role), Token: plain, ExpiresAt: expires,
				})
			return err
		}
		return nil
	})
	if err != nil {
		return CreateInviteOutput{}, err
	}

	return CreateInviteOutput{
		InvitationID: id,
		// The plaintext token exists in this response and in the email,
		// and NOWHERE else. Only its hash is stored, so a database dump
		// does not yield working invitations.
		URL:       s.baseURL + "/invite/" + plain,
		ExpiresAt: expires,
	}, nil
}

Redeeming

services/collab/internal/app/accept.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"net/netip"
	"strings"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/collab/internal/domain"
)

type AcceptInput struct {
	Token         string
	UserID        idgen.ID
	UserEmail     string
	EmailVerified bool
	IP            netip.Addr
}

type AcceptOutput struct {
	NotebookID idgen.ID
	Role       domain.Role
}

func (s *Service) AcceptInvite(ctx context.Context, in AcceptInput) (AcceptOutput, error) {
	// Brute-forcing a 256-bit token is not feasible, but limiting the
	// attempt rate also stops someone probing with harvested tokens and
	// keeps the audit log readable.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "accept:"+in.UserID.String(), 20, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return AcceptOutput{}, err
	}

	var out AcceptOutput

	err := pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// FOR UPDATE on the invitation row: two people redeeming the last
		// use of a link at the same moment must not both succeed and
		// push used_count past max_uses. The CHECK constraint would
		// catch it, but as an error rather than as correct behaviour.
		inv, err := q.FindInvitationForUpdate(ctx, domain.HashToken(in.Token))
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return domain.ErrInviteInvalid
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := inv.Usable(time.Now()); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// ── the email-invite binding ─────────────────────────────────
		if inv.Kind == string(domain.InviteEmail) {
			// Case-insensitive, because email addresses are.
			if !strings.EqualFold(inv.Email.String, in.UserEmail) {
				// Deliberately a DIFFERENT error from "invalid": the user
				// is signed in as the wrong account and telling them so
				// is the difference between a fixable confusion and a
				// support ticket.
				return domain.ErrInviteWrongUser
			}
			// Possession of the link plus an unverified address is not
			// proof of anything — anyone can type any address at signup.
			if !in.EmailVerified {
				return domain.ErrInviteEmailUnverified
			}
		}

		if inv.InviterID == in.UserID {
			return domain.ErrSelfInvite
		}

		// Already a member: succeed idempotently rather than erroring.
		// Clicking a link twice, or having been added by two routes, is
		// not a failure — but do NOT consume a use for it.
		if existing, err := q.GetMembership(ctx, GetMembershipParams{
			NotebookID: inv.NotebookID, UserID: in.UserID,
		}); err == nil {
			out = AcceptOutput{NotebookID: inv.NotebookID,
				Role: domain.Role(existing.Role)}
			return nil
		} else if !errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return err
		}

		// One redemption per user per link, enforced by the primary key.
		// Without it, one person could exhaust a 500-use link by
		// clicking it repeatedly after being removed.
		if err := q.InsertRedemption(ctx, InsertRedemptionParams{
			InvitationID: inv.ID, UserID: in.UserID,
			IpPrefix: domain.IPPrefix(in.IP),
		}); err != nil {
			if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrConflict) {
				return domain.ErrInviteInvalid
			}
			return err
		}

		revision, err := q.NextMembershipRevision(ctx)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertMembership(ctx, InsertMembershipParams{
			NotebookID: inv.NotebookID, UserID: in.UserID,
			Role: inv.Role, GrantedBy: inv.InviterID,
			GrantedVia: string(inv.Kind) + "_invite", Revision: revision,
		}); err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}

		if err := q.IncrementInviteUse(ctx, inv.ID); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertAudit(ctx, InsertAuditParams{
			NotebookID: inv.NotebookID, ActorID: in.UserID,
			Action: "invitation.accepted", TargetUserID: &in.UserID,
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{
				"invitation_id": inv.ID, "role": inv.Role, "kind": inv.Kind,
			}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// The event that updates every ACL replica (D10). Until it is
		// consumed, the user is a member here but cannot read notes —
		// a window of tens of milliseconds that the UI handles by
		// retrying once.
		if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "collab.membership_changed",
			MembershipChanged{
				NotebookID: inv.NotebookID, UserID: in.UserID,
				Role: inv.Role, Revision: revision, Action: "granted",
			}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Tell the inviter, so a link being redeemed by someone
		// unexpected is visible rather than silent.
		if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "collab.invite_redeemed",
			map[string]any{
				"notebook_id": inv.NotebookID, "inviter_id": inv.InviterID,
				"user_id": in.UserID, "kind": inv.Kind,
			}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		out = AcceptOutput{NotebookID: inv.NotebookID, Role: domain.Role(inv.Role)}
		return nil
	})
	return out, err
}
Three concurrency bugs this code avoids, all of which are easy to write

1 · Two people redeeming the last use of a link simultaneously — prevented by FOR UPDATE on the invitation row, so the second waits and then sees used_count == max_uses. 2 · One user consuming many uses by clicking repeatedly — prevented by the (invitation_id, user_id) primary key on redemptions. 3 · An already-member click consuming a use — prevented by returning early before the increment. All three look like edge cases until a link is posted in a team channel and thirty people click it within a second.

Revocation and membership changes

services/collab/internal/app/membership.go
package app

// RemoveMember is the flow that matters most for security: it is what an
// owner reaches for when someone leaves the company or a laptop is
// stolen, and it must take effect quickly and completely.
func (s *Service) RemoveMember(ctx context.Context, actorID, notebookID,
	targetID idgen.ID) error {

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		actorRole, err := s.roleOfTx(ctx, q, notebookID, actorID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// An owner may remove anyone; anyone may remove themselves.
		// Nobody else may remove anybody.
		if !actorRole.CanShare() && actorID != targetID {
			return domain.ErrForbidden
		}

		target, err := q.GetMembership(ctx, GetMembershipParams{
			NotebookID: notebookID, UserID: targetID,
		})
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return nil // already not a member: idempotent success
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if domain.Role(target.Role) == domain.RoleOwner {
			// The unique index enforces one owner, so removing them
			// would leave the notebook ownerless and unmanageable.
			return domain.ErrCannotRemoveOwner
		}

		revision, err := q.NextMembershipRevision(ctx)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.DeleteMembership(ctx, DeleteMembershipParams{
			NotebookID: notebookID, UserID: targetID,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Revoke every invitation that person could use to come straight
		// back in. Removing the membership without this is a revocation
		// that undoes itself the moment they re-click their email.
		if err := q.RevokeInvitesForUser(ctx, RevokeInvitesForUserParams{
			NotebookID: notebookID, Email: target.Email,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertAudit(ctx, InsertAuditParams{
			NotebookID: notebookID, ActorID: actorID,
			Action: "membership.removed", TargetUserID: &targetID,
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"previous_role": target.Role}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Two events. The ACL replicas must drop the row, and realtime
		// must disconnect any socket that user holds for this notebook —
		// otherwise they keep receiving change notifications for a
		// notebook they were just removed from.
		if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "collab.membership_changed",
			MembershipChanged{
				NotebookID: notebookID, UserID: targetID,
				Revision: revision, Action: "revoked",
			}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "collab.access_revoked",
			map[string]any{"notebook_id": notebookID, "user_id": targetID})
		return err
	})
}
Revocation has to reach five places, and it is easy to miss two

Removing a member must: delete the membership row; revoke any live invitation bound to their address; propagate to every ACL replica so reads stop working; disconnect their realtime subscriptions so they stop being told about changes; and — the one almost everyone forgets — the data already on their device stays there. Local-first means a removed collaborator keeps the local replica they had. That is not a bug you can fix server-side, so say it in the product: removing someone stops future access, it does not un-share what they already have.

The endpoints

EndpointWhoNotes
POST/v1/notebooks/{id}/invitationsownerReturns the URL once; never retrievable again
GET/v1/notebooks/{id}/invitationsownerMetadata only — never the token or its hash
DELETE/v1/invitations/{id}ownerImmediate; idempotent
POST/v1/invitations/acceptany signed-in userToken in the body, never the query string
GET/v1/invitations/previewany signed-in userNotebook name and inviter only, to show before accepting
GET/v1/notebooks/{id}/membersany memberDisplay names via identity.GetUsers
PATCH/v1/notebooks/{id}/members/{uid}ownerChange role; cannot set owner
DELETE/v1/notebooks/{id}/members/{uid}owner, or selfAlso revokes their invitations
GET/v1/notebooks/{id}/auditownerAppend-only history of every permission change
services/collab/internal/transport/http/invitations.go
package http

type acceptRequest struct {
	// In the BODY, not the path or query. URLs end up in access logs,
	// browser history, Referer headers and screen shares — and this
	// token is a credential.
	Token string `json:"token"`
}

func (h *Handler) accept(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	ctx := r.Context()
	sub := httpx.MustSubject(ctx)

	req, p := httpx.Decode[acceptRequest](w, r)
	if p != nil {
		problem.Write(ctx, w, p)
		return
	}
	if req.Token == "" {
		problem.Write(ctx, w, problem.BadRequest("token is required"))
		return
	}

	// The accepting user's verified email comes from the token claims,
	// not from the request body. Letting the client assert its own email
	// would make the email binding decorative.
	out, err := h.app.AcceptInvite(ctx, app.AcceptInput{
		Token: req.Token, UserID: sub.UserID,
		UserEmail: sub.Email, EmailVerified: sub.EmailVerified,
		IP: clientAddr(r),
	})
	if err != nil {
		h.writeInviteError(w, r, err)
		return
	}
	httpx.JSON(ctx, w, http.StatusOK, map[string]any{
		"notebook_id": out.NotebookID, "role": out.Role,
	})
}

func (h *Handler) writeInviteError(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request, err error) {
	ctx := r.Context()
	switch {
	case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrInviteInvalid):
		// Deliberately vague: expired, revoked, used up and never-existed
		// are one message, so a token cannot be probed for its state.
		problem.Write(ctx, w, problem.New(http.StatusGone, "invitation-invalid",
			"Invitation is no longer valid",
			"ask the owner to send you a new one"))
	case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrInviteWrongUser):
		// Specific ON PURPOSE. The user holds a valid invitation and is
		// simply signed in as the wrong account; telling them turns a
		// support ticket into a five-second fix, and reveals nothing an
		// attacker could not already infer from holding the token.
		problem.Write(ctx, w, problem.New(http.StatusForbidden, "invitation-wrong-account",
			"Wrong account", "this invitation was sent to a different address"))
	case errors.Is(err, domain.ErrInviteEmailUnverified):
		problem.Write(ctx, w, problem.New(http.StatusForbidden, "email-unverified",
			"Verify your email", "confirm your address, then open the link again"))
	default:
		h.writeError(w, r, err)
	}
}
Where to be vague and where to be specific

The rule is whether the message tells an attacker something they could not already determine. “Invalid or expired” for an unknown token is correctly vague — distinguishing “expired” from “never existed” would confirm that a guessed token was once real. But “this invitation was for a different address” is safe to say plainly, because the person reading it already holds the token, and the alternative is a user who cannot work out why a valid link does not work. Vagueness is a security tool, not a default.

The invitation email

services/mailer/internal/templates/invitation.gohtml — excerpt
{{/* Every interpolated value is user-controlled. html/template escapes
     contextually, and the inviter's display name in particular is
     attacker-controlled text arriving in someone else's inbox. */}}
<p>
  <strong>{{ .InviterName }}</strong> ({{ .InviterEmail }})
  invited you to collaborate on <strong>{{ .NotebookTitle }}</strong>
  as a <strong>{{ .Role }}</strong>.
</p>

<p><a href="{{ .AcceptURL }}" class="button">Open the notebook</a></p>

<p class="muted">
  This invitation was sent to {{ .RecipientEmail }} and expires on
  {{ .ExpiresAt.Format "2 January 2006" }}. It can only be accepted by
  an account using that address.
</p>

<p class="muted">
  If you were not expecting this, you can ignore it — no account has been
  created and nobody has access to anything of yours.
</p>
An invitation email is a message from a stranger, sent by you

The inviter's display name and the notebook title are both attacker-controlled strings arriving in a third party's inbox with your domain in the From header — which is a phishing vector if you let it be. Escape contextually (html/template, never text/template), cap the lengths so a “display name” cannot be a paragraph of instructions, strip control characters and bidirectional-override marks, and never let the inviter supply free-text body content. Rate limit per notebook and per inviter, monitor bounce and complaint rates, and be prepared to suspend an account that is using invitations as a mail relay.

Interview follow-up

“Design a sharing-by-link feature.” Start by naming it a bearer capability, because that framing produces the right requirements: mandatory expiry, a use cap, one-click revocation, no ability to grant the highest role, and an audit entry for every redemption so the owner can see who used it. Then contrast it with an email invitation, which is bound to a verified address and single-use, so possession alone is insufficient. The detail that shows real experience is the redemption race — several people clicking a nearly-exhausted link at once — and the answer that it needs a row lock plus a per-user redemption key, not an optimistic check.

D10

Authorization: the permission model

Authentication answers “who are you”; this chapter answers “may you”. The interesting problem in a distributed system is not the rule but the location: collab owns permissions, notes enforces them, and a network call per read would be unacceptable. The answer is a replicated read model, and the honest handling of the staleness it introduces.

The model

Four roles, strictly ordered viewer (1) read notes, read members commenter(2) + add comments editor (3) + create, edit and delete notes owner (4) + invite, remove members, publish, delete the notebook Ordering them means a check is a comparison rather than a chain of equality tests, and adding a role later does not require revisiting every call site. Three places a permission is enforced, deliberately 1 the query every read is scoped by the caller in SQL. Forgetting it returns nothing, not everything. 2 the service an explicit role check before any mutation, against the local ACL replica. 3 row-level security a Postgres policy behind both, so a query that escapes 1 and 2 still returns nothing. Layer 1 is the one that actually prevents the common bug. Layers 2 and 3 exist because layer 1 is written by humans, repeatedly, forever.
Broken object-level authorization is the most common real API vulnerability

It is number one on the OWASP API list and it is always the same shape: the endpoint authenticates correctly, then fetches by an ID taken from the URL without checking that the ID belongs to the caller — so changing /v1/notes/01HX…A to …B returns someone else's note. Middleware cannot see it, because middleware does not know what a note is. Only the query can. That is why every read query in Quill takes @user_id and every write takes a role check, and why neither is optional.

Where the truth lives, and where the copy lives

collab (source of truth) notes (read model) ┌────────────────────────┐ ┌────────────────────────┐ │ memberships │ │ acl_replica │ │ notebook_id │ event │ notebook_id │ │ user_id │ ───────▶ │ user_id │ │ role │ │ role │ │ granted_by │ │ revision │ │ granted_via │ └────────────────────────┘ │ revision ◀── monotonic│ │ └────────────────────────┘ ▼ every read is ONE INDEX LOOKUP in the same transaction as the data it guards Why not call collab on every read? · a 1 ms local lookup becomes a 5-15 ms network round trip · notes now fails when collab is restarting · collab must scale with notes' read traffic · the call is inside the transaction that reads the note, so it holds a database connection while waiting on the network — the pattern that exhausts a pool (B07) What it costs: a staleness window of tens of milliseconds between a permission change and every replica seeing it. That window is the subject of the rest of this chapter, and pretending it does not exist is how eventually-consistent systems become insecure ones.

Keeping the replica correct

services/notes/internal/events/acl.go
// Package events consumes collab's membership stream and maintains the
// local ACL replica. Every property that makes this safe is in this one
// file, so it is worth reading closely.
package events

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"fmt"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/eventbus"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
)

type MembershipChanged struct {
	NotebookID string `json:"notebook_id"`
	UserID     string `json:"user_id"`
	Role       string `json:"role"`
	Revision   int64  `json:"revision"` // monotonic, allocated by collab
	Action     string `json:"action"`   // granted | changed | revoked
}

func (c *Consumer) handleMembershipChanged(ctx context.Context, e outbox.Event) error {
	var m MembershipChanged
	if err := json.Unmarshal(e.Payload, &m); err != nil {
		// Permanent: retrying a malformed payload forever is a loop, not
		// a recovery. Dead-letter it and alert (B12).
		return fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", eventbus.ErrPermanent, err)
	}

	switch m.Action {
	case "granted", "changed":
		// The revision comparison is what makes this SAFE under
		// at-least-once, out-of-order delivery. Two events for the same
		// user can arrive in either order — a grant then a revoke, or
		// the reverse — and applying the older one last would be a
		// security bug. The WHERE clause makes an old event a no-op.
		return c.q.UpsertACLIfNewer(ctx, UpsertACLIfNewerParams{
			NotebookID: m.NotebookID, UserID: m.UserID,
			Role: m.Role, Revision: m.Revision,
		})

	case "revoked":
		return c.q.DeleteACLIfNewer(ctx, DeleteACLIfNewerParams{
			NotebookID: m.NotebookID, UserID: m.UserID, Revision: m.Revision,
		})

	default:
		return fmt.Errorf("%w: unknown action %q", eventbus.ErrPermanent, m.Action)
	}
}
services/notes/query.sql — the replica writes
-- name: UpsertACLIfNewer :exec
-- Idempotent AND order-independent. Replaying the same event does
-- nothing; an event that arrives late does nothing. Both properties are
-- required, because the bus is at-least-once and unordered across
-- partitions.
INSERT INTO acl_replica (notebook_id, user_id, role, revision)
VALUES (@notebook_id, @user_id, @role, @revision)
ON CONFLICT (notebook_id, user_id) DO UPDATE
   SET role = EXCLUDED.role,
       revision = EXCLUDED.revision,
       updated_at = now()
 WHERE acl_replica.revision < EXCLUDED.revision;

-- name: DeleteACLIfNewer :exec
-- A revoke is a delete, but ONLY if it is newer than what we hold —
-- otherwise a late revoke event could undo a subsequent re-grant.
DELETE FROM acl_replica
 WHERE notebook_id = @notebook_id
   AND user_id = @user_id
   AND revision < @revision;

-- name: ACLDrift :many
-- Used by the reconciliation job: everything this replica believes,
-- so it can be compared against collab's authoritative list.
SELECT notebook_id, user_id, role, revision FROM acl_replica
 WHERE updated_at < now() - interval '1 hour'
 ORDER BY notebook_id, user_id;
A revision number is what makes an at-least-once stream safe for permissions

Without it, the ordering of two events decides who has access — and NATS, Kafka and SQS all reserve the right to redeliver and to reorder across partitions. With a monotonic revision allocated by the source of truth, every write becomes “apply only if newer”, which is idempotent and commutative: any delivery order converges to the same state. This is the single most important detail in the whole read-model design, and it is three words in a WHERE clause.

The check itself

services/notes/internal/app/authz.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/notes/internal/domain"
	collabv1 "github.com/quillhq/quill/proto/collab/v1"
)

// roleFor resolves the caller's role from the LOCAL replica. One index
// lookup, inside the caller's transaction, no network.
func (s *Service) roleFor(ctx context.Context, q Querier,
	notebookID, userID idgen.ID) (domain.Role, error) {

	role, err := q.GetRole(ctx, GetRoleParams{
		NotebookID: notebookID, UserID: userID,
	})
	if err == nil {
		return domain.Role(role), nil
	}
	if !errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
		return "", err
	}
	// Absent from the replica. That is either "genuinely not a member"
	// or "we have not consumed the grant event yet" — and the two are
	// indistinguishable locally.
	return "", domain.ErrForbidden
}

// roleForStrong is the escape hatch, used ONLY where the staleness
// window is unacceptable. It asks collab directly and accepts the
// network cost, the extra failure mode, and the latency.
//
// Used by exactly two call sites in Quill:
//   · publishing a note to the public internet
//   · deleting a notebook
// Both are rare, both are irreversible from the user's point of view,
// and both are worth 10 ms.
func (s *Service) roleForStrong(ctx context.Context,
	notebookID, userID idgen.ID) (domain.Role, error) {

	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
	defer cancel()

	resp, err := s.collab.CheckPermission(ctx, &collabv1.CheckPermissionRequest{
		NotebookId: notebookID.String(), UserId: userID.String(),
	})
	if err != nil {
		// FAIL CLOSED. Unlike the rate limiter (D04), an authorization
		// check that cannot complete must deny. An unavailable collab
		// means publishing is briefly impossible, which is the correct
		// outcome — the alternative is publishing without a check.
		authzStrongFailures.Inc()
		return "", fmt.Errorf("permission check unavailable: %w", err)
	}
	return domain.Role(resp.GetRole()), nil
}

// requireRole is the shape every mutation uses, so the check cannot be
// half-written. Taking the minimum role as an argument means the call
// site reads as a sentence: requireRole(ctx, q, nb, user, RoleEditor).
func (s *Service) requireRole(ctx context.Context, q Querier,
	notebookID, userID idgen.ID, min domain.Role) error {

	role, err := s.roleFor(ctx, q, notebookID, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if !role.AtLeast(min) {
		// One error for "not a member" and "insufficient role". The
		// caller must not be able to distinguish them, or the endpoint
		// reveals which notebooks exist and who belongs to them.
		return domain.ErrForbidden
	}
	return nil
}
Fail open or fail closed, decided per mechanism

A rate limiter protects availability, so when it is unavailable, enforcing it would cause the outage it was meant to prevent — fail open, and alert. An authorization check protects data, so when it is unavailable the only safe answer is to deny — fail closed, and let the feature be briefly unusable. Writing both in the same codebase makes the asymmetry visible, which is the point: engineers who have not thought about it tend to pick one behaviour and apply it everywhere, and either choice is wrong half the time.

Handling the staleness window honestly

DirectionStale replica meansSeverityMitigation
Grant not yet appliedA new collaborator briefly gets 403AnnoyingThe accept response tells the client to retry once after 500 ms; collab also seeds the replica synchronously for the notebook owner
Revoke not yet appliedA removed collaborator can still read for tens of millisecondsA security windowPublish revocations on a dedicated high-priority subject, and additionally push a realtime disconnect so their client stops pulling
Event lost entirelyThe replica diverges permanentlySeriousThe outbox makes loss nearly impossible; the reconciliation job below catches what remains
Consumer stoppedEverything freezes at the last applied revisionSerious, and silentAlert on consumer lag and on replica age — a read model with no freshness metric is a liability
services/notes/internal/events/reconcile.go
package events

import (
	"context"
	"time"
)

// Reconcile compares the local replica against collab's authoritative
// list and repairs divergence. It is the honest answer to "what if an
// event is lost": not "that cannot happen", but "here is the job that
// notices and fixes it, and here is the metric that tells you how often".
//
// Runs hourly, behind a leader lease so only one replica does it (P05).
func (r *Reconciler) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	t := time.NewTicker(time.Hour)
	defer t.Stop()
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return nil
		case <-t.C:
			if err := r.once(ctx); err != nil {
				r.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "acl reconcile", "err", err)
			}
		}
	}
}

func (r *Reconciler) once(ctx context.Context) error {
	var cursor string
	var drift int

	for {
		// Page through collab's memberships. A full snapshot of a large
		// tenant in one response would be a memory and timeout problem,
		// so this is a cursor-paged gRPC stream.
		page, err := r.collab.ListMemberships(ctx, &collabv1.ListMembershipsRequest{
			Cursor: cursor, PageSize: 1000,
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		want := make(map[aclKey]aclVal, len(page.Memberships))
		for _, m := range page.Memberships {
			want[aclKey{m.NotebookId, m.UserId}] = aclVal{m.Role, m.Revision}
		}

		have, err := r.q.ACLForNotebooks(ctx, page.NotebookIDs())
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		for k, w := range want {
			h, ok := have[k]
			if !ok || h.role != w.role {
				drift++
				// Repair using collab's revision, so a subsequent real
				// event still wins if it is newer.
				if err := r.q.UpsertACLIfNewer(ctx, UpsertACLIfNewerParams{
					NotebookID: k.notebook, UserID: k.user,
					Role: w.role, Revision: w.revision,
				}); err != nil {
					return err
				}
			}
			delete(have, k)
		}
		// Anything left in `have` is a membership collab does not know
		// about — a missed revoke, which is the dangerous direction.
		for k := range have {
			drift++
			r.log.WarnContext(ctx, "acl replica has extra grant",
				"notebook_id", k.notebook, "user_id", k.user)
			if err := r.q.DeleteACL(ctx, k.notebook, k.user); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		if page.NextCursor == "" {
			break
		}
		cursor = page.NextCursor
	}

	// Drift should be ZERO. A non-zero value is not "self-healing
	// working as designed" — it is evidence that events are being lost,
	// and it deserves an alert rather than a dashboard nobody opens.
	aclDrift.Set(float64(drift))
	return nil
}
A read model without a freshness metric is a liability

The failure that actually hurts is not a lost event — the outbox makes that nearly impossible — it is a stopped consumer. The replica simply freezes, every read keeps working against last week's permissions, and nothing errors. Export three numbers and alert on all of them: consumer lag on the membership subject, the age of the oldest un-updated replica row, and the drift count from reconciliation. Without them, "eventually consistent" quietly becomes "consistent with a state from before the security incident".

Row-level security, measured

the cost of the policy, on a realistic table
quill=> EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id = '01HX…';

-- as the migration role (RLS bypassed)
Index Scan using notes_pkey on notes  (cost=0.43..8.45 rows=1)
  Index Cond: (id = '01HX…')
  Buffers: shared hit=4
Execution Time: 0.081 ms

-- as notes_svc, with quill.user_id set (policy applied)
Index Scan using notes_pkey on notes  (cost=0.43..16.92 rows=1)
  Index Cond: (id = '01HX…')
  Filter: (SubPlan 1)
  SubPlan 1
    ->  Index Scan using acl_replica_pkey on acl_replica a
          Index Cond: ((notebook_id = notes.notebook_id) AND
                       (user_id = current_user_id()))
  Buffers: shared hit=9
Execution Time: 0.119 ms

# 0.04 ms for a second wall that turns a forgotten WHERE clause from a
# data breach into an empty result set. That is a trade worth making.
#
# It is NOT always this cheap: the policy must be index-supported. A
# policy whose predicate cannot use an index turns every scan into a
# per-row subquery, and on a large table that is the difference between
# 0.1 ms and 400 ms. Always EXPLAIN both ways before shipping one.

Testing authorization

services/notes/internal/app/authz_test.go
package app_test

// A matrix test. Authorization is exactly the kind of logic where a
// table-driven test earns its keep: every (role, action) pair is one
// line, gaps are visible, and adding a role fails the test until every
// action is decided.
func TestPermissionMatrix(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	actions := []struct {
		name string
		do   func(context.Context, *app.Service, idgen.ID, idgen.ID) error
	}{
		{"read",      func(ctx context.Context, s *app.Service, nb, u idgen.ID) error { … }},
		{"comment",   …},
		{"edit",      …},
		{"delete",    …},
		{"invite",    …},
		{"publish",   …},
		{"delete_nb", …},
	}

	// The expected answer for every combination, written out in full.
	// An entry missing from this table is a compile error, not a silent
	// gap — which is the property that makes the test trustworthy.
	want := map[domain.Role]map[string]bool{
		domain.RoleViewer:    {"read": true, "comment": false, "edit": false, "delete": false, "invite": false, "publish": false, "delete_nb": false},
		domain.RoleCommenter: {"read": true, "comment": true,  "edit": false, "delete": false, "invite": false, "publish": false, "delete_nb": false},
		domain.RoleEditor:    {"read": true, "comment": true,  "edit": true,  "delete": true,  "invite": false, "publish": false, "delete_nb": false},
		domain.RoleOwner:     {"read": true, "comment": true,  "edit": true,  "delete": true,  "invite": true,  "publish": true,  "delete_nb": true},
	}

	for role, expectations := range want {
		for _, a := range actions {
			t.Run(string(role)+"/"+a.name, func(t *testing.T) {
				t.Parallel()
				env := newEnv(t)
				nb, user := env.notebookWithMember(t, role)

				err := a.do(env.ctx, env.svc, nb, user)
				allowed := !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrForbidden)

				if allowed != expectations[a.name] {
					t.Errorf("role %s action %s: allowed=%v want=%v (err=%v)",
						role, a.name, allowed, expectations[a.name], err)
				}
			})
		}
	}
}

// And the case the matrix cannot express: a complete stranger.
func TestNonMemberSeesNothing(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	env := newEnv(t)
	nb, _ := env.notebookWithMember(t, domain.RoleOwner)
	stranger := env.newUser(t)

	_, err := env.svc.GetNote(env.ctx, stranger, env.noteIn(nb))
	// NotFound, not Forbidden. A 403 confirms the note exists, which
	// turns the endpoint into an existence oracle for other people's ids.
	if !errors.Is(err, domain.ErrNotFound) {
		t.Fatalf("stranger got %v, want ErrNotFound", err)
	}
}
404 for a resource you may not see, 403 for one you may

The distinction matters. If the caller is a member of the notebook but lacks the role for this action, a 403 is correct and useful — they know the thing exists and that they need more access. If the caller has no relationship to the resource at all, a 403 confirms its existence, which lets an attacker map other people's ids. Return 404 there, and accept that the two cases are handled by different branches rather than one generic check. Quill's GetNoteForUser query produces this naturally because a non-member's query simply returns no rows.

Interview follow-up

“Where do you enforce authorization in a microservices architecture?” In the service that owns the data, never at the gateway — the gateway knows who you are but has no idea what a notebook is, and pushing resource-level decisions there recreates the monolith. Then the interesting half: if permissions live in another service, you do not call it on every read. You subscribe to its change events, keep a local read model, and make the check an index lookup inside the same transaction as the data. Say what that costs — a staleness window — and how you handle it: a monotonic revision so out-of-order events are safe, a strong synchronous check for the handful of irreversible actions, a reconciliation job, and a freshness metric you alert on.

D11

The sync protocol

This is the chapter to read twice. Local-first is what makes Quill feel instant — every read is a SQLite query, every write returns before the network is touched — and the entire cost of that is a protocol that must converge under arbitrary reordering, duplication, partition and clock skew. We design it here, in full, before writing a line of it.

The properties we need

PropertyWhat it means concretely
Local readsOpening a note is a SQLite query at tens of microseconds. No spinner, ever
Optimistic writesA keystroke updates local state and returns. The network happens later, or never
Offline capableA month offline, then reconnect, and nothing is lost
ConvergentTwo devices that have seen the same set of operations hold identical state, whatever order they arrived in
IdempotentA retried push after a timeout changes nothing. The network will make this happen
Gap-detectableA client can always tell whether it has missed something. This is the property that makes everything else safe
BoundedThe op log cannot grow forever, and a new device must not need to replay all history

The central decision: a total order per notebook

Every accepted mutation is appended to note_ops and receives a server_seq from a per-notebook counter. That gives one property everything else rests on: a client holding server_seq = 8791 knows EXACTLY what it is missing: everything from 8792 onward. notebook 01HX… server_seq ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ 8788 set_field note=A field=title lamport=44 actor=alice │ │ 8789 set_field note=A field=body lamport=45 actor=alice │ │ 8790 create note=B lamport=12 actor=bob │ │ 8791 set_field note=B field=title lamport=13 actor=bob │ ◀── you │ 8792 delete note=C lamport=46 actor=alice │ │ 8793 set_field note=A field=body lamport=47 actor=carol │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ pull since=8791 → 8792, 8793 Why per notebook rather than global? A global counter serialises every write in the service through one row. Per notebook, two notebooks never contend, and the ordering guarantee is exactly as strong as it needs to be — nobody cares about the relative order of edits in two unrelated notebooks. Why not timestamps? Clocks disagree, jump backwards on NTP correction, and collide. A counter allocated by the one process that can serialise is the only thing that gives a genuine total order.
Gap detection is the property, not a nice-to-have

A design where the server pushes changes over a socket and the client applies them has no way to notice a missed message — a dropped frame, a proxy timeout, a reconnect during a deploy, and the client is silently wrong forever with no error anywhere. Because server_seq is dense and monotonic, a Quill client that receives seq 8795 while holding 8791 knows immediately that it is missing three operations and pulls them. That is why the WebSocket carries notifications and the HTTP change feed carries data, and it is the single most important structural choice in the protocol.

Two clocks, doing different jobs

server_seq allocated by the server, per notebook, dense and monotonic. Answers "what have I not seen?" It is a cursor, not a causality claim: op 8793 arriving after 8792 says nothing about which edit happened first in the real world. lamport allocated by the client, per notebook, and merged on receipt. Answers "which of two concurrent edits to the same field wins?" The Lamport rule, in full: on local edit: lamport = max(seen) + 1 on receiving op: seen = max(seen, op.lamport) Two devices editing the same field while offline will produce the same or nearby counters — so ties are common and must be broken. The tie-break is the actor id, which is arbitrary but total: every replica computes the same winner, which is the only property that matters. alice: (lamport 47, actor "01HX…ALICE") bob: (lamport 47, actor "01HX…BOB") ──────────── bob wins everywhere, because "BOB" > "ALICE" byte-wise. Nobody's data is "better" — determinism is the goal. Why not just use server_seq for conflicts? Because arrival order at the server is decided by network luck. If alice edits at 09:00 offline and bob edits at 09:05 online, bob's op reaches the server first — and alice's later arrival would silently overwrite an edit made five minutes after hers. The Lamport clock preserves the causal story that the network destroyed.

The operation

platform/syncproto/op.go
// Package syncproto is the wire contract for sync. It is in platform/
// because BOTH the server and the client import it — one definition,
// so the two can never disagree about a field name.
package syncproto

import "github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"

type Kind string

const (
	KindCreate   Kind = "create"
	KindSetField Kind = "set_field"
	KindDelete   Kind = "delete"
	KindRestore  Kind = "restore"
)

type Op struct {
	// OpID is generated by the CLIENT, as a ULID. It is the idempotency
	// key: a retried push inserts nothing the second time, because of a
	// unique index. This is why ids must be client-generatable at all.
	OpID idgen.ID `json:"op_id"`

	NotebookID idgen.ID `json:"notebook_id"`
	NoteID     idgen.ID `json:"note_id"`
	Kind       Kind     `json:"kind"`

	// Field and Value are set for KindSetField only.
	Field string `json:"field,omitempty"`
	Value string `json:"value,omitempty"`

	// Lamport and Actor together are the merge clock. Actor is the USER
	// id, not the device: two devices belonging to one person editing
	// the same field concurrently is a real scenario, and the user
	// generally wants the later edit to win regardless of which laptop
	// it came from.
	Lamport int64    `json:"lamport"`
	Actor   idgen.ID `json:"actor"`
	Device  idgen.ID `json:"device"`

	// ClientTime is for the UI only ("edited 3 minutes ago"). It is
	// NEVER used for ordering — it is attacker-controlled and it is
	// wrong on any device with a bad clock.
	ClientTime int64 `json:"client_time"`
}

// ServerOp is what the change feed returns: the op plus the sequence the
// server assigned, plus whether it won the merge.
type ServerOp struct {
	Op
	ServerSeq int64 `json:"server_seq"`
	Applied   bool  `json:"applied"` // false = lost a merge; kept for audit
	ServerAt  int64 `json:"server_at"`
}

// ---- push ----------------------------------------------------------

type PushRequest struct {
	NotebookID idgen.ID `json:"notebook_id"`
	DeviceID   idgen.ID `json:"device_id"`
	Ops        []Op     `json:"ops"`
	// Since lets the server return everything the client is missing in
	// the SAME round trip as the push — one call instead of two, which
	// matters on a mobile connection.
	Since int64 `json:"since"`
}

type OpResult struct {
	OpID   idgen.ID `json:"op_id"`
	Status string   `json:"status"` // applied | superseded | duplicate | rejected
	Reason string   `json:"reason,omitempty"`
}

type PushResponse struct {
	Results []OpResult `json:"results"`
	// Changes made by OTHER devices since the client's cursor. Includes
	// nothing the client just pushed, because it already has those.
	Changes   []ServerOp `json:"changes"`
	ServerSeq int64      `json:"server_seq"` // the new cursor
	HasMore   bool       `json:"has_more"`
}

// ---- pull ----------------------------------------------------------

type ChangesResponse struct {
	Ops       []ServerOp `json:"ops"`
	ServerSeq int64      `json:"server_seq"`
	HasMore   bool       `json:"has_more"`
	// Set when the client's cursor is older than the compaction
	// horizon: the delta it asked for no longer exists and it must
	// re-baseline (see "Compaction" below).
	ResetRequired bool `json:"reset_required,omitempty"`
}

The four operation kinds, and why there are only four

KindCarriesMerge behaviour
createnote id, notebook idIdempotent by note id. A duplicate create is a no-op, not a conflict
set_fieldfield, value, clockPer-field last-writer-wins by (lamport, actor)
deletenote id, clockA tombstone. Wins over concurrent edits — see below
restorenote id, clockUndoes a tombstone, only if its clock is newer
Why set_field carries the whole value rather than a diff

A diff or patch operation would be smaller on the wire, and it would make the protocol far harder: patches must be transformed against concurrent patches (operational transformation) or expressed as a CRDT, and both require every replica to have applied the same prefix of history before a patch means anything. Whole-value writes with a clock are commutative and idempotent on their own, which is what lets a client apply ops in any order it receives them. The cost is bandwidth — a 40 KB note resends 40 KB per save — and the mitigation is debouncing on the client, not a cleverer protocol.

The conflict rules, stated precisely

1 Different fields never conflict. alice edits the title while bob edits the body → both apply. This is why the clock is per field and not per row. 2 Same field: highest (lamport, actor) wins. The loser's op is still stored with applied=false, so the history is complete and the UI can offer "see other version". 3 Delete beats concurrent edit. A tombstone with a clock at or above the edit's wins. The alternative — resurrect on edit — means a note deleted on one device keeps reappearing, which users read as a bug. Restore is an explicit, newer operation. 4 Visibility is NOT mergeable. A permission-shaped field must never be resurrected by a device that has been offline for three weeks. It travels the REST path with an authorization check and a version check (D07). 5 Body conflicts within a window produce a CONFLICT COPY. When two clients both wrote body and their clocks are within ±2 of each other, the loser's text is not discarded: a new note appears titled "Budget (conflicted copy — bob, 14:32)". Silently throwing away someone's paragraph is the behaviour that destroys trust in a sync product. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ alice (offline) server bob (online) │ │ ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │ │ body="AAA" L=47 body="BBB" L=47 │ │ ◀── bob's op │ │ apply: body="BBB" │ │ (47,BOB) wins │ │ ── reconnect ──▶ │ │ push body="AAA" L=47 │ │ (47,ALICE) LOSES │ │ |47-47| ≤ 2 ⇒ conflict copy │ │ create note "… (conflicted copy)" │ │ body="AAA" │ │ │ │ Both users end with body="BBB" AND a note containing "AAA". │ │ Nothing is lost; a human resolves it. │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Where last-writer-wins stops being acceptable

Per-field LWW is right for a note app: a title is a short value, and a body is usually edited by one person at a time. It is wrong for genuine simultaneous text editing — two people typing in the same paragraph — where one person's keystrokes vanishing mid-sentence is unusable, conflict copies or not. That needs a text CRDT such as Yjs or Automerge, which represents the body as a sequence of characters with identities rather than as a single value. Quill deliberately draws the line here: LWW plus conflict copies is what most note products ship, and adopting a CRDT is a decision to make when you add live cursors, not before.

The endpoints

EndpointPurpose
GET/v1/sync/changes?notebook_id=&since=&limit=Pull the delta. Cursor-paged, ordered by server_seq
POST/v1/sync/pushPush a batch of ops; returns per-op results and the delta
GET/v1/sync/snapshot?notebook_id=Full current state plus a cursor — for a new device, or after a reset
WS/v1/realtimeThe doorbell: {"type":"changed","notebook_id":…,"server_seq":…}

The loop, in full

Steady state ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ UI writes │ │ └─▶ SQLite: update notes, insert into pending_ops │ │ (one transaction, returns in ~50 µs) │ │ │ │ sync loop, every 2 s OR on doorbell OR on local write │ │ ├─▶ read pending_ops (max 200, oldest first) │ │ ├─▶ POST /v1/sync/push {ops, since: cursor} │ │ ├─▶ apply response.Changes to SQLite │ │ ├─▶ delete acked ops from pending_ops │ │ └─▶ cursor = response.ServerSeq │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Why ops are deleted only after the server acknowledges them The local note row is already updated — pending_ops is the outbox, not the state. If the process dies mid-push, the op is still there and is resent; the server dedupes it by op_id. That is the same transactional-outbox reasoning as on the server (B12), applied on the client. Cold start of a new device 1 GET /v1/sync/snapshot → all live notes + cursor 2 write them into SQLite in one transaction 3 enter the steady-state loop Never "pull all ops since 0": a notebook with two years of history has hundreds of thousands of ops, most of them superseded. The snapshot is the compacted view. Returning after a long offline period · cursor is still within the compaction horizon → normal delta pull, possibly many pages · cursor is older → the server sets reset_required, and the client takes a snapshot, then replays its own pending_ops on top — which is why pending_ops is kept separately from note state
The reset path must not lose local work

A reset replaces local note state with the server snapshot — and a client that has been offline for two months almost certainly has unpushed edits. If the reset simply overwrites, those are gone. Because pending_ops is a separate table that survives the snapshot write, the correct sequence is: take the snapshot, write it, then replay every pending op against it locally, then push them. The ops carry their original Lamport clocks, so they merge against the server's state by exactly the same rule as any other op. This path is the one to write a property test for (D15) — it is rare, it is hard, and it is where data loss lives.

Compaction

The op log grows without bound: every keystroke batch is a row. Three mechanisms keep it finite. 1 Debounce on the client. A body edit produces one op per 2 s of typing, not one per keystroke. This alone is a 50× reduction and it is the cheapest of the three by a wide margin. 2 Collapse superseded ops. Within a notebook, an op that lost a merge (applied=false) or that was overwritten by a newer op on the same (note, field) is only useful for audit. After 30 days they are deleted in batches. 3 The compaction horizon. Ops older than 90 days are deleted outright, and the notebook records compacted_before = N. A client asking for since < N gets reset_required and takes a snapshot instead. ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ seq 1 ─────────── 41200 ───────────── 88000 ───── 91433 │ │ └── deleted ──┘└── superseded ───┘└── live ──────────┘│ │ ▲ ▲ │ │ compacted_before 30-day boundary │ │ │ │ since=8791 → reset_required, take a snapshot │ │ since=52000 → delta pull works, ~3 pages │ │ since=91400 → delta pull, one small page │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Choosing 90 days is a product decision, not a technical one: it is the longest a device may be offline and still resume cheaply. Longer costs storage; shorter makes resets more common. Measure how many clients actually hit the horizon before changing it.

What the protocol deliberately does not do

Not doneWhy, and what you would do instead
Character-level text mergeNeeds a CRDT (Yjs, Automerge). Adopt when you add live cursors, not before
Peer-to-peer syncThe server's total order is what makes gap detection possible. P2P needs version vectors and gets much harder
End-to-end encryptionIncompatible with server-side search and public publishing as designed. It is a different product
Partial sync of a notebookThe cursor is per notebook. Syncing “only recent notes” breaks gap detection; sync whole notebooks and let the user choose which
Ordering across notebooksNobody needs it, and a global sequence would serialise every write in the service
Interview follow-up

“Design offline sync for a notes app.” Lead with the two decisions that determine everything else: an append-only operation log with a server-assigned monotonic sequence per document set, so a client can always tell exactly what it has missed; and a deterministic merge rule — per-field last-writer-wins with a Lamport clock and a total tie-break on actor id — so every replica computes the same result from the same set of operations regardless of arrival order. Then add the three things that separate a real answer from a whiteboard one: client-generated ids so offline creation works and pushes are idempotent, a realtime channel that carries notifications rather than data so a dropped socket is harmless, and an explicit statement of which fields are not mergeable — permissions and anything irreversible — because that is where last-writer-wins becomes a security bug.

D12

Sync: the server

Three endpoints implement the protocol from D11: push, changes and snapshot. The whole design lives in one transaction — allocate a sequence, dedupe, merge, append, enqueue — and this chapter writes it along with the compaction jobs that keep the log finite.

Push

services/notes/internal/app/sync_push.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"sort"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/syncproto"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/notes/internal/domain"
)

const (
	maxOpsPerPush   = 500
	maxChangesPage  = 500
	conflictWindow  = 2 // lamport distance within which we keep a conflict copy
)

func (s *Service) Push(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	req syncproto.PushRequest) (*syncproto.PushResponse, error) {

	if len(req.Ops) > maxOpsPerPush {
		return nil, domain.ErrBatchTooLarge
	}

	// Ops within a batch MUST be applied in Lamport order, not in the
	// order the client happened to serialise them. A client that edits
	// the title twice offline sends two ops for the same field, and
	// applying them out of order would leave the older value winning.
	ops := append([]syncproto.Op(nil), req.Ops...)
	sort.SliceStable(ops, func(i, j int) bool {
		if ops[i].Lamport != ops[j].Lamport {
			return ops[i].Lamport < ops[j].Lamport
		}
		return ops[i].OpID < ops[j].OpID // total, so the sort is deterministic
	})

	resp := &syncproto.PushResponse{
		Results: make([]syncproto.OpResult, 0, len(ops)),
	}

	err := pg.InTxAs(ctx, s.pool, userID.String(), func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// One authorization check for the batch. Every op must target
		// the notebook named in the request — validated below — so a
		// single check covers all of them.
		if err := s.requireRole(ctx, q, req.NotebookID, userID,
			domain.RoleEditor); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Take the notebook's sequence lock ONCE for the whole batch.
		// Allocating per op would mean N lock acquisitions and would
		// interleave this client's ops with another's mid-batch.
		seq, err := q.ReserveSeq(ctx, ReserveSeqParams{
			NotebookID: req.NotebookID, Count: int64(len(ops)),
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		for i, op := range ops {
			res := s.applyOp(ctx, q, tx, userID, req, op, seq+int64(i))
			resp.Results = append(resp.Results, res)
		}

		// One doorbell per batch, not per op. A client typing for a
		// minute should wake other devices a handful of times, not two
		// hundred (D14).
		if anyApplied(resp.Results) {
			if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "notes.changed", NotesChanged{
				NotebookID: req.NotebookID,
				ServerSeq:  seq + int64(len(ops)) - 1,
				ActorID:    userID, DeviceID: req.DeviceID,
			}); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		// Return the delta in the SAME response. One round trip instead
		// of two, which on a mobile connection is the difference between
		// a sync loop that feels instant and one that does not.
		changes, more, newSeq, err := s.changesSince(ctx, q, req.NotebookID,
			req.Since, req.DeviceID, maxChangesPage)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		resp.Changes, resp.HasMore, resp.ServerSeq = changes, more, newSeq
		return nil
	})
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return resp, nil
}
services/notes/internal/app/sync_apply.go
package app

// applyOp is the merge, and it is the most important function in Quill.
// Every branch here corresponds to a rule from D11.
func (s *Service) applyOp(ctx context.Context, q Querier, tx pgx.Tx,
	userID idgen.ID, req syncproto.PushRequest,
	op syncproto.Op, serverSeq int64) syncproto.OpResult {

	reject := func(reason string) syncproto.OpResult {
		return syncproto.OpResult{OpID: op.OpID, Status: "rejected", Reason: reason}
	}
