	// ── validation ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
	// Every field here is attacker-controlled. A client can send any
	// notebook id, any actor, any lamport value it likes.
	if op.NotebookID != req.NotebookID {
		return reject("notebook_mismatch") // no cross-notebook writes
	}
	if !op.OpID.Valid() || !op.NoteID.Valid() {
		return reject("malformed_id")
	}
	if op.Actor != userID {
		// A client must not be able to attribute an edit to someone
		// else. The actor is also the conflict tie-break, so forging it
		// would let a client always win merges.
		return reject("actor_mismatch")
	}
	if op.Lamport <= 0 || op.Lamport > maxLamport {
		// An unbounded Lamport value would let one client win every
		// future conflict forever by sending math.MaxInt64.
		return reject("bad_lamport")
	}

	// ── idempotency ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
	// The unique index on op_id does the work. A retried push after a
	// timeout inserts nothing and reports success — which is exactly
	// what the client needs to hear so it can drop the pending op.
	inserted, err := q.InsertOpIfAbsent(ctx, InsertOpIfAbsentParams{
		OpID: op.OpID, NotebookID: op.NotebookID, NoteID: op.NoteID,
		ServerSeq: serverSeq, ActorID: op.Actor, DeviceID: op.Device,
		Kind: string(op.Kind), Field: op.Field, Value: op.Value,
		Lamport: op.Lamport, Applied: false, // updated below if it wins
	})
	if err != nil {
		return reject("storage_error")
	}
	if !inserted {
		return syncproto.OpResult{OpID: op.OpID, Status: "duplicate"}
	}

	clk := domain.Clock{Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor}

	switch op.Kind {
	case syncproto.KindCreate:
		// Idempotent by note id: a create for a note that exists is a
		// no-op, not an error. Two devices creating the same note is
		// impossible (ULIDs), but a retried create is routine.
		if err := q.InsertNoteIfAbsent(ctx, InsertNoteIfAbsentParams{
			ID: op.NoteID, NotebookID: op.NotebookID,
			CreatedBy: op.Actor, Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
		}); err != nil {
			return reject("storage_error")
		}

	case syncproto.KindSetField:
		// Rule 4: permission-shaped fields are not mergeable.
		if op.Field != "title" && op.Field != "body" {
			return reject("field_not_mergeable")
		}
		if err := domain.ValidateFieldValue(op.Field, op.Value); err != nil {
			return reject(err.Error())
		}

		note, err := q.GetNoteForUpdate(ctx, op.NoteID)
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return reject("note_not_found")
		}
		if err != nil {
			return reject("storage_error")
		}
		if note.NotebookID != op.NotebookID {
			return reject("notebook_mismatch")
		}

		// Rule 3: a tombstone beats a concurrent edit.
		if note.DeletedAt.Valid && !clk.After(note.DeleteClock()) {
			return syncproto.OpResult{OpID: op.OpID, Status: "superseded",
				Reason: "note_deleted"}
		}

		// Rule 2: highest (lamport, actor) wins.
		current := note.ClockFor(op.Field)
		if !clk.After(current) {
			// Rule 5: a near-simultaneous body loss becomes a conflict
			// copy rather than silently vanishing.
			if op.Field == "body" && abs(current.Lamport-op.Lamport) <= conflictWindow {
				if err := s.createConflictCopy(ctx, q, note, op, serverSeq); err != nil {
					return reject("storage_error")
				}
				return syncproto.OpResult{OpID: op.OpID,
					Status: "superseded", Reason: "conflict_copy_created"}
			}
			return syncproto.OpResult{OpID: op.OpID, Status: "superseded"}
		}

		if err := q.SetFieldWithClock(ctx, SetFieldWithClockParams{
			ID: op.NoteID, Field: op.Field, Value: op.Value,
			Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
		}); err != nil {
			return reject("storage_error")
		}

	case syncproto.KindDelete:
		if err := q.TombstoneIfNewer(ctx, TombstoneIfNewerParams{
			ID: op.NoteID, Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
		}); err != nil {
			return reject("storage_error")
		}

	case syncproto.KindRestore:
		if err := q.RestoreIfNewer(ctx, RestoreIfNewerParams{
			ID: op.NoteID, Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
		}); err != nil {
			return reject("storage_error")
		}

	default:
		return reject("unknown_kind")
	}

	// Mark the op as having won, so the log records not just what was
	// attempted but what took effect.
	if err := q.MarkOpApplied(ctx, op.OpID); err != nil {
		return reject("storage_error")
	}
	return syncproto.OpResult{OpID: op.OpID, Status: "applied"}
}

// createConflictCopy preserves the losing text as a new note. The copy
// is itself an operation, so it propagates to every device by the normal
// mechanism rather than needing a special case on the client.
func (s *Service) createConflictCopy(ctx context.Context, q Querier,
	note db.Note, op syncproto.Op, serverSeq int64) error {

	copyID := idgen.New()
	title := fmt.Sprintf("%s (conflicted copy — %s)",
		note.Title, time.Now().UTC().Format("2 Jan 15:04"))

	if err := q.InsertNoteIfAbsent(ctx, InsertNoteIfAbsentParams{
		ID: copyID, NotebookID: note.NotebookID,
		CreatedBy: op.Actor, Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
	}); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if err := q.SetFieldWithClock(ctx, SetFieldWithClockParams{
		ID: copyID, Field: "title", Value: domain.NormaliseTitle(title),
		Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
	}); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	return q.SetFieldWithClock(ctx, SetFieldWithClockParams{
		ID: copyID, Field: "body", Value: op.Value,
		Lamport: op.Lamport, Actor: op.Actor,
	})
}
Every field in a pushed op is attacker-controlled

A client can claim any notebook id, any actor, any Lamport value. The three checks that matter: notebook must match the request's, so one push cannot write across notebooks after a single authorization check; actor must equal the authenticated user, or a client can attribute edits to a colleague and manipulate the conflict tie-break; and lamport must be bounded, or a client sending math.MaxInt64 wins every future conflict in that notebook forever. That last one is the kind of bug that only shows up when someone looks for it.

The sequence allocator, in batch

services/notes/query.sql — sync
-- name: ReserveSeq :one
-- Reserve a CONTIGUOUS RANGE for a whole batch in one statement, and
-- return the first value. One lock acquisition instead of N, and the
-- batch's ops get consecutive sequence numbers — so a client pulling
-- the delta sees them as one logical change.
INSERT INTO notebook_seq (notebook_id, last_seq)
VALUES (@notebook_id, @count)
ON CONFLICT (notebook_id) DO UPDATE
   SET last_seq = notebook_seq.last_seq + @count
RETURNING last_seq - @count + 1 AS first_seq;

-- name: InsertOpIfAbsent :one
-- ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING plus the RETURNING trick: the boolean tells us
-- whether this op is new, in one round trip and with no race between a
-- SELECT and an INSERT. This IS the idempotency mechanism.
INSERT INTO note_ops (
    op_id, notebook_id, note_id, server_seq, actor_id, device_id,
    kind, field, value, lamport, applied
) VALUES (
    @op_id, @notebook_id, @note_id, @server_seq, @actor_id, @device_id,
    @kind, @field, @value, @lamport, @applied
)
ON CONFLICT (op_id) DO NOTHING
RETURNING true AS inserted;

-- name: SetFieldWithClock :exec
-- The clock comparison is in the WHERE clause as well as being checked
-- in Go. Belt and braces: if two transactions somehow interleave, the
-- database still refuses to let an older write win.
UPDATE notes
   SET title         = CASE WHEN @field::text = 'title' THEN @value ELSE title END,
       body          = CASE WHEN @field::text = 'body'  THEN @value ELSE body  END,
       title_lamport = CASE WHEN @field::text = 'title' THEN @lamport ELSE title_lamport END,
       title_actor   = CASE WHEN @field::text = 'title' THEN @actor   ELSE title_actor   END,
       body_lamport  = CASE WHEN @field::text = 'body'  THEN @lamport ELSE body_lamport  END,
       body_actor    = CASE WHEN @field::text = 'body'  THEN @actor   ELSE body_actor    END,
       version    = version + 1,
       updated_at = now()
 WHERE id = @id
   AND (
        (@field::text = 'title' AND (@lamport > title_lamport
             OR (@lamport = title_lamport AND @actor > title_actor)))
     OR (@field::text = 'body'  AND (@lamport > body_lamport
             OR (@lamport = body_lamport  AND @actor > body_actor)))
   );

-- name: TombstoneIfNewer :exec
UPDATE notes
   SET deleted_at = now(), delete_lamport = @lamport, delete_actor = @actor,
       version = version + 1
 WHERE id = @id
   AND (@lamport > delete_lamport
        OR (@lamport = delete_lamport AND @actor > delete_actor));

-- name: ChangesSince :many
-- The change feed. The index on (notebook_id, server_seq) makes this a
-- range scan straight to the position — no sort, no filter, no offset.
SELECT op_id, note_id, server_seq, actor_id, device_id,
       kind, field, value, lamport, applied,
       extract(epoch FROM created_at)::bigint AS server_at
  FROM note_ops
 WHERE notebook_id = @notebook_id
   AND server_seq  > @since
   -- Skip the requesting device's OWN ops: it already has them, and
   -- echoing them back doubles the payload for an active editor.
   AND device_id <> @device_id
 ORDER BY server_seq
 LIMIT @page_size;

-- name: CompactedBefore :one
SELECT compacted_before FROM notebooks WHERE id = @notebook_id;

The change feed

services/notes/internal/app/sync_pull.go
package app

func (s *Service) Changes(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	notebookID, deviceID idgen.ID, since int64, limit int) (*syncproto.ChangesResponse, error) {

	limit = clamp(limit, 1, maxChangesPage)

	// Read access is enough to pull: a viewer syncs a notebook they can
	// read, they simply cannot push.
	if err := s.requireRoleDirect(ctx, notebookID, userID, domain.RoleViewer); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// If the cursor predates compaction, the delta the client wants no
	// longer exists. Telling it to re-baseline is the ONLY correct
	// answer — returning what remains would leave a silent gap, which
	// is the one failure this protocol exists to prevent (D11).
	horizon, err := s.q.CompactedBefore(ctx, notebookID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	if since > 0 && since < horizon {
		syncResets.Inc() // alert if this is common: the horizon is too short
		return &syncproto.ChangesResponse{ResetRequired: true}, nil
	}

	rows, err := s.q.ChangesSince(ctx, ChangesSinceParams{
		NotebookID: notebookID, Since: since,
		DeviceID: deviceID, PageSize: int32(limit + 1), // +1 to detect more
	})
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	hasMore := len(rows) > limit
	if hasMore {
		rows = rows[:limit]
	}

	out := &syncproto.ChangesResponse{
		Ops:     make([]syncproto.ServerOp, 0, len(rows)),
		HasMore: hasMore,
	}
	for _, r := range rows {
		out.Ops = append(out.Ops, toProtoOp(r))
	}

	// The cursor is the last sequence RETURNED, not the notebook's
	// current maximum. Advancing past ops we did not send would create
	// the gap we are trying to avoid.
	if n := len(out.Ops); n > 0 {
		out.ServerSeq = out.Ops[n-1].ServerSeq
	} else {
		// Nothing to send: advance to the head so the client stops
		// asking. Safe because we know there is nothing in between.
		head, err := s.q.HeadSeq(ctx, notebookID)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		out.ServerSeq = max(since, head)
	}
	return out, nil
}
The cursor must be the last sequence actually sent

It is tempting to return the notebook's current head as the new cursor — it is one query and it looks equivalent. It is not: if the page was truncated at the limit, the client advances past operations it never received and they are gone forever, with no error and no way to detect the loss. Return the sequence of the last op in the response, set has_more, and let the client loop. The only case where returning the head is correct is when the page is genuinely empty, because then there is nothing in between by definition.

Snapshot

services/notes/internal/app/sync_snapshot.go
package app

// Snapshot is the compacted view: current state plus a cursor, for a new
// device or after a reset. It streams rather than building one giant
// response, because a notebook with 20,000 notes is tens of megabytes.
func (s *Service) Snapshot(ctx context.Context, userID, notebookID idgen.ID,
	w io.Writer) error {

	if err := s.requireRoleDirect(ctx, notebookID, userID, domain.RoleViewer); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// Snapshot inside a REPEATABLE READ transaction, and read the cursor
	// INSIDE it. Reading the head first and then the rows would let a
	// write land in between, so the client would hold that change's
	// effect but a cursor from before it — and would never pull it.
	return pg.InTxRepeatable(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		head, err := q.HeadSeq(ctx, notebookID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		enc := json.NewEncoder(w)
		if err := enc.Encode(snapshotHeader{
			NotebookID: notebookID, ServerSeq: head, Format: "ndjson-v1",
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Cursor over rows rather than materialising them: constant
		// memory regardless of notebook size (P08).
		rows, err := q.AllLiveNotes(ctx, notebookID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		defer rows.Close()

		for rows.Next() {
			var n db.Note
			if err := rows.Scan(&n); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if err := enc.Encode(toSnapshotNote(n)); err != nil {
				return err // client disconnected, almost certainly
			}
		}
		if err := rows.Err(); err != nil { // the line everyone forgets
			return err
		}

		// Tombstones from the last 90 days too. A device that had a note
		// before going offline must learn it was deleted; omitting them
		// means the note reappears on that device forever.
		tombs, err := q.RecentTombstones(ctx, notebookID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		for _, t := range tombs {
			if err := enc.Encode(toSnapshotTombstone(t)); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}
		return nil
	})
}
A snapshot without tombstones resurrects deleted notes

The snapshot returns live notes, so a device that already holds a note deleted while it was offline never learns about the deletion — and the note sits there forever, reappearing after every reset. Including tombstones from the compaction window fixes it, and it is the reason the window and the tombstone retention must be the same number: a tombstone purged before the compaction horizon leaves exactly the same hole.

Compaction jobs

services/notes/internal/jobs/compact.go
package jobs

import (
	"context"
	"time"
)

// Two jobs, both batched and both throttled. A single DELETE over
// millions of rows holds locks, bloats the WAL, and makes replicas lag —
// which in a system where replicas serve reads is an outage (P05).
func (c *Compactor) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	t := time.NewTicker(time.Hour)
	defer t.Stop()
	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return nil
		case <-t.C:
			// Behind a leader lease: N replicas all compacting is N times
			// the load for no benefit (P05).
			if err := c.leader.Run(ctx, compactLockKey, c.once); err != nil {
				c.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "compaction", "err", err)
			}
		}
	}
}

func (c *Compactor) once(ctx context.Context) error {
	// 1 · superseded ops older than 30 days. These lost a merge or were
	//     overwritten, so they are audit data only.
	for {
		n, err := c.q.DeleteSupersededOps(ctx, DeleteSupersededOpsParams{
			Before: time.Now().Add(-30 * 24 * time.Hour), Limit: 10_000,
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if n < 10_000 {
			break
		}
		// Breathe. Without this, compaction saturates the primary's IO
		// and every user request slows down.
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return ctx.Err()
		case <-time.After(200 * time.Millisecond):
		}
	}

	// 2 · everything older than the horizon, per notebook, and advance
	//     compacted_before in the SAME transaction as the delete — or a
	//     crash between them leaves clients pulling ops that are gone.
	notebooks, err := c.q.NotebooksNeedingCompaction(ctx)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	for _, nb := range notebooks {
		if err := pg.InTx(ctx, c.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
			q := c.q.WithTx(tx)
			horizon, err := q.SeqAtAge(ctx, SeqAtAgeParams{
				NotebookID: nb, Age: 90 * 24 * time.Hour,
			})
			if err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if _, err := q.DeleteOpsBefore(ctx, DeleteOpsBeforeParams{
				NotebookID: nb, Seq: horizon,
			}); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			return q.SetCompactedBefore(ctx, SetCompactedBeforeParams{
				NotebookID: nb, Seq: horizon,
			})
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
	}
	return nil
}

The metrics that tell you sync is healthy

MetricHealthyWhat a bad value means
sync_push_ops_total{status}>98% appliedMany rejected means a client bug or an attack; many duplicate means pushes are timing out
sync_conflict_copies_totalRareRising means users are genuinely colliding — consider a CRDT for the body
sync_reset_required_totalNear zeroClients falling past the compaction horizon: the window is too short, or a client is stuck and not syncing
sync_push_batch_size p99< 100Large batches mean clients are offline for long periods, or debouncing is not working
sync_lag_secondsp99 < 2 sTime from an op being accepted to another device applying it — the number users actually feel
note_ops table sizeFlatGrowing means compaction is not keeping up
The one metric to put on the wall

sync_lag_seconds — the time between one device's edit being accepted and another device having applied it — is the only number that corresponds to what a user experiences. Everything else is a cause. Measure it end to end by stamping the op with its server timestamp and having clients report the delta when they apply it; a synthetic prober running two clients in a loop gives you the same number without depending on real users' telemetry, which is what you want during an incident.

Interview follow-up

“How do you make a sync push idempotent?” The client generates the operation id, so a retried batch carries the same ids as the original, and a unique index on that column plus ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING makes the second insert a no-op. The subtle part is the response: a duplicate must report success, not an error, or the client can never drop the operation from its outbox and retries forever. Then mention the ordering requirement most people miss — ops within a batch must be applied in logical-clock order rather than in whatever order the client serialised them, or two offline edits to the same field can apply backwards.

D13

Sync: the local client

This is where “local sync for better performance” becomes real. syncd is a Go daemon holding a complete SQLite replica: reads are local queries at tens of microseconds, writes return before the network is touched, and a background loop reconciles with the server. It is also a full Go program in its own right — with all the offline, retry and crash-recovery problems that implies.

The local schema

clients/syncd/internal/store/schema.sql
-- SQLite, in the user's config directory. Three tables do all the work.
PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL;      -- readers never block the writer, and a
                                -- crash mid-write cannot corrupt the file
PRAGMA synchronous  = NORMAL;   -- with WAL this is durable to process
                                -- crash; only an OS crash can lose the
                                -- last transaction, which for a cache
                                -- that resyncs is the right trade
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON;
PRAGMA busy_timeout = 5000;     -- wait rather than instantly returning
                                -- SQLITE_BUSY when the UI and the sync
                                -- loop collide

-- 1 · the replica. Mirrors the server's notes, plus tombstones.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes (
    id              TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    notebook_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
    title           TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    body            TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    visibility      TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'private',

    -- The SAME per-field clocks as the server. The client runs the
    -- identical merge rule, which is what makes convergence provable
    -- rather than hopeful.
    title_lamport   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    title_actor     TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    body_lamport    INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    body_actor      TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
    delete_lamport  INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    delete_actor    TEXT    NOT NULL DEFAULT '',

    deleted_at      INTEGER,        -- unix seconds; NULL = live
    updated_at      INTEGER NOT NULL,
    -- Set when this row has local edits not yet acknowledged. The UI
    -- shows a small dot; it is also how we know what to replay after a
    -- reset.
    dirty           INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS notes_notebook_idx
    ON notes (notebook_id, updated_at DESC) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL;

-- 2 · the outbox. Exactly the transactional-outbox pattern (B12), on
--     the client: the note row and the op row commit together, so a
--     crash can never leave a local edit that is never pushed.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS pending_ops (
    op_id           TEXT PRIMARY KEY,   -- ULID, generated HERE
    notebook_id     TEXT NOT NULL,
    note_id         TEXT NOT NULL,
    kind            TEXT NOT NULL,
    field           TEXT,
    value           TEXT,
    lamport         INTEGER NOT NULL,
    actor           TEXT NOT NULL,
    created_at      INTEGER NOT NULL,
    attempts        INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    last_error      TEXT
);
CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS pending_notebook_idx
    ON pending_ops (notebook_id, lamport, op_id);

-- 3 · per-notebook sync state.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sync_state (
    notebook_id     TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
    server_seq      INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,  -- the cursor
    lamport         INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,  -- our logical clock
    last_sync_at    INTEGER,
    last_error      TEXT
);

-- Full-text search locally too, so search works offline and is instant.
CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE IF NOT EXISTS notes_fts USING fts5(
    title, body, content='notes', content_rowid='rowid', tokenize='porter'
);
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS notes_fts_ins AFTER INSERT ON notes BEGIN
    INSERT INTO notes_fts(rowid, title, body) VALUES (new.rowid, new.title, new.body);
END;
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS notes_fts_del AFTER DELETE ON notes BEGIN
    INSERT INTO notes_fts(notes_fts, rowid, title, body)
    VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.title, old.body);
END;
CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS notes_fts_upd AFTER UPDATE ON notes BEGIN
    INSERT INTO notes_fts(notes_fts, rowid, title, body)
    VALUES ('delete', old.rowid, old.title, old.body);
    INSERT INTO notes_fts(rowid, title, body) VALUES (new.rowid, new.title, new.body);
END;
WAL mode is not optional for a local-first client

In SQLite's default rollback-journal mode a writer blocks every reader, so the UI freezes whenever the sync loop applies a batch. WAL lets readers proceed against the last committed state while a write is in flight, which is exactly the concurrency pattern here: one writer (the sync loop or a user edit) and many short reads. Pair it with busy_timeout so a collision waits rather than returning SQLITE_BUSY, and open the database with _txlock=immediate for write transactions so SQLite takes the write lock up front instead of failing on upgrade.

The local write path

clients/syncd/internal/store/write.go
package store

import (
	"context"
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/syncproto"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/notes/internal/domain"
)

// SetField is what the UI calls. It updates the replica AND appends to
// the outbox in ONE transaction, then returns — typically in well under
// a millisecond. No network is involved and none is waited for.
func (s *Store) SetField(ctx context.Context, noteID idgen.ID,
	field, value string) error {

	if err := domain.ValidateFieldValue(field, value); err != nil {
		return err // fail locally and immediately, not after a round trip
	}

	return s.inTx(ctx, func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
		var notebookID string
		if err := tx.QueryRowContext(ctx,
			`SELECT notebook_id FROM notes WHERE id = ?`, noteID).
			Scan(&notebookID); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("note %s: %w", noteID, err)
		}

		// Tick our Lamport clock: max(seen) + 1 for this notebook.
		lamport, err := s.tickLamport(ctx, tx, notebookID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Apply locally using the SAME merge rule the server will use.
		// This is the whole point of sharing domain.Clock between server
		// and client: the optimistic local result is the one the server
		// will also compute, so the UI does not flicker when the ack
		// arrives.
		if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			UPDATE notes
			   SET title         = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'title' THEN ?2 ELSE title END,
			       body          = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'body'  THEN ?2 ELSE body  END,
			       title_lamport = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'title' THEN ?3 ELSE title_lamport END,
			       title_actor   = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'title' THEN ?4 ELSE title_actor   END,
			       body_lamport  = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'body'  THEN ?3 ELSE body_lamport  END,
			       body_actor    = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'body'  THEN ?4 ELSE body_actor    END,
			       updated_at    = ?5,
			       dirty         = 1
			 WHERE id = ?6`,
			field, value, lamport, s.userID, time.Now().Unix(), noteID,
		); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// The outbox row. Committing these two together is what makes a
		// crash safe: either the edit and its op both exist, or neither
		// does. Writing the note first and the op after would lose edits
		// on a crash; the reverse would push phantom ops.
		_, err = tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			INSERT INTO pending_ops
			  (op_id, notebook_id, note_id, kind, field, value, lamport, actor, created_at)
			VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)`,
			idgen.New(), notebookID, noteID, syncproto.KindSetField,
			field, value, lamport, s.userID, time.Now().Unix())
		return err
	})
}

// tickLamport allocates the next logical timestamp for a notebook. It
// runs inside the caller's transaction so two concurrent local writes
// cannot receive the same value.
func (s *Store) tickLamport(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx, notebookID string) (int64, error) {
	var lamport int64
	err := tx.QueryRowContext(ctx, `
		INSERT INTO sync_state (notebook_id, lamport) VALUES (?, 1)
		ON CONFLICT (notebook_id) DO UPDATE SET lamport = lamport + 1
		RETURNING lamport`, notebookID).Scan(&lamport)
	return lamport, err
}
Debounce in the UI layer, not in the sync loop

Calling SetField on every keystroke produces one op per keystroke: a thousand rows for a paragraph, a thousand rows on the wire, and a thousand rows in the server's log forever. Debounce at the edit layer — coalesce two seconds of typing into one SetField — and the reduction is roughly fiftyfold. Doing it in the sync loop instead does not work, because the ops are already distinct rows with distinct ids by then; you would have to collapse them, which means reasoning about which are superseded, which is exactly the work the debounce avoids.

The sync loop

clients/syncd/internal/sync/loop.go
package sync

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"math"
	"math/rand"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/syncproto"
)

type Engine struct {
	store  *store.Store
	client *api.Client
	log    *slog.Logger

	// wake is how a local edit or a realtime doorbell asks for an
	// immediate cycle. Buffered with capacity 1 and written with a
	// non-blocking send: many wakes collapse into one, and nobody ever
	// blocks trying to notify.
	wake chan struct{}
}

func NewEngine(st *store.Store, c *api.Client, log *slog.Logger) *Engine {
	return &Engine{store: st, client: c, log: log, wake: make(chan struct{}, 1)}
}

// Wake is safe to call from anywhere, at any rate.
func (e *Engine) Wake() {
	select {
	case e.wake <- struct{}{}:
	default: // a cycle is already pending; nothing to add
	}
}

func (e *Engine) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	// Sync every notebook concurrently, but bounded — a user with fifty
	// notebooks must not open fifty connections (L14).
	g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)
	g.SetLimit(4)

	ticker := time.NewTicker(2 * time.Second)
	defer ticker.Stop()

	backoff := time.Duration(0)

	for {
		select {
		case <-ctx.Done():
			return nil
		case <-ticker.C:
		case <-e.wake:
		}

		if backoff > 0 {
			select {
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return nil
			case <-time.After(backoff):
			}
		}

		notebooks, err := e.store.NotebooksToSync(gctx)
		if err != nil {
			e.log.Error("list notebooks", "err", err)
			continue
		}

		var failed bool
		for _, nb := range notebooks {
			nb := nb
			g.Go(func() error {
				if err := e.syncNotebook(gctx, nb); err != nil {
					// One notebook failing must not stop the others, so
					// the error is recorded rather than returned.
					e.log.Warn("sync notebook", "notebook", nb, "err", err)
					_ = e.store.RecordSyncError(gctx, nb, err)
					failed = true
				}
				return nil
			})
		}
		_ = g.Wait()

		if failed {
			backoff = nextBackoff(backoff)
			syncFailures.Inc()
		} else {
			backoff = 0
		}
	}
}

// Exponential with FULL jitter, capped at five minutes. Without jitter,
// every client that lost connection during an incident reconnects in the
// same millisecond when the service recovers and knocks it over again
// (P04) — and a sync client is exactly the population that does this.
func nextBackoff(cur time.Duration) time.Duration {
	const base, max = 2 * time.Second, 5 * time.Minute
	next := base
	if cur > 0 {
		next = time.Duration(math.Min(float64(cur)*2, float64(max)))
	}
	return time.Duration(rand.Int63n(int64(next)))
}

One cycle for one notebook

clients/syncd/internal/sync/notebook.go
package sync

const maxOpsPerPush = 200

func (e *Engine) syncNotebook(ctx context.Context, notebookID idgen.ID) error {
	state, err := e.store.SyncState(ctx, notebookID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// Oldest first, in Lamport order — the server re-sorts anyway, but
	// sending them ordered means a truncated batch is a valid prefix
	// rather than an arbitrary subset.
	pending, err := e.store.PendingOps(ctx, notebookID, maxOpsPerPush)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// Push and pull in ONE round trip. On a mobile connection the
	// handshake dominates, so halving the number of calls halves the
	// perceived sync latency.
	resp, err := e.client.Push(ctx, syncproto.PushRequest{
		NotebookID: notebookID, DeviceID: e.deviceID,
		Ops: pending, Since: state.ServerSeq,
	})
	if err != nil {
		// A network failure leaves pending_ops untouched, so the next
		// cycle retries. The server dedupes by op_id, so a push that
		// actually succeeded but whose RESPONSE was lost is harmless.
		return fmt.Errorf("push: %w", err)
	}

	// Apply the results and the changes in ONE local transaction. A
	// crash between "acked" and "applied" would otherwise leave the
	// cursor advanced past changes we never wrote.
	if err := e.store.ApplyPushResponse(ctx, notebookID, resp); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("apply: %w", err)
	}

	// Drain the rest of the delta if the server truncated the page.
	for resp.HasMore {
		ch, err := e.client.Changes(ctx, notebookID, e.deviceID,
			resp.ServerSeq, 500)
		if err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("changes: %w", err)
		}
		if ch.ResetRequired {
			return e.reset(ctx, notebookID)
		}
		if err := e.store.ApplyChanges(ctx, notebookID, ch); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		resp.HasMore, resp.ServerSeq = ch.HasMore, ch.ServerSeq
	}

	// Keep draining the outbox if there was more than one batch of it —
	// a client returning from a week offline may have thousands.
	if len(pending) == maxOpsPerPush {
		e.Wake()
	}
	return nil
}
clients/syncd/internal/store/apply.go
package store

// ApplyPushResponse is the crash-safety boundary on the client. Results,
// changes and the new cursor all land in one SQLite transaction.
func (s *Store) ApplyPushResponse(ctx context.Context, notebookID idgen.ID,
	resp *syncproto.PushResponse) error {

	return s.inTx(ctx, func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
		for _, r := range resp.Results {
			switch r.Status {
			case "applied", "duplicate", "superseded":
				// All three mean "the server is done with this op".
				// `duplicate` is a SUCCESS — it means an earlier push
				// landed and only the response was lost. Treating it as
				// an error is how a client retries forever.
				if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
					`DELETE FROM pending_ops WHERE op_id = ?`, r.OpID); err != nil {
					return err
				}

			case "rejected":
				// The server will never accept this op. Retrying is
				// pointless, so drop it — but record it loudly, because
				// a rejection is either our bug or a permission change,
				// and silently discarding a user's edit is unacceptable.
				s.log.Error("op rejected by server",
					"op_id", r.OpID, "reason", r.Reason)
				opsRejected.WithLabelValues(r.Reason).Inc()
				if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
					`DELETE FROM pending_ops WHERE op_id = ?`, r.OpID); err != nil {
					return err
				}
				// Re-baseline this note from the server so the local copy
				// stops diverging from a state the server rejected.
				if err := s.markNoteForRefetch(ctx, tx, r.OpID); err != nil {
					return err
				}
			}
		}

		for _, op := range resp.Changes {
			if err := s.applyServerOp(ctx, tx, op); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		// The cursor advances LAST, inside the same transaction. If any
		// of the above fails, the cursor stays where it was and the
		// whole page is re-fetched — at-least-once on the client too.
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
			`UPDATE sync_state SET server_seq = ?, last_sync_at = ?, last_error = NULL
			  WHERE notebook_id = ?`,
			resp.ServerSeq, time.Now().Unix(), notebookID)
		return err
	})
}

// applyServerOp runs the IDENTICAL merge rule as the server. Sharing
// domain.Clock between the two is what makes convergence a property of
// the code rather than a hope.
func (s *Store) applyServerOp(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx,
	op syncproto.ServerOp) error {

	// The server records ops that lost a merge for audit; the client has
	// no use for them and applying one would be wrong.
	if !op.Applied {
		return s.observeLamport(ctx, tx, op.NotebookID, op.Lamport)
	}

	// Advance our clock past anything we have seen. This is the other
	// half of the Lamport rule, and forgetting it means our next local
	// edit gets a lower counter than an edit we already know about — so
	// our own change loses the merge and appears to be ignored.
	if err := s.observeLamport(ctx, tx, op.NotebookID, op.Lamport); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	switch op.Kind {
	case syncproto.KindCreate:
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			INSERT INTO notes (id, notebook_id, updated_at)
			VALUES (?,?,?) ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING`,
			op.NoteID, op.NotebookID, op.ServerAt)
		return err

	case syncproto.KindSetField:
		// The clock comparison is in the WHERE clause, so an op that
		// loses is simply a no-op — no branching, no read-modify-write
		// race with a concurrent local edit.
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			UPDATE notes
			   SET title         = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'title' THEN ?2 ELSE title END,
			       body          = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'body'  THEN ?2 ELSE body  END,
			       title_lamport = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'title' THEN ?3 ELSE title_lamport END,
			       title_actor   = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'title' THEN ?4 ELSE title_actor   END,
			       body_lamport  = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'body'  THEN ?3 ELSE body_lamport  END,
			       body_actor    = CASE WHEN ?1 = 'body'  THEN ?4 ELSE body_actor    END,
			       updated_at    = ?5
			 WHERE id = ?6
			   AND ( (?1 = 'title' AND (?3 > title_lamport
			            OR (?3 = title_lamport AND ?4 > title_actor)))
			      OR (?1 = 'body'  AND (?3 > body_lamport
			            OR (?3 = body_lamport  AND ?4 > body_actor))) )`,
			op.Field, op.Value, op.Lamport, op.Actor, op.ServerAt, op.NoteID)
		return err

	case syncproto.KindDelete:
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			UPDATE notes SET deleted_at = ?1, delete_lamport = ?2, delete_actor = ?3
			 WHERE id = ?4
			   AND (?2 > delete_lamport OR (?2 = delete_lamport AND ?3 > delete_actor))`,
			op.ServerAt, op.Lamport, op.Actor, op.NoteID)
		return err

	case syncproto.KindRestore:
		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			UPDATE notes SET deleted_at = NULL, delete_lamport = ?1, delete_actor = ?2
			 WHERE id = ?3
			   AND (?1 > delete_lamport OR (?1 = delete_lamport AND ?2 > delete_actor))`,
			op.Lamport, op.Actor, op.NoteID)
		return err
	}
	return nil
}

func (s *Store) observeLamport(ctx context.Context, tx *sql.Tx,
	notebookID idgen.ID, seen int64) error {
	_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
		UPDATE sync_state SET lamport = MAX(lamport, ?) WHERE notebook_id = ?`,
		seen, notebookID)
	return err
}
Advancing the local clock on receipt is not optional

The Lamport rule has two halves, and clients that implement only the first are subtly broken. Ticking on local edit is obvious. Advancing lamport = max(lamport, received) on every op you see is the half that gets forgotten — and without it, a device that has been quiet while others edited will issue its next edit with a counter lower than changes it already knows about. That edit loses the merge, and to the user it looks exactly like “my change was ignored”, intermittently, with no error anywhere.

Reset, without losing local work

clients/syncd/internal/sync/reset.go
package sync

// reset runs when the client's cursor has fallen past the server's
// compaction horizon: the delta it needs no longer exists. The danger is
// obvious — this device may hold weeks of unpushed edits — so the order
// of operations here is the whole thing.
func (e *Engine) reset(ctx context.Context, notebookID idgen.ID) error {
	e.log.Warn("re-baselining notebook", "notebook", notebookID)
	syncResets.Inc()

	// 1 · Take the snapshot BEFORE touching anything local. If this
	//     fails we have changed nothing and will retry.
	snap, err := e.client.Snapshot(ctx, notebookID)
	if err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("snapshot: %w", err)
	}
	defer snap.Close()

	// 2 · Read the pending ops out first. They are about to survive a
	//     wholesale replacement of the note rows, which is exactly why
	//     they live in a SEPARATE table rather than as a flag on notes.
	pending, err := e.store.AllPendingOps(ctx, notebookID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// 3 · Replace the replica and replay, in ONE transaction. A crash
	//     midway leaves the old state intact rather than a half-written
	//     replica with the pending ops already consumed.
	if err := e.store.ReplaceFromSnapshot(ctx, notebookID, snap, pending); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("replace: %w", err)
	}

	// 4 · The ops are still in pending_ops, so the next cycle pushes
	//     them normally. They carry their ORIGINAL Lamport clocks, so
	//     they merge against the server's current state by exactly the
	//     same rule as any other op — an edit made three weeks ago
	//     correctly loses to one made yesterday.
	e.Wake()
	return nil
}
clients/syncd/internal/store/snapshot.go
package store

func (s *Store) ReplaceFromSnapshot(ctx context.Context, notebookID idgen.ID,
	snap *api.SnapshotReader, pending []syncproto.Op) error {

	return s.inTx(ctx, func(tx *sql.Tx) error {
		// Clear only THIS notebook. A user with ten notebooks resetting
		// one must not lose the other nine.
		if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx,
			`DELETE FROM notes WHERE notebook_id = ?`, notebookID); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// The snapshot is NDJSON streamed from the server, so a notebook
		// with twenty thousand notes uses constant memory here rather
		// than tens of megabytes (P08).
		for {
			n, err := snap.Next()
			if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {
				break
			}
			if err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if _, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
				INSERT INTO notes (id, notebook_id, title, body, visibility,
				    title_lamport, title_actor, body_lamport, body_actor,
				    delete_lamport, delete_actor, deleted_at, updated_at, dirty)
				VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?,0)`,
				n.ID, notebookID, n.Title, n.Body, n.Visibility,
				n.TitleLamport, n.TitleActor, n.BodyLamport, n.BodyActor,
				n.DeleteLamport, n.DeleteActor, n.DeletedAt, n.UpdatedAt,
			); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		// Replay local edits on top, using the shared merge rule. Some
		// will win and some will lose — and losing is CORRECT when the
		// server has a newer change. What matters is that none of them
		// is silently dropped.
		for _, op := range pending {
			if err := s.applyLocalOp(ctx, tx, op); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		_, err := tx.ExecContext(ctx, `
			INSERT INTO sync_state (notebook_id, server_seq, lamport, last_sync_at)
			VALUES (?1, ?2, MAX(?3, ?2), ?4)
			ON CONFLICT (notebook_id) DO UPDATE
			   SET server_seq = ?2, lamport = MAX(lamport, ?3), last_sync_at = ?4`,
			notebookID, snap.ServerSeq, snap.MaxLamport, time.Now().Unix())
		return err
	})
}

The doorbell

clients/syncd/internal/realtime/client.go
package realtime

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"time"

	"github.com/coder/websocket"
)

// The socket is a LATENCY OPTIMISATION and nothing else. Every message
// it carries could be replaced by polling two seconds later, and the
// client would still converge. That is what makes reconnect logic easy:
// there is nothing to recover.
type Client struct {
	url    string
	token  func(context.Context) (string, error)
	engine *sync.Engine
	log    *slog.Logger
}

func (c *Client) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	backoff := time.Duration(0)

	for ctx.Err() == nil {
		if backoff > 0 {
			select {
			case <-ctx.Done():
				return nil
			case <-time.After(backoff):
			}
		}
		if err := c.connectOnce(ctx); err != nil && ctx.Err() == nil {
			c.log.Debug("realtime disconnected", "err", err)
			backoff = nextBackoff(backoff)
			continue
		}
		backoff = 0
	}
	return nil
}

func (c *Client) connectOnce(ctx context.Context) error {
	tok, err := c.token(ctx)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// The access token goes in a header, never a query string: URLs end
	// up in proxy logs, and this one is a credential.
	conn, _, err := websocket.Dial(ctx, c.url, &websocket.DialOptions{
		HTTPHeader: http.Header{"Authorization": {"Bearer " + tok}},
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	defer conn.CloseNow()

	// A read deadline longer than the server's ping interval. Without
	// one, a connection killed by a NAT timeout or a mobile handover
	// looks alive forever and the client silently stops receiving
	// notifications — the failure that a doorbell design tolerates and
	// a data-carrying socket does not.
	for {
		readCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 45*time.Second)
		_, data, err := conn.Read(readCtx)
		cancel()
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		var msg struct {
			Type       string   `json:"type"`
			NotebookID idgen.ID `json:"notebook_id"`
			ServerSeq  int64    `json:"server_seq"`
		}
		if err := json.Unmarshal(data, &msg); err != nil {
			continue // a malformed frame is not worth dropping the socket
		}

		switch msg.Type {
		case "changed":
			// We do NOT apply anything from the socket. We pull.
			c.engine.Wake()
		case "access_revoked":
			// Stop syncing a notebook we have been removed from. The
			// local copy stays — local-first means removal stops future
			// access, it does not un-share what is already on disk (D09).
			_ = c.engine.StopNotebook(ctx, msg.NotebookID)
		}
	}
}

What the user actually experiences

Operation Latency Network? open a note ~60 µs no type a character ~0 no save (debounced) ~400 µs no search across 50,000 notes ~8 ms no (SQLite FTS5) see a collaborator's edit ~300 ms yes (doorbell + pull) create a note on a plane ~400 µs no reconnect after a week ~2 s yes (delta, paged) first sync on a new device ~4 s yes (snapshot) Compare with a conventional client, where every one of the first six rows is a network round trip: 40-200 ms on a good connection, 600 ms on a train, and an error message on a plane. That gap is the entire argument for local-first, and the price is this chapter plus D11 and D12. It is a real price. It is worth paying for a writing tool, where latency is felt on every keystroke, and not worth paying for an admin dashboard nobody uses offline.
What local-first costs you, stated honestly

Three things. Complexity: the merge rule, the reset path and the clock discipline are genuinely hard, and they are now in two codebases that must agree — which is why domain.Clock and syncproto are shared rather than reimplemented. Storage on the device: a full replica, growing with the corpus. And an irreversible disclosure property: once data is on someone's disk you cannot take it back, so revoking access stops future sync but does not unshare history. If any of those three is unacceptable for your product, do not build local-first — build a good cache instead and be honest that it is a cache.

Interview follow-up

“How would you make an app work offline?” Start with the data model rather than the network: a complete local replica the UI reads from directly, and an outbox of pending operations written in the same local transaction as the state change — otherwise a crash between the two loses an edit or pushes a phantom. Then the three properties that make the sync loop safe: client-generated ids so operations are idempotent when retried, a server cursor so gaps are detectable, and a deterministic merge rule shared by both sides so the optimistic local result matches what the server will compute. Finish with the path nobody asks about and everybody gets wrong — what happens when the client has been offline past the server's history horizon, and how you replay local work on top of a fresh snapshot without losing any of it.

D14

The event backbone, realtime and mail

Three pieces that share one mechanism. Every service publishes through its outbox to NATS JetStream; the realtime service turns those events into WebSocket doorbells; the mailer turns them into email. All of it is at-least-once, so every consumer here is idempotent by construction.

The event bus

platform/eventbus/nats.go
// Package eventbus wraps NATS JetStream. Every service publishes through
// its outbox relay (D03) and consumes through this, so delivery
// semantics are identical everywhere: at-least-once, unordered across
// subjects, deduped by event id.
package eventbus

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"log/slog"
	"time"

	"github.com/nats-io/nats.go"
	"github.com/nats-io/nats.go/jetstream"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
)

// ErrPermanent marks a failure that retrying cannot fix — a malformed
// payload, an unknown event type. It goes straight to the dead-letter
// stream instead of looping forever (B12).
var ErrPermanent = errors.New("permanent failure")

type Bus struct {
	nc  *nats.Conn
	js  jetstream.JetStream
	log *slog.Logger
}

func Connect(ctx context.Context, url, name string, log *slog.Logger) (*Bus, error) {
	nc, err := nats.Connect(url,
		nats.Name("quill-"+name),
		nats.MaxReconnects(-1),            // never give up reconnecting
		nats.ReconnectWait(2*time.Second),
		nats.ReconnectJitter(500*time.Millisecond, 2*time.Second),
		nats.DisconnectErrHandler(func(_ *nats.Conn, err error) {
			log.Warn("nats disconnected", "err", err)
			natsConnected.Set(0)
		}),
		nats.ReconnectHandler(func(c *nats.Conn) {
			log.Info("nats reconnected", "url", c.ConnectedUrl())
			natsConnected.Set(1)
		}),
	)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("nats connect: %w", err)
	}
	js, err := jetstream.New(nc)
	if err != nil {
		nc.Close()
		return nil, err
	}
	return &Bus{nc: nc, js: js, log: log}, nil
}

// EnsureStreams is idempotent and runs at startup. Declaring topology in
// code rather than by hand means a fresh environment comes up correctly
// and a drifted one is repaired.
func (b *Bus) EnsureStreams(ctx context.Context) error {
	for _, cfg := range []jetstream.StreamConfig{
		{
			Name:      "QUILL",
			Subjects:  []string{"identity.*", "notes.*", "collab.*"},
			Retention: jetstream.LimitsPolicy,
			// Long enough that a consumer down for a day catches up,
			// short enough that the stream is bounded.
			MaxAge:    7 * 24 * time.Hour,
			MaxBytes:  8 << 30,
			Storage:   jetstream.FileStorage,
			Replicas:  3,
			Discard:   jetstream.DiscardOld,
			// Belt and braces on top of the outbox: JetStream itself
			// deduplicates identical Nats-Msg-Id values within a window.
			Duplicates: 5 * time.Minute,
		},
		{
			Name:     "QUILL_DLQ",
			Subjects: []string{"dlq.>"},
			MaxAge:   30 * 24 * time.Hour,
			Storage:  jetstream.FileStorage,
			Replicas: 3,
		},
	} {
		if _, err := b.js.CreateOrUpdateStream(ctx, cfg); err != nil {
			return fmt.Errorf("stream %s: %w", cfg.Name, err)
		}
	}
	return nil
}

// Publish satisfies outbox.Publisher, so the relay knows nothing about
// NATS and could be pointed at Kafka by changing one constructor.
func (b *Bus) Publish(ctx context.Context, e outbox.Event) error {
	msg := &nats.Msg{
		Subject: e.Subject,
		Data:    e.Payload,
		Header: nats.Header{
			// JetStream dedupes on this within the Duplicates window,
			// which covers the relay republishing after a failed commit.
			"Nats-Msg-Id": []string{e.ID.String()},
			"Quill-Trace": []string{e.TraceID},
		},
	}
	// A publish that blocks forever holds an outbox transaction open and
	// a database connection with it (B07).
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 5*time.Second)
	defer cancel()

	_, err := b.js.PublishMsg(ctx, msg)
	return err
}

The consumer, with retries and a dead-letter path

platform/eventbus/consumer.go
package eventbus

type Handler func(context.Context, outbox.Event) error

type ConsumerConfig struct {
	Durable     string   // survives restarts; this IS the consumer's identity
	Subjects    []string
	MaxDeliver  int
	AckWait     time.Duration
	MaxInFlight int
}

func (b *Bus) Consume(ctx context.Context, cfg ConsumerConfig, h Handler) error {
	cons, err := b.js.CreateOrUpdateConsumer(ctx, "QUILL", jetstream.ConsumerConfig{
		Durable:        cfg.Durable,
		FilterSubjects: cfg.Subjects,
		AckPolicy:      jetstream.AckExplicitPolicy,
		// Longer than the slowest handler, or a slow message is
		// redelivered while still being processed — which turns one
		// event into two and makes idempotency load-bearing rather
		// than defensive.
		AckWait:    cfg.AckWait,
		MaxDeliver: cfg.MaxDeliver,
		// Exponential backoff between redeliveries, so a failing
		// dependency is not hammered by the retry stream.
		BackOff: []time.Duration{
			1 * time.Second, 5 * time.Second, 30 * time.Second,
			2 * time.Minute, 10 * time.Minute,
		},
		MaxAckPending: cfg.MaxInFlight,
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	sub, err := cons.Consume(func(msg jetstream.Msg) {
		start := time.Now()
		md, _ := msg.Metadata()

		// Per-message context with a deadline. A handler that hangs
		// forever would otherwise occupy an in-flight slot permanently
		// and eventually stall the whole consumer.
		mctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, cfg.AckWait-time.Second)
		defer cancel()

		// Re-attach the producing trace so the consumer's span links
		// back to the request that caused it.
		mctx = withTraceHeader(mctx, msg.Headers().Get("Quill-Trace"))

		e := outbox.Event{
			ID:      idgen.ID(msg.Headers().Get("Nats-Msg-Id")),
			Subject: msg.Subject(),
			Payload: msg.Data(),
		}

		err := h(mctx, e)
		eventDuration.WithLabelValues(msg.Subject()).Observe(time.Since(start).Seconds())

		switch {
		case err == nil:
			_ = msg.Ack()

		case errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent):
			// Retrying cannot help. Dead-letter it now rather than
			// burning five redeliveries first.
			b.deadLetter(ctx, msg, err)
			_ = msg.Ack()
			eventsDLQ.WithLabelValues(msg.Subject(), "permanent").Inc()

		case md != nil && md.NumDelivered >= uint64(cfg.MaxDeliver):
			// Out of attempts. The DLQ is not a graveyard — alert on its
			// depth, because these are events a user expected to have
			// taken effect (B12).
			b.deadLetter(ctx, msg, err)
			_ = msg.Ack()
			eventsDLQ.WithLabelValues(msg.Subject(), "exhausted").Inc()

		default:
			b.log.WarnContext(mctx, "event failed, will retry",
				"subject", msg.Subject(), "attempt", md.NumDelivered, "err", err)
			_ = msg.Nak() // let the BackOff schedule decide when
		}
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	<-ctx.Done()
	sub.Stop()
	return nil
}

func (b *Bus) deadLetter(ctx context.Context, msg jetstream.Msg, cause error) {
	md, _ := msg.Metadata()
	payload, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
		"subject": msg.Subject(), "error": cause.Error(),
		"delivered": md.NumDelivered, "data": json.RawMessage(msg.Data()),
		"failed_at": time.Now().UTC(),
	})
	// Best effort: if even the DLQ publish fails, log loudly. Losing the
	// event silently is the one outcome that must not happen quietly.
	if _, err := b.js.Publish(ctx, "dlq."+msg.Subject(), payload); err != nil {
		b.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "DEAD LETTER PUBLISH FAILED",
			"subject", msg.Subject(), "err", err, "payload", string(msg.Data()))
	}
}
AckWait must exceed your slowest handler, or you manufacture duplicates

If a handler takes forty seconds and AckWait is thirty, JetStream redelivers while the first attempt is still running — so the same event is processed twice concurrently, which is a far harder problem than processing it twice sequentially. The symptom is duplicate side effects that appear only under load, when handlers are slowest. Set AckWait from the p99 handler duration with headroom, give each handler its own context deadline just below it, and if a handler genuinely needs minutes, extend the ack in a heartbeat rather than raising AckWait globally.

The realtime service

services/realtime/internal/hub/hub.go
// Package hub holds the WebSocket connections. It is entirely in-memory
// and entirely disposable: killing every realtime pod costs clients two
// seconds of extra latency and nothing else, because the socket is a
// doorbell and the HTTP change feed is the source of truth (D11).
package hub

import (
	"context"
	"sync"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
)

type conn struct {
	id     idgen.ID
	userID idgen.ID
	// Buffered, and written with a NON-BLOCKING send. A slow client must
	// never block the fan-out goroutine — one stalled mobile connection
	// would otherwise stall notifications for everyone.
	out    chan []byte
	cancel context.CancelFunc
}

type Hub struct {
	mu sync.RWMutex
	// notebook → set of connections. A map of maps rather than a slice,
	// because unsubscribe on disconnect must be O(1) and disconnects are
	// constant in a mobile population.
	subs  map[idgen.ID]map[idgen.ID]*conn
	conns map[idgen.ID]*conn
}

func New() *Hub {
	return &Hub{
		subs:  make(map[idgen.ID]map[idgen.ID]*conn),
		conns: make(map[idgen.ID]*conn),
	}
}

const sendBuffer = 16

func (h *Hub) Broadcast(notebookID idgen.ID, payload []byte, exceptDevice idgen.ID) {
	// Copy the target list under a READ lock, then send outside it.
	// Sending while holding the lock would let one slow channel block
	// every subscribe and unsubscribe in the process.
	h.mu.RLock()
	targets := make([]*conn, 0, len(h.subs[notebookID]))
	for _, c := range h.subs[notebookID] {
		targets = append(targets, c)
	}
	h.mu.RUnlock()

	for _, c := range targets {
		select {
		case c.out <- payload:
			messagesSent.Inc()
		default:
			// The buffer is full: this client is not keeping up. DROP
			// the message and close the connection. Dropping is safe
			// precisely because the notification carries no data — the
			// client reconnects and pulls, and converges anyway.
			messagesDropped.Inc()
			c.cancel()
		}
	}
}

// Revoke disconnects a user from a notebook, driven by
// collab.access_revoked (D09). Without it, a removed collaborator keeps
// receiving change notifications for a notebook they can no longer read.
func (h *Hub) Revoke(notebookID, userID idgen.ID) {
	h.mu.Lock()
	defer h.mu.Unlock()
	for id, c := range h.subs[notebookID] {
		if c.userID == userID {
			delete(h.subs[notebookID], id)
			c.cancel()
		}
	}
}
services/realtime/internal/transport/ws/handler.go
package ws

import (
	"context"
	"encoding/json"
	"net/http"
	"time"

	"github.com/coder/websocket"
	"github.com/coder/websocket/wsjson"
)

const (
	pingInterval = 25 * time.Second
	writeTimeout = 10 * time.Second
	readLimit    = 4 << 10 // clients send only small subscribe frames
)

func (h *Handler) ServeHTTP(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	ctx := r.Context()
	sub := httpx.MustSubject(ctx)

	conn, err := websocket.Accept(w, r, &websocket.AcceptOptions{
		// An explicit origin allowlist. Without it, any website can open
		// an authenticated socket in a logged-in user's browser — the
		// WebSocket equivalent of a missing CORS policy, and it is not
		// covered by the same-origin policy.
		OriginPatterns:  h.allowedOrigins,
		CompressionMode: websocket.CompressionDisabled, // small frames
	})
	if err != nil {
		return
	}
	defer conn.CloseNow()
	conn.SetReadLimit(readLimit)

	// Bound the connection's total lifetime. A socket held for days
	// accumulates against every limit you have and outlives the access
	// token that authorised it; forcing a reconnect re-authenticates.
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 4*time.Hour)
	defer cancel()

	c := h.hub.Add(ctx, cancel, sub.UserID)
	defer h.hub.Remove(c)

	g, gctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)

	// reader: subscribe frames, and liveness. We do not act on anything
	// else a client sends.
	g.Go(func() error {
		for {
			var msg clientMessage
			if err := wsjson.Read(gctx, conn, &msg); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if msg.Type != "subscribe" {
				continue
			}
			// EVERY subscription is authorised. A socket authenticated
			// as user X must not be able to subscribe to a notebook X
			// cannot read — the check belongs here, not at connect time,
			// because the notebook list arrives after the handshake.
			role, err := h.collab.CheckPermission(gctx, msg.NotebookID, sub.UserID)
			if err != nil || !role.CanRead() {
				_ = wsjson.Write(gctx, conn, errorMessage{
					Type: "error", Code: "forbidden", NotebookID: msg.NotebookID})
				continue
			}
			h.hub.Subscribe(c, msg.NotebookID)
		}
	})

	// writer: fan-out plus keepalive.
	g.Go(func() error {
		ticker := time.NewTicker(pingInterval)
		defer ticker.Stop()
		for {
			select {
			case <-gctx.Done():
				return gctx.Err()
			case payload := <-c.Out():
				wctx, wcancel := context.WithTimeout(gctx, writeTimeout)
				err := conn.Write(wctx, websocket.MessageText, payload)
				wcancel()
				if err != nil {
					return err
				}
			case <-ticker.C:
				// Ping detects the connection a NAT or a mobile handover
				// killed without telling either side — otherwise the
				// socket looks alive forever and silently delivers
				// nothing.
				pctx, pcancel := context.WithTimeout(gctx, writeTimeout)
				err := conn.Ping(pctx)
				pcancel()
				if err != nil {
					return err
				}
			}
		}
	})

	_ = g.Wait()
	conn.Close(websocket.StatusNormalClosure, "")
}
services/realtime/internal/events/consume.go
package events

// The realtime service consumes with an EPHEMERAL consumer per pod, not
// a durable shared one. Every pod must see every event, because it holds
// a different set of connections — a queue group would deliver each
// event to one pod and the other pods' clients would never hear about it.
func (c *Consumer) Run(ctx context.Context) error {
	return c.bus.ConsumeEphemeral(ctx, []string{
		"notes.changed", "collab.access_revoked", "collab.membership_changed",
	}, func(ctx context.Context, e outbox.Event) error {
		switch e.Subject {
		case "notes.changed":
			var p NotesChanged
			if err := json.Unmarshal(e.Payload, &p); err != nil {
				return fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", eventbus.ErrPermanent, err)
			}
			// The doorbell. Sequence only — no note content, so a leaked
			// or misrouted frame discloses nothing, and the payload is
			// the same tiny size whether the note is 1 KB or 1 MB.
			payload, _ := json.Marshal(map[string]any{
				"type": "changed", "notebook_id": p.NotebookID,
				"server_seq": p.ServerSeq,
			})
			c.hub.Broadcast(p.NotebookID, payload, p.DeviceID)

		case "collab.access_revoked":
			var p AccessRevoked
			if err := json.Unmarshal(e.Payload, &p); err != nil {
				return fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", eventbus.ErrPermanent, err)
			}
			c.hub.Revoke(p.NotebookID, p.UserID)
		}
		return nil
	})
}
Ephemeral consumers for stateless fan-out, durable for work

The distinction trips people up. A durable, queue-grouped consumer delivers each message to exactly one member of the group — correct for the mailer, where sending an email twice is a bug. An ephemeral per-pod consumer delivers every message to every pod — correct for realtime, where each pod holds different connections and a queue group would mean most clients never hear anything. Getting this backwards produces a system that works perfectly with one replica and breaks the moment you scale out, which is a memorable way to learn it.

The mailer

services/mailer/internal/app/send.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"fmt"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/eventbus"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
)

// Handle turns an event into an email. The dedupe table is what makes
// at-least-once delivery safe: without it, a redelivered event sends a
// second password-reset email, which is confusing at best and a
// support-load problem at worst.
func (s *Service) Handle(ctx context.Context, e outbox.Event) error {
	tmpl, ok := s.templates[e.Subject]
	if !ok {
		return nil // an event we do not mail on; ack and move on
	}

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// The unique constraint IS the dedupe. Insert first: if this is
		// a redelivery, the conflict short-circuits before we spend a
		// provider call.
		inserted, err := q.ClaimDelivery(ctx, e.ID)
		if err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}
		if !inserted {
			return nil // already sent; acknowledging is correct
		}

		msg, err := tmpl.Render(ctx, e.Payload)
		if err != nil {
			// A template that cannot render this payload will never
			// render it. Permanent.
			return fmt.Errorf("%w: render %s: %v", eventbus.ErrPermanent, e.Subject, err)
		}

		// Suppression list: bounces, complaints and unsubscribes. Sending
		// to a hard-bounced address damages domain reputation for
		// everyone else's mail.
		if suppressed, err := q.IsSuppressed(ctx, msg.To); err != nil {
			return err
		} else if suppressed {
			s.log.InfoContext(ctx, "suppressed", "to", hashEmail(msg.To))
			return nil
		}

		if err := s.provider.Send(ctx, msg); err != nil {
			var perr *ProviderError
			if errors.As(err, &perr) && perr.Permanent {
				// A malformed address or a rejected domain: no retry.
				return fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", eventbus.ErrPermanent, err)
			}
			// Transient. Returning a plain error rolls back the claim,
			// so the redelivery genuinely retries rather than being
			// deduped away — the subtle reason the claim lives in the
			// SAME transaction as the send.
			return fmt.Errorf("send: %w", err)
		}

		return q.MarkDelivered(ctx, e.ID)
	})
}
The claim and the send must share a transaction, and that is a real trade

If the claim commits before the send, a provider failure leaves the event marked as delivered and the email is never sent. If the claim is rolled back on failure, a send that actually succeeded but whose response was lost will be retried — and the user gets two emails. There is no third option: a network call and a database write cannot be made atomic. Quill chooses “possibly twice” over “possibly never”, because a duplicate invitation is an annoyance and a missing password reset is a support ticket. Say which way you chose and why, because reviewers will ask.

Event catalogue

SubjectPublished byConsumed by
identity.user_registeredidentitymailer — verification link
identity.password_reset_requestedidentitymailer
identity.password_changedidentitymailer — “your password changed”
identity.token_reuse_detectedidentitymailer, and your alerting
notes.notebook_creatednotescollab — creates the owner membership
notes.changednotesrealtime — the doorbell
notes.published / unpublishednotesgateway — cache purge
collab.invitation_createdcollabmailer
collab.membership_changedcollabnotes — the ACL replica (D10)
collab.access_revokedcollabrealtime — disconnect; notes — drop ACL
collab.invite_redeemedcollabmailer — tells the inviter
Name events for what happened, never for what should happen next

collab.membership_changed is a fact; notes.update_acl would be a command. The distinction matters because a fact can have any number of consumers added later without the publisher knowing or changing — realtime, notes, an audit pipeline, a billing counter — while a command couples the publisher to one specific handler and quietly turns your event bus into an awkward RPC mechanism with worse error handling. Past tense in the name is a small discipline that keeps the coupling honest.

What to alert on

SignalMeans
Outbox backlog (unpublished rows older than 60 s)The relay is stuck or NATS is unreachable. Everything downstream is frozen
Consumer lag on collab.membership_changedThe ACL replica is stale — a security-relevant staleness window (D10)
DLQ depth > 0Work a user expected has not happened. This is never “fine”
Redelivery rate risingA handler is failing or slower than AckWait
WebSocket drops (buffer full)Clients not keeping up, or a fan-out storm from missing batching
Mail bounce rate > 2%Domain reputation is at risk; check for an invite-spam account
identity.token_reuse_detected at allPage someone. A refresh token was replayed — either a bug, or a theft
Interview follow-up

“How do you make an event consumer safe under at-least-once delivery?” Idempotency, and be specific about the mechanism: a unique constraint on the event id claimed in the same transaction as the side effect, so the claim and the effect commit together. Then the two refinements that show experience — separating permanent failures from transient ones, so a malformed payload dead-letters immediately instead of burning five retries, and setting AckWait above the slowest handler, because a redelivery that overlaps a still-running attempt turns sequential duplication into concurrent duplication, which is a far harder problem and only appears under load.

D15

Testing the system

Six services, an event bus and a sync protocol that must converge under arbitrary reordering. This chapter is the test strategy: what to fake, what to run for real, and the property test that is the only honest way to verify that sync works.

What gets tested where

count runs in needs domain unit merge rules, ~400 < 1 s nothing validation, roles app + fakes use cases with ~150 ~2 s nothing in-memory stores store integration real SQL against ~80 ~25 s postgres a real Postgres container transport handlers through ~60 ~3 s fakes the real middleware beneath contract each consumer vs ~25 ~2 s recorded the producer's shape payloads sync property randomised ~8 ~40 s postgres convergence + in-proc clients end to end the whole stack, ~12 ~90 s compose real browsers absent The shape is deliberate: the expensive tests are few and they test the things cheap tests cannot — whether the SQL is valid, whether two services agree about a payload, and whether the sync protocol actually converges. Everything provable in the domain is proved there, where a full run costs a second.

The domain layer, where the merge rule is proved

services/notes/internal/domain/clock_test.go
package domain_test

// The merge rule is the highest-risk code in Quill and it has no
// dependencies at all, so it gets the most thorough test and that test
// runs in microseconds.
func TestClockAfter(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	alice, bob := idgen.ID("01HXALICE"), idgen.ID("01HXBOB")

	tests := []struct {
		name string
		a, b domain.Clock
		want bool
	}{
		{"higher lamport wins",
			domain.Clock{5, alice}, domain.Clock{4, bob}, true},
		{"lower lamport loses",
			domain.Clock{3, alice}, domain.Clock{4, bob}, false},
		{"tie broken by actor, higher wins",
			domain.Clock{4, bob}, domain.Clock{4, alice}, true},
		{"tie broken by actor, lower loses",
			domain.Clock{4, alice}, domain.Clock{4, bob}, false},
		{"identical is not after itself",
			domain.Clock{4, alice}, domain.Clock{4, alice}, false},
		{"zero clock loses to anything",
			domain.Clock{0, ""}, domain.Clock{1, alice}, false},
	}
	for _, tt := range tests {
		t.Run(tt.name, func(t *testing.T) {
			t.Parallel()
			if got := tt.a.After(tt.b); got != tt.want {
				t.Errorf("After() = %v, want %v", got, tt.want)
			}
		})
	}
}

// The three algebraic properties the protocol depends on. If any of
// these is false, convergence is not merely unlikely — it is impossible,
// and no amount of integration testing would reliably catch it.
func TestClockIsTotalOrder(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()

	f := func(l1, l2 int64, a1, a2 string) bool {
		c1 := domain.Clock{Lamport: l1, Actor: idgen.ID(a1)}
		c2 := domain.Clock{Lamport: l2, Actor: idgen.ID(a2)}

		// ANTISYMMETRY: never both after each other.
		if c1.After(c2) && c2.After(c1) {
			return false
		}
		// TOTALITY: distinct clocks always have a winner. Without this,
		// two replicas can disagree about which edit won and stay
		// disagreeing forever.
		if c1 != c2 && !c1.After(c2) && !c2.After(c1) {
			return false
		}
		// IRREFLEXIVITY: a clock is not after itself, so replaying an op
		// is a no-op rather than a spurious rewrite.
		if c1.After(c1) {
			return false
		}
		return true
	}
	if err := quick.Check(f, &quick.Config{MaxCount: 10_000}); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
}

// Transitivity, checked over random triples: if a beats b and b beats c,
// a must beat c. A merge rule without it gives you rock-paper-scissors,
// where the final state depends on arrival order.
func TestClockTransitive(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	f := func(l1, l2, l3 int64, a1, a2, a3 string) bool {
		c1 := domain.Clock{l1, idgen.ID(a1)}
		c2 := domain.Clock{l2, idgen.ID(a2)}
		c3 := domain.Clock{l3, idgen.ID(a3)}
		if c1.After(c2) && c2.After(c3) {
			return c1.After(c3)
		}
		return true
	}
	if err := quick.Check(f, &quick.Config{MaxCount: 10_000}); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
}
Property tests earn their keep exactly here

Example-based tests confirm the cases you thought of. For a merge rule, the cases you did not think of are the whole risk — and the properties are simple enough to state precisely: antisymmetry, totality, irreflexivity, transitivity. Ten thousand random triples take eight milliseconds and cover a space no table could. Use property tests where the correctness condition is an algebraic law, and tables everywhere else; using them the other way round produces slow tests that assert very little.

Integration, against a real Postgres

platform/testsupport/postgres.go
// Package testsupport gives every service the same container harness, so
// the integration setup is written once rather than six times.
package testsupport

import (
	"context"
	"database/sql"
	"fmt"
	"os"
	"testing"

	"github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go"
	tcpostgres "github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go/modules/postgres"
	"github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go/wait"
)

// StartPostgres boots ONE container for the whole package and returns a
// factory for isolated databases. Starting a container per test would
// add ~2 s each; per package it is amortised to nothing.
func StartPostgres(ctx context.Context, m *testing.M, migrate func(string) error) (string, func()) {
	c, err := tcpostgres.Run(ctx, "postgres:16-alpine",
		tcpostgres.WithDatabase("quill_test"),
		tcpostgres.WithUsername("test"),
		tcpostgres.WithPassword("test"),
		// Two occurrences: Postgres logs "ready" once during its own
		// init and again when it is genuinely accepting connections.
		// Waiting for the first is the classic flaky-test cause.
		testcontainers.WithWaitStrategy(
			wait.ForLog("database system is ready to accept connections").
				WithOccurrence(2).WithStartupTimeout(60*time.Second)),
		// Durability is irrelevant for tests and fsync dominates the
		// runtime — this is worth roughly 3× on a migration-heavy suite.
		testcontainers.WithCmd("postgres", "-c", "fsync=off",
			"-c", "full_page_writes=off", "-c", "synchronous_commit=off"),
	)
	if err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	dsn, _ := c.ConnectionString(ctx, "sslmode=disable")
	if err := migrate(dsn); err != nil {
		panic(err)
	}
	return dsn, func() { _ = c.Terminate(ctx) }
}

// WithTx gives each test its own transaction, rolled back at the end.
// Fast, and fully isolated — so every test can be t.Parallel() without
// any of them seeing another's rows.
func WithTx(t *testing.T, pool *pgxpool.Pool) pgx.Tx {
	t.Helper()
	tx, err := pool.Begin(context.Background())
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}
	t.Cleanup(func() { _ = tx.Rollback(context.Background()) })
	return tx
}
services/notes/internal/store/store_integration_test.go
//go:build integration

package store_test

// The tests worth running against a real database are the ones where the
// DATABASE is doing the work — constraints, partial indexes, row locks,
// RLS. A fake would happily accept all of these and prove nothing.

func TestRLSHidesOtherUsersNotes(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	env := newEnv(t)

	alice, bob := env.newUser(t), env.newUser(t)
	nb := env.notebookOwnedBy(t, alice)
	note := env.noteIn(t, nb)

	// Read as bob, who has no membership. Even with a query that
	// "forgets" the ACL scope, the policy must return nothing.
	err := pg.InTxAs(env.ctx, env.pool, bob.String(), func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		var id string
		// Deliberately the UNSCOPED query — this is the bug we are
		// testing the second wall against.
		return tx.QueryRow(env.ctx,
			`SELECT id FROM notes WHERE id = $1`, note).Scan(&id)
	})
	if !errors.Is(err, pgx.ErrNoRows) {
		t.Fatalf("RLS did not hide the note: err = %v", err)
	}
}

func TestSeqIsMonotonicUnderConcurrency(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	env := newEnv(t)
	nb := env.notebook(t)

	const writers, each = 16, 25
	seen := make([][]int64, writers)

	// The whole sync protocol rests on server_seq being a gapless total
	// order per notebook. This test is what turns that from an
	// assumption into a verified property.
	var g errgroup.Group
	for w := 0; w < writers; w++ {
		w := w
		g.Go(func() error {
			for i := 0; i < each; i++ {
				seq, err := env.store.ReserveSeq(env.ctx, nb, 1)
				if err != nil {
					return err
				}
				seen[w] = append(seen[w], seq)
			}
			return nil
		})
	}
	if err := g.Wait(); err != nil {
		t.Fatal(err)
	}

	all := slices.Concat(seen...)
	slices.Sort(all)
	if len(all) != writers*each {
		t.Fatalf("got %d sequences, want %d", len(all), writers*each)
	}
	for i, v := range all {
		if v != int64(i+1) {
			t.Fatalf("sequence %d is %d — gaps or duplicates", i+1, v)
		}
	}
}

func TestLinkInviteCannotExceedMaxUses(t *testing.T) {
	t.Parallel()
	env := newEnv(t)
	inv := env.linkInvite(t, withMaxUses(3))

	// Ten people redeem simultaneously. Exactly three must succeed —
	// enforced by the row lock plus the CHECK constraint (D09).
	var succeeded atomic.Int64
	var g errgroup.Group
	for i := 0; i < 10; i++ {
		g.Go(func() error {
			_, err := env.collab.AcceptInvite(env.ctx, app.AcceptInput{
				Token: inv.Token, UserID: env.newUser(t), EmailVerified: true,
			})
			if err == nil {
				succeeded.Add(1)
			}
			return nil
		})
	}
	_ = g.Wait()

	if got := succeeded.Load(); got != 3 {
		t.Fatalf("%d redemptions succeeded, want exactly 3", got)
	}
}

The sync convergence property test

clients/syncd/internal/sync/converge_test.go
//go:build integration

package sync_test

// This is the test that actually proves the product works. Everything
// else verifies a piece; this verifies the guarantee: given any
// interleaving of edits, partitions and reconnections, every client
// ends in the SAME state.
func TestConvergence(t *testing.T) {
	env := newSyncEnv(t) // real Postgres, real notes service, in-process HTTP

	const (
		clients = 5
		rounds  = 200
		seed    = 20260915 // fixed: a failing run must be reproducible
	)
	rng := rand.New(rand.NewSource(seed))

	nb := env.notebook(t)
	cs := make([]*fakeClient, clients)
	for i := range cs {
		cs[i] = env.newClient(t, nb) // its own SQLite file and device id
	}

	noteID := cs[0].createNote(t, "shared")
	cs[0].syncNow(t)
	for _, c := range cs[1:] {
		c.syncNow(t)
	}

	// Randomised interleaving: edit, go offline, come back, sync, delete.
	// The partitions are the point — a client that never disconnects
	// exercises none of the interesting paths.
	for r := 0; r < rounds; r++ {
		c := cs[rng.Intn(clients)]
		switch rng.Intn(10) {
		case 0, 1, 2, 3:
			c.setField(t, noteID, "body", fmt.Sprintf("body-%d-%d", r, c.id))
		case 4, 5:
			c.setField(t, noteID, "title", fmt.Sprintf("title-%d", r))
		case 6:
			c.goOffline() // subsequent edits queue in pending_ops
		case 7:
			c.goOnline()
		case 8:
			c.syncNow(t)
		case 9:
			if rng.Intn(20) == 0 {
				c.deleteNote(t, noteID)
			}
		}
	}

	// Everyone comes back and syncs until quiescent. Several passes,
	// because one client's push produces changes another must pull.
	for _, c := range cs {
		c.goOnline()
	}
	for pass := 0; pass < clients*3; pass++ {
		for _, c := range cs {
			c.syncNow(t)
		}
	}

	// THE ASSERTION: identical state everywhere, including the server.
	want := cs[0].noteState(t, noteID)
	for i, c := range cs[1:] {
		if got := c.noteState(t, noteID); got != want {
			t.Errorf("client %d diverged:\n got %+v\nwant %+v", i+1, got, want)
		}
	}
	if got := env.serverNoteState(t, noteID); got != want {
		t.Errorf("server diverged:\n got %+v\nwant %+v", got, want)
	}

	// And nothing may be left unpushed — a client stuck with permanent
	// pending ops is a silent data-loss bug.
	for i, c := range cs {
		if n := c.pendingCount(t); n != 0 {
			t.Errorf("client %d has %d unpushed ops after quiescence", i, n)
		}
	}
}

// The reset path deserves its own test, because it is rare, hard, and
// exactly where data loss lives (D11).
func TestResetPreservesLocalEdits(t *testing.T) {
	env := newSyncEnv(t)
	nb := env.notebook(t)
	a, b := env.newClient(t, nb), env.newClient(t, nb)

	noteID := a.createNote(t, "original")
	a.syncNow(t)
	b.syncNow(t)

	// b goes offline and writes. a keeps working, and the server
	// compacts past b's cursor.
	b.goOffline()
	b.setField(t, noteID, "title", "edited-offline-by-b")

	for i := 0; i < 50; i++ {
		a.setField(t, noteID, "body", fmt.Sprintf("a-%d", i))
		a.syncNow(t)
	}
	env.compactAllOpsBefore(t, nb, env.headSeq(t, nb))

	// b reconnects into a forced reset.
	b.goOnline()
	b.syncNow(t)

	if b.pendingCount(t) != 0 {
		t.Fatal("b still has unpushed ops after reset")
	}
	// b's offline edit had a LOWER lamport than a's fifty subsequent
	// edits, so it correctly loses on body — but the title, which a
	// never touched, must have survived the reset and been pushed.
	if got := env.serverNoteState(t, noteID).Title; got != "edited-offline-by-b" {
		t.Errorf("b's offline title edit was lost: got %q", got)
	}
}
Seed the randomness, and print the seed on failure

A property test that uses an unseeded source finds a bug once and never again, which is worse than not finding it — you now know a bug exists and cannot reproduce it. Fix the seed so every run is identical, and when you want broader coverage run a nightly job that iterates over a range of seeds and reports which one failed. The failing seed then reproduces the exact interleaving on any machine, which turns “sync sometimes diverges” from a week of guessing into a debugging session.

Contract tests

platform/testsupport/contract.go
package testsupport

// The failure this prevents: notes renames a field in NotesChanged,
// every test passes because each service tests its own half, and
