	if !ok {
		return nil, domain.ErrChallengeExpired
	}
	// Bind the challenge to the user who started it. Without this, a
	// challenge issued for one account could be completed against
	// another — a genuine session-fixation shaped hole.
	if string(session.UserID) != userID.String() {
		return nil, domain.ErrChallengeMismatch
	}

	parsed, err := protocol.ParseCredentialCreationResponseBody(body)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", domain.ErrPasskeyInvalid, err)
	}

	u, err := s.webAuthnUser(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// CreateCredential performs the verification: challenge, origin,
	// RP ID hash, user-present flag, and the signature itself. Every one
	// of those checks matters, which is why this is a maintained library
	// rather than something to hand-roll.
	cred, err := s.wa.CreateCredential(u, session, parsed)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", domain.ErrPasskeyInvalid, err)
	}

	auth := &domain.Authenticator{
		ID: idgen.New(), UserID: userID, Kind: domain.KindPasskey,
		// Name it from the AAGUID so the list says "iCloud Keychain" or
		// "YubiKey 5 Series" instead of "Passkey". A user with three
		// keys cannot otherwise tell which one to remove.
		DisplayName: cmp.Or(name, aaguidName(cred.Authenticator.AAGUID)),
	}

	err = pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.InsertAuthenticator(ctx, auth); err != nil {
			return pg.Translate(err)
		}
		if err := q.InsertPasskeyDetails(ctx, InsertPasskeyDetailsParams{
			AuthenticatorID: auth.ID,
			CredentialID:    cred.ID,
			PublicKey:       cred.PublicKey,
			SignCount:       int64(cred.Authenticator.SignCount),
			Aaguid:          uuidFrom(cred.Authenticator.AAGUID),
			Transports:      transportStrings(cred.Transport),
			// From the authenticator data flags. BackupEligible means
			// the key CAN sync to a cloud keychain; BackupState means it
			// currently is. A synced key is not hardware-bound, which is
			// what stops it being AAL3 (A01).
			BackupEligible: cred.Flags.BackupEligible,
			BackupState:    cred.Flags.BackupState,
			UvCapable:      cred.Flags.UserVerified,
			AttestationFmt: cred.AttestationType,
		}); err != nil {
			// A duplicate credential id means this key is already
			// enrolled — on this account or, more interestingly, on
			// another one.
			if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrConflict) {
				return domain.ErrPasskeyAlreadyRegistered
			}
			return err
		}
		// ONLY NOW is it usable. Everything up to here was provisional.
		if err := q.ConfirmAuthenticator(ctx, auth.ID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "authenticator.added",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{
				"kind": "passkey", "name": auth.DisplayName,
				"backup_eligible": cred.Flags.BackupEligible,
			}),
		})
	})
	return auth, err
}
Four things that must be server state, and are routinely not

1 · The challenge — if it comes back from the client and is merely compared to itself, the ceremony proves nothing. 2 · The user id it was issued for, or a challenge for one account can be completed against another. 3 · Single-use — Take deletes as it reads, so a replayed finish finds nothing. 4 · A short TTL, two minutes, because a challenge sitting in Redis for an hour is an hour-long replay window. In a multi-replica deployment all four mean Redis rather than process memory, because begin and finish routinely land on different pods.

Authentication, including the “just tap” flow

services/identity/internal/app/passkey_login.go
package app

// BeginPasskeyLogin has two modes, and the difference is a product
// decision as much as a technical one.
//
//   DISCOVERABLE ("usernameless"): we send no credential list. The
//   authenticator shows the user which accounts it holds for this site
//   and they pick one. This is the flow that feels like magic — open the
//   page, tap, you are in — and it requires resident keys.
//
//   NON-DISCOVERABLE: the user types their email first, we look up their
//   credential ids and send them. Works with older security keys that
//   cannot store resident keys, at the cost of an extra step AND of
//   leaking whether that address has an account (A07).
func (s *Service) BeginPasskeyLogin(ctx context.Context, email string) (
	*protocol.CredentialAssertion, string, error) {

	var (
		options *protocol.CredentialAssertion
		session *webauthn.SessionData
		err     error
	)

	if email == "" {
		// Discoverable. No user lookup at all, so this path cannot be
		// used to enumerate accounts — which is a real advantage on top
		// of the better experience.
		options, session, err = s.wa.BeginDiscoverableLogin(
			webauthn.WithUserVerification(protocol.VerificationPreferred))
	} else {
		u, uerr := s.webAuthnUserByEmail(ctx, domain.NormaliseEmail(email))
		if uerr != nil {
			// Return a challenge for a PHANTOM user rather than an
			// error. An attacker learns nothing about whether the
			// address exists; the ceremony simply fails at the end,
			// exactly as a wrong password does (D04).
			options, session, err = s.wa.BeginDiscoverableLogin()
		} else {
			options, session, err = s.wa.BeginLogin(u)
		}
	}
	if err != nil {
		return nil, "", err
	}

	ref := idgen.New().String()
	if err := s.challenges.Put(ctx, "auth:"+ref, session, 2*time.Minute); err != nil {
		return nil, "", err
	}
	return options, ref, nil
}

func (s *Service) FinishPasskeyLogin(ctx context.Context, ref string,
	body io.Reader, dev DeviceInfo) (LoginOutput, error) {

	var session webauthn.SessionData
	ok, err := s.challenges.Take(ctx, "auth:"+ref, &session)
	if err != nil || !ok {
		return LoginOutput{}, domain.ErrChallengeExpired
	}

	parsed, err := protocol.ParseCredentialRequestResponseBody(body)
	if err != nil {
		return LoginOutput{}, domain.ErrPasskeyInvalid
	}

	var (
		userID idgen.ID
		cred   *webauthn.Credential
	)

	if len(session.UserID) == 0 {
		// Discoverable: the USER HANDLE in the response tells us who
		// this is. It must be verified against the credential we stored,
		// not merely trusted — the handler below does exactly that.
		cred, err = s.wa.ValidateDiscoverableLogin(
			func(rawID, userHandle []byte) (webauthn.User, error) {
				u, err := s.webAuthnUserByHandle(ctx, userHandle)
				if err != nil {
					return nil, err
				}
				// The credential must belong to the claimed handle.
				// Skipping this check lets a caller present their own
				// valid passkey with someone else's user handle.
				if !u.HasCredential(rawID) {
					return nil, domain.ErrPasskeyUnknown
				}
				userID = u.QuillID()
				return u, nil
			}, session, parsed)
	} else {
		userID = idgen.ID(session.UserID)
		u, uerr := s.webAuthnUser(ctx, userID)
		if uerr != nil {
			return LoginOutput{}, domain.ErrPasskeyInvalid
		}
		cred, err = s.wa.ValidateLogin(u, session, parsed)
	}
	if err != nil {
		s.recordFailure(ctx, userID, dev, "passkey_invalid")
		return LoginOutput{}, domain.ErrPasskeyInvalid
	}

	// ── clone detection ──────────────────────────────────────────────
	// The authenticator increments a counter on every use. If the value
	// we receive is not greater than the one we stored, either the key
	// has been cloned, or the authenticator does not implement counters
	// at all (many platform authenticators report 0 permanently).
	//
	// Distinguishing the two is the whole subtlety: 0 always means "not
	// supported", and a non-zero value going backwards is a real signal.
	if cred.Authenticator.CloneWarning {
		s.log.WarnContext(ctx, "passkey clone warning",
			"user_id", userID, "credential", base64.RawURLEncoding.EncodeToString(cred.ID))
		passkeyCloneWarnings.Inc()
		// We do NOT block. False positives are common — some
		// authenticators reset counters across firmware updates — and
		// locking people out of a phishing-resistant credential on an
		// ambiguous signal is worse than the risk. Record, notify, and
		// let the user decide.
		if err := s.recordSecurityEvent(ctx, userID, "passkey.clone_warning", nil); err != nil {
			s.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "record clone warning", "err", err)
		}
	}

	methods := []domain.Method{domain.MethodWebAuthn}
	if parsed.Response.AuthenticatorData.Flags.UserVerified() {
		methods = append(methods, domain.MethodUserVerif)
	}

	return s.completeLogin(ctx, userID, methods, cred, dev)
}
Sign-count clone detection is weaker than it sounds

Many platform authenticators — iCloud Keychain and Google Password Manager among them — report a constant zero, because a synced credential has no single counter to increment. So the check applies to a shrinking minority of hardware keys, and even there a firmware update can reset it. Treat a regression as a signal worth recording and notifying on, never as grounds for an automatic block: refusing a legitimate hardware key on an ambiguous counter is a worse outcome than the attack it is guarding against, and the user has no way to diagnose it.

Naming a key so a human recognises it

services/identity/internal/domain/aaguid.go
package domain

// The AAGUID identifies the authenticator MODEL — not the individual
// key, so it reveals nothing about the user. Mapping it to a name is the
// difference between a security page that says
//
//     Passkey · added 14 Jan        Passkey · added 2 Mar
//
// and one that says
//
//     iCloud Keychain · added 14 Jan     YubiKey 5C NFC · added 2 Mar
//
// Only the second lets a user decide which to remove.
//
// The community AAGUID list (passkeydeveloper/passkey-authenticator-aaguids)
// is refreshed by `go generate`; unknown values fall back gracefully
// rather than showing a raw UUID.
//go:generate go run ./internal/gen/aaguid

var aaguidNames = map[string]string{
	"adce0002-35bc-c60a-648b-0b25f1f05503": "Chrome on Mac",
	"08987058-cadc-4b81-b6e1-30de50dcbe96": "Windows Hello",
	"fbfc3007-154e-4ecc-8c0b-6e020557d7bd": "iCloud Keychain",
	"ea9b8d66-4d01-1d21-3ce4-b6b48cb575d4": "Google Password Manager",
	"cb69481e-8ff7-4039-93ec-0a2729a154a8": "YubiKey 5 Series",
	"d8522d9f-575b-4866-88a9-ba99fa02f35b": "YubiKey Bio Series",
	"6028b017-b1d4-4c02-b4b3-afcdafc96bb2": "Windows Hello (software)",
	// … generated
}

func AAGUIDName(id [16]byte, transports []string) string {
	if name, ok := aaguidNames[formatUUID(id)]; ok {
		return name
	}
	// Fall back to something descriptive rather than a UUID. The
	// transports tell us roughly what kind of thing it is.
	switch {
	case slices.Contains(transports, "internal"):
		return "This device"
	case slices.Contains(transports, "nfc"), slices.Contains(transports, "usb"):
		return "Security key"
	case slices.Contains(transports, "hybrid"):
		return "Phone or tablet"
	}
	return "Passkey"
}

The product decisions

DecisionQuill's choiceReasoning
RP IDquill.app, the registrable domainWorks across subdomains. Changing it later invalidates every passkey, with no migration path
User verificationpreferred, recorded per useRequiring it turns away PIN-less hardware keys; recording it lets the assurance level be accurate
Resident keyspreferredEnables the usernameless flow, degrades gracefully on older keys
AttestationnoneVerifying it properly means trust roots and vendor quirks, and buys nothing unless you enforce a hardware policy
Multiple passkeysEncouraged, prompted after the firstOne passkey on one lost phone is a lockout. This is the single most important passkey UX decision
Passkey-only accountsAllowed, with two enrolledThe floor is then the email-recovery path, unless the user disables it (A01)
Conditional UIYesPasskeys offered in the browser's autofill, so signing in needs no button at all
clients/web/src/auth/passkey.ts — the browser half
// Conditional UI: the passkey is offered inside the browser's own
// autofill dropdown on the email field, so a returning user signs in
// without pressing anything. This is the flow that makes passkeys feel
// better than passwords rather than merely safer.
export async function armConditionalUI(signal) {
  // Feature-detect properly. Calling get() with mediation:"conditional"
  // where it is unsupported throws, and the catch would hide a real bug.
  if (!window.PublicKeyCredential?.isConditionalMediationAvailable) return;
  if (!(await PublicKeyCredential.isConditionalMediationAvailable())) return;

  const { options, ref } = await api.post('/v1/auth/passkey/begin', {});

  try {
    const assertion = await navigator.credentials.get({
      publicKey: decodeOptions(options),
      // The request stays pending until the user picks a passkey from
      // autofill. It MUST be abortable, or navigating away leaves a
      // dangling request that blocks the next one.
      mediation: 'conditional',
      signal,
    });
    if (!assertion) return;
    await finishLogin(assertion, ref);
  } catch (err) {
    // AbortError is normal — the user typed a password instead, or
    // navigated. Anything else is worth reporting.
    if (err.name !== 'AbortError') reportError(err);
  }
}

// The explicit "Sign in with a passkey" button, for users who did not
// use autofill and for browsers without conditional mediation.
export async function signInWithPasskey() {
  const { options, ref } = await api.post('/v1/auth/passkey/begin', {});
  const assertion = await navigator.credentials.get({
    publicKey: decodeOptions(options),
  });
  return finishLogin(assertion, ref);
}
Prompt for a second passkey, immediately after the first

A user who enrols one passkey on one phone and loses the phone is locked out of a credential that was supposed to be their strongest. The moment after a successful first enrolment is when they understand what a passkey is and are most willing to add another — on a laptop, on a hardware key, on a second phone. Waiting until later means never. This single prompt does more for real-world passkey outcomes than any amount of cryptographic care in the verification path.

The endpoints

EndpointAuthPurpose
POST/v1/auth/passkey/beginnoneAssertion options; discoverable when no email is supplied
POST/v1/auth/passkey/finishnoneVerify and issue a session
POST/v1/account/passkeys/beginsession + step-upCreation options, with exclusions
POST/v1/account/passkeys/finishsession + step-upVerify and enrol
GET/v1/account/passkeyssessionList, with model name, added date, last used
PATCH/v1/account/passkeys/{id}sessionRename
DELETE/v1/account/passkeys/{id}session + step-upRemove, subject to the last-credential rule (A01)
Enrolling a passkey must be behind step-up

Adding an authenticator is a persistence mechanism: an attacker holding a stolen session does not need the password if they can simply enrol their own passkey and return whenever they like. So POST /account/passkeys/begin requires a recent, strong authentication (A04) — not merely a valid session. The same applies to removing one, to changing the email address, and to raising the device limit. The rule is that anything which changes how the account can be accessed in future requires proving who you are now.

Migration, and what to measure

Rolling passkeys out to an existing password userbase 1 Offer, never force. A prompt after sign-in, dismissible, re-offered at a decreasing rate. Forcing enrolment on a device that cannot do it well produces support tickets, not security. 2 Enrol silently on sign-in where the platform allows it, so the user's next visit is one tap. 3 Once a user has two confirmed passkeys, offer to remove the password. Not before — one passkey plus no password is one lost phone away from recovery-by-email, which is the floor we were trying to raise. 4 Never remove the password automatically. The metrics that tell you it is working passkey_enrolments_total{result} started vs completed — a large gap means the ceremony is failing on some platform passkey_logins_total / logins_total adoption passkey_login_failures{reason} origin mismatch, expired challenge, unknown credential passkeys_per_user histogram how many users have exactly 1 ← the lockout population passkey_clone_warnings_total expect a trickle; a spike is worth investigating
Interview follow-up

“Why are passkeys phishing-resistant when TOTP is not?” Because the signature is bound to the origin by the browser rather than by the user. A phishing site can relay a TOTP code within its 30-second window, and the human has no way to tell it is being relayed. With WebAuthn the browser puts the actual origin into the signed payload, so a signature produced on quiII.app simply does not verify against a relying party ID of quill.app — and the user cannot be socially engineered past it, because they were never the one doing the check. The follow-up worth pre-empting is that this only holds if the server actually verifies origin and RP ID hash, which is exactly why those checks are non-negotiable.

A04

Two-factor authentication and step-up

Two related mechanisms that are usually conflated. Two-factor asks for a second proof at sign-in. Step-up asks for a fresh proof before a dangerous action, hours into an existing session. You need both, and the second is the one that stops a stolen session becoming a stolen account.

TOTP, done properly

services/identity/internal/app/totp.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"crypto/subtle"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"time"

	"github.com/pquerna/otp"
	"github.com/pquerna/otp/totp"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
)

// Enrolment is TWO steps, and the separation is not ceremony: generating
// a secret must not enable 2FA, or a user who mis-scans the QR code is
// locked out of their own account with no way back.
func (s *Service) BeginTOTPEnrolment(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID) (
	secret, uri string, err error) {

	u, err := s.q.GetUser(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return "", "", err
	}

	key, err := totp.Generate(totp.GenerateOpts{
		Issuer:      "Quill",
		AccountName: u.Email, // shown in the authenticator app
		Period:      30,
		Digits:      otp.DigitsSix,
		Algorithm:   otp.AlgorithmSHA1, // SHA1 here is NOT a weakness:
		// it is what every authenticator app implements, and the
		// security of TOTP rests on the shared secret's entropy rather
		// than on the hash. Choosing SHA256 means users' apps silently
		// produce codes that never match.
		SecretSize: 20,
	})
	if err != nil {
		return "", "", err
	}

	enc, err := domain.SealSecret([]byte(key.Secret()), s.masterKey)
	if err != nil {
		return "", "", err
	}

	// confirmed_at stays NULL. Until the user proves they can produce a
	// code, this authenticator does not exist for any purpose: not for
	// login, not for the last-factor rule, not in the list (A01).
	auth := &domain.Authenticator{
		ID: idgen.New(), UserID: userID, Kind: domain.KindTOTP,
		DisplayName: "Authenticator app",
	}
	if err := s.insertUnconfirmedTOTP(ctx, auth, enc); err != nil {
		return "", "", err
	}
	return key.Secret(), key.URL(), nil
}

func (s *Service) ConfirmTOTPEnrolment(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	code string) ([]string, error) {

	auth, secret, err := s.unconfirmedTOTP(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	valid, step, err := s.validateTOTP(secret, code, 0)
	if err != nil || !valid {
		return nil, domain.ErrInvalidCode
	}

	var plain []string
	err = pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.ConfirmAuthenticator(ctx, auth.ID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.SetTOTPLastStep(ctx, auth.ID, step); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Recovery codes are generated WITH the first second factor, not
		// as a separate optional step nobody completes. A user who
		// enables 2FA and loses their phone before generating codes is
		// the most common 2FA support case there is.
		var hashes [][]byte
		plain, hashes = domain.NewRecoveryCodes(10)
		if err := q.ReplaceRecoveryCodes(ctx, userID, hashes); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		return q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "mfa.enabled",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"method": "totp"}),
		})
	})
	// Shown once, never retrievable. Regenerating is the only way to see
	// them again, and regenerating invalidates the old set.
	return plain, err
}

// verifyTOTP is the checking path, and three things here are load-bearing.
func (s *Service) verifyTOTP(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID, code string) error {
	// 1 · RATE LIMIT. Six digits is a million possibilities; without a
	//     limit, a 30-second window is brute-forceable in hours by a
	//     script that simply keeps trying.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "totp:"+userID.String(), 5, time.Minute); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	auth, secret, err := s.confirmedTOTP(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return domain.ErrInvalidCode
	}

	// 2 · A SMALL SKEW. ±1 period tolerates clock drift on the user's
	//     phone. A larger window widens the replay opportunity for a
	//     code read over someone's shoulder or captured by a proxy.
	valid, step, err := s.validateTOTP(secret, code, 1)
	if err != nil || !valid {
		s.recordSecurityEvent(ctx, userID, "mfa.challenge_failed", nil)
		return domain.ErrInvalidCode
	}

	// 3 · SINGLE USE. Without this, a code captured by a phishing proxy
	//     is replayable for the rest of its window — which is precisely
	//     the attack real-time phishing kits perform. Storing the last
	//     accepted step and refusing anything at or below it closes it.
	ok, err := s.q.AdvanceTOTPStep(ctx, AdvanceTOTPStepParams{
		AuthenticatorID: auth.ID, Step: step,
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if !ok {
		// The code was valid but already used. Report it as invalid —
		// telling the caller "already used" confirms they had a real
		// code, which is information only an attacker benefits from.
		return domain.ErrInvalidCode
	}
	return nil
}
services/identity/query.sql — TOTP replay prevention
-- name: AdvanceTOTPStep :one
-- The comparison and the write are ONE statement, so two concurrent
-- submissions of the same code cannot both succeed. A read-then-write
-- in Go would have exactly that race, and it is a race an attacker
-- controls the timing of.
UPDATE totp_details
   SET last_step = @step
 WHERE authenticator_id = @authenticator_id
   AND last_step < @step
RETURNING true AS accepted;
A TOTP code must be single-use, and almost no implementation does it

Real-time phishing kits proxy the login page, capture the code the user types, and replay it to the real site within its thirty-second window. Rate limiting does not stop this — the attacker needs one attempt. Recording the last accepted time step and refusing anything at or below it does, and it costs one UPDATE … WHERE last_step < $1. It is the single highest-value line in a TOTP implementation, and it is the reason a passkey is categorically better: there is no code to capture.

Recovery codes

services/identity/internal/domain/recovery.go
package domain

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"strings"
)

// Recovery codes are printed, photographed and pasted into password
// managers, so the alphabet matters: no 0/O, no 1/l/I, grouped for
// transcription, and case-insensitive on input.
const recoveryAlphabet = "ABCDEFGHJKMNPQRSTUVWXYZ23456789" // 31 chars

// 10 codes × 10 characters ≈ 49 bits each — far beyond brute force,
// and short enough to write down without error.
func NewRecoveryCodes(n int) (plain []string, hashes [][]byte) {
	plain = make([]string, n)
	hashes = make([][]byte, n)
	for i := range plain {
		var b strings.Builder
		for j := 0; j < 10; j++ {
			if j == 5 {
				b.WriteByte('-') // "K7M2P-QR94X" transcribes better
			}
			b.WriteByte(recoveryAlphabet[randIndex(len(recoveryAlphabet))])
		}
		plain[i] = b.String()
		hashes[i] = HashRecoveryCode(plain[i])
	}
	return plain, hashes
}

// SHA-256 rather than Argon2: these are 49 bits of uniform randomness,
// so there is nothing to brute-force and no reason to pay a memory-hard
// cost. That reasoning does NOT transfer to passwords, which are
// low-entropy by nature (D04).
func HashRecoveryCode(code string) []byte {
	// Normalise on input so a user typing lowercase, or omitting the
	// separator, still matches what we stored.
	norm := strings.ToUpper(strings.ReplaceAll(strings.TrimSpace(code), "-", ""))
	sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte("quill-recovery:" + norm))
	return sum[:]
}
services/identity/internal/app/recovery.go
package app

// UseRecoveryCode is the "I lost my phone" path. It must be reliable,
// because the alternative is a support ticket from someone who cannot
// prove who they are — and it must be loud, because it is also what an
// attacker who has stolen a printed code would use.
func (s *Service) UseRecoveryCode(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	code string, dev DeviceInfo) error {

	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "recovery:"+userID.String(), 5, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var remaining int
	err := pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// Single use, enforced atomically: the UPDATE both checks and
		// consumes, so the same code cannot be redeemed twice by two
		// concurrent requests.
		ok, err := q.ConsumeRecoveryCode(ctx, ConsumeRecoveryCodeParams{
			UserID: userID, CodeHash: domain.HashRecoveryCode(code),
			UsedIp: dev.IPPrefix,
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if !ok {
			return domain.ErrInvalidCode
		}

		remaining, err = q.CountUnusedRecoveryCodes(ctx, userID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Always notify. Using a recovery code is either the user
		// recovering, in which case the email is reassuring, or someone
		// else, in which case it is the only warning they will get.
		if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.recovery_code_used",
			map[string]any{
				"user_id": userID, "remaining": remaining,
				"location": dev.Location, "device": dev.Name,
			}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "recovery.code_used",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"remaining": remaining}),
		})
	})
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// Running out silently is a lockout waiting to happen. Nudge at two,
	// and make the UI insistent at zero.
	if remaining <= 2 {
		s.log.InfoContext(ctx, "recovery codes running low",
			"user_id", userID, "remaining", remaining)
	}
	return nil
}

Trusted devices

services/identity/internal/app/trust.go
package app

// "Remember this device for 30 days" is the setting that makes 2FA
// tolerable — a user prompted for a code on every sign-in from their own
// laptop will turn 2FA off, and a disabled second factor protects
// nothing.
//
// Three properties make it safe:
//   · the trust lives on the DEVICE (A02), not the session, so signing
//     out does not lose it and removing the device does
//   · it is bounded in time, and the bound is short enough that a
//     stolen laptop stops being trusted
//   · it is ignored for step-up: trusting a device means "I have seen
//     this device before", NOT "this person is verified right now"
func (s *Service) shouldChallengeMFA(ctx context.Context, userID, deviceID idgen.ID,
	risk RiskSignals) (bool, string) {

	// Risk overrides trust. A trusted device signing in from a country
	// it has never been in is exactly when you want the prompt (A09).
	if risk.NewCountry || risk.ImpossibleTravel || risk.KnownBadASN {
		return true, "unusual_activity"
	}

	trusted, err := s.q.IsDeviceTrusted(ctx, IsDeviceTrustedParams{
		UserID: userID, DeviceID: deviceID,
	})
	if err != nil || !trusted {
		return true, "untrusted_device"
	}
	return false, ""
}

// Trust is granted only AFTER a successful second factor, and only if
// the user asked for it. Granting it automatically turns the first
// sign-in from any device into a permanent bypass.
func (s *Service) trustDevice(ctx context.Context, q Querier,
	userID, deviceID idgen.ID, remember bool) error {
	if !remember {
		return nil
	}
	return q.TrustDevice(ctx, TrustDeviceParams{
		UserID: userID, DeviceID: deviceID,
		TrustedUntil: time.Now().Add(30 * 24 * time.Hour),
	})
}
Anything that changes the account's security must clear every device trust

Changing the password, adding or removing an authenticator, disabling 2FA, changing the email address — each of these is either the user reasserting control or an attacker establishing it, and in both cases the old “remember this device” grants are no longer meaningful. Clear them all, alongside revoking sessions. The cost is that the user re-enters a code once on each of their devices; the benefit is that an attacker who obtained trust on their own machine loses it the moment the user starts cleaning up.

Step-up: the mechanism that matters most

A session is eight hours old. The user — or someone holding their laptop, or their stolen session cookie — clicks "remove passkey". A plain permission check passes: they are authenticated, they are the account holder, the endpoint is theirs. And the account is gone. Step-up asks a different question: not "who are you" but "have you proved it recently enough, and strongly enough, for THIS?" ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ action needs AAL needs fresh window │ ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │ read / edit notes 1 no — │ │ publish a note publicly 1 yes 15m │ │ invite a collaborator 1 yes 15m │ │ change password 2 yes 5m │ │ add or remove an authenticator 2 yes 5m │ │ change email address 2 yes 5m │ │ disable two-factor 2 yes 5m │ │ raise the device limit 2 yes 5m │ │ sign out everywhere 2 yes 5m │ │ delete the account 2 yes 5m │ └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Freshness is measured from authenticated_at, not from when the session was created and not from the access token's iat — the token is reissued every ten minutes by refresh, and using its age would mean every session is permanently "fresh". The rule of thumb: anything that changes how the account can be accessed in future requires proving who you are now.
platform/authn/stepup.go
package authn

import (
	"net/http"
	"time"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/httpx"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/problem"
)

type Requirement struct {
	MinAAL   domain.AAL
	MaxAge   time.Duration // how recently the user must have authenticated
	Reason   string        // shown to the user: "to remove a passkey"
}

// RequireStepUp is middleware, so the requirement sits next to the route
// and cannot be forgotten inside a handler. A requirement expressed in
// the router is reviewable; one buried in a function body is not.
func RequireStepUp(req Requirement) func(http.Handler) http.Handler {
	return func(next http.Handler) http.Handler {
		return http.HandlerFunc(func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
			ctx := r.Context()
			sub := httpx.MustSubject(ctx)

			age := time.Since(sub.AuthenticatedAt)

			switch {
			case sub.AAL < req.MinAAL:
				// The user needs a STRONGER proof, not merely a fresher
				// one. The response tells the client which methods are
				// available, so it can render the right prompt rather
				// than guessing.
				writeChallenge(ctx, w, "step_up_required", req, sub, age)
				return
			case age > req.MaxAge:
				writeChallenge(ctx, w, "reauthentication_required", req, sub, age)
				return
			}
			next.ServeHTTP(w, r)
		})
	}
}

// The challenge response is a 401 with a MACHINE-READABLE body. A bare
// 401 would make the client sign the user out, which is exactly the
// wrong reaction — the session is fine, it simply is not fresh enough.
func writeChallenge(ctx context.Context, w http.ResponseWriter, code string,
	req Requirement, sub httpx.Subject, age time.Duration) {

	p := problem.New(http.StatusUnauthorized, code,
		"Confirm it is you", "please confirm your identity "+req.Reason)
	p.Extra = map[string]any{
		"required_aal":  req.MinAAL,
		"current_aal":   sub.AAL,
		"max_age_sec":   int(req.MaxAge.Seconds()),
		"authenticated_seconds_ago": int(age.Seconds()),
		// Offer the STRONGEST method the user has enrolled first: a
		// passkey prompt is one tap, while a password prompt is a
		// typing exercise and a phishing opportunity.
		"methods": sub.AvailableStepUpMethods,
	}
	problem.Write(ctx, w, p)
}
services/identity/internal/transport/http/routes.go — requirements at the route
package http

func (h *Handler) Routes() http.Handler {
	mux := http.NewServeMux()

	// Two named requirements, used everywhere. Inlining the numbers at
	// each route is how they drift apart.
	sensitive := authn.Requirement{
		MinAAL: domain.AAL2, MaxAge: 5 * time.Minute,
	}
	moderate := authn.Requirement{
		MinAAL: domain.AAL1, MaxAge: 15 * time.Minute,
	}

	stepUp := func(req authn.Requirement, reason string, h http.Handler) http.Handler {
		req.Reason = reason
		return authn.RequireStepUp(req)(h)
	}

	// ── anything that changes how the account can be accessed ────────
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/account/passkeys/begin",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to add a passkey", http.HandlerFunc(h.beginPasskeyReg)))
	mux.Handle("DELETE /v1/account/passkeys/{id}",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to remove a passkey", http.HandlerFunc(h.deletePasskey)))
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/account/totp/begin",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to set up an authenticator app", http.HandlerFunc(h.beginTOTP)))
	mux.Handle("DELETE /v1/account/totp",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to turn off two-factor authentication", http.HandlerFunc(h.deleteTOTP)))
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/account/password",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to change your password", http.HandlerFunc(h.changePassword)))
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/account/email/change",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to change your email address", http.HandlerFunc(h.changeEmail)))
	mux.Handle("PATCH /v1/account/security/limits",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to change your device limit", http.HandlerFunc(h.setLimits)))
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/account/sessions/revoke-all",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to sign out everywhere", http.HandlerFunc(h.revokeAll)))
	mux.Handle("DELETE /v1/account",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to delete your account", http.HandlerFunc(h.deleteAccount)))
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/account/oauth/{provider}/unlink",
		stepUp(sensitive, "to unlink an account", http.HandlerFunc(h.unlinkOAuth)))

	// ── outward-facing, but not account-structural ───────────────────
	mux.Handle("POST /v1/notes/{id}/publish",
		stepUp(moderate, "to publish a note publicly", h.proxyNotes()))

	// ── the step-up ceremony itself ──────────────────────────────────
	mux.HandleFunc("POST /v1/account/reauth/begin", h.beginReauth)
	mux.HandleFunc("POST /v1/account/reauth/finish", h.finishReauth)

	return mux
}
services/identity/internal/app/reauth.go
package app

// Re-authentication upgrades the EXISTING session in place: it does not
// issue a new one, and it does not create a device. The user stays where
// they were; only authenticated_at, aal and amr move.
func (s *Service) Reauthenticate(ctx context.Context, sessionID idgen.ID,
	userID idgen.ID, proof Proof) error {

	// Rate limit per session. Without it, a stolen session becomes an
	// offline-speed password oracle against the account.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "reauth:"+sessionID.String(), 8, 10*time.Minute); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	var methods []domain.Method
	var pk *domain.PasskeyProperties

	switch proof.Kind {
	case "passkey":
		cred, uid, err := s.verifyPasskeyAssertion(ctx, proof.Ref, proof.Body)
		if err != nil || uid != userID {
			// The passkey must belong to THIS user. Verifying the
			// assertion without binding it to the session's subject
			// would let anyone with a valid passkey step up any session.
			return domain.ErrInvalidCredentials
		}
		methods = append(methods, domain.MethodWebAuthn)
		if cred.UserVerified {
			methods = append(methods, domain.MethodUserVerif)
		}
		pk = cred.Properties()

	case "password":
		if err := s.verifyPassword(ctx, userID, proof.Password); err != nil {
			s.recordSecurityEvent(ctx, userID, "mfa.challenge_failed", nil)
			return domain.ErrInvalidCredentials
		}
		methods = append(methods, domain.MethodPassword)
		// A password alone is AAL1. If the requirement is AAL2 the
		// caller will be challenged again for a second factor — which is
		// correct, and is why the response tells the client what is
		// still missing rather than simply failing.
		if proof.TOTPCode != "" {
			if err := s.verifyTOTP(ctx, userID, proof.TOTPCode); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			methods = append(methods, domain.MethodOTP)
		}

	case "totp":
		if err := s.verifyTOTP(ctx, userID, proof.TOTPCode); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		methods = append(methods, domain.MethodOTP)

	default:
		return domain.ErrUnsupportedProof
	}

	aal := domain.Classify(methods, pk)

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.UpgradeSession(ctx, UpgradeSessionParams{
			SessionID: sessionID, UserID: userID,
			Aal: int16(aal), Amr: methodStrings(methods),
			AuthenticatedAt: time.Now(),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "session.reauthenticated", SessionID: sessionID,
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"aal": aal, "amr": methods}),
		})
	})
}
The access token must be reissued after a step-up, or nothing changes

The gateway reads acr, amr and auth_time from the access token, so upgrading the session row alone has no effect until a new token is minted — and the client is holding one that is valid for up to ten more minutes. The re-auth response must therefore return a fresh access token carrying the upgraded claims, and the client must use it for the retried request. Forgetting this produces the most confusing possible bug: the user completes a passkey prompt, the server records the upgrade, and the action still fails.

Disabling two-factor

services/identity/internal/app/mfa_disable.go
package app

// Turning 2FA off is the single most attractive action for an attacker
// holding a session, so it is the most protected. Note what is required:
// step-up (from the route), AND a current second-factor proof, AND the
// last-factor rules, AND a notification that cannot be suppressed.
func (s *Service) DisableTOTP(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	currentCode string) error {

	// Proving the factor you are removing still works is deliberate: it
	// means an attacker who has the session but not the phone cannot
	// remove the phone.
	if err := s.verifyTOTP(ctx, userID, currentCode); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	set, err := s.loadAuthenticators(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		if err := set.CanRemove(set.TOTP); err != nil {
			return err // last-factor rule (A01)
		}
		if err := q.RevokeAuthenticator(ctx, RevokeAuthenticatorParams{
			ID: set.TOTP.ID, UserID: userID, Reason: "user_removed",
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Every "remember this device" grant is now meaningless.
		if err := q.ClearAllDeviceTrust(ctx, userID); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "mfa.disabled",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"method": "totp"}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Unconditional. A user who did not do this needs to know
		// immediately, and it is the one notification that must not be
		// switchable off in settings — because an attacker would switch
		// it off first.
		_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.mfa_disabled",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID})
		return err
	})
}

Enforcing 2FA, and the endpoints

EndpointRequiresNotes
POST/v1/account/totp/beginstep-upReturns the secret and otpauth:// URL; 2FA stays off
POST/v1/account/totp/confirmstep-upEnables it, returns ten recovery codes, once
DELETE/v1/account/totpstep-up + a current codeClears all device trust; notifies unconditionally
POST/v1/account/recovery-codesstep-upRegenerate; invalidates the previous set
POST/v1/auth/mfa/verifythe MFA token from loginSecond step of sign-in; accepts TOTP, passkey or recovery code
POST/v1/account/reauth/beginsessionStarts a step-up; returns available methods
POST/v1/account/reauth/finishsessionUpgrades the session, returns a fresh access token
PATCH/v1/account/security/mfa-requiredstep-upRefuses unless ≥1 second factor is confirmed
Offer the strongest enrolled method first, and let the user pick

A step-up prompt that always demands a password is bad on three counts: it is the slowest to complete, it is the most phishable thing the user owns, and it trains people to type their password into any dialog that looks official. Sort the offered methods by strength — passkey, then TOTP, then password — and let a passkey-only account step up without ever having a password at all. The response from writeChallenge carries that list precisely so the client does not have to guess.

Interview follow-up

“An attacker steals a valid session cookie. What can they do, and what stops them?” They can read and edit, because that is what the session authorises — and step-up is what stops it becoming permanent. Anything that changes how the account can be accessed in future (adding a passkey, changing the password or email, disabling 2FA, raising the device limit) requires a fresh, strong proof within minutes, so the attacker cannot establish their own access. Then name the two details that make it real: freshness is measured from authenticated_at rather than the token's iat, which is reissued on every refresh; and the step-up must mint a new access token, or the gateway keeps reading the old claims and the upgrade silently does nothing.

A05

Social sign-in: Google, GitHub and Apple

One OAuth flow and three sets of provider-specific problems. Google is textbook OIDC, GitHub is OAuth 2.0 with no identity layer at all, and Apple sends a POST to your callback, gives you the user's name exactly once, and makes you mint a JWT as your client secret. This chapter builds the shared client and then the three adapters.

The flow, and the two parameters that carry all the security

Authorization Code with PKCE — the only flow to use for anything new. Implicit is deprecated; the password grant is dead. browser ──▶ GET /v1/auth/oauth/google/start server generates: state 32 random bytes, stored server-side nonce 32 random bytes, goes in the id_token code_verifier 64 random bytes code_challenge = base64url(sha256(code_verifier)) 302 to the provider user ──▶ provider: authenticate, consent browser ◀── 302 back with ?code=…&state=… server ──▶ POST to the token endpoint code + code_verifier + client credentials server ◀── access_token, id_token, (refresh_token) verify: signature against the provider's JWKS · iss · aud · exp · nonce state is the CSRF defence. Without it, an attacker can complete their own authorization and redirect the victim's browser to your callback with the attacker's code — silently linking the victim's Quill account to the attacker's Google account. It must be server-side, single-use and bound to the browser. nonce is the replay defence for the id_token. It ties the token to THIS authorization request, so a token captured elsewhere cannot be presented here. PKCE binds the code to the client that started the flow. Originally for mobile apps that cannot keep a secret; now recommended for confidential clients too, because it also defends against a code leaked through a referrer or a log.
The redirect URI must be an exact-match allowlist

Prefix matching is the classic open-redirect-to-account-takeover bug: if https://quill.app/callback is registered as a prefix, then https://quill.app/callback.attacker.com or https://quill.app/callback/../../evil may match depending on the provider's comparison, and the authorization code is delivered to the attacker. Register the full URI, compare it byte for byte, and never build it from a request header — Host and X-Forwarded-Host are attacker-controlled, and constructing the redirect from them is how this becomes exploitable even with exact matching.

The shared client

services/identity/internal/oauth/client.go
// Package oauth is one client and three thin adapters. The differences
// between providers are real but small, and pulling them into a
// Provider interface keeps them from leaking into the login flow.
package oauth

import (
	"context"
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/base64"
	"errors"
	"fmt"
	"net/url"
	"time"

	"golang.org/x/oauth2"
)

// Identity is what every provider must ultimately produce. Everything
// downstream — linking, account creation, the security log — works
// against this and never against a provider-specific shape (A06).
type Identity struct {
	Provider      string
	Subject       string // the provider's STABLE user id, never the email
	Email         string
	EmailVerified bool
	Name          string
	AvatarURL     string
	Raw           map[string]any
}

type Provider interface {
	Name() string
	Config() *oauth2.Config
	// Identify turns a token response into an Identity. This is where
	// each provider's peculiarities live.
	Identify(ctx context.Context, tok *oauth2.Token, nonce string) (*Identity, error)
	// ExtraAuthParams are appended to the authorization URL.
	ExtraAuthParams() []oauth2.AuthCodeOption
}

// flowState is everything we must remember between the start and the
// callback. It lives in Redis with a short TTL — NOT in a cookie the
// client could tamper with, and NOT in process memory, because the two
// requests routinely land on different pods.
type flowState struct {
	Provider     string    `json:"p"`
	Nonce        string    `json:"n"`
	CodeVerifier string    `json:"v"`
	RedirectTo   string    `json:"r"`  // where to send the user afterwards
	LinkUserID   string    `json:"u"`  // non-empty = linking, not signing in
	CreatedAt    time.Time `json:"t"`
}

func (s *Service) Start(ctx context.Context, provider, redirectTo, linkUserID string) (string, error) {
	p, ok := s.providers[provider]
	if !ok {
		return "", fmt.Errorf("unknown provider %q", provider)
	}

	state := randomToken()
	verifier := oauth2.GenerateVerifier()
	nonce := randomToken()

	// The returned URL must be validated against an allowlist of OUR
	// paths. Echoing back an arbitrary `redirect_to` turns the callback
	// into an open redirect, which is a phishing primitive even when it
	// does not leak the code.
	if !isSafeRedirect(redirectTo) {
		redirectTo = "/"
	}

	if err := s.flows.Put(ctx, "oauth:"+state, flowState{
		Provider: provider, Nonce: nonce, CodeVerifier: verifier,
		RedirectTo: redirectTo, LinkUserID: linkUserID, CreatedAt: time.Now(),
	}, 10*time.Minute); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	opts := append([]oauth2.AuthCodeOption{
		oauth2.S256ChallengeOption(verifier),
		oidc.Nonce(nonce),
	}, p.ExtraAuthParams()...)

	return p.Config().AuthCodeURL(state, opts...), nil
}

var (
	ErrStateInvalid = errors.New("the sign-in link has expired — please try again")
	ErrProviderDenied = errors.New("sign-in was cancelled")
)

func (s *Service) Callback(ctx context.Context, provider string,
	q url.Values) (*Identity, *flowState, error) {

	// The provider may report an error instead of a code. `access_denied`
	// is the user pressing cancel and must not be logged as a failure.
	if e := q.Get("error"); e != "" {
		if e == "access_denied" {
			return nil, nil, ErrProviderDenied
		}
		return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("provider error: %s: %s", e, q.Get("error_description"))
	}

	// Take() deletes as it reads: state is single-use, so a replayed
	// callback finds nothing.
	var st flowState
	ok, err := s.flows.Take(ctx, "oauth:"+q.Get("state"), &st)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, err
	}
	if !ok || st.Provider != provider {
		// Mismatched provider means the state was minted for a different
		// flow — either a bug or an attempt to cross the wires.
		return nil, nil, ErrStateInvalid
	}

	p := s.providers[provider]

	// Exchange with a hard timeout. A hanging token endpoint must not
	// hold the user's browser — or a goroutine — indefinitely (B11).
	ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 10*time.Second)
	defer cancel()

	tok, err := p.Config().Exchange(ctx, q.Get("code"),
		oauth2.VerifierOption(st.CodeVerifier))
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, fmt.Errorf("token exchange: %w", err)
	}

	id, err := p.Identify(ctx, tok, st.Nonce)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, nil, err
	}
	return id, &st, nil
}

Google — textbook OIDC

services/identity/internal/oauth/google.go
package oauth

import (
	"context"
	"errors"

	"github.com/coreos/go-oidc/v3/oidc"
	"golang.org/x/oauth2"
)

type Google struct {
	cfg      *oauth2.Config
	verifier *oidc.IDTokenVerifier
}

func NewGoogle(ctx context.Context, clientID string, secret config.Secret,
	redirect string) (*Google, error) {

	// Discovery fetches the JWKS URL and endpoints. The provider caches
	// keys internally and refetches on an unknown kid, so this is one
	// call at startup rather than one per sign-in.
	p, err := oidc.NewProvider(ctx, "https://accounts.google.com")
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return &Google{
		cfg: &oauth2.Config{
			ClientID: clientID, ClientSecret: secret.Reveal(),
			RedirectURL: redirect, Endpoint: p.Endpoint(),
			Scopes: []string{oidc.ScopeOpenID, "email", "profile"},
		},
		verifier: p.Verifier(&oidc.Config{ClientID: clientID}),
	}, nil
}

func (g *Google) Identify(ctx context.Context, tok *oauth2.Token, nonce string) (*Identity, error) {
	raw, ok := tok.Extra("id_token").(string)
	if !ok {
		return nil, errors.New("google: no id_token in response")
	}

	// Verifies signature against the JWKS, plus iss, aud and exp.
	idt, err := g.verifier.Verify(ctx, raw)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("google: verify id_token: %w", err)
	}
	// The nonce check is SEPARATE and must not be skipped: it is what
	// binds this token to the authorization request we started.
	if idt.Nonce != nonce {
		return nil, errors.New("google: nonce mismatch")
	}

	var c struct {
		Sub           string `json:"sub"`
		Email         string `json:"email"`
		EmailVerified bool   `json:"email_verified"`
		Name          string `json:"name"`
		Picture       string `json:"picture"`
		HD            string `json:"hd"` // the Workspace domain, if any
	}
	if err := idt.Claims(&c); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// `sub` is the stable identifier. The EMAIL is not: a Workspace
	// admin can rename a user, and a consumer account can change its
	// address. Keying on email is how two people end up sharing an
	// account after a rename (A06).
	return &Identity{
		Provider: "google", Subject: c.Sub,
		Email: c.Email, EmailVerified: c.EmailVerified,
		Name: c.Name, AvatarURL: c.Picture,
		Raw: map[string]any{"hd": c.HD},
	}, nil
}

func (g *Google) ExtraAuthParams() []oauth2.AuthCodeOption {
	return []oauth2.AuthCodeOption{
		// Without prompt=select_account, a user with two Google accounts
		// is silently signed in as whichever one the browser prefers —
		// and cannot switch. It is the most common complaint about
		// Google sign-in and it is one parameter.
		oauth2.SetAuthURLParam("prompt", "select_account"),
	}
}

GitHub — OAuth without an identity layer

services/identity/internal/oauth/github.go
package oauth

// GitHub is OAuth 2.0 and NOT OpenID Connect: there is no id_token, no
// nonce, and no signed identity assertion at all. Identity comes from
// calling the API with the access token, which means:
//
//   · no signature to verify — the transport IS the security
//   · the nonce parameter is meaningless here
//   · two API calls, because the primary email is not in /user
type GitHub struct{ cfg *oauth2.Config }

func (g *GitHub) Identify(ctx context.Context, tok *oauth2.Token, _ string) (*Identity, error) {
	client := g.cfg.Client(ctx, tok)

	var u struct {
		ID        int64  `json:"id"`
		Login     string `json:"login"`
		Name      string `json:"name"`
		Email     string `json:"email"`     // only if PUBLIC; usually empty
		AvatarURL string `json:"avatar_url"`
	}
	if err := getJSON(ctx, client, "https://api.github.com/user", &u); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	// The /user endpoint returns the public email, which most users do
	// not set. The real address needs a second call, and the `user:email`
	// scope.
	email, verified, err := g.primaryEmail(ctx, client)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return &Identity{
		Provider: "github",
		// The numeric id, not the login. Usernames on GitHub are
		// RENAMEABLE and the old one becomes available for anyone else
		// to claim — keying on it is a direct account-takeover path.
		Subject:       strconv.FormatInt(u.ID, 10),
		Email:         email,
		EmailVerified: verified,
		Name:          cmp.Or(u.Name, u.Login),
		AvatarURL:     u.AvatarURL,
		Raw:           map[string]any{"login": u.Login},
	}, nil
}

func (g *GitHub) primaryEmail(ctx context.Context, c *http.Client) (string, bool, error) {
	var emails []struct {
		Email    string `json:"email"`
		Primary  bool   `json:"primary"`
		Verified bool   `json:"verified"`
	}
	if err := getJSON(ctx, c, "https://api.github.com/user/emails", &emails); err != nil {
		// The scope may have been declined. Continue without an email
		// rather than failing the sign-in — the account can be linked
		// by other means (A06).
		return "", false, nil
	}
	for _, e := range emails {
		if e.Primary {
			// GitHub's `verified` flag is authoritative and must be
			// carried through: an UNVERIFIED address must never be used
			// to match an existing Quill account.
			return e.Email, e.Verified, nil
		}
	}
	return "", false, nil
}

func (g *GitHub) ExtraAuthParams() []oauth2.AuthCodeOption {
	return []oauth2.AuthCodeOption{
		// GitHub reuses an existing authorization silently, so a user
		// who wants to switch accounts cannot. This forces the picker.
		oauth2.SetAuthURLParam("prompt", "consent"),
	}
}
Never key an identity on a username or an email

GitHub logins can be changed, and the vacated name becomes claimable by anyone — so an account keyed on login can be taken over by someone who registers the old username. Google addresses change on a Workspace rename. Apple's relay addresses change if the user unlinks and relinks. The only stable identifier is the provider's opaque subject: GitHub's numeric id, Google's sub, Apple's sub. Store that, index on (provider, subject), and treat the email as a mutable attribute that happens to travel alongside it.

Apple — four things nobody expects

services/identity/internal/oauth/apple.go
package oauth

import (
	"context"
	"crypto/ecdsa"
	"time"

	"github.com/golang-jwt/jwt/v5"
)

// Apple differs in four ways, and each one breaks an assumption that
// holds for every other provider.
//
//  1 · the CLIENT SECRET is a JWT you sign yourself with a .p8 key from
//      Apple, valid at most six months — so it must be REGENERATED, and
//      a hardcoded one silently stops working half a year after launch
//  2 · the callback is a form POST, not a GET, when you request the
//      name or email scope — which breaks SameSite=Strict cookies
//  3 · the user's NAME is sent exactly ONCE, in the first callback, and
//      never again. Miss it and it is gone forever
//  4 · the email may be a private relay address that forwards to the
//      real one and changes if the user unlinks
type Apple struct {
	cfg      *oauth2.Config
	verifier *oidc.IDTokenVerifier
	teamID   string
	keyID    string
	key      *ecdsa.PrivateKey
}

// clientSecret mints a fresh JWT on demand. Caching it for an hour is
// ample and avoids signing on every request; regenerating is cheap.
func (a *Apple) clientSecret() (string, error) {
	now := time.Now()
	t := jwt.NewWithClaims(jwt.SigningMethodES256, jwt.MapClaims{
		"iss": a.teamID,
		"iat": now.Unix(),
		// Apple permits up to six months. One hour means a leaked
		// secret is worthless almost immediately.
		"exp": now.Add(time.Hour).Unix(),
		"aud": "https://appleid.apple.com",
		"sub": a.cfg.ClientID, // the Services ID, not the App ID
	})
	t.Header["kid"] = a.keyID
	return t.SignedString(a.key)
}

func (a *Apple) Identify(ctx context.Context, tok *oauth2.Token, nonce string) (*Identity, error) {
	raw, _ := tok.Extra("id_token").(string)
	idt, err := a.verifier.Verify(ctx, raw)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, fmt.Errorf("apple: verify id_token: %w", err)
	}
	if idt.Nonce != nonce {
		return nil, errors.New("apple: nonce mismatch")
	}

	var c struct {
		Sub            string `json:"sub"`
		Email          string `json:"email"`
		EmailVerified  any    `json:"email_verified"`   // string OR bool
		IsPrivateEmail any    `json:"is_private_email"` // string OR bool
	}
	if err := idt.Claims(&c); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}

	return &Identity{
		Provider: "apple", Subject: c.Sub,
		Email: c.Email,
		// Apple sends booleans as the STRINGS "true"/"false" in some
		// responses and as real booleans in others. Decoding into a bool
		// therefore fails intermittently, which is a delightful bug to
		// receive in production.
		EmailVerified: parseLooseBool(c.EmailVerified),
		Raw: map[string]any{
			"is_private_email": parseLooseBool(c.IsPrivateEmail),
		},
	}, nil
}
services/identity/internal/transport/http/oauth.go
package http

// Apple POSTs to the callback when the name/email scope is requested,
// which means the browser treats it as a cross-site POST — and a
// SameSite=Strict or Lax cookie is NOT sent. Any state kept in a cookie
// is simply absent, which is why flowState lives in Redis keyed by the
// `state` parameter instead.
func (h *Handler) oauthCallback(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	ctx := r.Context()
	provider := r.PathValue("provider")

	var params url.Values
	switch r.Method {
	case http.MethodPost:
		// Apple, and any provider configured with response_mode=form_post.
		if err := r.ParseForm(); err != nil {
			h.redirectWithError(w, r, "invalid_request")
			return
		}
		params = r.PostForm
	default:
		params = r.URL.Query()
	}

	// Apple's ONE-TIME name. It arrives as a JSON blob in the form body
	// on the very first authorization and never again — so it must be
	// captured here, before anything else can fail, and stashed with the
	// flow. Forgetting it means every Apple user is called "User".
	var firstName string
	if u := params.Get("user"); u != "" {
		var payload struct {
			Name struct{ FirstName, LastName string } `json:"name"`
		}
		if json.Unmarshal([]byte(u), &payload) == nil {
			firstName = strings.TrimSpace(
				payload.Name.FirstName + " " + payload.Name.LastName)
		}
	}

	identity, flow, err := h.oauth.Callback(ctx, provider, params)
	if err != nil {
		switch {
		case errors.Is(err, oauth.ErrProviderDenied):
			// The user pressed cancel. Not an error worth logging.
			h.redirect(w, r, flow.SafeRedirect(), "")
		case errors.Is(err, oauth.ErrStateInvalid):
			h.redirectWithError(w, r, "session_expired")
		default:
			h.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "oauth callback", "provider", provider, "err", err)
			h.redirectWithError(w, r, "sign_in_failed")
		}
		return
	}
	if firstName != "" && identity.Name == "" {
		identity.Name = firstName
	}

	// Everything from here is the LINKING decision, which is where the
	// real security lives — see A06.
	result, err := h.app.CompleteOAuth(ctx, app.OAuthInput{
		Identity: identity, LinkUserID: flow.LinkUserID,
		Device: deviceFrom(r),
	})
	if err != nil {
		h.writeOAuthError(w, r, flow, err)
		return
	}

	setRefreshCookie(w, result.Tokens.RefreshToken, refreshTTL, h.prod)
	h.redirect(w, r, flow.SafeRedirect(), result.Notice)
}
Apple's client secret expires, and it will be someone else's problem

It is a JWT you sign, valid for at most six months, and the failure mode is that Apple sign-in stops working entirely on a random Tuesday with a generic invalid_client — long after whoever generated it has moved on. Generate it on demand from the .p8 key with a one-hour expiry, as above, rather than pasting a long-lived one into a secret store. The same instinct applies generally: anything that expires should be minted by code that runs, not by a human who will not be there.

Storing what you get back

services/identity/internal/app/oauth_store.go
package app

// Store the minimum. For pure sign-in we need the subject and the email
// and nothing else — and NOT storing an access token is strictly better
// than storing one well.
func (s *Service) upsertOAuthAuthenticator(ctx context.Context, q Querier,
	userID idgen.ID, id *oauth.Identity, tok *oauth2.Token) (*domain.Authenticator, error) {

	auth := &domain.Authenticator{
		ID: idgen.New(), UserID: userID, Kind: domain.KindOAuth,
		// "Google (masud@example.com)" rather than "Google": a user with
		// two Google accounts linked needs to tell them apart.
		DisplayName: providerLabel(id),
	}
	if err := q.InsertAuthenticator(ctx, auth); err != nil {
		return nil, pg.Translate(err)
	}

	params := InsertOAuthDetailsParams{
		AuthenticatorID: auth.ID,
		Provider:        id.Provider,
		Subject:         id.Subject,
		ProviderEmail:   nullIfEmpty(id.Email),
		EmailVerified:   id.EmailVerified,
	}

	// Only keep tokens if we will actually call the provider's API
	// later. Quill does not, so this branch is off — but the encryption
	// is here because the day someone adds "import from GitHub Gists",
	// a plaintext token column is what they will otherwise find.
	if s.storeProviderTokens && tok != nil {
		enc, err := domain.SealSecret([]byte(tok.AccessToken), s.masterKey)
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		params.AccessTokenEnc = enc
		params.TokenExpiresAt = nullTime(tok.Expiry)
		if tok.RefreshToken != "" {
			renc, err := domain.SealSecret([]byte(tok.RefreshToken), s.masterKey)
			if err != nil {
				return nil, err
			}
			params.RefreshTokenEnc = renc
		}
	}

	if err := q.InsertOAuthDetails(ctx, params); err != nil {
		// The unique index on (provider, subject) means this provider
		// account is already linked — to this user or another one (A06).
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrConflict) {
			return nil, domain.ErrProviderAlreadyLinked
		}
		return nil, err
	}
	if err := q.ConfirmAuthenticator(ctx, auth.ID); err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	return auth, nil
}
Ask for the narrowest scopes, and ask later for more

Requesting repo from GitHub or Drive access from Google at sign-in produces a consent screen that frightens people and a token that is a liability if you are breached. For authentication you need openid email profile from Google, user:email from GitHub, and name email from Apple — nothing more. If a feature later needs broader access, run a second authorization for that specific scope at the moment the user asks for the feature, which is both better security and a markedly better consent conversation.

Interview follow-up

“What does the state parameter actually protect against?” Login CSRF, and the consequence is worse than it sounds. Without it an attacker starts their own authorization at the provider, captures the resulting code, and then causes the victim's browser to hit your callback with it — so the victim's session is now signed in as, or linked to, the attacker's identity. If the victim then stores something in that account, the attacker can read it. State must therefore be random, server-side, single-use and bound to the flow that created it; putting it in a cookie fails for Apple specifically, because the form-post callback is cross-site and a SameSite cookie is not sent.

A06

Account linking and identity resolution

Someone signs in with Google using an address that already has a Quill password account. Do you link them? That one question has produced account-takeover vulnerabilities in a remarkable number of products, and the answer is more subtle than “match on email”.

The takeover, step by step

The naive rule: "if the provider's email matches an existing account, sign them into it." 1 victim has a Quill account: masud@example.com, password 2 attacker creates an account at a provider that does not verify email ownership — a self-hosted OIDC server, a small social app, or a provider whose verified flag you ignore — and sets the address to masud@example.com 3 attacker clicks "Sign in with that provider" on Quill 4 Quill matches on email and signs them into the victim's account 5 attacker now reads every note, adds their own passkey, and removes the victim's password Nothing was compromised. No password was stolen, no token leaked. The vulnerability is entirely in step 4 — trusting an email address asserted by a third party as proof of ownership. The fix is one condition and one confirmation: · link automatically ONLY if the provider says the address is verified AND we independently know it is the same person · otherwise, require the user to prove control of the EXISTING account before attaching anything to it
An email_verified flag from a provider is a claim, not a proof

Google and Apple verify addresses and their flag is meaningful. GitHub verifies per-address and exposes it. But a provider you add later may set the flag unconditionally, may let a user edit their profile email without re-verification, or may simply not have the concept — and your linking logic will silently treat all of them as equivalent. So the flag gates automatic linking only, the set of providers permitted to link automatically is an explicit allowlist rather than “anything with the flag set”, and every other path requires the user to prove the existing account.

The resolution state machine

A provider identity arrives. Six outcomes, and exactly one applies. 1 (provider, subject) already linked to account X → sign in as X. Nothing else matters: this is the same provider account we saw before. Refresh the stored email if it changed. 2 linking flow (the user was signed in and clicked "link") → attach to their account, if that provider identity is not already attached elsewhere. 3 no email from the provider → create a NEW account. We have nothing to match on, and guessing is the vulnerability above. 4 email matches an account, provider says VERIFIED, provider is on the auto-link allowlist → link and sign in. Notify the account owner that a new sign-in method was added. 5 email matches an account, but NOT verified → do not link, do not sign in. Send the user to a page that says an account exists and offers to sign in the normal way, after which the link can be completed from settings. 6 no match at all → create a new account, email pre-verified if the provider verified it. ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ The dangerous transition is 4 vs 5, and the difference is │ │ entirely whether a third party's boolean is trustworthy. │ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
services/identity/internal/app/oauth_complete.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"slices"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/idgen"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/oauth"
)

// Providers permitted to link automatically on a verified email. An
// explicit allowlist, not a property check: adding a provider must be a
// deliberate decision recorded in code review, because getting it wrong
// is the takeover above.
var autoLinkProviders = []string{"google", "apple"}
// GitHub is deliberately absent: its verified flag is per-address and
// correct, but a user can add and verify any address they control to a
// GitHub account — which is fine for identity and NOT sufficient to
// grant access to a pre-existing Quill account.

type OAuthInput struct {
	Identity   *oauth.Identity
	LinkUserID idgen.ID // non-empty: an explicit link from settings
	Device     DeviceInfo
}

type OAuthResult struct {
	Tokens  TokenPair
	Created bool
	Linked  bool
	Notice  string // shown after the redirect
}

func (s *Service) CompleteOAuth(ctx context.Context, in OAuthInput) (OAuthResult, error) {
	id := in.Identity
	email := domain.NormaliseEmail(id.Email)

	// ── 1 · already linked ───────────────────────────────────────────
	existing, err := s.q.FindOAuthAuthenticator(ctx, FindOAuthParams{
		Provider: id.Provider, Subject: id.Subject,
	})
	switch {
	case err == nil:
		// Same provider account as before. Refresh the cached email —
		// a Workspace rename or an Apple relay change must not orphan
		// the link — and sign in.
		if err := s.refreshOAuthEmail(ctx, existing.AuthenticatorID, email, id.EmailVerified); err != nil {
			s.log.WarnContext(ctx, "refresh oauth email", "err", err)
		}
		if in.LinkUserID != "" && in.LinkUserID != existing.UserID {
			// They are signed in as A and tried to link a provider
			// account already attached to B. Refusing is the only safe
			// answer; merging accounts is not something to do silently.
			return OAuthResult{}, domain.ErrProviderLinkedElsewhere
		}
		tokens, err := s.completeOAuthLogin(ctx, existing.UserID, id, in.Device)
		return OAuthResult{Tokens: tokens}, err

	case !errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound):
		return OAuthResult{}, err
	}

	// ── 2 · explicit link from settings ──────────────────────────────
	// The user is already authenticated and asked for this, so the
	// email does not need to match anything. This is the path users
	// should be steered to whenever automatic linking is refused.
	if in.LinkUserID != "" {
		if err := s.linkProvider(ctx, in.LinkUserID, id); err != nil {
			return OAuthResult{}, err
		}
		return OAuthResult{Linked: true,
			Notice: providerLabel(id) + " has been added to your account"}, nil
	}

	// ── 3 · nothing to match on ──────────────────────────────────────
	if email == "" {
		return s.createAccountFromProvider(ctx, id, in.Device)
	}

	user, err := s.q.FindActiveUserByEmail(ctx, email)
	if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
		// ── 6 · no match: a new account ──────────────────────────────
		return s.createAccountFromProvider(ctx, id, in.Device)
	}
	if err != nil {
		return OAuthResult{}, err
	}

	// ── 4 · auto-link, but only under both conditions ────────────────
	if id.EmailVerified && slices.Contains(autoLinkProviders, id.Provider) {
		if err := s.linkProvider(ctx, user.ID, id); err != nil {
			return OAuthResult{}, err
		}
		tokens, err := s.completeOAuthLogin(ctx, user.ID, id, in.Device)
		if err != nil {
			return OAuthResult{}, err
		}
		// Tell the owner. If this was not them, this email is the only
		// warning they get that a new way into their account exists.
		s.notify(ctx, user.ID, "identity.oauth_linked", map[string]any{
			"provider": id.Provider, "auto": true,
		})
		return OAuthResult{Tokens: tokens, Linked: true}, nil
	}

	// ── 5 · an account exists, and we cannot prove this is its owner ──
	// Refuse. The message is careful: it must help a legitimate user
	// without confirming to a stranger that this address has an account
	// — so it says the same thing either way and pushes to normal
	// sign-in, where the usual enumeration defences apply (D04).
	return OAuthResult{}, domain.ErrLinkRequiresVerification
}
Outcome 5 is where the product pressure is, and where you must not give in

It is a genuinely worse experience: the user clicked “Continue with GitHub” and got told to sign in another way. Every product manager will ask you to just link it. The compromise that is actually safe is to make the recovery path excellent rather than to weaken the check — remember the pending provider identity for ten minutes, let the user sign in with their password or passkey, and complete the link automatically the moment they do, with a single confirmation. They experience one extra step instead of a dead end, and nobody has been trusted who should not have been.

Completing the link after a normal sign-in

services/identity/internal/app/pending_link.go
package app

// When automatic linking is refused, we stash the provider identity
// against a short-lived token and hand it to the client. After the user
// proves the existing account, the link completes with one tap.
type PendingLink struct {
	Identity  *oauth.Identity `json:"identity"`
	Email     string          `json:"email"`
	CreatedAt time.Time       `json:"created_at"`
}

func (s *Service) StashPendingLink(ctx context.Context, id *oauth.Identity) (string, error) {
	ref := randomToken()
	// Ten minutes. Long enough to sign in, short enough that a stashed
	// identity is not a standing credential.
	return ref, s.flows.Put(ctx, "pendinglink:"+ref, PendingLink{
		Identity: id, Email: domain.NormaliseEmail(id.Email), CreatedAt: time.Now(),
	}, 10*time.Minute)
}

// ConsumePendingLink runs AFTER a successful normal sign-in. By this
// point the user has proved the account, so the link is safe.
func (s *Service) ConsumePendingLink(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	userEmail, ref string) error {

	var pl PendingLink
	ok, err := s.flows.Take(ctx, "pendinglink:"+ref, &pl)
	if err != nil || !ok {
		return domain.ErrLinkExpired
	}

	// The address the provider asserted must still match the account
	// that just authenticated. Without this check, a stashed identity
	// could be attached to whichever account happens to sign in next —
	// including an attacker's, who would then be able to sign in as the
	// victim at that provider.
	if !strings.EqualFold(pl.Email, userEmail) {
		return domain.ErrLinkMismatch
	}
	return s.linkProvider(ctx, userID, pl.Identity)
}

func (s *Service) linkProvider(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	id *oauth.Identity) error {

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// One provider account links to at most ONE Quill account,
		// enforced by the unique index on (provider, subject). Allowing
		// two would mean signing in with Google is ambiguous.
		if _, err := s.upsertOAuthAuthenticator(ctx, q, userID, id, nil); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Linking a provider whose email is verified and matches also
		// verifies the Quill address, if it was not already — reaching
		// that inbox proves control of it.
		u, err := q.GetUser(ctx, userID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if id.EmailVerified && strings.EqualFold(domain.NormaliseEmail(id.Email), u.Email) {
			if err := q.MarkEmailVerified(ctx, userID); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "oauth.linked",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{
				"provider": id.Provider, "email": id.Email,
			}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.oauth_linked",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID, "provider": id.Provider})
		return err
	})
}

Unlinking

services/identity/internal/app/unlink.go
package app

// Unlinking is where the last-credential rule earns its keep (A01). A
// user who signed up with Google, never set a password, and then
// unlinks Google has just deleted their only way in — and will contact
// support from an address they can no longer prove they own.
func (s *Service) UnlinkProvider(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	provider string) error {

	set, err := s.loadAuthenticators(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	target := set.OAuthFor(provider)
	if target == nil {
		return domain.ErrNotLinked
	}

	// The generic rule handles it: is this the last thing that can
	// START a sign-in?
	if err := set.CanRemove(target); err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		if err := q.RevokeAuthenticator(ctx, RevokeAuthenticatorParams{
			ID: target.ID, UserID: userID, Reason: "user_unlinked",
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Sessions created BY this provider are no longer backed by a
		// credential the user has. Revoking them is the consistent
		// choice: unlinking should mean "that route into my account is
		// closed", including routes already taken.
		revoked, err := q.RevokeSessionsByAuthenticator(ctx, target.ID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		s.denylist.Add(ctx, revoked, accessTTL) // immediate (A02)

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "oauth.unlinked",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{
				"provider": provider, "sessions_revoked": len(revoked),
			}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.oauth_unlinked",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID, "provider": provider})
		return err
	})
}
The sign-up path that creates a locked-out account

A user signs up with Google, so no password is ever set. Months later they unlink Google — perhaps they are leaving that ecosystem — and now nothing can start a sign-in. Their email may not even be verified if the provider did not assert it. The CanRemove check refuses this, but the product fix is better: after a provider-created sign-up, prompt once to add a passkey, and make the unlink button in settings explain what is missing rather than merely refusing. “Add a passkey first” is a solvable instruction; “Cannot unlink” is a support ticket.

What the account page must show

services/identity/internal/app/authenticator_list.go
package app

type AuthenticatorView struct {
	ID          idgen.ID   `json:"id"`
	Kind        string     `json:"kind"`
	Name        string     `json:"name"`
	AddedAt     time.Time  `json:"added_at"`
	LastUsedAt  *time.Time `json:"last_used_at"`
	// Whether the UI should enable the remove button, and if not, WHY.
	// Returning both means the client never has to reimplement the
	// last-credential rule — and never gets it subtly different.
	Removable   bool   `json:"removable"`
	RemoveBlockedReason string `json:"remove_blocked_reason,omitempty"`
	// Provider-specific extras, e.g. the linked address.
	Detail map[string]any `json:"detail,omitempty"`
}

type SecurityOverview struct {
	Authenticators []AuthenticatorView `json:"authenticators"`
	// The summary line the page leads with.
	SignInMethods  int    `json:"sign_in_methods"`
	MFAEnabled     bool   `json:"mfa_enabled"`
	MFARequired    bool   `json:"mfa_required"`
	RecoveryCodesRemaining int `json:"recovery_codes_remaining"`
	ActiveSessions int      `json:"active_sessions"`
	Devices        int      `json:"devices"`
	MaxSessions    int      `json:"max_sessions"`
	SessionPolicy  string   `json:"session_policy"`
	// Concrete, ordered suggestions rather than a security "score".
	// A score tells a user they are at 60%; this tells them what to do.
	Recommendations []Recommendation `json:"recommendations"`
}

type Recommendation struct {
	Code   string `json:"code"`
	Title  string `json:"title"`
	Action string `json:"action"` // the endpoint or route to send them to
	Severity string `json:"severity"` // critical | warning | suggestion
}

func (s *Service) SecurityOverview(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID) (*SecurityOverview, error) {
	set, err := s.loadAuthenticators(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return nil, err
	}
	// … assemble the views …

	var recs []Recommendation
	switch {
	case set.PrimaryCount() == 1 && len(set.Passkeys) == 1:
		recs = append(recs, Recommendation{
			Code: "add_second_passkey", Severity: "critical",
			Title:  "Add a second passkey",
			Action: "/account/security/passkeys/new",
		})
	case set.PrimaryCount() == 1 && set.Password != nil:
		recs = append(recs, Recommendation{
			Code: "add_passkey", Severity: "warning",
			Title:  "Add a passkey so you can sign in without a password",
			Action: "/account/security/passkeys/new",
		})
	}
	if !set.HasSecondFactor() && set.Password != nil {
		recs = append(recs, Recommendation{
			Code: "enable_mfa", Severity: "warning",
			Title: "Turn on two-factor authentication", Action: "/account/security/2fa",
		})
	}
	if set.HasSecondFactor() && s.recoveryRemaining(ctx, userID) <= 2 {
		recs = append(recs, Recommendation{
			Code: "regenerate_recovery", Severity: "warning",
			Title: "You are running low on recovery codes", Action: "/account/security/recovery",
		})
	}
	// … etc
	return overview, nil
}
