Recommendations, not a security score

A percentage tells a user they are at 60% and gives them nothing to do about it; worse, it implies the remaining 40% is optional decoration. An ordered list of concrete actions — “add a second passkey”, “you have two recovery codes left” — is actionable, and the severity ordering does the work a score was supposed to do. Compute it server-side so every client shows the same advice, and derive the removability flags from the same Set the enforcement uses, so the button state and the API can never disagree.

The endpoints

EndpointRequiresPurpose
GET/v1/auth/oauth/{provider}/startnoneBegin sign-in; state, nonce and PKCE stored server-side
GETPOST/v1/auth/oauth/{provider}/callbacknoneBoth methods — Apple POSTs (A05)
POST/v1/auth/oauth/pending-linka fresh sessionCompletes a link refused by outcome 5, after normal sign-in
GET/v1/account/oauth/{provider}/startsession + step-upLink from settings
POST/v1/account/oauth/{provider}/unlinksession + step-upSubject to the last-credential rule; revokes its sessions
GET/v1/account/securitysessionThe whole overview: authenticators, devices, recommendations

Merging two accounts

Quill does not merge accounts, and that is a deliberate choice

Users do end up with two — one from a password sign-up and one from a provider sign-up with a different address — and merging looks like the obvious kindness. It is also a one-way, irreversible operation that has to reconcile two sets of notebooks, two sets of memberships in other people's notebooks, two billing states and two sets of sync cursors, while proving the person controls both. Getting any part wrong destroys data that cannot be recovered. Quill instead offers to transfer notebooks between accounts using the existing invitation machinery (D09), which is reversible, auditable, and built already. If you do build a merge, make it support-operated with a confirmation from both addresses, a full export taken first, and a reversal window.

Interview follow-up

“A user signs in with Google using an email that already has a password account. What do you do?” The answer that matters is the one you refuse to do: never link on an email match alone, because a provider that does not verify ownership turns that into account takeover — the attacker registers your address there and walks in. Link automatically only when the provider verifies the address and is on an explicit allowlist you maintain; otherwise ask the user to sign in the existing way first and complete the link from a short-lived pending token. Then add the detail that shows you have shipped this: key the link on the provider's stable subject, never the email or username, because both change and a vacated GitHub username is claimable by anyone.

A07

Email codes and magic links

Passwordless sign-in by email is the easiest thing in this part to implement and the easiest to implement badly. This chapter builds the code flow, explains why a six-digit code beats a magic link in almost every case, and covers the four attacks that a naive version is open to.

Code or link?

Six-digit codeMagic link
Cross-deviceWorks — read on the phone, type on the laptopOpens on the wrong device, which is the top complaint
Email scannersUnaffectedConsumed before the user sees it — corporate link-rewriting and preview fetchers follow every URL
Brute forceOne million values — needs strict rate limiting256 bits; not feasible
PhishingRelayable in real time, like TOTPRelayable; the link is a bearer credential
Leak surfaceBody text onlyURL: browser history, Referer, proxy logs, shared screens
Session fixationBound to the requesting browser naturallyNeeds explicit binding, or an attacker's link signs in the victim
Clicks to sign inCopy, pasteOne click — genuinely nicer when it works
Email security scanners will consume your magic links

Microsoft Defender's Safe Links, Proofpoint, Mimecast and most corporate gateways fetch every URL in an inbound message to check it — with a GET, before the human ever opens the email. A single-use magic link is therefore already spent by the time it is clicked, and the user sees “this link has expired” on their first attempt, every time, on their work email. Mitigations exist (require a POST to complete, put the link behind an interstitial), but they cost the one-click simplicity that was the entire point. Quill defaults to a code and offers a link alongside it.

The code flow

services/identity/migrations/000007_email_codes.up.sql
SET search_path TO identity;

CREATE TABLE email_codes (
    id           text        PRIMARY KEY,
    -- Not a user_id: a code may be requested for an address with no
    -- account, and the request must look identical either way (D04).
    email        citext      NOT NULL,
    code_hash    bytea       NOT NULL,

    purpose      text        NOT NULL
                 CHECK (purpose IN ('sign_in','verify_email','step_up')),

    -- Binds the code to the browser that asked for it. Without this,
    -- an attacker who can read the victim's inbox — or who simply
    -- guesses a code — can complete a sign-in the victim started.
    request_id   text        NOT NULL,

    attempts     integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
    max_attempts integer     NOT NULL DEFAULT 5,

    expires_at   timestamptz NOT NULL,
    consumed_at  timestamptz,
    created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
    ip_prefix    inet
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX email_codes_hash_key ON email_codes (code_hash)
    WHERE consumed_at IS NULL;
-- At most one live code per (address, purpose): requesting a new one
-- supersedes the old, so an email from ten minutes ago stops working.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX email_codes_live_key
    ON email_codes (email, purpose) WHERE consumed_at IS NULL;
CREATE INDEX email_codes_expiry_idx ON email_codes (expires_at)
    WHERE consumed_at IS NULL;
services/identity/internal/domain/emailcode.go
package domain

import (
	"crypto/rand"
	"crypto/sha256"
	"encoding/binary"
	"fmt"
	"math/big"
)

// Six digits is a million possibilities. That is only safe because the
// code is short-lived, attempt-limited and single-use — the three
// properties together, not any one of them.
//
// Eight digits would be safer and measurably worse to type on a phone;
// the right lever is the attempt limit, not the length.
const (
	CodeDigits     = 6
	CodeTTL        = 10 * time.Minute
	CodeMaxAttempts = 5
)

// NewEmailCode uses crypto/rand with rejection sampling. The obvious
// `rand.Int63() % 1000000` is biased toward low values, and while the
// bias is tiny it is exactly the sort of thing that is embarrassing to
// explain and free to avoid.
func NewEmailCode() (plain string, hash []byte) {
	n, err := rand.Int(rand.Reader, big.NewInt(1_000_000))
	if err != nil {
		panic("crypto/rand failed: " + err.Error())
	}
	plain = fmt.Sprintf("%06d", n.Int64())
	return plain, HashEmailCode(plain)
}

// Hashed with the PURPOSE mixed in, so a code issued for email
// verification cannot be presented to the sign-in endpoint. Domain
// separation costs one string concatenation and closes a whole class of
// cross-protocol confusion.
func HashEmailCode(code string) []byte {
	sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte("quill-email-code:" + code))
	return sum[:]
}
services/identity/internal/app/email_code.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"crypto/subtle"
	"errors"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
)

type RequestCodeInput struct {
	Email     string
	Purpose   string
	RequestID string // generated by the client, returned in the response
	Device    DeviceInfo
}

// RequestCode ALWAYS reports success. The response, the status code and
// the timing are identical whether or not the address has an account —
// otherwise this endpoint is a user-enumeration oracle with a friendly
// interface (D04).
func (s *Service) RequestCode(ctx context.Context, in RequestCodeInput) error {
	email := domain.NormaliseEmail(in.Email)

	// Three limits, each closing a different hole:
	//
	//   per ADDRESS   stops using Quill as a mail bomb against one person
	//   per NETWORK   stops enumerating many addresses from one source
	//   global        a circuit breaker on our own sending reputation
	//
	// All three are checked BEFORE the lookup, so which addresses get
	// limited cannot itself be used to enumerate.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "code:email:"+email, 5, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return nil // still report success
	}
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "code:ip:"+in.Device.IPPrefix.String(), 30, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return nil
	}
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "code:global", 10_000, time.Hour); err != nil {
		s.log.ErrorContext(ctx, "global email-code limit reached — possible abuse")
		return nil
	}

	user, err := s.q.FindActiveUserByEmail(ctx, email)
	if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
		// No account. Send NOTHING — sending a "you do not have an
		// account" email would turn the endpoint into an oracle
		// operated through someone else's inbox. Burn a comparable
		// amount of time and return success.
		domain.BurnHashTime()
		return nil
	}
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	plain, hash := domain.NewEmailCode()

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// Supersede any live code for this address and purpose, so a
		// previous email stops working the moment a new one is sent.
		if err := q.ConsumeLiveEmailCodes(ctx, ConsumeLiveEmailCodesParams{
			Email: email, Purpose: in.Purpose,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.InsertEmailCode(ctx, InsertEmailCodeParams{
			ID: idgen.New(), Email: email, CodeHash: hash,
			Purpose: in.Purpose, RequestID: in.RequestID,
			MaxAttempts: domain.CodeMaxAttempts,
			ExpiresAt:   time.Now().Add(domain.CodeTTL),
			IpPrefix:    in.Device.IPPrefix,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// The email is an EVENT in the same transaction (B12): if the
		// commit fails no mail is sent, and if it succeeds the mail is
		// guaranteed to go out even if the mailer is down.
		_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.sign_in_code",
			map[string]any{
				"user_id": user.ID, "email": email, "code": plain,
				// Context in the email lets a user spot a request they
				// did not make: "requested from Berlin, Chrome on macOS".
				"location": in.Device.Location, "device": in.Device.Name,
				"expires_in_minutes": int(domain.CodeTTL.Minutes()),
			})
		return err
	})
}

var ErrCodeInvalid = errors.New("that code is not valid")

func (s *Service) VerifyCode(ctx context.Context, email, code, requestID string,
	purpose string, dev DeviceInfo) (idgen.ID, error) {

	email = domain.NormaliseEmail(email)

	// A per-address verification limit on top of the per-code attempt
	// counter: without it, an attacker can request a fresh code every
	// time they exhaust the five attempts on the last one, and get
	// unlimited guesses across a sequence of codes.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "verify:"+email, 10, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return "", err
	}

	var userID idgen.ID

	err := pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// Look up by ADDRESS and lock, not by code hash. Fetching by
		// hash would mean a wrong code finds no row and therefore never
		// increments the attempt counter — so the limit would never
		// engage and the code is brute-forceable.
		row, err := q.FindLiveEmailCodeForUpdate(ctx, FindLiveEmailCodeParams{
			Email: email, Purpose: purpose,
		})
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return ErrCodeInvalid
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if row.Attempts >= row.MaxAttempts {
			// Burn it. An attacker who exhausts the attempts must not be
			// able to keep the row alive and keep guessing.
			_ = q.ConsumeEmailCode(ctx, row.ID)
			return ErrCodeInvalid
		}
		if time.Now().After(row.ExpiresAt) {
			return ErrCodeInvalid
		}

		// Bind to the browser that requested it. Without this check, a
		// code read from the victim's inbox — or a request the attacker
		// initiated — can be completed in the attacker's browser.
		if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare([]byte(row.RequestID), []byte(requestID)) != 1 {
			_ = q.IncrementEmailCodeAttempts(ctx, row.ID)
			return ErrCodeInvalid
		}

		// Constant-time comparison of the hashes. Comparing the codes as
		// strings with == leaks how many leading digits matched, which
		// over enough samples reduces a million to a few thousand.
		if subtle.ConstantTimeCompare(row.CodeHash, domain.HashEmailCode(code)) != 1 {
			if err := q.IncrementEmailCodeAttempts(ctx, row.ID); err != nil {
				return err
			}
			return ErrCodeInvalid
		}

		// Single use, atomically: the UPDATE both checks and consumes, so
		// two concurrent submissions cannot both succeed.
		ok, err := q.ConsumeEmailCodeChecked(ctx, row.ID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if !ok {
			return ErrCodeInvalid
		}

		userID = row.UserID

		// Receiving the code proves control of the inbox, so it also
		// verifies the address if it was not already.
		if err := q.MarkEmailVerified(ctx, userID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		return q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "sign_in.email_code",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"purpose": purpose}),
		})
	})
	return userID, err
}
Look the code up by address, not by hash

It is tempting to index on the code hash and fetch directly — it is one query and it looks cleaner. But then a wrong code matches no row, so nothing increments the attempt counter, so the per-code limit never fires and a million guesses are available at whatever rate your rate limiter permits. Fetching the live code for that address and comparing in constant time means every wrong guess costs an attempt. Combine it with a per-address verification limit so requesting a fresh code does not reset the budget, or the attacker simply loops: request, five guesses, request again.

If you offer a magic link as well

services/identity/internal/transport/http/magiclink.go
package http

// A magic link is a bearer credential in a URL, so it needs three
// protections a code does not.
func (h *Handler) magicLink(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
	ctx := r.Context()
	token := r.URL.Query().Get("t")

	// 1 · NEVER complete a sign-in on GET. Email scanners issue GET
	//     requests to every URL before the human sees the message, so a
	//     GET that consumes the token means the link is already spent.
	//     The GET renders an interstitial with a form; the POST from
	//     that form completes it.
	if r.Method == http.MethodGet {
		if !h.magicLinkLooksValid(ctx, token) {
			h.renderExpired(w, r)
			return
		}
		// The page also carries a CSRF token, so the POST cannot be
		// forged by a third-party site.
		h.renderConfirm(w, r, token, h.csrfFor(r))
		return
	}

	// 2 · Bind to the browser. The link carries a request id that must
	//     match a cookie set when the link was requested. If it does
	//     not, the user opened it on a different device — which is
	//     legitimate and common, so we do not refuse: we require the
	//     code instead, which works cross-device by design.
	if !h.requestIDMatches(r, token) {
		h.renderUseCodeInstead(w, r)
		return
	}

	userID, err := h.app.VerifyMagicLink(ctx, token, deviceFrom(r))
	if err != nil {
		h.renderExpired(w, r)
		return
	}

	// 3 · Redirect immediately after consuming, so the token leaves the
	//     address bar. Otherwise it sits in browser history, is sent in
	//     the Referer of any outbound click, and is visible on a shared
	//     screen — long after it was used.
	tokens, err := h.app.IssueSession(ctx, userID, deviceFrom(r))
	if err != nil {
		h.renderError(w, r)
		return
	}
	setRefreshCookie(w, tokens.RefreshToken, refreshTTL, h.prod)
	http.Redirect(w, r, "/app", http.StatusSeeOther)
}

Passwordless as the primary method

A Quill account can have no password at all. Sign-in is then: passkey ← the good path: phishing-resistant, one tap provider ← as strong as that account is email code ← the floor What the floor means, stated honestly: if email codes are enabled, the account's security is the email account's security. That is true of any product with email-based recovery, including ones with strong passwords and 2FA — the difference is that passwordless makes it visible rather than hiding it behind a reset flow. So the product has to say it, and offer a way out: · a user with two confirmed passkeys may turn email sign-in and email recovery off entirely (A01) · doing so is irreversible without support, and the confirmation dialog says exactly that · until then, treat email as a single factor and never present it as "two-factor authentication" when paired with a password (A01) Assurance: an email code alone is AAL1. It does not combine with a password to make AAL2, because the password can be reset through the same inbox — the two are not independent.
Put context in the email, not just the code

“Your code is 481902” tells a user nothing about whether they should be suspicious. “Your code is 481902 — requested from Berlin, Germany on Chrome (macOS) at 14:02” lets them notice a request they did not make, which is the only defence against a code phished over the phone by someone who has their address. Add a plain line saying Quill will never ask for the code over chat or phone, and the “please read me this code” scam stops working on most people. This costs four lines in a template and is the highest-value thing in the whole flow.

The endpoints

EndpointResponseNotes
POST/v1/auth/email/codeAlways 202Returns a request_id the client must echo back. Never reveals whether the address exists
POST/v1/auth/email/verifysession, or 400Attempt-limited per code and per address
GET/v1/auth/magican interstitialNever consumes the token — scanners hit this
POST/v1/auth/magicsessionConsumes it; CSRF-protected; redirects immediately
POST/v1/account/email/code202Re-send a verification code for the signed-in user

What to watch

SignalMeans
email_codes_requested_total spikingEnumeration, or someone using you as a mail bomb. Check the per-IP distribution
Verify failure rate > 20%Codes arriving late, being superseded by re-requests, or a brute-force attempt
request_id mismatches risingUsers opening links on a second device — or an attempt to complete someone else's flow
Bounce or complaint rate > 2%Domain reputation at risk; the global limit exists for this
Median delivery latency > 30 sThe code expires before it arrives, and every user sees a failure
Delivery latency is a security setting, not an infrastructure detail

A ten-minute code TTL assumes the mail arrives in seconds. When your provider queues for four minutes — which happens during a reputation incident, a provider outage, or a greylisting spike — users receive codes that expire almost immediately, and the flood of retries makes it worse. Monitor median and p99 time from enqueue to delivery, alert on it, and have a documented lever: raise the TTL, fall back to a secondary provider, or disable the flow and tell people to use a passkey. Deciding that during an incident is much worse than deciding it now.

Interview follow-up

“Is a six-digit email code secure enough?” Only because of three properties together, and removing any one breaks it: a short TTL, a hard per-code attempt limit, and single use. Then the detail that catches most implementations — the attempt limit has to be enforced on a lookup by address, because indexing by code hash means a wrong guess matches no row and never increments the counter. And there must be a second limit on verification attempts per address, or an attacker just requests a fresh code every time they burn five guesses. Finish by naming what it is not: an email code is a single factor, and pairing it with a password that can be reset through the same inbox does not make two.

A08

The password lifecycle

Four flows — forgot, reset, change, and remove — plus the policy questions that surround them. D04 built the hashing; this chapter builds everything that happens to a password after it exists, and the revocation each change has to trigger.

Forgot: the request

services/identity/internal/app/password_forgot.go
package app

import (
	"context"
	"errors"
	"time"

	"github.com/jackc/pgx/v5"

	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/outbox"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/platform/pg"
	"github.com/quillhq/quill/services/identity/internal/domain"
)

// RequestPasswordReset ALWAYS reports success, and the four observables
// a caller can measure — status code, body, headers and LATENCY — are
// identical whether or not the address exists.
func (s *Service) RequestPasswordReset(ctx context.Context, rawEmail string,
	dev DeviceInfo) error {

	email := domain.NormaliseEmail(rawEmail)

	// Limit BEFORE the lookup. Limiting after means an attacker can
	// infer existence from which addresses start returning 429, which
	// defeats the whole exercise.
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "reset:email:"+email, 3, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return nil
	}
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "reset:ip:"+dev.IPPrefix.String(), 20, time.Hour); err != nil {
		return nil
	}

	user, err := s.q.FindActiveUserByEmail(ctx, email)
	if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
		domain.BurnHashTime() // equalise the timing (D04)
		return nil
	}
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	set, err := s.loadAuthenticators(ctx, user.ID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// An account with no password cannot "reset" one — but the reply
	// must still be identical, so instead of an error we send a
	// DIFFERENT email explaining how they actually sign in. The user
	// gets something useful; an attacker learns nothing.
	template := "identity.password_reset"
	if set.Password == nil {
		template = "identity.no_password_set"
	}

	plain, hash := domain.NewActionToken()

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// The partial unique index means inserting supersedes: a second
		// request invalidates the first link, so an email harvested
		// last week stops working the moment the user asks again (D03).
		if err := q.InsertActionToken(ctx, InsertActionTokenParams{
			ID: idgen.New(), UserID: user.ID, Purpose: "reset_password",
			TokenHash: hash,
			// 30 minutes. A reset link sitting in an inbox is a standing
			// credential, and half an hour is ample for a real user.
			ExpiresAt: time.Now().Add(30 * time.Minute),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: user.ID, Kind: "password.reset_requested",
			IpPrefix: dev.IPPrefix,
			Detail:   jsonb(map[string]any{"location": dev.Location}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, template, map[string]any{
			"user_id": user.ID, "email": email, "token": plain,
			// Context so the user can spot a request they did not make.
			"location": dev.Location, "device": dev.Name,
			"expires_in_minutes": 30,
			// What second factors they will still need afterwards, so
			// the email sets expectations honestly.
			"mfa_enabled": set.HasSecondFactor(),
		})
		return err
	})
}
Send an email even when there is nothing to reset

The naive alternatives both leak: returning an error reveals that no account exists, and sending nothing reveals it through the absence of mail. Sending a different message — “you asked to reset a password, but you sign in with Google; here is how” — keeps the observable behaviour identical and is genuinely helpful to the confused user who is the overwhelmingly likely cause. The same trick applies at registration (D04): an address that is already taken gets a “someone tried to sign up with your address” email rather than an error.

Reset: the redemption

services/identity/internal/app/password_reset.go
package app

// ResetPassword is the most consequential endpoint in the service: it
// grants access to an account without any prior session. Six things
// have to be right.
func (s *Service) ResetPassword(ctx context.Context, in ResetInput) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// 1 · Single use, atomically. The UPDATE checks purpose, expiry
		//     and consumption in one statement, so two concurrent
		//     redemptions cannot both win.
		row, err := q.ConsumeActionToken(ctx, ConsumeActionTokenParams{
			TokenHash: domain.HashToken(in.Token), Purpose: "reset_password",
		})
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return domain.ErrTokenInvalid
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		set, err := s.loadAuthenticatorsTx(ctx, q, row.UserID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// 2 · A RESET MUST NOT BYPASS 2FA. This is the single most
		//     commonly missed control in the whole flow: if possession
		//     of the inbox is sufficient to reset the password AND sign
		//     in, then the second factor protects nothing — an attacker
		//     with inbox access simply resets their way past it.
		if set.HasSecondFactor() && !in.SecondFactorVerified {
			return domain.ErrSecondFactorRequired
		}

		user, err := q.GetUser(ctx, row.UserID)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// 3 · The same policy as registration: length, breach corpus,
		//     not similar to the address (D04).
		if probs := domain.CheckPassword(in.NewPassword, user.Email, s.breaches); len(probs) > 0 {
			return domain.PasswordRejected(probs)
		}

		// 4 · Refuse reuse of a recent password. Bounded history, and
		//     the comparison is against hashes, so we never store or
		//     compare plaintext.
		if set.Password != nil {
			reused, err := domain.MatchesPrevious(in.NewPassword, set.Password.PreviousHashes)
			if err != nil {
				return err
			}
			if reused {
				return domain.ErrPasswordReused
			}
		}

		hash, err := domain.HashPassword(in.NewPassword, domain.DefaultParams())
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.UpsertPassword(ctx, UpsertPasswordParams{
			UserID: row.UserID, Hash: hash, KeepPrevious: 5,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// 5 · REVOKE EVERYTHING. If the reset happened because the
		//     account was compromised, leaving the attacker's sessions
		//     alive defeats the entire exercise. This includes device
		//     trust (A04): a "remembered" device is no longer meaningful.
		revoked, err := q.RevokeAllSessions(ctx, RevokeAllSessionsParams{
			UserID: row.UserID, Reason: "password_reset",
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.ClearAllDeviceTrust(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// Also invalidate any OTHER live action token — a second reset
		// link, an email-change confirmation — since we cannot tell
		// which were requested by the attacker.
		if err := q.ConsumeAllActionTokens(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		s.denylist.Add(ctx, revoked, accessTTL) // immediate (A02)

		// 6 · Reaching the inbox proves control of it.
		if err := q.MarkEmailVerified(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: row.UserID, Kind: "password.reset",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"sessions_revoked": len(revoked)}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// Unconditional notification — and it goes to the address on
		// file, which is why the email-change flow (A09) is careful.
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.password_changed",
			map[string]any{"user_id": row.UserID, "email": user.Email})
		return err
	})
}
A password reset must not be a 2FA bypass

This is the control that is missed most often, and it quietly negates every second factor on the account. If an attacker with inbox access can request a reset, set a new password, and be signed in, then the TOTP app and the hardware key are decorative — the attacker never encounters them. The reset flow must therefore still require the second factor before completing, and offer recovery codes as the alternative for a user who has genuinely lost their phone. The only account that should be recoverable by email alone is one that never had a second factor.

Change, while signed in

services/identity/internal/app/password_change.go
package app

// ChangePassword sits behind step-up (A04), so the caller has already
// proved who they are recently. It STILL asks for the current password.
func (s *Service) ChangePassword(ctx context.Context, in ChangeInput) error {
	set, err := s.loadAuthenticators(ctx, in.UserID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	// Asking for the current password on top of step-up is not
	// redundant belt-and-braces: step-up may have been satisfied by a
	// passkey, and someone with physical access to an unlocked laptop
	// can complete a biometric prompt. Knowing the old password is a
	// different proof, and it is cheap to require.
	if set.Password != nil {
		ok, _, err := domain.VerifyPassword(in.CurrentPassword, set.Password.Hash)
		if err != nil || !ok {
			s.recordSecurityEvent(ctx, in.UserID, "password.change_failed", nil)
			return domain.ErrInvalidCredentials
		}
	}

	user, err := s.q.GetUser(ctx, in.UserID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if probs := domain.CheckPassword(in.NewPassword, user.Email, s.breaches); len(probs) > 0 {
		return domain.PasswordRejected(probs)
	}
	if set.Password != nil {
		reused, err := domain.MatchesPrevious(in.NewPassword, set.Password.PreviousHashes)
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if reused {
			return domain.ErrPasswordReused
		}
	}

	hash, err := domain.HashPassword(in.NewPassword, domain.DefaultParams())
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.UpsertPassword(ctx, UpsertPasswordParams{
			UserID: in.UserID, Hash: hash, KeepPrevious: 5,
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Revoke every OTHER session, not this one. Signing the user out
		// of the browser they just used to change their password is
		// gratuitous, and it trains people to distrust the flow.
		revoked, err := q.RevokeOtherSessions(ctx, RevokeOtherSessionsParams{
			UserID: in.UserID, KeepSessionID: in.SessionID, Reason: "password_changed",
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.ClearAllDeviceTrust(ctx, in.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		s.denylist.Add(ctx, revoked, accessTTL)

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: in.UserID, Kind: "password.changed", SessionID: in.SessionID,
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"sessions_revoked": len(revoked)}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.password_changed",
			map[string]any{"user_id": in.UserID, "email": user.Email})
		return err
	})
}
services/identity/internal/domain/reuse.go
package domain

// MatchesPrevious checks a candidate against a bounded history of
// hashes. Each comparison is a full Argon2 evaluation, so the history is
// SHORT — five is plenty, and fifty would make every password change
// take several seconds of CPU.
//
// Note what is NOT stored: plaintext, reversible ciphertext, or a fast
// hash "just for comparison". A reuse check that weakens the storage is
// worse than no reuse check.
func MatchesPrevious(candidate string, previous []string) (bool, error) {
	for _, encoded := range previous {
		ok, _, err := VerifyPassword(candidate, encoded)
		if err != nil {
			// A corrupt historical hash is our bug, not the user's.
			// Skip it rather than blocking a legitimate change.
			continue
		}
		if ok {
			return true, nil
		}
	}
	return false, nil
}

Policy: what to require, and what not to

RuleQuillWhy
Minimum length12 runesLength is the one composition rule that measurably helps
Maximum length128 bytesBounds hashing cost; also stops a 10 MB request body
Character classesNoneUsers satisfy them predictably (Password1!), which reduces entropy, and it trains people to write passwords down
Breach-corpus checkYes, k-anonymityCatches the passwords actually used in credential stuffing. The one check worth adding
Similar to the emailRejectedTrivially guessable and common
Reuse of the last 5RejectedCheap to check, prevents the “reset to the same one” cycle
Forced rotationNeverProduces Summer2026! → Summer2027!. NIST removed it from its guidance for exactly this reason
Rotation on breachYesRotate when there is a reason, not on a calendar
Paste allowedAlwaysBlocking paste breaks password managers, which is the single biggest thing users can do for their own security
Show-password toggleYesFewer failed attempts, fewer resets, and shoulder-surfing is not the threat model
services/identity/internal/breach/hibp.go
// Package breach checks a password against the Have I Been Pwned corpus
// using k-anonymity: we send the first five hex characters of the SHA-1
// and match the suffix locally, so the password — and even its full
// hash — never leaves the process.
package breach

import (
	"context"
	"crypto/sha1"
	"encoding/hex"
	"strings"
	"time"
)

type HIBP struct {
	client *http.Client
	cache  *lru.Cache[string, []string] // prefix → suffixes
}

func (h *HIBP) Breached(ctx context.Context, password string) (bool, error) {
	sum := sha1.Sum([]byte(password)) // SHA-1 here is HIBP's protocol,
	full := strings.ToUpper(hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])) // not our storage
	prefix, suffix := full[:5], full[5:]

	// 5 hex characters is ~1 million buckets, so the prefix identifies
	// roughly 800 candidate hashes — enough anonymity that the query
	// reveals nothing useful about the password.
	suffixes, ok := h.cache.Get(prefix)
	if !ok {
		ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 2*time.Second)
		defer cancel()

		var err error
		suffixes, err = h.fetch(ctx, prefix)
		if err != nil {
			// FAIL OPEN. A third party being down must not stop people
			// signing up or changing their password — but count it,
			// because silently failing open for a week is not a check.
			breachCheckErrors.Inc()
			return false, err
		}
		h.cache.Add(prefix, suffixes)
	}

	for _, s := range suffixes {
		// Constant-time is unnecessary here — the attacker supplied the
		// password and already knows it — but the comparison must be
		// case-insensitive, which is the actual bug people ship.
		if strings.EqualFold(s, suffix) {
			return true, nil
		}
	}
	return false, nil
}
Reject breached passwords at set time, not at sign-in time

Checking during sign-in seems thorough and is actively harmful: you are blocking a user who is trying to get into their own account, at the moment they most need in, and the corpus changes under them so it happens without warning. Check when the password is set — registration, reset, change — where rejecting costs the user one retry. If a password already in use later appears in a breach, the right response is a notification asking them to change it and, for a confirmed credential-stuffing match, a forced reset on next sign-in — not a locked door with no explanation.

Removing the password entirely

services/identity/internal/app/password_remove.go
package app

// Going passwordless is a real feature, and the guard rails matter: a
// user who removes their password and then loses their only passkey is
// down to email recovery, which is the floor they were trying to leave.
func (s *Service) RemovePassword(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID) error {
	set, err := s.loadAuthenticators(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if set.Password == nil {
		return nil // idempotent
	}

	// The generic last-credential rule is necessary but not sufficient
	// here: it would permit removing the password when exactly one
	// passkey remains, and one passkey on one lost phone is a lockout.
	if err := set.CanRemove(set.Password); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if len(set.Passkeys) < 2 {
		return domain.ErrNeedTwoPasskeys
	}

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.RevokeAuthenticator(ctx, RevokeAuthenticatorParams{
			ID: set.Password.ID, UserID: userID, Reason: "user_removed",
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "authenticator.removed",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"kind": "password"}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.password_removed",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID})
		return err
	})
}

What each change must revoke

EventSessionsDevice trustAction tokensNotify
Password reset (forgot)AllAllAllAlways
Password change (signed in)All othersAllAllAlways
Password removedNoneNoneNoneYes
2FA disabledNoneAllNoneAlways
Passkey removedThose it createdNoneNoneYes
Provider unlinkedThose it createdNoneNoneYes
Email changedAll othersAllAllBoth addresses
Token reuse detectedThat familyThat deviceNoneAlways
Notifications about security changes must not be switchable off

Every other email in the product can have a preference toggle. These cannot, because the first thing an attacker with account access would do is turn them off — and then every subsequent change is silent. Password changed, 2FA disabled, a new sign-in method added, an email change requested: these go out unconditionally, to the address on file, and in the email-change case to both the old and the new address. It is the one place where the user's stated preference is correctly overridden, and it is worth saying so in the settings UI rather than hiding it.

Interview follow-up

“Walk me through a password reset.” The mechanics are easy — a single-use token, hashed at rest, short TTL, superseding any previous one — so spend the answer on the four things that are usually missing. It must not bypass 2FA, or the second factor protects nothing against an attacker with inbox access. It must revoke every session and every device trust, because the reset is often a response to compromise. It must look identical for an address with no account, in body, status and timing. And it must notify unconditionally, because the notification is the only signal a victim gets when the reset was not theirs.

A09

The rest of production

The parts that are not a login flow but decide whether the login flows matter: telling users when something changed, noticing when a sign-in is wrong, changing an email address without creating a takeover path, deleting an account properly, and letting support help without handing them the keys.

Notifications

services/identity/internal/app/notify.go
package app

// Security notifications are the only control that works when every
// other one has failed. An attacker who has the password, the session
// and the device cannot stop the email arriving — unless you let them
// turn it off, which is why these are not switchable.
type NotificationClass int

const (
	// Always sent. No preference, no digest, no batching.
	ClassCritical NotificationClass = iota
	// Sent unless the user has opted out, and batched if frequent.
	ClassInformational
)

var notificationPolicy = map[string]NotificationClass{
	"password.changed":        ClassCritical,
	"password.reset":          ClassCritical,
	"mfa.disabled":            ClassCritical,
	"mfa.enabled":             ClassCritical,
	"authenticator.added":     ClassCritical,
	"authenticator.removed":   ClassCritical,
	"oauth.linked":            ClassCritical,
	"oauth.unlinked":          ClassCritical,
	"email.change_requested":  ClassCritical,
	"email.changed":           ClassCritical,
	"recovery.code_used":      ClassCritical,
	"token.reuse_detected":    ClassCritical,
	"account.deletion_requested": ClassCritical,

	"sign_in.new_device":      ClassInformational,
	"session.evicted":         ClassInformational,
	"sign_in.blocked":         ClassInformational,
}

// The consumer that turns security events into email, running behind the
// event bus (D14) so a mailer outage never blocks the security-relevant
// write itself.
func (c *NotifyConsumer) handle(ctx context.Context, e outbox.Event) error {
	var ev SecurityEvent
	if err := json.Unmarshal(e.Payload, &ev); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("%w: %v", eventbus.ErrPermanent, err)
	}

	class, known := notificationPolicy[ev.Kind]
	if !known {
		return nil // logged but not mailed
	}

	if class == ClassInformational {
		if muted, err := c.q.HasMutedNotifications(ctx, ev.UserID); err == nil && muted {
			return nil
		}
		// Batch the noisy ones. A user syncing on five devices does not
		// need five "new device" emails in a minute.
		if recent, _ := c.recentlyNotified(ctx, ev.UserID, ev.Kind, 15*time.Minute); recent {
			return nil
		}
	}

	// The dedupe claim and the send share a transaction, so a
	// redelivered event cannot notify twice (D14).
	return c.mailer.SendSecurityNotice(ctx, SecurityNotice{
		UserID: ev.UserID, Kind: ev.Kind,
		When: ev.At, Location: ev.Location, Device: ev.Device,
		// Every security email ends with the same line and the same
		// link. A user who thinks "that was not me" must have one
		// obvious action, and it must work without signing in first.
		SecureAccountURL: c.baseURL + "/account/secure?t=" + c.recoveryToken(ctx, ev.UserID),
	})
}
Every security email needs a one-click “that was not me”

Telling a user their password changed and leaving them to work out what to do is most of the way to useless — by the time they find the settings page, the attacker has changed the email address too. The link in the notification should lead to a flow that requires no sign-in (because they may no longer be able to), revokes every session, invalidates every action token, locks the account pending verification, and mails the support queue. A short-lived token in the URL authorises exactly that one destructive-but-safe action and nothing else.

Risk signals

services/identity/internal/risk/risk.go
// Package risk computes cheap, explainable signals at sign-in. It is
// deliberately not machine learning: a rule a support agent can read out
// to a confused user beats a score nobody can explain, and the false
// positives are borne by real people trying to get into their accounts.
package risk

import (
	"context"
	"math"
	"time"
)

type Signals struct {
	NewDevice        bool
	NewCountry       bool
	ImpossibleTravel bool
	NewASN           bool
	KnownBadASN      bool // hosting ranges, Tor exits, known proxies
	CredentialStuffingPattern bool

	Score  int      // 0-100, for logging and thresholds
	Reasons []string // human-readable, shown to support and in the log
}

// Evaluate runs on every sign-in. Budget: a few milliseconds and two
// index lookups — this is in the critical path of every login.
func (e *Evaluator) Evaluate(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	dev DeviceInfo) (Signals, error) {

	var s Signals
	last, err := e.q.LastSuccessfulSignIn(ctx, userID)
	if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
		return s, nil // first ever sign-in: nothing to compare against
	}
	if err != nil {
		// A risk evaluator that is broken must not block sign-in. Fail
		// open, count it, and carry on with no signals.
		riskErrors.Inc()
		return s, nil
	}

	if dev.Country != "" && dev.Country != last.Country {
		s.NewCountry = true
		s.Reasons = append(s.Reasons, "first sign-in from "+dev.Country)
		s.Score += 25
	}

	// Impossible travel: the implied speed between two sign-ins exceeds
	// what any aircraft does. Crude, and it catches real account
	// compromise — but it also catches VPNs constantly, which is why it
	// raises a CHALLENGE rather than blocking.
	if dist := haversine(last.Lat, last.Lon, dev.Lat, dev.Lon); dist > 500 {
		hours := time.Since(last.At).Hours()
		if hours > 0 && dist/hours > 900 { // km/h
			s.ImpossibleTravel = true
			s.Reasons = append(s.Reasons, fmt.Sprintf(
				"%.0f km from the previous sign-in %.1f hours ago", dist, hours))
			s.Score += 40
		}
	}

	if dev.ASN != 0 && dev.ASN != last.ASN {
		s.NewASN = true
		s.Score += 10
	}
	if e.badASNs.Contains(dev.ASN) {
		s.KnownBadASN = true
		s.Reasons = append(s.Reasons, "sign-in from a hosting or anonymising network")
		s.Score += 20
	}

	// Credential stuffing looks different from a targeted attack: many
	// DIFFERENT accounts attempted from one network in a short window,
	// mostly failing. Counted per network, not per account, because per
	// account it is invisible.
	if n, _ := e.q.DistinctAccountsAttemptedFrom(ctx, dev.IPPrefix, time.Hour); n > 20 {
		s.CredentialStuffingPattern = true
		s.Reasons = append(s.Reasons, "many accounts attempted from this network")
		s.Score += 50
	}

	return s, nil
}

// Action maps a score to a decision. Three outcomes, and BLOCK is
// deliberately rare: a false positive there means a legitimate user
// cannot get in, which is a worse outcome than a false negative on a
// challenge.
func (s Signals) Action(hasSecondFactor bool) Decision {
	switch {
	case s.Score >= 70 && s.CredentialStuffingPattern:
		return DecisionBlock
	case s.Score >= 30:
		// Challenge means "prove it again", not "go away". If the user
		// has a second factor we demand it even on a trusted device
		// (A04); if not, we send an email code (A07).
		return DecisionChallenge
	default:
		return DecisionAllow
	}
}
Challenge, do not block — and never on geolocation alone

IP geolocation is wrong often enough that “sign-in from an unusual country” fires for anyone on a VPN, a corporate proxy, a mobile carrier that routes through another country, or a train crossing a border. Blocking on it produces a steady stream of users who cannot access their own accounts and have no idea why, and support has no mechanism to help. A challenge — a second factor, or an email code — costs a legitimate user fifteen seconds and stops an attacker who has only the password. Reserve outright blocking for signals about the source rather than the user, such as one network attempting twenty different accounts in an hour.

Lockout, without the denial-of-service

services/identity/internal/app/lockout.go
package app

// The classic design — "five failures locks the account for 30 minutes"
// — is a denial-of-service primitive: anyone who knows an address can
// lock its owner out at will, indefinitely, for free. Quill does not
// have account lockout in that form.
//
// What it has instead:
//
//   1 · progressive DELAY on the failing path, per account
//   2 · a per-NETWORK limit, which is what actually stops stuffing
//   3 · a challenge, not a lock, once failures are elevated
//   4 · a genuine lock ONLY on a signal that cannot be faked by a
//       third party — a token reuse, or a confirmed compromise report
func (s *Service) beforePasswordCheck(ctx context.Context, email string,
	dev DeviceInfo) (delay time.Duration, err error) {

	fails, err := s.q.RecentFailures(ctx, RecentFailuresParams{
		Email: email, Since: time.Now().Add(-time.Hour),
	})
	if err != nil {
		return 0, nil // never block sign-in on a metrics query
	}

	// Exponential, capped. At 10 failures this is 2 seconds, which is
	// invisible to a human and ruinous to a script — while never
	// preventing the real user from trying again.
	switch {
	case fails >= 20:
		delay = 5 * time.Second
	case fails >= 10:
		delay = 2 * time.Second
	case fails >= 5:
		delay = 500 * time.Millisecond
	}

	// The per-network limit is the one that stops credential stuffing,
	// because an attacker spraying a leaked list hits it long before
	// any single account's counter moves (D04).
	if err := s.limiter.Check(ctx, "login:ip:"+dev.IPPrefix.String(), 60, time.Minute); err != nil {
		return 0, err
	}
	return delay, nil
}

// LockAccount is the real thing, and it is reserved for signals a third
// party cannot manufacture.
func (s *Service) LockAccount(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID, reason string) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)
		if err := q.SetUserStatus(ctx, userID, "locked"); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		revoked, err := q.RevokeAllSessions(ctx, RevokeAllSessionsParams{
			UserID: userID, Reason: reason,
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		s.denylist.Add(ctx, revoked, accessTTL)
		if err := q.ConsumeAllActionTokens(ctx, userID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "account.locked",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"reason": reason}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// A locked account must be recoverable without support where
		// possible — the email explains what happened and how to unlock.
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.account_locked",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID, "reason": reason})
		return err
	})
}

Changing the email address

The address is the recovery channel, so changing it is changing who can take the account over. Six steps, and each one closes something. 1 step-up (A04) — a fresh, strong proof, not just a session 2 verify the NEW address by sending a token to it → proves the user controls where recovery will point 3 notify the OLD address, unconditionally, with a "this was not me" link that cancels the change → this is the step that stops a silent takeover 4 a waiting period for high-risk accounts — 24 hours before the change takes effect, during which the old address can cancel it → gives a victim time to react to step 3 5 on completion: revoke every other session, clear device trust, invalidate every action token → anything issued against the old address is now void 6 notify BOTH addresses that it completed The attack this prevents: attacker gets a session, changes the email to their own, requests a password reset to that address, and now owns the account with no way for the victim to recover — because every recovery path points at the attacker's inbox. Step 3 alone breaks it; steps 1 and 4 make it much harder to reach.
services/identity/internal/app/email_change.go
package app

func (s *Service) RequestEmailChange(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID,
	newEmail string, dev DeviceInfo) error {

	newEmail = domain.NormaliseEmail(newEmail)
	user, err := s.q.GetUser(ctx, userID)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}
	if newEmail == user.Email {
		return nil // idempotent
	}

	// Check availability WITHOUT revealing it. If the address is taken,
	// we proceed exactly as normal and simply fail at confirmation time
	// — otherwise this endpoint enumerates accounts for anyone with a
	// session (D04).
	taken, _ := s.q.EmailExists(ctx, newEmail)

	plain, hash := domain.NewActionToken()

	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		if err := q.InsertActionToken(ctx, InsertActionTokenParams{
			ID: idgen.New(), UserID: userID, Purpose: "change_email",
			TokenHash: hash,
			// The new address is the PAYLOAD, not a separate mutable
			// column — so the token authorises a change to exactly this
			// address and cannot be redirected after the fact.
			Payload:   jsonb(map[string]any{"new_email": newEmail, "taken": taken}),
			ExpiresAt: time.Now().Add(2 * time.Hour),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// To the NEW address: the confirmation link.
		if !taken {
			if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.email_change_confirm",
				map[string]any{
					"user_id": userID, "email": newEmail, "token": plain,
				}); err != nil {
				return err
			}
		}

		// To the OLD address: the warning, with a cancel link. This one
		// is sent whether or not the new address is available, because
		// the attempt itself is what the owner needs to know about.
		cancelTok, cancelHash := domain.NewActionToken()
		if err := q.InsertActionToken(ctx, InsertActionTokenParams{
			ID: idgen.New(), UserID: userID, Purpose: "cancel_email_change",
			TokenHash: cancelHash, ExpiresAt: time.Now().Add(30 * 24 * time.Hour),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if _, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.email_change_requested",
			map[string]any{
				"user_id": userID, "email": user.Email,
				"new_email_masked": maskEmail(newEmail), // m•••d@e•••e.com
				"cancel_token": cancelTok,
				"location": dev.Location, "device": dev.Name,
			}); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		return q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: userID, Kind: "email.change_requested",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"new_email": maskEmail(newEmail)}),
		})
	})
}
Mask the new address in the warning email

The message to the old address has to be specific enough to be actionable and must not hand an attacker a working address to spear-phish with, nor confirm a guess. m•••d@e•••e.com is enough for the owner to recognise their own alternative address or to see that it is not theirs, and not enough for anything else. The same masking belongs in the security event detail, because that log is shown to the user and may be exported.

Deletion and export

services/identity/internal/app/account_delete.go
package app

// Deletion is a saga across services: identity owns the user, notes owns
// the notebooks, collab owns the memberships. No distributed
// transaction exists, so it is an event with idempotent consumers and a
// reconciliation sweep (B12).
func (s *Service) RequestDeletion(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// A grace period, not an immediate delete. It turns an
		// irreversible mistake into a recoverable one, and it is the
		// window in which a victim of a compromised session can cancel.
		if err := q.ScheduleDeletion(ctx, ScheduleDeletionParams{
			UserID: userID, DeleteAfter: time.Now().Add(30 * 24 * time.Hour),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// Sign out everywhere immediately: the account is closing, and
		// leaving sessions alive during the grace period is pointless
		// exposure.
		revoked, err := q.RevokeAllSessions(ctx, RevokeAllSessionsParams{
			UserID: userID, Reason: "deletion_requested",
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		s.denylist.Add(ctx, revoked, accessTTL)

		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.deletion_requested",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID, "grace_days": 30})
		return err
	})
}

// Execute runs after the grace period, from a scheduled job.
func (s *Service) executeDeletion(ctx context.Context, userID idgen.ID) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		// Anonymise rather than DELETE in identity. The row is
		// referenced by audit logs, by other users' notebook
		// memberships, and by billing records that must be retained for
		// tax purposes — a hard delete would either cascade into other
		// people's data or leave dangling references.
		if err := q.AnonymiseUser(ctx, AnonymiseUserParams{
			UserID: userID,
			// The address becomes a tombstone so it cannot be reused to
			// claim the old identity, and cannot be reversed to the
			// original.
			Email:       fmt.Sprintf("deleted-%s@invalid", hashEmail(userID)),
			DisplayName: "Deleted user",
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// Credentials, however, are deleted outright: there is no
		// retention argument for a password hash or a passkey public key
		// belonging to a closed account.
		if err := q.DeleteAllAuthenticators(ctx, userID); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Downstream services do their own part idempotently. A
		// reconciliation job re-emits for any user still marked deleted
		// whose services have not acknowledged (D10).
		_, err := outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.user_deleted",
			map[string]any{"user_id": userID})
		return err
	})
}
Deletion cannot cascade into other people's data

A departing user owns notebooks that other people are members of, and has edited notes in notebooks they do not own. Hard-deleting their row breaks those references; deleting their notebooks destroys other people's work. Quill's rule: notebooks they own are offered for transfer before deletion and archived if nobody takes them; their edits elsewhere remain, attributed to an anonymised user; and the identity row is anonymised rather than removed. Say this in the deletion dialog — a user who expects their collaborators' copies to disappear and finds they have not will report it as a privacy failure, and they will be right to, if you did not tell them.

Support access, without the keys

services/identity/internal/app/impersonate.go
package app

// "Log in as user" is the feature that turns a compromised support
// account into a total breach. If it exists at all, every one of these
// constraints has to hold.
func (s *Service) BeginImpersonation(ctx context.Context, in ImpersonateInput) (TokenPair, error) {
	// 1 · The ADMIN must be at AAL2 with a fresh authentication. A
	//     support session that has been open all day is not enough.
	if in.Admin.AAL < domain.AAL2 || time.Since(in.Admin.AuthenticatedAt) > 5*time.Minute {
		return TokenPair{}, domain.ErrStepUpRequired
	}
	// 2 · A REASON, and a ticket reference. Free text is not enough —
	//     it must be greppable and auditable.
	if in.TicketRef == "" || len(in.Reason) < 20 {
		return TokenPair{}, domain.ErrReasonRequired
	}
	// 3 · The USER must have consented, within a window. Support asks;
	//     the user clicks a link; only then is the session mintable.
	consent, err := s.q.ActiveImpersonationConsent(ctx, in.TargetUserID)
	if err != nil {
		return TokenPair{}, domain.ErrConsentRequired
	}

	pair, err := s.issueImpersonationSession(ctx, in.TargetUserID, in.Admin.UserID)
	if err != nil {
		return TokenPair{}, err
	}

	// 4 · The token is MARKED. Every service sees act.sub in the claims
	//     and logs it, so a support action is never indistinguishable
	//     from the user's own.
	// 5 · SHORT: 15 minutes, non-renewable.
	// 6 · READ-ONLY by default. Writing requires a second, separately
	//     justified grant.
	// 7 · Both the user and a security channel are notified, now.
	s.notify(ctx, in.TargetUserID, "account.impersonation_started", map[string]any{
		"admin": in.Admin.Email, "ticket": in.TicketRef, "reason": in.Reason,
		"consent_id": consent.ID,
	})
	s.alertSecurityChannel(ctx, in)

	return pair, nil
}
If impersonation is read-only by default, most support tickets still resolve

The overwhelming majority of “can you look at my account” requests need someone to see the state, not change it. Making writes a separate, separately justified grant removes almost all of the risk while removing almost none of the utility — and it makes the audit trail meaningful, because a write by a support agent is now a rare, deliberate, individually-reasoned event rather than one line in thousands. The marked token matters for the same reason: every downstream log line carries act.sub, so “who actually did this” is answerable months later.

The security page the user sees

EndpointShows
GET/v1/account/securityAuthenticators, devices, session counts, limits, recommendations (A06)
GET/v1/account/security/eventsThe activity log, paged, most recent first
POST/v1/account/secure“That was not me” — no session required, token from an email
POST/v1/account/email/changeStep-up; notifies both addresses
POST/v1/account/email/cancel-changeFrom the old address's warning email; no session required
POST/v1/account/exportAsync; produces a signed, expiring download link
DELETE/v1/accountStep-up; 30-day grace; offers notebook transfer first
POST/v1/account/deletion/cancelDuring the grace period
services/identity/internal/app/secure_account.go
package app

// SecureAccount is the "that was not me" button from every security
// email. It deliberately requires NO session — a victim may already have
// been locked out — and it is safe to expose because the only thing it
// can do is make the account more locked down.
func (s *Service) SecureAccount(ctx context.Context, token string) error {
	return pg.InTx(ctx, s.pool, func(tx pgx.Tx) error {
		q := s.q.WithTx(tx)

		row, err := q.ConsumeActionToken(ctx, ConsumeActionTokenParams{
			TokenHash: domain.HashToken(token), Purpose: "secure_account",
		})
		if errors.Is(pg.Translate(err), pg.ErrNotFound) {
			return domain.ErrTokenInvalid
		}
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}

		// Everything at once. This is the one place where being
		// aggressive is correct: the user has told us something is
		// wrong, and the cost of over-reacting is that they sign in
		// again.
		revoked, err := q.RevokeAllSessions(ctx, RevokeAllSessionsParams{
			UserID: row.UserID, Reason: "user_reported_compromise",
		})
		if err != nil {
			return err
		}
		s.denylist.Add(ctx, revoked, accessTTL)

		if err := q.ClearAllDeviceTrust(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// Cancel every pending change an attacker may have started —
		// an email change, a password reset, a deletion.
		if err := q.ConsumeAllActionTokensExcept(ctx, row.UserID, "secure_account"); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.CancelPendingEmailChange(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		if err := q.CancelScheduledDeletion(ctx, row.UserID); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		// Lock pending verification. The user recovers through the
		// normal reset flow, which now requires their second factor.
		if err := q.SetUserStatus(ctx, row.UserID, "locked"); err != nil {
			return err
		}

		if err := q.InsertSecurityEvent(ctx, InsertSecurityEventParams{
			UserID: row.UserID, Kind: "account.secured_by_user",
			Detail: jsonb(map[string]any{"sessions_revoked": len(revoked)}),
		}); err != nil {
			return err
		}
		_, err = outbox.Enqueue(ctx, tx, "identity.account_secured",
			map[string]any{"user_id": row.UserID})
		return err
	})
}

What to monitor, and what should page

SignalHealthyAction
token_reuse_detected_total0Page. One user is a client bug; many is a breach (D05)
account_secured_by_user_total~0Page. Users are reporting compromise
Failed sign-ins per network, p99lowAlert — credential stuffing in progress
Distinct accounts attempted per IP< 5/hourAlert; feed the risk evaluator
mfa_disabled_totalrareDashboard. A spike means either a UX problem or an attack
Passkey enrolments started vs completed> 80%Dashboard — a gap means the ceremony fails on some platform (A03)
Email-code delivery p99< 30 sAlert. Slow mail expires codes and looks like a broken login (A07)
Step-up challenge ratestableDashboard. A jump means a risk rule is misfiring on real users
Support impersonation sessionsfew, all ticketedWeekly review. Every one, by a human

The Part VI checklist

Model □ every credential is an authenticator row with a shared spine □ the last-credential rule is one function, used everywhere □ assurance level and methods recorded per session, in the token Devices & sessions □ device ≠ session; both listable, both revocable □ current device marked unmistakably and shown first □ deny-list makes revocation immediate, not eventual □ limit policy is per user; eviction is notified, never silent Factors □ passkeys with origin and RP-ID verification; challenges server-side □ TOTP codes single-use, with the last accepted step stored □ recovery codes generated WITH the first factor, not later □ device trust cleared by every security change Step-up □ every account-structural action behind a requirement in the ROUTER □ freshness measured from authenticated_at, not the token's iat □ re-auth returns a NEW access token Federated □ keyed on (provider, subject), never on email or username □ auto-link only on a verified email AND an allowlisted provider □ state, nonce and PKCE server-side; exact-match redirect URIs Recovery □ reset does not bypass 2FA □ reset revokes everything, including device trust □ email change warns the old address with a cancel link □ every security email has a working "that was not me" Operations □ every security-relevant change writes an event in the SAME transaction as the change □ critical notifications cannot be switched off □ no account lockout that a third party can trigger □ impersonation: consented, marked, short, read-only, reviewed
Interview follow-up

“How do you know an account has been compromised?” Honestly: usually you do not, and the user tells you — which is why the detection story starts with notification rather than with detection. Send unconditional mail on every security-relevant change, give each one a one-click “that was not me” that needs no sign-in and locks everything down, and make the account's own activity log readable. Then the signals that genuinely help: refresh-token reuse, which is unambiguous and should page; many distinct accounts attempted from one network, which catches stuffing; and impossible travel, which is worth a challenge and never a block. The instinct that separates a good answer here is preferring a challenge to a block, because a false positive on a block is a user permanently locked out of their own data.

The question bank

503 questions with written answers, grouped by topic — language semantics, the runtime, concurrency, backend engineering and production. Everything is searchable and every answer is deep-linkable.

How to use it

Do not read it front to back. Search for the area you are weakest on, open ten questions, and answer each aloud before expanding it. The gap between “I recognise this” and “I can explain this” is the entire difference in an interview, and only speaking out loud reveals which side of it you are on.
